paragraphs.text: “Search the Scriptures,” Christ said to the crowds of the Jews. He was stating most plainly that no one could attain eternal life in any other way than by digging up the letter of the law like a treasure and carefully searching out the pearl hidden in it, that is, Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,” as the blessed Paul says. Of this wisdom or knowledge, so venerable and so worthy of admiration, Solomon also says somewhere: “If you seek her like silver and search for her as for treasures, then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God.” Nothing could weigh as much as this for those who praise the blameless life, who have chosen to achieve what is best and most excellent of all, and who fill their own minds with the divine light. For this reason we must delight endlessly in the words about God and make the sacred Scripture a kind of lamp, as the holy Psalmist cries out and says: “Your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.” Since, then, it is clearly and manifestly a means to eternal life, and a path to every gladness for us, to love searching out the mystery of Christ, come, let us once again add our profitable sweat. For our own sake before anyone else’s, let us take pains to gather together the passages through which the mystery of Christ may be most clearly signified, and to explain the meaning each one holds. Then what we say, though it may offer only faint impressions, and at times only of the truer contemplations, may become a good starting point for the more apt learners, and in a way a set of steps that carries them up to a better and higher knowledge. It will be useful to set out first what took place as history. When we have explained this in due measure, and have reshaped the narrative as if from type and shadow, we will make the account clear, with our discourse turning toward the mystery of Christ and having him as its goal, if indeed it is true that Christ is the end of the law and the prophets. And if anywhere we happen to fall short of what is more fitting, because our thoughts are thin and much is obscure, our readers ought to be forgiving. It should be known, however, that since we have composed seventeen books On Worship and Service in Spirit and Truth, and gathered a great many ideas in them, we have deliberately passed over in the present work the chapters treated there and left them unexamined, even if here and there we have had to mention one of them out of necessity. We will begin, then, with our more elegant comments on Genesis. After that, running in order through the five books of Moses, we will also examine, in addition to them, whatever in the rest of Scripture is useful for our present purpose.

Paul, truly learned in the law and most holy, having perceived the mystery of the salvation that comes through Christ, says that in him there took place a summing up of things in heaven and things on earth, according to the good pleasure and will of God the Father. By the word "summing up" he makes plain the restoration of all things, and the return of what had been corrupted to what it was in the beginning. For he no doubt remembered, as is likely, that God said through the voice of the prophets: "Do not remember the former things, and do not consider the things of old. Behold, I am making new things, which will now spring up, and you will know them." Accordingly he too, as one nourished on the divine words, showed that the prediction made to us in these words had in a sense already been fulfilled in Christ, saying: "So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new." For we have been refashioned in Christ and have become a new creation. In him alone, indeed, we have been enriched with the new name, for we are called Christ's. And again the inspired Paul himself says somewhere about us: "Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires." For the life of those who are in Christ befits saints, and rises beyond fleshly passions and earthly impurity. That the new name given to us in Christ was to come upon us becomes clear from God's having cried aloud through the voice of the saints: "Those who serve me shall be called by a new name, which shall be blessed on the earth. For they shall bless the true God." Since, then, no one who has chosen to think rightly and reasonably would doubt that things have become new in Christ, come, let us examine what the growing-old was, and of what the restoration to something better might be said to have taken place, as being from what was not wholly sound and unharmed, that is, from what had been corrupted and had unexpectedly been brought into a state it was not in at the beginning. For in this way one would know, and quite rightly, where the aim of the discourse before us is heading, and what is sound would in no way be lost.

So then God, the supreme craftsman of all things, using his own all-working power, that is, the Son, for everything whatsoever that was to be done—for "all things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being"—in the beginning, before everything else, fashioned heaven and earth and called them into being, though they had never existed. But if someone should ask how, and from what, he will hear from us that wise and truly excellent saying: "Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?" For if anyone chose to learn such things thoroughly, it is beyond dispute that he would certainly need a mind and understanding like that which is conceived to be in God. But that what is in us is small, or rather nothing at all, compared with God, he himself will make clear when he says: "For my counsels are not like your counsels, nor are my ways like your ways. But as far as heaven is from the earth, so far is my way from your ways, and your thoughts from my mind." Let the examination of these matters, then, be set aside as superfluous and in no way attainable. For God creates as he knows how, and as he is able.

When heaven and earth had been made in the beginning, and then the mass of waters had been drawn together into one place—for they had to yield to the one who said, "Let the water be gathered into one gathering"—the earth was uncovered and was everywhere decked with flowers by grasses of so many kinds, and became wonderfully rich in trees, having received the coming into being of fruit-bearing trees. The disks of the sun and moon appeared, and a law from God apportioned to each the measure of its rule. For the one was appointed to dawn and daylight, the other to night and darkness; and the whole heaven itself was sprinkled with stars for us. And he also laid down the purpose for which they had come into being, saying: "And let them be for signs and for seasons, and for days and for years, and let them be for light in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth." And since the Creator of all is life by nature, he made the very nature of the waters a mother of the creatures that swim and of those that fly in the air. And again he commanded the earth to bring forth the many-shaped nature of cattle and the untamed kinds of wild beasts. And what he willed was accomplished without effort and beyond understanding. For each of the things made, the Word was the maker, and a mere nod was their coming into being.

And since the good order of the things made pleased even the Craftsman of all himself, another deliberation then came in, which brought in last of all the one for whose sake those things had been brought into existence—I mean man. For it was necessary, truly necessary, that the Creator of all, being good by nature, or rather being the Good itself, should be known by us as what he is. It was necessary that the earth be filled with those who know how to give glory, and who, as it is written, contemplate the glory of the Maker from the beauty of created things. For as the prophet Isaiah says, "You did not make it in vain"—clearly meaning the earth—"but to be inhabited." It was necessary, therefore, that a rational living being be formed upon it, once everything that serves for his delight, and that would show him to have been well provided for, had been displayed beforehand. For this reason, having first displayed earth and heaven and what is in them in fitting order, he proceeded to the fashioning of man. Of man's creation he made a deliberation beforehand, although he had produced all the rest of creation on the spot by a word, and established it by his own Word, as God. And since man is a truly gifted and most godlike living being, so that the copy of the supreme glory might not seem to have received the same treatment in its making as things not so constituted, he honored this work with prior deliberation and with his own handiwork. Having molded a statue from earth, he makes it a rational living being; and so that it might reach back to the principles of his own nature, he at once impressed on it an incorruptible, life-giving spirit. For it is written: "And he breathed into his face the breath of life, and the man became a living soul." Then he counted him worthy of paradise and delight, and allotted to him dominion over all things on earth. He set him as ruler over the creatures that swim and those that fly, yoked herds of wild beasts beneath him, and laid even the venomous kinds themselves at his feet along with the rest. And he commanded that they be persuaded by natural laws that they ought to fear man. Man, then, was the impress of the supreme glory, and an image on earth of a God-befitting authority.

But the one who had come to such glory and delight surely had to know that he had God as his overseer, king and lord, lest through excessive prosperity he should all too readily slip into thinking that he had perhaps been freed from authority and from the supremacy of the one who rules. So God at once gave him a law, and set the threat of punishment right beside any transgression. For there was as yet no way of sinning on the earth, since he was one and alone. But so that he too might be under law, a way of keeping a commandment was devised for him: "From every tree," he says, "that is in paradise you may eat for food. But from the tree of knowing good and evil, you shall not eat of it. On the day you eat of it, you shall surely die." Then one of Adam's ribs was taken away, and the woman is formed, to serve him in bearing children and to share his life as one of the same kind; and indeed she goes on living with him in simplicity. But when she was led astray into transgression by the slanders of the devil and made the forbidden tree her food, and the forefather Adam himself slipped down along with her, their nature was at once condemned to death. And God said to the woman, "In sorrow you will bear children," and to Adam, "Cursed is the earth in your labors." And besides this, they were sent out of the much-desired dwellings of the beginning and out of the delight of paradise. Only then did they learn, with difficulty, that they were naked and unclothed and in need of garments from then on; and for this they had garments of skin, God having taken pity on them. They were enrolled with the earth as their mother, and were brought under the nets of corruption; and nothing at all, I think, was lacking to bring them to the utmost misery.

"But what then?" someone might say, I suppose. "If man, once made, was going to sink into such great wretchedness, how could it not reasonably be thought far better for him not to exist at all? Yet God makes so splendid and admirable one who before long would be pitiable and wretched, under a curse and a penalty. Now the Creator, being God by nature, was by no means ignorant of what was to come. But since he worked with full knowledge, how will he escape being convicted of having wronged rather than benefited, if it is truly better for those who will be wretched never to come into being at all—as the Savior himself said concerning the disciple who betrayed him: 'It would have been good for that man if he had not been born'?"

To such objections I would say that it is extremely dangerous, and close to stupefaction carried to its very limit—or rather well inside it and far beyond it—to censure the divine counsels as not rightly made, and to suppose that the supreme nature either disregarded what was fitting, or at any rate failed to achieve what was useful and better, as happens in our own affairs. It would be more fitting to ascribe blamelessness to it in its counsels and deeds, to decline to think beyond what one ought to think, and not to let curiosity in these matters go unrebuked. Besides this, I think we must also take the following into account: for those who have received being together with well-being, is it better not to come into being, or to exist and share in the Creator's kindness? No one, I imagine, would hesitate over this. For just as, for those who will be wretched if brought into being, not attaining it would reasonably be thought better and preferable, in the same way, I think, for those who will be in no such condition it is a good and desirable thing to come into existence and to live.

What then, tell me? For I say that our argument must be raised to this point, to things far beyond our own condition—I mean, again, the blessed angels. They were made by God and have their passage from non-being into being: Angels and Archangels, Thrones and Authorities, Powers and Principalities, and besides these the highest Seraphim themselves. And the apostate dragon himself was counted among the things made, together with the evil powers that are with him; and they were together with the other holy and rational creatures, filling the dwellings above, distinguished in glory, far superior to our condition, and possessing an incomparable preeminence. Indeed, God said somewhere: "I placed you with the Cherubim." But the holy Cherubim have their glory firmly established and securely keep their own rank. "Thousands upon thousands minister to God, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him." Satan, however, fell along with others and was deprived of his own glory. Was it necessary, then, because he was going to abandon his own rank by willingly turning to offend God, that the Creator of all should hesitate—I mean over making the holy angels—and cast away so splendid and admirable a creation? Then how would that creation not seem to have been wronged, if the multitude that stands by him and ministers to this day had not been brought into being—the multitude that keeps its true loyalty to the God who fashioned it and will not allow itself to forget its own rank? For what, tell me, is so very grievous if some, through arrogance, have perhaps fallen away from well-being? Those who are better than they stand with God, and, richly filled with his kindness, honor him with long and unceasing doxologies. It is of them, I think, that the blessed David says: "Blessed are all who dwell in your house; they will praise you forever and ever." Since this is how the matter stands with them, come, let us set the inquiry aside and consider the following with regard to ourselves.

Man was made in the beginning entrusted with the reins of his own will, and having a free inclination toward whatever he might choose. For the Godhead, in whose likeness he had been formed, is free. In this way, I think, and in no other, he would possess what is admirable: if he were seen to be a willing worker of virtue, having integrity in his deeds as the fruit of his own judgment, and not as the product of a natural necessity that would not allow him to be carried outside the good at all, even if he chose to do what was not good. So in the beginning man had been endowed with an unconstrained and unfettered inclination of mind in all that was to be done; but through the deceits of the dragon he was foolishly carried off toward what was not fitting, and thought nothing of transgression. For this reason he was condemned to death and corruption, God, I think, foreseeing what would be more profitable in the circumstances. For once man had inclined toward sin, and his nature had grown sick with the tendency toward evil, he would perhaps, like the unclean spirits, have proved to be an everlasting evil on the earth. The death of the flesh was therefore devised for our benefit. It did not send the living creature to total destruction; rather, it was kept for renewal and, so to speak, for refashioning in due time, like some shattered vessel. For the Creator was not ignorant that the creature would in the meantime suffer corruption; but he knew, together with this, the undoing of these evils, the abolition of corruption, the restoration to something better, and the recovery of the original goods. For he knew that in due time he would send his own Son in human form to die for us and to destroy the power of death, so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.

What then? Even if not all have believed, still the multitude of the saved, being beyond number, will, as it were, dance in triumph over the destruction of the others, and will declare any grief over them stale, all but saying: "Therefore they shall eat the fruits of their own way." For although they could be saved if they wished, and escape the harms that crept in meanwhile, they do not receive the Redeemer, that is, Christ. Tell me: if someone skilled in husbandry filled his own garden with the finest trees, and then not all of them escaped the harms that arise from various causes, would anyone think that the one who chose to farm had been wrong to choose that labor? No one, I think, would find fault with him—far from it. For he took due care of what he had planted, but the plants fell sick and suffered. Shall we then say that it would have been better for no one to take up farming at all, and for the garden not to flourish with the noblest plants, but rather to do away with every method of cultivation altogether, so that none of the plants might be wronged? And how is it not utterly senseless to think that this is right?

So it would be unjust for us to indict the Creator for bringing us into existence. If we are in our right minds and senses, we will instead blame ourselves, since the harm we have suffered is of our own choosing. The inspired Paul clearly persuades us that, even as he was bringing man into being, the Creator knew that man would fall into corruption, and was not ignorant of the means of healing either; for Paul bears witness that salvation through Christ is ancient, held in the Spirit's foreknowledge. He writes thus to Timothy, his own disciple: "Do not be ashamed, then, of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel by the power of God, who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and the grace that was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal ages, but has been made manifest in the last times through the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ." And again, to others: "We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined he also called; and those whom he called he also justified; and those whom he justified he also glorified." You hear how he says that the grace in Christ was given before eternal ages, and that those who would be conformed to the image of his Son were plainly foreknown and predestined by God the Father. For, as I said, the manner of the incarnation was foreknown, and the cure for our ailments was being stored up for the fitting time. Paul will bear witness to this again, writing as follows: "Now to him who is able to strengthen us according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept silent for eternal ages but has now been made manifest through the prophetic Scriptures, by the command of the eternal God, and made known to all the nations for the obedience of faith, to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, be glory forever. Amen." The mystery had been kept silent, but it has now been made manifest through both the law and the prophets, according to the will of God the Father. For in Christ we have been refashioned into what we were in the beginning, and the things that had crept in meanwhile through the devil's deceit have been overturned. Paul again said this about Christ, the Savior of us all: "In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his kindness, which he lavished on us in all wisdom and insight, making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he set forth in him as a plan for the fullness of the times, to sum up all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth, in him. In him we have also obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we who first hoped in Christ might be to the praise of his glory." See, once again: we have been predestined according to the Father's purpose, and we have been enriched with a hope that is, as it were, older than our very existence, since God foreknew the matter and recorded in his own counsels what would follow for us. In the beginning the inventor of sin deceived Adam and made him liable to the charge of negligence, and so Adam came to be brought down to death. The penalty then passed on to all human beings, as the affliction spread from the root to what grows from it, for death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam's transgression. So the Creator necessarily took forethought for his own creatures, and he devised for us what was, as it were, a second root of our race, one that would raise us back up to our former incorruption. Just as the image of the first man, the one from the earth, stamped on us the necessity of dying and of being caught in the snares of corruption, so in turn the second beginning after him, that is, Christ, and our likeness to him through the Spirit, would imprint on us imperishability. And just as in the first man disobedience brought us under punishment, so in this one yielding and complete obedience would show us to be partakers of the blessing from above, from the Father. For he says, "The first man Adam became a living soul; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit." And again he made the same thing clear to us in another way, saying: "The first man was from the earth, made of dust; the second man is the Lord from heaven. As was the man of dust, so are those who are of dust; and as is the heavenly man, so are those who are heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly man." And again: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us." For he humbled himself, as it is written. The only-begotten Word of God came down willingly into our condition. He did not come to be ruled by death along with us, as though Adam had passed his deadness on even to him, since he is the one who gives life to all things. He came so that he might take as his own the nature held fast by corruption and transform it into life. That is why he became flesh. So also the wise Paul writes: "For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead has also come through a man; and as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive." It would be ignorant to think that Adam, who was a man born of the earth, passed the power of the curse that came upon him on to the whole race, so that it ran through them by nature like an inheritance, while Emmanuel, who is from above and from heaven and is God by nature, and who took on likeness to us and became a second Adam for us, would not in turn make richly partakers of his own life those who choose to share by faith in kinship with him. For we have become of one body with him through the mystical blessing. And we are united with him in another way as well, since we have become partakers of his divine nature through the Spirit. For he dwells in the souls of the saints, as the blessed John says: "By this we know that he is in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us." He himself, then, is our life; he is our justification. And again it is written: "So then, as through one trespass condemnation came to all people, so also through one act of righteousness justification of life came to all people." And again: "For as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous." It is therefore quite clear that the mystery of Christ was already being sketched out back then in the first Adam. It was not reproduced there in an exactly identical form, but in a different way and as a reversed pattern. For Adam was a beginning for the race leading to death, to curse, to condemnation; Christ was a beginning leading to the very opposite: to life, to blessing, to justification. Adam took the woman into one flesh with himself and was ruined through her. But Christ joins the Church to himself through the Spirit, and he rescues and saves her and makes her stronger than the devil's deceit. That is why he moves her to cry out: "For we are not ignorant of his designs." Our forefather Adam received corruption as the wages of sin and the penalty for transgression. But in the senseless stupidity of the Jews, it was righteousness itself that was charged against Christ. Therefore, because he suffered death, he is crowned with honor and glory, in the words of the blessed Paul. To Adam only the things on earth were made subject, and even those barely; but to Christ all things are subject. For every knee shall bow to him, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. Amen.

As I said just now, human nature fell under death and sin at the very beginning of the race, in Adam. And it has been redeemed in no other way than through Christ alone. As his disciple wrote, "There is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved." It was necessary, truly necessary, that the one through whom all things were brought into existence should become the renewer of what had been corrupted and should drive out the maiming that came from sin. He had to abolish what causes grief and once more give well-being richly to those who came into being through him. For my part, I would say that divine power and authority show their brilliance in both these acts: in being able to bring something from non-being into being, and in calling back to well-being, as if recovering them, those who had lost their good and unblemished state. The type of this has been shown in Adam. But one could see it no less depicted in those who were born from him. For in Christ the God and Father sums up the things in the heavens and the things on earth. What slipped into a state that did not befit it is lifted back up to what it was in the beginning, through him alone. The things that crept in between have now passed away into nothing, and the things on earth are re-formed into the newness of creation. For in him there is a new creation, and the saying is true. Look, then, look at the mystery of Christ in Abel and Cain too, the mystery through which we have been saved. It is written in Genesis: "Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, and said, 'I have acquired a man through God.' And she bore again, his brother Abel. And Abel became a shepherd of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground. And it came to pass after some days that Cain brought of the fruits of the ground a sacrifice to the Lord, and Abel also brought of the firstborn of his sheep and of their fat. And God looked upon Abel and upon his gifts, but to Cain and to his sacrifices he paid no heed. And Cain was greatly grieved, and his face fell. And the Lord God said to Cain, 'Why have you become grieved, and why has your face fallen? If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be still; his turning will be toward you, and you will rule over him.'" And a little later: "And Cain said to Abel his brother, 'Let us go out into the field.' And it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him. And the Lord God said to Cain, 'Where is Abel your brother?' And he said, 'I do not know. Am I my brother's keeper?' And God said, 'What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me from the ground. And now you are cursed upon the earth, which opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand. For you will work the ground, and it will no longer yield its strength to you. Groaning and trembling you shall be on the earth.' And Cain said to the Lord, 'My guilt is too great to be forgiven. If you cast me out today from the face of the earth, I shall also be hidden from your face, and I shall be groaning and trembling on the earth, and anyone who finds me will kill me.' And the Lord God said to him, 'Not so: whoever kills Cain will undo seven punishments.' And the Lord God set a sign for Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him. And Cain went out from the presence of God."

Cain and Abel were both born of Adam. They were like tender, blossoming shoots springing up from the first root at the beginning. In them human nature was practising fruitfulness, and the command to "increase and multiply" was just beginning to show itself and from then on to take effect. Cain came first in order of birth, and Abel followed after him. While they were tender and young, their parents reared them like nestlings. But when the young men reached manhood and were now counted among men, they turned to different occupations. Cain was delighted, I suppose, with the green earth. He saw that it was full of trees and very fertile, and adorned with ripe fruits, and he thought he should make what he saw look gentler through careful tending. He reasoned, probably, that things lovely in themselves and by nature, which reached their beauty on their own, would easily grow incomparably finer if they had the benefit of a farmer's sweat. So he equipped himself as a farmer and put all his strength into achieving his aim. Perhaps nature itself gave him the knowledge of these things, and a divine and unspoken law engraved in his mind the knowledge of what he should choose. These were the things Cain thought worthy of his zeal and toil. But Abel the wise left aside sweat over trees and the mattock, and would have nothing to do with the sickle either; he devoted himself to flocks of sheep. Perhaps the lambs drew him to this decision, still bleating thinly to their mothers and scarcely able to cry, skipping a little on the flowering grass on tender, newly steady feet; and the bleating goats too, leaping effortlessly over the highest rocks. Being very wise, I think, he chose to crown the shepherd's life with a most excellent vote. He regarded the occupation as a kind of preparatory exercise for ruling over men, and believed this to be so. For both the divinely inspired Scripture itself and the learned men of the Greeks customarily call those who preside over nations, cities, or peoples "shepherds of the people." So the two young men took their different paths, the one toward farming, the other toward something better, the shepherd's life. As time went on, it made Cain's gardens thick with foliage and laden with ripe fruits, and it increased Abel's flocks to the greatest possible number. Then the law within us, our innate knowledge of God, summoned the men to offer thank-offerings to the Creator of all, God, the giver of every good thing to us. Among idol-worshippers, perhaps, the effort to know who the maker of the universe is appears corrupted and false. Nevertheless an innate and compelling law prods them, and a self-prompted knowledge awakens them, to the conviction that they must conceive of something higher and incomparably better than ourselves, that is, God. So the holy and all-wise Abel brings the choicest of the flock, picked out as the very best. "For he brought," it says, "of the firstborn of the lambs and of their fat," that is, the foremost and choicest. And since he knew how sacred rites should be performed, he set out the fat portions. Not so Cain, who acted very carelessly: he kept the most outstanding of the ripe fruits for his own pleasures, and offended the God who is over all with second-rate ones. So God sent fire down from heaven upon Abel's gifts and caused the offerings to be consumed. "But to Cain and to his sacrifices," it says, "he paid no heed"; for he did not send the customary fire upon what was offered. At this Cain is deeply grieved and terribly distraught. He was taught the reason for his rejection, and that Abel had won the better verdict, yet he did not turn instead to correcting his faults. Glaring like a bull in untimely rage, he became the first among men to give birth to savage envy. As though taking revenge on the God of all for rejecting him, he pursues by treachery the one whom God had admired. He trampled on the law of natural affection. His mind was filled to the brim with diabolical wickedness and unholy schemes, while he put on a show of kindness in his words: "Let us go out," he says, "into the field." Do you hear how he invited him into the fields, as if Abel were to view how carefully he had tended them and enjoy the varied sight of the flowers? But he commits an unholy deed: he gives his own blood brother to death like the first spoils of war and an offering of firstfruits, and he became the teacher of the way to murder for human nature. When God inquires, saying, "Where is Abel your brother?" the wretch lies and answers harshly, "I do not know." When he was convicted as a murderer and fell under the curses, he supposed in turn that he too would die, even if God did not wish it, and that this would be his release from God's wrath. For he said, "If you cast me out today from the face of the earth, I shall also be hidden from your face, and I shall be groaning and trembling on the earth, and anyone who finds me will kill me." But he was clearly assured that he would be subject to the curses wholly and completely, and would pay the penalty for his own unholy deeds by living a thrice-wretched life on earth, when God said, "Not so: whoever kills Cain will undo seven punishments." He puts "seven" for "many." It is as if he said: whoever releases the fratricide Cain from bodily life will grant him remission of the penalty for many unholy offenses. But if someone prefers to say that the punishments are seven in number, it is not hard to count them up. Cain's first sin was not dividing rightly, that is, not dedicating the choicest of everything to God. The second was that, having learned of his sin, he did not turn to repentance and correct his faults by returning to better ways. Instead he was whetted to anger and goaded by his neighbor's good repute, when he surely ought to have chosen to emulate him rather than regard him as an enemy and look askance at him with unjust eyes. The third, a kind of prelude to the savagery that leads to murder, was his ruthless envy. The fourth was the very words "Let us go out into the field," which prove his treachery and deceit. The fifth was the guilt of the unholy murder. The sixth offense that might be counted against him was lying to God. The seventh was thinking that he could escape the punishments against God's will by departing from life in the body, which he would not have been unwilling to do. "But God gave Cain a sign," it says, "so that no one who found him would kill him. And Cain went out from the presence of God." He was at once subject to the curses, and the form his rejection took followed. For how could the all-pure and most holy nature look upon one who had already gone the whole way to the utmost limit of evil?

Let this much be said for now, broadly and as a matter of history. Now, as though recoloring the outline of a picture and recasting the shadow in the letter into the truth, come, come, let us examine each detail very closely and say this: one might see the mystery of Christ foreshadowed at the beginning, as in a shadow, in what happened. For it was necessary, truly necessary, once human nature had been brought into sin and unexpectedly caught in the snares of death, that the mystery of its restoration to something better should be proclaimed beforehand, and that Christ, who in due time would die for our sake and on our behalf, should not be unknown. According to the faith of the sacred Scriptures, our forefather Adam was made in the image and likeness of God. From him were born and came forth first Cain, and second, after him, Abel. To Cain we shall assign the role of Israel. For Christ himself also judged that Cain prefigured the Jewish peoples, since they were of like character to him. He said, "If you abide in my word, you will truly be my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free." But they did not understand the beauty of the freedom the Father gives, and set about glorying in fleshly boasts, saying, "We are Abraham's seed and have never been slaves to anyone. How can you say, 'You will be made free'?" What does Christ say to this? "If you were children of Abraham," he says, "you would do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth which I heard from the Father; Abraham did not do this." And he assigns them Satan as their father, saying, "You do the works of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because he is a liar, as is his father also." If we understand rightly, we shall by no means suppose that Christ was speaking here of the wicked demon who was the origin of evil. Rather, to the Jews, who were raging and in labor with the unholy murder of him, he gives as father the first murderer and practitioner of lies, I mean Cain, and gives Satan, the inventor of sin, as Cain's father. For let someone teach us what father we shall assign to the devil, or what we say was the archetype of his perversity! Rather, Christ assigns to Cain, as to an archetype, like an image, those who are said to be afflicted with a likeness in every respect to the impiety that was in him. That it was the custom of Christ the Savior to call "Satan" anyone who resembled Satan in his ways, we may see very easily when he says to the holy disciples, "Did I not choose you, the twelve, and one of you is a devil?" Israel, then, is to be likened to Cain; of Israel it is written, "Israel is my firstborn son." After the firstborn Israel, Christ appeared second, as it were, in time and youngest, he too a son of Adam. For this reason, wisely and in keeping with the divine plan, he everywhere called himself the Son of Man. Israel thought to honor God by offering things temporary and quickly withering, of no great account, and set its whole mind, as it were, on earthly pursuits. For Cain turned to farming, but Abel was a shepherd of sheep. Emmanuel led the rational flock: he is the Good Shepherd, "in a rich place and in good pasture," as it is written, shepherding the flocks both above and on earth. To him the prophetic word also cried out, "Shepherd your people with your rod of guarding, the sheep of your inheritance." So Israel thought fit to honor God with earthier things, bearing the fruits of the law and offering him sacrifices he did not want. Therefore it also heard through the voice of the saints: "The whole burnt offerings of your rams, the fat of lambs, and the blood of goats and bulls I do not want, not even if you come to appear before me. For who required these things from your hands? You shall no longer tread my court. If you bring fine flour, it is futile; incense is an abomination to me." And again: "Why do you bring me frankincense from Sheba and cinnamon from a distant land? Your whole burnt offerings are not acceptable, and your sacrifices have not pleased me." This is plainly what is meant by God's paying no heed to Cain's sacrifices. But Abel the righteous, that is, Christ, brought to God as gifts the firstborn of the rational flocks. These are the tender of heart, those who are infants in wickedness and choice in virtues, who bear the glory of the firstborn through their likeness to him. For the divine Paul names the multitude of those called through faith to sanctification "the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven." Of this holy multitude, then, the flock of the firstborn, Christ became the priest who offers the sacrifice. For through him we have access in the Spirit to the God and Father. And we have become a fine and acceptable sacrifice, more pleasing than a young calf putting forth horns and hooves. Offering by means of blood is lowly and earthy and has no sweet savor before God, but worship in spirit and through Christ is very pleasing indeed to the Father. Indeed, to those of Israel who brought the things of the earth, God cried out: "I will not accept bulls from your house, nor he-goats from your flocks. For all the beasts of the field are mine, the cattle on the mountains and the oxen. I know all the birds of the sky, and the beauty of the field is with me. If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is mine and all that fills it." But to us, who have been justified in Christ and sanctified in the Spirit, he called out, saying, "Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High; and call upon me in the day of your affliction, and I will rescue you, and you will glorify me." Spiritual things, then, are better than earthly ones, and the sacrifice through Christ is far superior to the sacrifice under the law. So God inclined not to Cain's sacrifices but to Abel's. For what reason? Israel offered rightly, for it was right to sacrifice to God. But it did not divide rightly: it always clung to the types and thought that God took delight in things that were mere shadows. Therefore it both sinned and was ordered to be still, that is, to cease from the ancient customs of the law and to take Christ as its leader. For it was said to Cain, "You have sinned; be still," and with regard to Abel, "his turning will be toward you, and you will rule over him." If Israel had been willing to set aside the offering of earthier things and the unprofitable worship of the law, and to make Christ its ruler and guide on the road to something better, it would have been free along with us, and "in the book of the living," as the Scriptures say. But since, just like Cain, it made our Savior's good repute a pretext for envy and the beginning of murder, it fell under a curse and became liable to seven punishments. The wretches have become liable to many penalties, subjected to savage punishments, and they go on groaning and trembling; for everywhere they are strangers, newcomers, and fearful, lacking that freedom of speech which above all befits the free. Yet Cain received a sign so that no one would kill him. For Israel has not perished entirely; the remnant has been saved, as the prophet's voice says. Knowing this, he proclaimed it beforehand: "Unless the Lord of Hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah." Moreover, the divine Psalmist too begged the God of all that Israel should not be wiped out entirely: "Do not kill them, lest they forget your law." Yet Cain went out from the presence of God. For so it is written: "And Cain went out from the presence of God." Those of Israel have suffered something of this kind; to them it was said through the prophet's voice: "When you stretch out your hands to me, I will turn my eyes away from you; and if you multiply your prayer, I will not listen to you; for your hands are full of blood." For they killed the Lord of all, and in their great impiety they dared to say, "His blood be on us and on our children." Abel's blood, perhaps, cried out only against his murderer. The precious blood of Christ cried out against the cruelty and ingratitude of the Jews, but it also freed the world from sin, since it was poured out for the world. Therefore the divine Paul says that we who have been justified in faith have come "to a sprinkled blood that speaks better than Abel's." It would be fitting, I think, to add this as well to what has been said. After Abel's death, it says, "Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore a son and called his name Seth, saying, 'For God has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.'" Then, after other things, it says: "Adam lived two hundred and thirty years and begot a son according to his form and according to his image, and called his name Seth." Notice, then, that after Abel's death a son, Seth, is born again, closely resembling the one made in the image and likeness of God, that is, Adam. For after Emmanuel died according to the flesh, another seed at once sprang up for Adam, which possesses in abundance the supreme beauty of the divine image; for we who believe are re-formed into Christ through the Spirit. That Christ's death became for these believers a kind of root of their race and the occasion of their birth, he himself confirms when he says, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless the grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit." So when he fell into the earth like a grain, he sprang up manifold like an ear of wheat, and in him human nature was refashioned into the original image in which the first man was made.

It is also worth our while to look closely into the descendants of both, I mean those of Cain and those of Seth, for from this too we shall gain something to our profit. It is written thus: “And Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enosh; and he was building a city, and he named the city after the name of his son Enosh. And to Enosh was born Irad, and Irad begot Mehujael. And Mehujael begot Methushael, and Methushael begot Lamech. And Lamech took for himself two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the second Zillah. And he said to his wives Adah and Zillah: Hear my voice, you wives of Lamech; give ear to my words: for I have killed a man to my wounding, and a young man to my bruising; for vengeance has been taken sevenfold for Cain, but for Lamech seventy times seven.” Here you have a clear account of Cain’s offspring; let us see also what came from Seth. It is written again as follows: “Seth lived two hundred and five years, and begot Enosh”; and of him the sacred text says: “He hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God.” “And all the days of Seth were nine hundred and twelve years, and he died. And Enosh lived a hundred and ninety years, and begot Cainan; and all the days of Enosh were nine hundred and five years, and he died. And Cainan lived a hundred and seventy years, and begot Mahalalel. And all the days of Cainan were nine hundred and ten years, and he died. And Mahalalel lived a hundred and sixty-five years, and begot Jared. And all the days of Mahalalel were eight hundred and ninety-five years, and he died. And Jared lived a hundred and sixty-two years, and begot Enoch.” Then it says: “And Enoch pleased God, and he was not found, because God had taken him away.” Observe, then, first of all, that the descendants of Cain are named, and the account of the succession of generations moves along; but it is not clearly stated to how many years the span of each one’s life extended, as is certainly done for those born from Seth. For the time of each of these is recorded exactly, and one could learn from the sacred Scriptures, finely and precisely, what each lived and how long, both before the begetting of children and after it. This too, then, is no obscure indication to those who have chosen to examine such matters carefully, that God would not bear to know the life of those who love sin. Indeed, they will hear Christ saying at the divine judgment seat: “Truly I say to you, I never knew you.” For nothing at all escapes the knowledge of the God of all; yet though he knows them, he does not know those who love sin, because of the great intensity of his aversion toward them. So the length of life of Cain’s descendants is passed over in silence. For they did nothing worth hearing about, but rather such things as would likely bring harm to those who read an account of them. They were therefore, and quite justly, left without any share in God’s remembrance. But he does take account of knowing the life of the saints in detail, and nothing of what concerns them, I think, could slip from the divine and pure mind. Our Lord Jesus Christ will confirm this when he says: “Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground without our Father who is in heaven. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered.” And if even the number of their hairs is taken into account by God, since he knows clearly everything that concerns them and keeps it in his care, how could the span of their very life go unknown? For “the eyes of the Lord,” it says, “are upon the righteous.” Now Enosh, second in line directly from Cain, had a city on earth named after him; and yet the saints have counted it as a kind of boast to think and say: “Here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one to come, whose builder and maker is God.” They regard life in this world as a sojourn, and call it so. And somewhere the divine David sings: “Let me be, for I am a sojourner on the earth and a stranger, as all my fathers were.” But concerning those whose minds are set on earthly things he says in the forty-eighth psalm: “They called their names upon their generations.” From Seth, on the other hand, sprang the divine Enosh, of whom it is written: “He hoped to be called by the name of the Lord his God.” For the race that is in Christ is holy and sacred, and lives in hope of a glory beyond what is human. For although we are from the earth, we have been called to adoption as sons of the Master of all and to brotherhood with Christ, who for our sake became as we are, so that we too, through him, might gain the glory of being gods, raised to better things beyond the human, by grace, that is, and loving-kindness. For “I said,” it says, “You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.” So Enosh hoped to be called by others by the name of the Lord his God, that is, “God.” For since he was not without admiration, being adorned with the glories of holiness, some of the more upright perhaps called him God, choosing to crown him with the highest honor. But let our discourse now come to its proper aim. The Jews, who are images of Cain’s descendants, are known by the God of all to exist; but that they are not enrolled in the book of life would be made clear by the silence about the life of Cain’s descendants. That the race in Christ is enrolled and held in God’s remembrance would be shown, I think, by the clear recording of the life of the righteous, I mean of Seth’s descendants. And Enosh, second directly from Cain, had a city named after him; for the wretched Jews think only of the things on earth, neither knowing the church of the firstborn nor hastening toward the city above. But the one from Seth, that is, Enosh, is highly esteemed, for he is even called God. And we who have run to Christ and cling tightly to our hope in him have, through faith, been enriched with the glory this implies. I would add to what I have said yet another necessary observation. If one chooses to trace the genealogy of the descendants of Cain and of Seth, setting down Adam first as the root, so to speak, of each, he will find Lamech to be seventh in the line coming through Cain, and Enoch himself seventh in the line through Seth. The enumeration of the generations on both sides is as follows: Adam, Cain, Enosh, Irad, Mehujael, Methushael, Lamech. And again: Adam, Seth, Enosh, Cainan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch. Let us see, then, what the state of each was. Lamech confided to his wives, saying: “Hear my voice, you wives of Lamech; give ear to my words: for I have killed a man to my wounding, and a young man to my bruising; for vengeance has been taken sevenfold for Cain, but for Lamech seventy times seven.” But the righteous Enoch was taken away by faith so that he should not see death, in the words of the blessed Paul, “and he was not found, because God had taken him away.” For in the last times, in which the Sabbath rest in Christ has appeared, Israel is seen full of fear and fallen into dread of punishment, as one who has killed a man and is henceforth judged for holy blood, and much more severely than Cain himself. For Cain, who sinned against one like ourselves, became liable to sevenfold vengeance; but Israel, who committed impiety against Emmanuel himself, is called to account far more severely. For vengeance has been taken sevenfold for Cain, but for Israel seventy times seven, since punishment will follow in proportion to impieties. But those who have found favor in Christ through faith at the time of his coming will no longer be found when Satan seeks them. For they will be taken away by God to a life incomparably better and more glorious, from death and corruption to everlasting life, from minding the things of the flesh to willing to do what pleases God, from dishonor to glory, from weakness to power, in Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom and with whom be glory to the Father with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

Noah was a good man. He was a true lover of the highest devotion to God, and he valued nothing above being well regarded for it. Because he was distinguished, conspicuous, renowned and widely celebrated, and richly crowned with honors, he was rightly admired. So our discourse now turns to him. If we present what God arranged in his time as an image and type, so to speak, of the salvation through Christ, it should, I think, be of no small benefit to those who read it. Come then, let us tell each thing about him as well as we can, thinning out the coarseness of the history and skillfully recoloring the things that visibly happened into spiritual contemplation.

Seth, then, was born to Adam after Abel was slain. From Seth came Enosh, who hoped to call on the name of the Lord his God. The people of that time called Enosh "God." They were amazed at how great his righteousness was, and so they at once named him God, thinking the title especially fitting for the man's virtue. From Enosh, the one called God, others were born, and after them came Lamech, the father of Noah. At the birth of his son, Lamech was at once revealed as a prophet, just as Zechariah was at the birth of the blessed Baptist. Lamech named his son Noah, which means "rest" if the word is translated into our language. And giving, as it were, the reason for this name, Lamech says: "This one will give us rest from our works, and from the earth which the Lord God has cursed." With such bright and rich hopes, then, the people of old announced Noah's birth in advance. In the genealogy he was the tenth from Adam through Seth, and the custom that all who descended from Enosh, the one called God, should be called gods by everyone extended down to him. "But Noah," it says, "was five hundred years old, and he fathered three sons: Shem, Ham and Japheth." Translated from Hebrew into Greek, Shem would mean "perfection" or "planting," Ham "heat," and Japheth "enlargement." Then the sacred Scripture says: "And it came to pass, when people began to multiply on the earth and daughters were born to them, that the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives for themselves any of them they chose. And the Lord God said: My spirit shall not remain among these people forever, because they are flesh. His days shall be a hundred and twenty years. Now the giants were on the earth in those days." And after that: "Whenever the sons of God went in to the daughters of men, they bore children for themselves. These were the giants of old, the men of renown." For when the human race was already growing into a great multitude, the sons of God, it says, fell into an utterly outlandish desire for women and took as wives for themselves any of them they chose. Now, we know that some of the manuscripts plainly read: "The angels of God saw the daughters of men." Some people then shift the charges of fleshly lust elsewhere and pin the blame for so abominable a desire on the fallen angels, who did not keep their own position, as it is written. For my part, I would say, and I will agree, that every sickness of mind may well befit them. But to let belief in the matter be carried as far as possible from sound reasoning would, it seems to me, be utterly absurd. Our aim is to examine with care the truth in each thing that is written, and certainly not to dwell on the sicknesses of the herd of demons. We see that desires always follow chiefly the impulses that are within us and innate in us. Either we love the passions of the flesh, or we are used to setting the highest value on the means by which the things of the flesh come about. But pleasures do not carry us outside the laws of nature, as it seems to me, rightly and truly. For example, eating and drinking, and natural intercourse with women, would be works and passions of the flesh. Desires for wealth and glory, in turn, serve the pleasures of the flesh, and nearly all the passions of the world come through these, as the wise disciple said: "All that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life." The bitter and terrible desires for such things easily net us, so that we choose to think and do the things of the flesh. But no argument will persuade us to love what lies outside the body and against nature. How, then, would it not be close to folly to say that spirits who are above the flesh and removed from it fell in love with fleshly things? What natural impulse would they have toward this? What law would stir them up to thirst for such passions, as one does in our own case? Not that we are clearing the throng of demons of blame in such matters. It is unholy and profane, and ready for anything at all that is outrageous. Let it be sick, if you like, with unnatural pleasures as well as everything else. But when the divine Scripture says that they had intercourse with women, and the women bore the so-called giants, that is, extraordinary monsters, yet rational human beings, what are we to think about that? Human seed could not be placed in a woman by spirits utterly remote from the flesh. Some people tell idle tales and try to be clever about the matter, slipping the impossible past us with arguments they think persuasive: they say that the evil demons entered into men and through them deposited the seed. But we will find their argument quite crude and full of ignorance. For how shall we accept what the divine Scripture has not said and count it among the things that are true? So we will read instead: "The sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives for themselves any of them they chose." The renderings of the other translators also confirm for us that this reading is correct. Aquila says: "The sons of the gods saw the daughters of men." Symmachus, for his part, has "the sons of the powerful" in place of "the sons of the gods." They called the descendants of Seth and Enosh sons of gods and of the powerful because of their holiness and their devotion to God, and because they could crush all who opposed them. God was presumably helping them and making that most sacred and holy race illustrious. It was a race unmixed with the other, that is, with the descendants of Cain and of Lamech. Lamech followed in his father's footsteps and became a murderer, for he confessed: "I have killed a man to my wounding, and a young man to my bruising." So as long as the holy race remained by itself and unmixed with the worse one, the beauty of their piety toward God still shone in them pure and unspoiled, and made them admirable. But they slipped into love of the flesh and, swept away by the beauty of women, were driven to apostasy. "For they took," it says, "any of the daughters of men they chose," that is, of the descendants of Cain. Then, though they were called gods, sons of gods and sons of the powerful, they were carried off into the customs of those people and into a shameful and profane way of life. And the women bore monsters, for God now debased even the beauty of human bodies because the people of that time had no restraint in their lustful appetites. Those who were born were giants, that is, wild and powerful, deeply hideous, and larger in body than the rest. It should be noted that the inspired Scripture is somehow in the habit of calling exceptionally strong men giants. Thus it said of the Persians and Medes through the voice of the prophets: "Giants are coming to carry out my wrath, rejoicing and insolent alike." We will in no way adhere to the falsehoods of the Greeks. Their learned men, and especially their poets, are in the habit of describing and inventing the nature of things as they please. They think they should exalt small and contemptible things and dignify them with outrageous fables, even if the story strays far from what is fitting. One of them says that the whole of Sicily was hurled up to heaven by one of the giants, and another tells an even bigger and more outlandish lie about another. As I said, they were terrible to look at, immense in strength, harsh and hard to face, and probably rose a little above others in bodily stature. But they did not touch the very clouds, as those in the habit of making up myths about them say.

So when the races had mingled with one another and all had turned aside into unbridled sin, "the Lord God saw," it says, "that the wickedness of people had multiplied on the earth, and that everyone was intently devising evil things in his heart all day long. And God took it to heart" (or "repented," as in another version, I mean Aquila's) "that he had made man on the earth, and he considered it, and said: I will wipe out man whom I have made from the face of the earth, from man to beast, and from the creeping things to the birds of heaven, for I regret that I made them. But Noah found favor before the Lord God." You see that he wills the wiping out of every human being. But since Noah was adorned with the ways of piety, God has regard for him alone. He does not destroy him along with the others, but saves him with his whole household. And he says to him: "The time of every human being has come before me, for the earth is filled with injustice because of them. Behold, I am destroying them along with the earth. So make yourself an ark of squared timbers. You shall make nests throughout the ark, and you shall coat it inside and outside with pitch. This is how you shall make the ark: the length of the ark three hundred cubits, its breadth fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits. You shall make the ark narrowing upward, and finish it to a cubit at the top." And again, after other things: "You shall go into the ark, you and your sons and your wife," it says, "and your sons' wives with you, and of all the wild animals, of all the livestock and of all flesh, two by two. You shall bring some of every kind into the ark to keep them alive with you; they shall be male and female. Of all the birds according to their kind, of the livestock according to their kind, and of all the creeping things that creep on the earth according to their kind, two by two. Of every kind they shall come in to you to be fed with you, male and female." And of the clean animals, it says, you shall gather seven pairs each, but of the unclean, two. When all this had been done, just as the God of all had commanded, all flesh was drowned: rains and hail and a most violent downpour of waters from above and from heaven flooded the whole world under heaven. But the ark floated, carrying a cargo of righteous souls. When the waters had subsided a little, "the ark," it says, "came to rest on the mountains of Ararat." And Noah opened the door of the ark and sent out the raven to see whether the water had abated from the face of the earth, but it did not return. Then after it he released a dove, "and the dove," it says, "found no resting place for her feet and returned to him into the ark, for there was water over the whole face of the earth. And Noah stretched out his hand, took her, and brought her back to himself into the ark." After seven days she was sent out a second time, and she came back toward evening with an olive twig in her mouth. After another seven days he released her a third time, and she "no longer returned," it says, "to him." So he understood at last that all the water had been swallowed up from the earth, and the dry land and everything on it had appeared again. When he came out with his own children and all the creatures that had been gathered, and saw the earth freed from the waters, he at once built an altar. He was eager to offer as whole burnt offerings the clean and unblemished livestock and birds, presenting, I suppose, thank offerings to the God who had saved him. When this was done, "the Lord God," it says, "smelled the pleasing aroma, and the Lord God, having considered, said: I will never again curse the earth because of the deeds of men, for the mind of man is intently set on evil from his youth. So I will never again strike down all living flesh as I have done. As long as the earth endures, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and spring, day and night shall not cease." And besides this, "The Lord God also blessed," it says, "Noah and his sons, and said to them: Increase and multiply, fill the earth and rule over it. The fear and dread of you shall be upon all the wild animals of the earth, upon all the livestock, upon all the birds of heaven, upon everything that moves on the earth, and upon all the fish of the sea. I have given them into your hands."

Now that our discourse has come this far, nothing at all, I think, is lacking as far as the literal and historical narrative is concerned. Come then, following in the track of what has been said, let us bring out the contemplation hidden within. Let us depict the mystery of Christ, and show that Noah himself, and the wise and ineffable dispensation of the ark, are an image of the salvation that comes through him. Noah, then, was born of Lamech: not the Lamech who had murdered a man and a young man, but his namesake descended through Seth. Our Lord Jesus Christ also sprang from Israel, a people holy because of the fathers, but like Lamech in character and like-minded with the murderer, and indeed his namesake inasmuch as it was murderous. For it was said to the Jews somewhere: "Which of the prophets did your fathers not kill?" And Christ said: "Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers." And through the voice of Isaiah, too, he says: "When you stretch out your hands to me, I will turn my eyes away from you; even if you multiply your prayers, I will not listen to you, for your hands are full of blood." Noah was the eleventh from Adam; and Christ, in turn, was born according to the flesh at the last, the eleventh, hour, as it were, and began his dispensation on our behalf. You may learn that this is so, and true, so that you will affirm it completely and without reservation, persuaded by the sacred Scriptures. The one who hired workers for the vineyard called out to some at the eleventh hour (these would be those from the nations): "Why do you stand here idle all day?" They said plainly, "No one hired us," for before the coming of our Savior no one had called the nations to the knowledge of God. And he says kindly and compassionately: "You also go into the vineyard, and whatever is right I will give you." The law given through Moses also commanded that the sheep be slaughtered between the evenings, toward evening and already by lamplight. For when the time had, as it were, already reached its setting, and the present age was all but drawing to its close, the only-begotten Word of God became man and endured slaughter on behalf of all. He freed believers from penalty and punishment and set them as far as possible from every such fear. For he is the true Noah, that is, righteousness and rest, since this is how the name is interpreted. According to the Scriptures, we have been justified not by works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his great mercy. Christ, then, has become righteousness for us who have believed, and rest as well, if indeed it is true that he was bruised for our iniquities and handed over for our sins, and by his wound we were healed. And, as the prophet's voice says: "The Lord handed him over for our sins." Since Christ, then, suffered for us in the flesh, [?] blessed and enviable. And why not? Have we not been called over to such things? Do we not delight in heavenly gifts and grow rich in sharing them? Having thrown off the heavy burden of sin, are we not released at last into spiritual well-being? For he himself called us to this, saying: "Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls." That Christ was going to give us rest, the archangel Gabriel also announced in advance to the holy Virgin, saying: "Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins." The divinely inspired prophets, too, were eager to announce in advance the rest that would come through him. One said: "Take courage, Zion; do not let your hands grow slack. The Lord your God is mighty in your midst; he will save you and renew you in his love." Isaiah, in turn, all but set it before our eyes, saying: "Be strong, you slack hands and feeble knees. Take comfort, you who are fainthearted in mind; be strong, do not fear. Behold our God! Behold, the Lord comes with strength, and his arm with dominion. Like a shepherd he will tend his flock; he will gather the lambs with his arm and comfort the ewes that are with young." Christ, then, has become righteousness and rest for us, and he has also saved us from the earth which the Lord God cursed. This is what Lamech said, prophesying to us about Noah. It is beyond dispute that the charges arising from the transgression in Adam have been undone in Christ. For, as it is written, he became a curse for us, freeing the earth from the ancient curse. We say that through him the God and Father restores all things to what they were in the beginning: the old things have passed away, all things have become new, and if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. For he is the second Adam, who by obedience overturns the charge against the first-formed man, I mean the disobedience that took place in the beginning, his refusal of the command. The divinely inspired Paul also seemed to think this way, for he writes: "For just as through the disobedience of the one man people were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one many will be made righteous." Christ became obedient to the Father to the point of death, even death on a cross. So just as the earth was cursed because of the transgression in Adam at the beginning, so it has become blessed because of the obedience of Christ. He also redeemed us in another way from the earth that had become cursed. For according to his promises we await new heavens and a new earth, as the Savior's wise disciple also said. He also opened for us the new way of ascent to the things above and to the heavens. As our forerunner he entered on our behalf into the holy land, which he said the meek would inherit, that is, those who are trained to meekness by the teachings of the Gospel. For the law commanded that wrongdoers be repaid eye for eye, tooth for tooth, and wound for wound. But Christ says to us: "If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well." Noah, then, was eleventh from Adam through Seth and through Enosh, "who hoped to call on the name of the Lord his God" because of his very great holiness and his God-loving way of life. Our Lord Jesus Christ is likewise traced by the holy evangelists from Adam down to Joseph himself, the line of the genealogy running, so to speak, entirely through holy men.

But come, let us speak of the mixing, as it were, and the confusion of the generations with one another: I mean the holy line and the one that was not holy, that is, the profane and most abominable. The descendants of Enos, who was called by the name of God, went mad for the daughters of men. When this happened they at once changed their character, and, choosing to live by those people's customs and laws, they sickened with a corruption that reached every kind of outrage. In the same way, those of the blood of Israel, as long as they practised a holy way of life and were excellent imitators of their ancestors' piety, shunned every kind of wickedness and kept the glories of their renowned way of life entirely unadulterated, at least among themselves. But when they became entangled with the neighbouring nations, although the law had condemned the practice, they were at once filled with the loathsomeness found among those nations. They became easily driven to frenzy and exceedingly fickle. Indeed, which of the very worst evils were they not caught suffering from? And what is more astonishing still: the nations, though they worshipped the creation rather than the Creator and Maker and had turned aside into the error of many gods, honoured the herds of demons with genuine devotion. But Israel, holy from of old and from its fathers, made of apostasy a matter of very little account. That is why God says to them through a holy voice: "Go over to the islands of Kittim and see, and send to Kedar and consider carefully, and see whether such things have ever happened: whether nations will exchange their gods, though these are no gods. But my people have exchanged their glory for what will not profit them. Heaven was astonished at this, and the earth shuddered exceedingly, says the Lord, because my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns that will not be able to hold water." And again: "For as many as your cities were your gods, O Judah, and as many as the streets of Jerusalem were the sacrifices they offered to Baal. Why do you speak to me? You have all acted lawlessly, and all of you have been ungodly toward me, says the Lord." For they had sunk so far into perversity of thought, or rather of deed, as to unite with women who were still in error. And when these women bore children, the marks of Jewish worship ought to have been set upon the infants at once: circumcision on the eighth day and the sacrifices made for them. Instead, they offered the offspring of the sanctified peoples as a votive gift to the unclean demons. And this, I think, is what was said about them through the voice of the prophet: "For alien children have been born to them." So when the holy race had at last been corrupted by its union with what was worse, and Israel and the nations had been brought together into one in the quality and character of their mind, their manners, and even their customs, the Creator of all justly decreed the destruction of all who were on the earth. Yet, overcome by his innate gentleness, he did not make his wrath equal to their sins. And so that the race on earth might not be utterly destroyed, he showed beforehand through Noah justification by faith, as it were, and the remission that comes through water. For this reason the Only-begotten became man and lived among men, as it is written. He is the truer Noah, and, as in a type of that famous ark of the beginning, he has, so to speak, built the Church. Those who leap into it escape the destruction that hangs over the world. So too the divine Paul interprets the mystery of the ark, saying: "By faith Noah, being divinely warned, prepared an ark for the saving of his household." In it, as Peter also says, a few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water. "And baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves us: not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience to God." How, then, was the ark constructed? "You shall make the length of the ark three hundred cubits," he says, "its breadth fifty, and its height thirty. You shall make the ark drawing it in, and you shall finish it to a cubit at the top." That such a construction would signify the mystery of Christ, even if very dimly, would quickly and easily become clear to anyone. For the divine Paul writes to those justified in faith that he prays for them unceasingly, "that they may be strong enough to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge."

What, then, is the meaning of the ark's measurements? They are a correct and finely wrought declaration of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, and of the one Godhead's perfect completeness and its all-perfection in every respect. One may see this indicated in the numbers before us by considering the following. It is the custom of divinely inspired Scripture to make numbers that circle back again a symbol of perfection. What do I mean? The week, beginning from the first day, is completed on the Sabbath, the seventh. Then we count the next week, beginning again from the first day up to the seventh. Likewise, when we reach the number ten, we begin again from the first number of the next ten. In the same way and by the same reasoning, the perfect number made up of perfect numbers, that is, the hundred formed from ten tens, also has a cycle and a return back to one. So, as I said, in divine Scripture every number that goes back, as it were, after reaching its proper and appointed limit is a symbol of perfection. See, then, the all-perfection of the Holy Trinity in the three hundreds of cubits, for this is the ark's length. And the breadth, which reaches fittingly to fifty cubits, would suggest that the Godhead, as in a unity, is, so to speak, the perfection of perfections. That is, it is seven sevens with one added to them, because the nature of the Godhead is one. The height, too, conveys to us no other idea than this. It reaches its full extent in the third ten of cubits, but then comes to an end again in the one cubit that lies above and is highest. "Its height," he says, "is thirty cubits, and you shall finish it to one cubit." For the Holy Trinity, broadened as it were into the distinctions of three hypostases, that is, of individual persons, is drawn together, as it were, into one nature of Godhead. The Greeks honour the road that wanders into many gods. But we, while reckoning and positing Father, Son and Holy Spirit truly in individual hypostases, are accustomed to crown them with unity of nature.
