And by raising them up together through the identity of their essence, we, as it were, finish the long, broad and high ark to one cubit. Christ, then, saves us in faith and settles the Church as if into an ark. Once inside it, we shall float above the terror of death and escape being condemned with the world. For the righteous Noah, that is, Christ, will be with us.

It is worth inquiring carefully, I think, who might be meant by those who hurry with Noah into the ark and win the salvation that comes through faith and water. It is written, then: "Noah went into the ark, and his sons, and his wife, and his sons' wives with him." With them he also brought in some of every animal and of the birds: seven of the clean and two each of the unclean. For this is what God saw fit to ordain. The names of his sons are Shem, Ham and Japheth. Shem is interpreted as "planting" and "perfect", Ham as "heat", and Japheth as "broadening". For we who have been saved in Christ through faith have been planted like tender saplings, moving from the imperfect way of life under the law, so to speak, into the perfection of the gospel teaching. That is why the divine David rebuked the peoples of the Jews who did not accept justification in Christ, saying: "You loved evil more than good, unrighteousness more than speaking righteousness. You loved all words that drown, a deceitful tongue." For they blasphemed the Son without restraint. "Therefore," he says, "God will destroy you for ever. May he pluck you up and remove you from your dwelling, and your root from the land of the living." But concerning those who loved justification and life in Christ he says: "Planted in the house of the Lord, they will flourish in the courts of our God." That Emmanuel did not work his grace in us without the divine, spiritual fire, without, as it were, the heat that comes through the Spirit, the divine Paul will also convince us, since he wishes those called in sanctification to be seen "fervent in spirit." No less does the wise John assure us, saying: "I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who comes after me is mightier than I, and I am not worthy to carry his sandals. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire." For the love of the Jews has grown cold because "lawlessness has multiplied" among them, as it is written. But we are very hot, especially in this love. That is why we say: "What will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or persecution, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?" Ham, then, whose name is understood as "heat", would be a very clear type of those who are fervent in spirit. And the third son, Japheth, whose name translates as "broadening", would suggest to us that we have swum out into broadness of heart, leaving behind the affliction of life under the law. For God addressed the Jews through the voice of Isaiah: "Hear the word of the Lord, you afflicted men and rulers of the people in Jerusalem." And again: "Learn to hear, you who are hemmed in." But Paul, having passed beyond the narrowness of the law, addressed some who had already believed: "Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections. In return (I speak as to children), be enlarged as well. Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers." For they were still following the commandments of the Jews and their useless, rash counsels. And David somewhere sings to Christ, the Saviour of all, as if speaking for the new people in Christ: "I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart." For our mind has been enlarged into wisdom, since Emmanuel has taken up lodging and made his dwelling in the souls of all through the Spirit. Such, then, are those who are in Christ through faith.

The most pure multitude of those justified in faith is very great, while the number from the Jews is smaller. One may learn this from the following without any effort. Noah brought into the ark seven of the clean animals, but only two each of the unclean, that is, of the Jews who killed the Lord. For it is the remnant that has been saved, as the prophet says. Yet the type also foreshadowed that from time to time some of the blood of Israel would revolt and depart from the faith. For he sent out the raven from the ark, Scripture says, to see whether the water had abated, but it did not return. It drowned in the waters, I think, since it found no support or footing. So slipping away from faith in Christ and withdrawing from it is surely a cause of destruction. So too the blessed Paul says to those who after coming to faith sought perfection in the law, or rather imagined they would become perfect: "You have been severed from Christ, you who are being justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace. For through the Spirit, by faith, we eagerly await the hope of righteousness." Notice that the raven, the deserter, belongs to the unclean birds. For it was from among the Jews that some went back to the shadows of the law after being justified in Christ. It is about them, I think, that the wise John also writes: "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us." And since the Spirit also says clearly that "in later times some will depart from the faith, paying heed to deceiving spirits," see a clear type of this too given through Noah. He sent out a first and a second dove to look around, as if to see whether the flood had subsided. They returned to the ark as to a nest, and one of them had a twig in its mouth, as it is written, and this was an olive shoot. For the saints are sent out by Christ to look over the world and those in it, and they return, as it were, speaking peace. This, I think, is what the olive shoot lying in the dove's mouth indicates indirectly, for that plant has always in some way been a symbol of peace. Those cleansed by faith, then, love God and are chosen by God, living in the meekness, so to speak, of the gospel way of life. Yet the type would show that even some of these will fall away in the last times, as I said just now. For a third and final dove is sent out, and it had no thought of returning: it stayed away. When the flood had subsided, the ark settled on the mountains of Ararat, a name interpreted as "testimony of descent." For those who are in Christ through faith are lofty, as if on mountains, because the gospel way of life rises so high. They proclaim to people everywhere God the Word, who came down from above and from heaven. God himself called to them through the voice of the prophet: "Be my witnesses, and I am a witness, says the Lord God, and so is the servant whom I have chosen." The glories of those who are in Christ, then, are above the lowliness of the world.

Emmanuel has also become our High Priest. Through him we have gained access to the God and Father and been renewed to our original state, once the curse was lifted, I mean the curse laid on the first-formed man. See this by looking into what is written next. "When the earth was dried," it says, "Noah went out of the ark, and all who were with him. And he built an altar to God, and took some of all the clean cattle and of all the clean birds, and offered whole burnt offerings on the altar. And God smelled a sweet-smelling savour. And the Lord God considered and said: I will not curse the earth again because of the deeds of men." And again, further on: "And the Lord God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth and rule over it. The fear and dread of you shall be upon all the wild beasts, upon all the cattle of the earth, upon all the birds of the sky, upon everything that moves on the earth, and upon all the fish of the sea. I have given them into your hands." So when Christ became our high priest, and we were brought by him spiritually to God the Father as a sweet-smelling savour, we were then also richly granted his favour. We have received firm assurance that death will no longer have power over us. The effects of wrath have been undone, and those of that ancient curse have vanished. For we have been blessed in Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

Now that everything concerning the ark has been concluded, the flood is past, and Noah is already working the land, our discourse will again look closely into what it was that Ham did against him. For it will persuade those who choose to live lawfully to regard nothing whatever as equal in weight to reverence for their fathers, and plainly to shun, as one of the most perilous of things, mocking them in any way at all, even if they should stray a little beyond what is fitting, overcome by the weaknesses of nature. That parents are always in some way to be revered, the divine law itself teaches us. For having first commanded that we must love the one God, who is God by nature, with our whole soul and heart, it says, "Honor your father and your mother, that it may go well with you, and that you may live long on the earth." For those who have begotten us may be reckoned as being, so to speak, in the image and likeness of God. "Remember," it says, "that through them you were born." For this reason it says again, "The eye that mocks a father and dishonors the old age of a mother, may the ravens of the valleys pick it out." That to think one need not honor one's fathers, or indeed count them worthy of all reverence, brings curse and punishment, one could learn very easily from Ham as well. For it says: "The sons of Noah who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth; and Ham was the father of Canaan. These three are the sons of Noah; from them people were scattered over all the earth. And Noah began to be a man who tilled the earth, and he planted a vineyard, and he drank of the wine and became drunk, and was uncovered in his house. And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father's nakedness, and went out and told his brothers outside. And Shem and Japheth took the garment and laid it on both their backs, and walked backward, and covered their father's nakedness; their faces were turned away, and they did not see their father's nakedness. And Noah awoke from his wine and learned what his younger son had done to him, and he said, 'Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a household slave to his brothers.' And he said, 'Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem, and Canaan shall be his slave. May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his slave.'" Noah, then, having planted a vineyard, was enjoying the fruits of his own labors, and became drunk, which was not his habit. Having suffered an unwilled exposure, an unexpected charge of fondness for wine, he was at home and out of sight of most people. But the one whose mind was unsound, I mean Ham, made the indecency of the sight an occasion for unholy laughter, although he ought to have covered his father, and all but come to the aid of the one who begot him, overpowered as he was by drunkenness and brought low by the lapses that wine causes. But passing over such duties, and slighting in no small measure the honor due to his father, he hurries to share the spectacle with the others, and, setting up the old man like some show on a stage, he urges his brothers to laugh. They, however, were better than his wicked counsel: dealing wisely with what had happened, and hiding the unsightliness of the spectacle with the covering, they walked backward. For it seemed to them a matter of piety to show reverence even to their father's thighs, through which they had come into being. And when the father awoke and became aware of what had happened, he at once curses the one who had so senselessly disregarded what was fitting and the reverence owed to him, and justly lays on him the yoke of slavery, naming Canaan because of the Canaanites descended from him, who were to share his punishment with him. For he was punished together with his whole race. But he blessed those who had honored him.

This, again, would also reveal in a figure the mystery concerning the Jews. For there have been three peoples in all: the one in the first time, corresponding to Shem; the one in between, corresponding to the accursed Ham; and the third, the last, which may be understood as Japheth, coming at the end, whose name means "enlargement." Now when God the Father revealed to us his own Son, who is signified by the thighs, and who, measured, so to speak, against the intelligible beauty of the Godhead, was unseemly and unlovely because of his humanity ("for he had neither form nor beauty," in the prophet's words), then indeed, as the very outcome of events would bear witness, the first people and the last, that is, those who believed at the beginning and first, and also the one called in the last times, showed reverence to Emmanuel, and they have been blessed through him by God the Father. But the one that came between the two, mocking Christ, as it were, for the unloveliness of his humanity, and dishonoring in many ways the Son who appeared from God, has remained in the condition of slavery and has slipped away from the freedom of the fathers. And that those from among the Jews who would believe in the last times were to be partners of the first, all but sharing the same household with them, since they would be brought together into one city, or court, or hearth, that is, the Church, he indicated by saying, "May God enlarge Japheth" (that is, the third, the one in the last times, for Japheth is the third), "and let him dwell in the tents of Shem" (that is, of the first), "and let Canaan be their slave." This, I think, is what Christ said to the crowds of the Jews: "Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free." For the wretched Jews, having mocked the saving dispensation of our Savior and having failed to honor his revelation, made to us by God the Father, have remained in the spirit of slavery.

Human nature lacked nothing for well-being and prosperity, for the Maker of all made it complete and filled with every good. But what was once great was brought down to something less, losing little by little the things through which it might be seen as venerable and perfectly fitted for great dignity. For example, it forfeited incorruption in Adam, for it was said to him, "Earth you are, and to earth you will return." After this it was deprived of the Spirit. For when God saw that those on earth wished to think only of the unholy and most abominable passions of the flesh, he says, "My Spirit shall not remain in these people, because they are flesh." But see, it suffers yet another loss. For some, condemned for unholy schemes and crazed rashness, carry it off into a different and discordant speech. "The whole earth," it says, "had one lip, and there was one language for all. And as they moved from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there. And each said to his neighbor, 'Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire.' And brick served them as stone, and bitumen was their mortar. And they said, 'Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose top will reach to heaven, and let us make a name for ourselves before we are scattered over all the earth.'" Then God comes down (for so the holy Scripture has said), and confuses their tongues and scatters them over all the earth. The God of all rebuked their undertaking, yet he did not fear its outcome; but since they had planned something arrogant, he used his innate gentleness and stopped their undertaking by the multitude of tongues, showing that he does not leave unrebuked designs that go beyond what is human, even if they are somehow aimed at the impossible. And he confuses the tongues themselves; for what requires the skill, and indeed the authority, of the Creator alone would befit no one else at all, but him alone. The reshaping of language, and the broadening of speech into different sounds, one might reasonably ascribe to him who alone is truly and by nature Creator. And the enterprise itself would by no means escape deserving to be thoroughly laughed at.

For they supposed, I know not how, that they would by every means succeed in raising a tower of brick and earth to the very heavens. These too, I think, would be a type of the folly of the Jews, who supposed they would find intimacy with God, and indeed all but the very journey upward, not by choosing to do what seems good and dear to him, nor through faith in Christ, but, as though erecting a kind of tower, by ignorantly thinking high thoughts on the bare and sole basis of the glory of their fathers. For, naming Abraham over and over, and building up their own glory, as it were, with earthly boasts, they were always being condemned. But God rebuked those who were building the tower and divided them into many tongues. And we say that what happened to those people then was a kind of advance proclamation of what befell the Jews. For since they thought very high thoughts and sought the way upward by the means least fitting, he scattered them into the multitude of tongues, that is, among all the nations. For they were scattered, driven from their own land and city and homes, and became wanderers among the nations, as the prophet says. But in Christ the multitude of tongues was a good sign. For when the disciples were gathered together into one house on the day of Pentecost, "suddenly," it says, "there came from heaven a sound like the rush of a violent wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And there appeared to them tongues as of fire, divided among them, and one rested on each of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." And what were they speaking of? Of the way upward that the Spirit provides, the ascent to heaven in Christ through faith, the coming together into unity in the Spirit of all the tongues throughout the world, that is, of peoples or nations. For every tongue of mortals confessed Christ and spoke of his mysteries. So in the case of the tower, the multitude of tongues was a sign of scattering and of dispersal among all the nations; but in the case of Christ, it was a sign of coming together into unity through the Spirit, and of the journey upward. For Christ has become for us a tower of strength, as the Psalmist says, carrying us to the city above and joining those on earth to the choirs of the holy angels.

The God of all gave the law as a help, for so it is written. Yet the law serves as a tutor, while it is the mystery of Christ that brings us to perfection, and this is not at all hard to see from the sacred Scriptures themselves, if we gather the proof for it carefully and collect the truth. The inspired Paul is enough, I think, when he speaks about the two covenants: "On the one hand, the former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness, for the law made nothing perfect; on the other hand, a better hope is brought in, through which we draw near to God." So a person could quite easily come into close fellowship with God, though not through the first, Mosaic commandment. It is through the hope that is said to have been brought in, which the one who initiates us into the mysteries, looking toward the truth, saw fit to crown with the verdict "better." He says plainly that what is in the law has been set aside, and, laying down that the former commandment can perfect nothing, he writes to the Hebrews: "For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion sought for a second. For he finds fault with them when he says: Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they did not remain in my covenant, and I paid no heed to them, says the Lord. For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and I will write them on their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And they shall not teach each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, Know the Lord; for all shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest. For I will be merciful toward their sins, and I will remember their iniquities no more." And to this he immediately adds: "In speaking of a new covenant, he has made the first old; and what is growing old and aging is near to vanishing away." The law, then, is weak, and is plainly seen to be largely powerless, powerless, I mean, to bring anyone to perfection in holiness. Justification and worship in Christ are better, and you will hear this plainly from God himself, crying out through the voice of the prophets to those who honored the worship of the law and clung tightly, as it were, to the commandment that had grown old. At one time he says, "Wash yourselves, become clean"; and at another, "I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than whole burnt offerings." For we have received mercy in Christ, and in him we have spiritually beheld the Father, and have come to know the one who is God by nature.

It would be very easy to heap countless further points onto what has been said, and to add the voices of the holy prophets, through which one could see quite plainly that the worship of the law is unacceptable to God. But we do not want to drag the discussion away from the purpose before us and let the narrative wander off somewhere far away, as if it were going down another path. So we will now proceed to the inspired Abraham himself. He learned that his nephew Lot had unexpectedly fallen into danger. Lot was living in Sodom, and had now been taken captive in war and counted among the slaves. So Abraham armed the servants born in his household, together with some of his allies, Eshcol, Aner and Mamre. He led them out against the victors, and nobly, and freed the man from their greed. Along with him he rescued a very great multitude who had been wronged with him and were in danger. As Abraham returned home, bearing the honored tokens of his valor against the enemy, those who had benefited from his labors naturally came out to meet him. For it is written thus: "And the king of Sodom went out to meet him, after he returned from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, to the valley of Shaveh." This was the King's Valley. And it goes on: "And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out to him bread and wine; and he was a priest of God Most High. And he blessed Abraham and said: Blessed be Abraham by God Most High, who created heaven and earth. And blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hands. And he gave him a tenth of everything." Observe, then, how the types of the perfection that is in Christ shine out clearly in Melchizedek, and how the worship of the law is shown to be of lesser measure. For it is beyond doubt that the lesser is in every case blessed by the greater, as it is written. Now the inspired Abraham is, as it were, the root of those who are from Israel, and what was preeminent and choice in him was Levi, crowned with the glories of the divine priesthood. But Levi was still lying in the loins, for blessed Abraham was potentially the father of those who would come from him in due time. And this, I think, is what is wisely said about Levi: "For he was still in the loins of his father when Melchizedek met him." So the righteousness of the law has been blessed by the worship that is in Christ, of which Melchizedek is a type. And who could doubt that the blessing is superior, indeed incomparably so, coming as it does from what is not in the same condition [?]? But we shall examine such matters in fine and careful detail before long.

But perhaps the one who has chosen to fight against Christ will want to ask, before anything else, who Melchizedek actually was. For some people get drunk on various opinions about him. They have senselessly slipped into idle nonsense, and have paid little attention to the ways of the divinely inspired Scripture. Some say that it was the Holy Spirit who met the victorious Abraham, in an apparition and merely in our outward form, and that he was only seen. Others do not say this, since they fear, I suppose, what veers too far into the unseemly. Instead they insist that he was a power from the multitude of the angels, an illustrious and select one. A feeble and unsteady mind, it seems, has led them astray into this opinion. "Since Salem," they say, "is interpreted 'peace,' and Melchizedek is named king of Salem, let him not be thought of as a man; let it be the Spirit that is meant. For peace belongs properly to God, and he alone will rule over peace." And they add: "If he has neither beginning of days nor end of life, how could it not be a foolish thing to write that a man is without beginning and without end? So again let the Spirit be understood. For if," one of them says, "he has been made like the Son of the Most High and remains a priest forever, how could we not conclude on every count that Melchizedek was not a man?" Then, weaving other reasonings in with these, they think they can establish as truth an argument they got from who knows where. But we must say what comes to mind, since we have chosen to set against their conjectures what seems best and right. First, if they have resolved to think reasonably, they themselves will agree that Salem is a city, and that Melchizedek was neither its first nor its only king. There were certainly a great many kings, some before him and others after him. If anyone thinks we are speaking falsely, let him come and show us Melchizedek reigning over Salem to this day, since it is one of the cities of Judea, and was perhaps renamed Jerusalem. This name too is interpreted "vision of peace." But no one could show it. It is ignorant, then, to pay attention to the interpretations of names and dare to overturn what is clear and agreed by all. That the whole notion is ignorant and the argument for it full of senselessness we shall see without effort, if we consider this as well. Jerusalem, as I said just now, is interpreted "vision of peace," or "raised above death." Israel, again, means "a mind seeing God," and Judah means "praise and hymning." Yet the sacred Scripture has clearly proclaimed how many impious and profane kings of Jerusalem there have been in their times, over Israel and over Judah. So, if no earthly king could reign over a vision of peace, over praise and hymning, and over a mind that sees God, and if such a thing would not befit a man, then come, let us pay attention to the interpretations of the names and say that those who reigned in their times were shadows and phantoms and not men at all, but rather the Spirit, as in the case of Melchizedek! You can learn from this too that the force of names, or of their interpretations, can in no way compel the nature of things to conform to itself. Would one not suppose, or rather declare it entirely true, that if Jerusalem is a vision of peace, it surely ought not to have failed to know Christ? For he himself is our peace, according to the Scriptures. Yet it did not behold with the eyes of the mind the one through whom we have obtained access and have been joined in unity in the Spirit to the Father, the one who made both into one and created the two peoples into one new man. How then is it a vision of peace, if it did not behold Christ? And if it is "raised above death," that is, stronger than death and higher than it, how did the wretched city perish through its unbelief in Christ? For he himself addressed the Jews, saying: "Truly I tell you, unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins." And if Israel is interpreted "a mind seeing God," why did it not behold the glory of Christ, through whom and in whom we have come to know the Father himself? How were they overtaken by the darkness? Or how could it be said of them and of those appointed to lead them, "Leave them; they are blind guides of the blind"? For what blindness could be conceived in a mind that sees God? It is full of ignorance, then, to grant the qualities of names complete mastery over the realities themselves. Nothing at all, I think, will prevent us any longer from rightly and fittingly holding that Melchizedek was a man, and reigned over Salem in his time, even if the name perhaps means "peace."

To what has been said we must add this further consideration. For now we see the divine mysteries only barely, through a mirror and in a riddle. And since nothing among created things is wholly like the divine and ineffable nature, we gather from countless examples a modest ability to understand or say something about it, as far as we can. No less obscure is the mystery of Christ, and the account of the incarnation is not to be grasped by just anyone. Deep indeed is the account of the divine plan. For the Only-begotten, being God and from God by nature, became man and dwelt among us. He has also been called our Apostle and High Priest. He released us from the slow-tongued law and brought us over to the eloquence of the gospel teachings. Not only this, but he also set us free when we were captives, having overthrown the ruler of this age. He rescued those who had fallen asleep from the depths of Hades. He founded the Church and has been appointed ruler over us. He brought us across the Jordan in faith, gave us circumcision in the Spirit, and brought us into the kingdom of heaven. That he became as we are, it will be enough, I think, to hear the inspired evangelist saying: "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us." That he has been anointed as priest and apostle, the appointment of Aaron would show quite clearly. For Aaron was anointed with the consecrated oil and set as ruler and leader of priests and people. Moreover, on the top of his forehead he received the golden band, that is, the plate, which had the name of the Lord written on it. This was a clear symbol of our Savior as king, a bright and conspicuous diadem, as it were. That the worship through Christ is better than the worship of the law can be seen in Aaron, just as it certainly can in Melchizedek. For the Levites received tithes from the sons of Israel according to the laws. But God commanded that a tithe of the Levites' tithe be given to Aaron as their leader, since in the office of priesthood he flourished with the highest honors. Understand, then, how in the person of Aaron, Levi, who receives tithes, has himself paid tithes. For Aaron has been set in the place of Christ. All the other Levites and priests performed the sacrifices of the law, having their station in the first tent. But Aaron alone of all of them entered the Holy of Holies once a year, as it is written, and not without blood, according to the law. This too would be a type of Christ, who died once for our sins, according to the Scriptures, and entered into the most holy tent above. For he opened this way for us, sanctifying the Church with his own blood. And when the inspired Moses was chosen for a mission, he entreated God, saying: "I pray you, Lord, I have not been eloquent, neither yesterday nor the day before, nor since you began to speak to your servant; I am weak of voice and slow of tongue." And he added: "Choose another who is able, whom you will send." Then the God of all said to him: "No. Behold, Aaron your brother, the Levite. I know that he will speak for you. And behold, he will come out to meet you, and when he sees you he will rejoice within himself. You shall speak to him and put my words in his mouth, and I will instruct you both in what you are to do. He shall speak for you to the people, and he shall be your mouth." For the ancient law was admittedly slow of tongue and did not know how to speak well. Through a long, roundabout route, that of the letter, I mean, it barely conveyed God's will to us, almost stammering it out. But the most eloquent mouth of Moses is Christ, who changes the types into truth and sets the knowledge of what is necessary readily before people everywhere. That is why it says in the forty-eighth Psalm: "Hear this, all you nations; give ear, all you who dwell in the world." So Christ was prefigured, as it were, in Aaron. And there is something more remarkable still. Do not be surprised that he sketched out the greatness of his own preeminence among those who knew him and had knowledge of the laws. For he also appeared as it were in a foreign man, one who freed Israel from captivity, laid the foundations of the holy and sacred city, and held invincible power over all. I will make the account clear, keeping it as brief as possible.

Judea was once carried off into captivity, and the people of Israel were worn down for many years in Babylon, weighed down by a harsh and barbarous slavery. But Cyrus, son of Cambyses, having gained the power of both the Medes and the Persians, took up war against the Assyrians, who were his neighbors and bordered on his lands. It was then that he took Babylon itself by force and set the Jews free. They had come running to him, not without tears, lamenting the greed of the Assyrians. They affirmed that God had foretold through the voice of the saints that he would come in due time, would prevail over those who opposed him, and would himself release the wronged from their bonds. They said too that he would raise up again the house in Jerusalem, which the Assyrians had burned, committing impiety against God. And if we examine the writings of the holy prophets closely, we shall not find the Israelites speaking falsely in this. For God spoke thus through the voice of Isaiah: "Thus says the Lord, who redeems you and who formed you from the womb: I am the Lord who accomplishes these things. I alone stretched out the heaven and made the earth firm. Who else will scatter the signs of ventriloquists and divinations from the heart, turning the wise back and making their counsel foolish, confirming the words of his servant and making the counsel of his messengers come true? It is he who says to Jerusalem, You shall be inhabited, and to the cities of Judea, You shall be built, and its desolate places shall spring up. It is he who says to the deep, You shall be made desolate, and I will dry up your rivers; who tells Cyrus to be wise, and he shall do all my will; who says to Jerusalem, You shall be built, and I will lay the foundation of my holy house. Thus says the Lord God to my anointed, Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, so that nations may obey before him; and I will break the strength of kings. I will open doors before him, and cities shall not be shut. I will go before you and level mountains; I will shatter bronze doors and break iron bars. I will give you treasures of darkness; hidden, unseen ones I will open to you, so that you may know that I am the Lord God who calls you by your name, the God of Israel. For the sake of Jacob my servant and Israel my chosen, I will call you by your name and receive you. But you did not know that I am the Lord God, and there is no other God besides me; and you did not know me." You hear how plainly he says, "You did not know me." He does not even think fit to count among those who know God this man so illustrious, whom he himself made greater than kings and master of countless nations. For what concerned Cyrus were types of the achievements of Christ. God foretold that Cyrus would scatter the false divinations of the Babylonians and the signs of the ventriloquists, and that he would show that the counsels, that is, the predictions, of God's own prophets, whom he also called messengers, were not false. He announced beforehand that Cyrus would build the cities of Judea, make the deep desolate, and dry up all its rivers. By "the deep," I suppose, he means Babylon, because of the multitude of its inhabitants, and by its rivers the nations that streamed together from every side to its aid. But come, let us set out clearly what concerns Cyrus, and skillfully reshape what was accomplished through him into the mystery of Christ.

Cyrus, then, was born of Mandane, daughter of Astyages the ruler of the Medes, and of Cambyses, a Persian by race but a man of very gentle character. For this reason some of the ancients called Cyrus a mule and a half-breed, because, I think, his father and mother came from different races. For the Persians are a different nation from the Medes. You can see something like this in the case of Christ as well. According to the flesh he was born of a mother, the holy Virgin, who was like us and human by nature; but his father was not one of us. Rather, if we may put it this way, his father was of an altogether different nature, exalted in nature, and transcending everything that is counted among created things. That is why he said to the Jews, who thought that he was like us and had come into being as we do: "You are from below; I am from above." Cyrus conquered countless nations, and every city received him. He also took treasures that were dark, hidden and unseen, and released Israel from long slavery. But Emmanuel has become king of all that lies under heaven, and every city welcomes him as the Savior and Redeemer of all. Every race that had been overpowered by the devil's greed and forced to act under him has now been released from that slavery. And going down even into Hades, he emptied out treasures that were dark, hidden and unseen. He shattered the doors of bronze and crushed the bars of iron. For he said to those in bonds, "Come out," and to those in darkness, "Show yourselves." That is why, long ago, he said to Job, that most long-suffering and unconquerable athlete: "Have you come to the source of the sea, and walked in the tracks of the deep? Do the gates of death open to you in fear, and did the gatekeepers of Hades cower when they saw you?" We shall read these words as a question, since the passage points to the achievements of Christ, accomplished in the very depths of Hades. "For to this end Christ died and lived, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living." Long ago Cyrus gave money and ordered the temple in Jerusalem to be rebuilt. But Emmanuel founded the Church, the truly holy and renowned city, after he had utterly shaken arrogant and insolent idolatry as though it were a Babylon. Concerning Cyrus, God says: "He shall do all my will." And somewhere the Savior of us all said to the Jewish people who despised him: "You judge according to the flesh." And elsewhere: "And if I judge, my judgment is true, because I do not seek my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me." To Cyrus, God said: "I have called you by my name." But Emmanuel is truly Lord, even though he appeared as a man. That the things concerning Cyrus were set down as a type of Christ, the Lord of glory, will be made plain by the words that follow, spoken through the voice of the prophet: "I made the earth and man upon it. With my hand I established the heaven, and I gave command to all the stars. I raised him up in righteousness, and all his ways are straight. He shall build my city and turn back the captivity of my people, not for ransom nor for gifts, says the Lord of hosts. Thus says the Lord: Egypt has toiled, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians, and the Sabeans, men of stature, shall come over to you and shall be your slaves. They shall follow behind you bound in manacles, and they shall bow down to you and pray in you, because God is in you, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it, the God of Israel, the Savior. All who oppose him shall be ashamed and confounded, and they shall go in shame." For he who made the earth and man upon it, who adorned the heaven with stars, raised up Jesus for us as righteousness, the one who redeems freely (for we have been justified by faith). He releases us from bonds and captivity. He spiritually builds the spiritual Jerusalem, and he founds the Church so that it cannot be shaken even by the gates of Hades and cannot be taken by enemies. Recognizing that he is God by nature, those who once went astray say: "For you are our God, and we did not know it. And there is no God besides you." To him they will bow down; to him every knee shall bend, and every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. Some from Israel dared to oppose him. But they were put to shame and fell, and they went away in rout, as the prophet's voice foretold. So Cyrus son of Cambyses laid the foundation of the house of God in Jerusalem as a type of Christ. That Emmanuel himself would bring the matter to completion in a spiritual and intelligible way can be learned at once through yet another image. For when Cyrus released Israel from slavery in Babylon, there immediately appeared as guides and, so to speak, leaders of the people Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and Joshua son of Jozadak, the high priest. When they had arrived in Jerusalem, God charged them through the voice of Haggai the prophet to devote themselves diligently to the work on the house. For it is written thus: "In the second year of King Darius, in the sixth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying: Speak to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and to Joshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: This people says, The time has not come to build the house of the Lord. And the word came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying: Is it a time for you to live in paneled houses, while the house of the Lord lies desolate?" And again, after other things: "And the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, and the spirit of the remnant of all the people; and they came in and did the work in the house of the Lord Almighty, their God." See, then, Emmanuel in a double type and image. He appears as king in Zerubbabel, who was of the tribe of Judah, the tribe that then had the lot of ruling in Israel. He appears again as high priest in his namesake, Joshua the high priest. And he appears, moreover, as the one who leads the way to the holy city out of a land of foreigners, by which I mean, once again, Babylon. See him also as the craftsman and overseer of the holy temple. For when we follow Christ by faith as our guide, as king and high priest, we come out of the devil's greed, as if out of a foreign land, and out of worldly deception, and we enter the holy city, the Church of the firstborn, which Christ himself will raise up as if from spiritual stones. Paul will bear witness to this when he writes to those who have been redeemed by faith and have chosen to follow in the footsteps of Christ: "In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place of Christ in the Spirit." And that the glory of the Church is greater than the first glory of the beginning, I mean the glory of the temple built of stones, he made clear by saying again through the voice of Haggai: "Who among you saw this house in its former glory? And how do you see it now, as though it were nothing before you?" And again, after other things: "Mine is the silver and mine the gold, says the Lord Almighty; for the latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former, says the Lord Almighty. And in this place I will give peace, and peace of soul as a possession to everyone who builds, so as to raise up this temple." One could collect without effort the passages in which Christ was depicted for us in the ancient writings. But so that our discourse may not seem to be carried away from what is fitting by a multitude of examples, we shall for now forgo going through any more of them, and we say this: we shall certainly have to choose one of two options. Either we shall do away altogether with the people through whom those things came about, deciding that the types are not entirely free of fault if they are understood as having come about through men like us, even though they contain a great deal that is worthy of God. Or else, by saying that the Spirit is always taking on a form like ours, we shall be forced to confess that it was once fashioned into Cyrus as well, a man who did not know God. For it was said to him: "But you did not know me." And if those who serve as types are done away with, Aaron perhaps becomes a mere shadow, while Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and indeed Joshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, would be nothing but bare names.

But I think that, persuaded by reasonable argument, they will rather agree, and rightly, that Melchizedek was a man, king of the city of Salem, and that Paul, with his subtle mind for spiritual contemplation, made him a type of Christ for us. But suppose that after this they object, and still say that Melchizedek was not a man but rather the Holy Spirit, or at any rate some other power from above and from heaven belonging to the ministering rank, for some do hold this view. Then we must say that they will err in two ways. They drag the divine and ineffable nature of the Spirit down to a condition that does not befit it, and they foolishly raise begotten and made creation to an excessive glory. I will explain how. It is written of Melchizedek that he was a priest of God Most High. If, then, Melchizedek is the Holy Spirit, the Spirit has been brought down among those who perform priestly service, and its role is that of a minister. In that case it too will praise the most high God together with the holy angels. For it is written: "Bless the Lord, all his angels, his ministers who do his will." It could hardly be unclear that whoever performs priestly service always does so for another and not for himself, and that he serves as priest to God, who is superior to him. So if we say that the Spirit acts as a priest, it is certainly placed beneath the divine nature. It will instead be counted among created things, and it will worship along with us. Nor will it sanctify itself, since whatever is sanctified is surely sanctified by something superior to itself in nature. It will be sanctified along with us. How, then, can what is sanctified still be God by nature? For is not every priest sanctified, and only then does he take up the duty of performing priestly service? "For no one takes this honor for himself," as it is written, "but only when called by God, just as Aaron was." And Paul added: "So also Christ did not glorify himself in becoming high priest, but was appointed by the one who said to him, You are my Son, today I have begotten you; as he also says in another place, You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." For we must understand that not even the Son himself, the Word from God the Father, would be said to act as priest and to belong to the ministering rank unless he were understood to have become like us. Just as he is called a prophet, and indeed an apostle, because of his humanity, so too he is called a priest. For in the form of a servant, the things proper to a servant befit him; and this is the self-emptying. He exists in the form of the Father and in equality with him. The very Seraphim above stand before him, and thousands upon thousands of angels serve him. Yet when he emptied himself, then indeed he is said to have been revealed as a minister of the holy things and of the true tabernacle. Then too he who is above all creation was sanctified with us. "For the one who sanctifies," it says, "and those who are sanctified are all from one. For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, I will declare your name to my brothers." So he who sanctifies as God is said to be sanctified with us at the time when he became man, dwelt among us, and was called our brother according to his humanity. Both the need to act as priest and the being sanctified with us therefore belong to the economy in the flesh. Since we have chosen to think rightly and blamelessly, we shall ascribe such things to the measure of the self-emptying. But if we say that the Spirit, which never underwent self-emptying, acts as priest, we shall strip it of the glory that befits God and reckon it among the beings that are subject to God, assigning it the measure of what is begotten. Otherwise, let them show us that the Spirit became man and underwent a descent in the divine economy, just as the Son did. For it does not follow, from the fact that the holy and worshipped Trinity is consubstantial, that one may assign the incarnation to whichever person one likes. It was not the Father himself who became man, nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone. This is what the divine Scriptures have taught us. Why, then, do they do violence to the truth? Why do they bring down into the measure of the self-emptying that which has no reason to be emptied, I mean the Holy Spirit, if it is truly to be numbered among those appointed to perform priestly service? For Melchizedek was a priest. "But," they say, "the Spirit took on this form by itself in honor of the Son, as a type of the priesthood that would be his in due time." Then, I shall ask, has the Holy Spirit neglected the honor and love it owes the Son, and does it think fit to care little for the matter? Yet how is it not nonsense to think or say such a thing? For the Paraclete, that is, the Spirit, glorifies the Son, and the Son says about him: "He will glorify me." So if the Spirit chose to honor the Son, and to do so unceasingly, why did it not rather become Aaron? Why did it not become Cyrus, who ruled the Persians and the Medes? Or Joshua son of Jozadak, or Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah? Or Moses, who displayed in himself the mediation of Christ, and to whom it was said: "I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he will speak to them whatever I command him"? Why did it not also become Joshua son of Nun, the general after Moses, who brought the sons of Israel across the Jordan, circumcised them with knives of stone, and led them into the land of promise? Or have we not been baptized in Christ, circumcised through the Spirit with a circumcision not made with hands, and made heirs of the kingdom of heaven? And how is this not plain? So either we shall grant that the Spirit is always taking on a form, as it would have in each of those named, in order to honor the Son, or else the charge will turn out to be true that it is caught having cared little for what was fitting, since it allowed some of the ancients to be fashioned into a type and likeness of the Son. Away with such absurd reasoning! Melchizedek, then, was a man, and not the Holy Spirit.

Nor could he be understood to be a holy ministering power, as some have seen fit to think. Let us now show this, gathering arguments from reasonable considerations to demonstrate the truth. These people have put together an argument of the following kind, a wise one, as they suppose among themselves. "Since," they say, "it is written of Melchizedek that he was without father, without mother, and indeed without genealogy, and since he blessed Abraham, great as Abraham was, and since beyond all dispute the lesser is blessed by the better and greater, let him not be thought of as one of us. Let him instead be an angel by nature, that is, one of the ministering powers above, august and glorified." But I, beloved, am greatly astonished that a kind of reverence for the divine Abraham has carried them away from the pursuit of what is useful and fitting, and has lured them away from the reasoning needed to find the truth. For while they present Melchizedek to us as a likeness and type of Emmanuel, they do not look at the character of the events or examine the nature of the priesthood. Instead they scrutinize the natures of those who were brought forward for this purpose. One might reasonably ask them: what harm would there be in Abraham being blessed by Melchizedek, who might well be a man, even if he were not thought to be superior to him? For in these matters it is not the natures that are examined, but the meaning of what is done; and the realities of the truth, which are better than the enigmas in shadows, are revealed beforehand. It is utterly absurd not to set what is signified alongside the shadows, and instead to fix on the very natures of those who are brought forward. You will see this from the following as well. Aaron was chosen. He presided over and led the holy tabernacle, and he was crowned with the highest honors of the priesthood. How, then, was he sanctified? Was not a ram slaughtered, and was not the tip of his right ear anointed with its blood, and likewise his hand and his foot, and was he not consecrated in this way for priestly service? My good sirs, I would say to them, if it is right to fix on the natures of those who sanctify and those who are sanctified, rather than to move from type and shadow to the very beauty of the truth, how can the lesser still be blessed by the greater? Let them tell us which is the better in these cases. Are we then to rank Aaron below even a ram? The rational is consecrated by an irrational animal! Are we to say that the man chosen for the priesthood was sanctified by the blood of sheep? And the ashes of a heifer, when sprinkled, sanctify those who have been defiled, so as to purify the flesh. What, then, is the point of all this? What is the depth of its meaning? The rites were types and images, and, if we may put it so, an advance showing of the sanctification that comes through Christ. The type is found in the actions, not in the nature of those who sanctify or those who are sanctified. Otherwise, as I said just now, the greater is blessed by the lesser, if indeed human nature ranks above a heifer and a ram. So let them not blush if Abraham, though far superior to Melchizedek, is said to have been blessed by him. For what prevailed was the type, not the nature of the one who gave the blessing. I am also astonished that while they shape him into a likeness and type of the Son, they say he is without mother and without father as an angel would be, even though Christ in a sense has both parents. For he had a mother on earth, the holy Virgin, and he had, and has, a Father in heaven, God. I think that images ought to be drawn to match their archetypes. And since the divine Paul said that Melchizedek has "neither beginning of days nor end of life," they insist for this reason that he is a rational and priestly power. They do not realize that they are overlooking something essential. For nothing that is counted among created things will be without a beginning in time. Whatever has been brought into existence at all has a beginning of life and of days. What, then, was blessed Paul's aim in these words? How did he present Melchizedek as a type and likeness of Christ? Let us withdraw our minds from random notions, and come, let us examine the question and speak as well as we can.

Being thoroughly learned in the Law, Paul does not build his argument against the Jews on bare ideas, but on the writings of Moses, to which even those who had resolved to make war on the truth would likely have to yield, however unwillingly. So he takes Melchizedek as a likeness and outline of Christ, because he is called king of righteousness and also king of peace. These titles, I think, would fit Emmanuel alone, when they are understood in the mystical sense. For he was revealed to those on earth as the ruler of righteousness and peace. We have been justified in him, having cast off the burden of sin. And we have gained peace with God the Father, having washed away the impurity of our ways that stood between us and kept us apart, and being united, as it were, to him through the Spirit. "For whoever is joined to the Lord," it says, "is one spirit." Now in Greek, "Melchi" means "king" and "Sedek" means "righteousness." So one can see that Melchizedek was endowed in his very name, by the force of its meaning, with the title "king of righteousness"; and in being called king of Salem, he was "king of peace." The divine Paul, then, applied these things to Christ on the basis of a likeness in Melchizedek that was already clear and plain. He also takes Melchizedek's blessing of Abraham, and his providing him with wine and bread, as a symbol of the priesthood that is above the Law. For we are blessed in no other way than by Christ, the great and true priest. And we are blessed as the divine Abraham was, when we have fought most valiantly against the rulers of this age, proved stronger than the hand of our enemies, and needed nothing that is in the world, but have counted the things of God as spiritual wealth, together with the glorious and unfading bestowal of the gifts from above. For notice that Melchizedek blessed Abraham when he had won his victory and was returning from the slaughter of the kings, as it is written, and had refused to take anything from the ruler of Sodom as his own possession. The leader of the Sodomites said to Abraham, as to the victor, "Give me the men, and take the horses for yourself." But Abraham, having resolved to claim nothing of his, said, "I will stretch out my hand to God Most High, who created heaven and earth, that I will not take anything of all that is yours, from a thread to a sandal strap, so that you may not say, 'I made Abraham rich.'" For it is the way of the saints not to rejoice in worldly wealth. So when we have overcome enemies both visible and invisible, accepting nothing from the world but honoring rather the wealth from above, we are blessed through Christ, the king of peace. And we are blessed when we receive the mysteries as a gift of hospitality from heaven, as it were, and as provision for life. But let that be left unsaid for now, if you please. We are also blessed by Christ through his intercessions for us before the Father. For Melchizedek blessed Abraham with these words: "Blessed be God Most High, who delivered your enemies into your hands." But our Lord Jesus Christ, the atoning sacrifice for us all, says, "Holy Father, keep them in your truth." So Paul seizes on what is useful even from the meaning of the names, to show a foreshadowing of Christ. And he also made the very manner of the priesthood serve clearly to demonstrate the point, for Melchizedek brought out bread and wine. But nowhere does the sacred Scripture state that Melchizedek was without father or without mother, that is, without genealogy, or that he had neither beginning of days nor end of life. Someone might perhaps say, then, that the divine Paul has deceived us. We say no such thing, God forbid! For he speaks the truth. Rather, as a skilled guide into the mysteries, he takes even the way the story is told about these very matters and refers it to a type of the glory of Emmanuel. For the God-inspired Scripture has told us only that Melchizedek was a priest. It does not name his family, or say from what father or mother he was born, and we do not find that it adds how many years he lived, or what succession he had in the priesthood. So the narrative, by treating all this as it does, sketches for us, as it were, the everlasting and beginningless being of Christ, insofar as he is understood as God. By "beginningless" I mean in terms of quantity, that is, of time, for he himself is the maker of the ages. It also hints at the unending nature of his priesthood. That is why blessed Paul says of Melchizedek that, "having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever." But Paul seems also to have had another wise purpose in mind, and I shall try to explain what it is as best I can.

The Jews opposed the preaching about Christ and all but dared to laugh at the apostles' efforts, putting forward these two objections. The first was that it was impossible for the commandment laid down for the fathers through the voice of the all-wise Moses to become void and for the Law to be set aside, with another way of life, known to none of the ancients, being unexpectedly brought in. The second was their insistence that the glory of the priesthood must not pass outside the chosen tribe, that is, the tribe of Levi, since God again and again drove away from the temple service those who did not belong to it, and at once set the severest penalty for such presumption. Paul, then, being learned in the Law, takes up the contest and tries to convince them, both from reason and from the God-inspired Scripture itself, that a new law and a change of the priesthood itself had both been announced beforehand, and that the sign of each had already shone out in types. So he takes Melchizedek, who was not of the Levitical tribe, and then shows that he was a priest of God Most High and that he offered bread and wine, and speaks of him as follows: "See how great this man was, to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils. Those of the sons of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment in the Law to collect tithes from the people, that is, from their brothers, even though these also are descended from Abraham. But this man, whose descent is not traced from them, collected tithes from Abraham and blessed the one who had the promises. And beyond all dispute the lesser is blessed by the greater." Yet we say that Melchizedek's superiority lay not in his nature but in the manner of his priesthood. Our forefather Abraham did not refuse him this; rather, he granted him precedence through the honors he chose to pay him, and by the very offering of the tithes. For those of Levi's blood collect tithes from the people, even though they are their brothers; but he whose descent is not traced from them, that is, Melchizedek (for he was not of the tribe of Levi), collected tithes from Abraham and blessed him. Such is the type in these events. Christ, however, who is portrayed in the shadows, has no place in the genealogy of those appointed to serve as priests under the Law, for he sprang from the tribe of Judah, about which Moses said nothing concerning priests. Yet he has collected tithes from the sons of Levi, that is, from the priesthood under the Law. He did so of old in Melchizedek, and later in Aaron as well. For Aaron too collected tithes from the sons of Levi, since he bore the type of Christ's priesthood, as we have already said.

It has therefore been shown in Melchizedek that the office of the priesthood would one day pass away from the tribe that served as priests under the Law, and indeed that another mode and law of sacred service would shine forth. For it was in some way necessary that the Law itself should also be changed along with the sacred rites, and depart with them. Accordingly the divine Paul too reasons about these things and says, "If, then, perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people received the Law), what further need would there have been for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, rather than one named according to the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood is changed, there must also be a change of law." And again: "It is even more evident if another priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek, one who has become a priest not according to the law of a fleshly commandment, but according to the power of an indestructible life. For it is testified, 'You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.'" You see how he condemns the priesthood under the Law as able to perfect nothing, and shows how very beneficial the introduction of the better commandment is. For if what was needed had been found in that priesthood, why, he asks, is another priest not appointed according to the order of Aaron rather than according to the order of Melchizedek, who was a likeness and type of Christ? For Christ no longer serves as priest in a fleshly way at all, but rather according to the power of an indestructible life. He nourishes us for unfading life through the mystical rites, whereas Aaron served as priest in a fleshly way. Through him there were sacrifices of oxen and slaughterings of sheep, and the ashes of heifers sprinkled on the defiled for the purification of the flesh, and certain other things besides, which could not perfect the worshipers in conscience. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls to take away sins. Since, then, another mode of sacred service has been brought in for us, which removes us from the first and more ancient customs, there must surely be another priest as well. And if God has promised a new covenant, the first having grown old, then the priest according to the order of Melchizedek, to whom the word "forever" may fittingly be applied, can be none other than our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

The inspired Paul writes that Christ became the high priest and apostle of our confession. Indeed, he clearly affirmed that, because Christ brought us something incomparably better and more excellent than the ancient commandment given through Moses (I mean the commandment of the gospel), he has become the guarantor of a better covenant. And what he says is true, since the law brings about wrath and points out sin, while the grace ministered through the gentleness of our Savior justifies us. For, as he himself says somewhere, he did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him. Our discourse has already shown sufficiently that, even though he did not happen to come from the tribe of Levi according to the flesh, he has been named and is a high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek's priesthood. But there are further points. The mystery of righteousness by faith was foretold earlier than circumcision under the law. The type was laid down beforehand for those of Israel that they could never be saved in any other way than through Christ alone, who justifies the ungodly and remits their offenses. And beyond this, those who are of the promise made in Isaac to blessed Abraham are heirs of God and are ranked among his most truly legitimate children. Come, then, let us speak of these things, drawing them from the sacred Scriptures themselves and offering the proofs for each point carefully and after close examination.

So the most holy Paul writes to the Romans: "What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, has found? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God. For what does the Scripture say? 'Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.' Now to one who works, the wage is not reckoned as a favor but as a debt. But to one who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness. So David also speaks of the blessedness of the man to whom God reckons righteousness apart from works: 'Blessed are those whose lawless deeds have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered; blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will not reckon.' Is this blessing, then, for the circumcised, or for the uncircumcised as well? For we say that faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it reckoned? When he was circumcised, or when he was uncircumcised?" "Not when he was circumcised," he says, "but when he was uncircumcised. And he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of the faith he had while uncircumcised, so that he might be the father of all who believe while uncircumcised, so that it might be reckoned to them as righteousness, and the father of circumcision to those who are not only of the circumcision but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had while uncircumcised." And besides this, he examines the mystery even more precisely, speaking as follows: "For the promise to Abraham or to his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who are of the law are heirs," he says, "faith has been emptied and the promise made void. For the law brings about wrath; but where there is no law, there is no transgression either. That is why it is of faith, so that it may be by grace, in order that the promise may be secure to all the offspring, not only to those of the law but also to those of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all (as it is written, 'I have made you the father of many nations'), in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls the things that do not exist as though they did." You hear him affirming over and over, and saying without reserve, that the grace which justified Abraham through faith was given to him when he did not yet have circumcision but was still uncircumcised. He affirms too that the heirs of God's gifts are those who wish to follow in the track of the faith that our forefather Abraham had while uncircumcised, and imitate it. They are certainly not those who habitually pride themselves on the shadow ministered through Moses and boast of Abraham as their father according to the flesh. For Abraham was named "father of many nations," yet Israel is a single nation, even if it should happen to grow into a countless multitude. This is because he became the father of those who live by faith, who have been gathered from practically every city and country, have become one body in Christ, and have been called into a spiritual brotherhood. The Jews were indeed born from Abraham. Yet not all who are descended from Israel are Israel, nor are all of them children because they are Abraham's offspring. Rather, it is faith that makes those who believed while uncircumcised his kin. For the promise was made, and the justifying grace was given, to Abraham when he did not yet have circumcision but was still uncircumcised, as the sacred [?] attest.

Even though the promise was made in Abraham, the gift of righteousness by faith would not extend to him alone, but has gone out, as it were, to all who have believed since. The most wise Paul assures us of this again, adding to the words I have just quoted: "But the words 'it was reckoned to him as righteousness' were not written for his sake alone, but for ours as well. It is going to be reckoned to us who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification." Therefore the grace that justifies us by faith is heaven's gift to its guests and a present from the gentleness above. Those who would be counted among Abraham's children are by no means those born from him according to the flesh. They are all who have been enriched with conformity to him, and who, being like-minded as brothers, believe in our Lord Jesus Christ. These will also be heirs of God's gifts, while Israel according to the flesh has been thrust aside for unbelief. This too was sketched out for us, and very clearly, in the mystery concerning Isaac. But come, let us speak again as best we can, setting the very writings of Moses before you so that you may know them. They read as follows: "After these words," it says, "the word of the Lord came to Abraham in a vision, saying: 'Do not be afraid, Abraham; I will shield you. Your reward will be very great.' And Abraham said: 'Master, what will you give me? I am departing childless. And the son of Masek, my household servant, this is Damascus Eliezer.' And Abraham said: 'Since you have not given me offspring, my household servant will be my heir.' And at once the voice of the Lord came to him, saying: 'This man will not be your heir; the one who will come forth from you, he will be your heir.' And he brought him outside and said to him: 'Look up now to heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.' And he said: 'So shall your offspring be.' And Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness." Blessed Sarah, whose name is interpreted as "ruler," was joined to him and shared his home. She was a woman of outstanding beauty and very fair of face, for so the sacred text testifies. The household servant, that is, Hagar, whose name is interpreted as "sojourning," also attended him, serving a second and, as it were, illegitimate union. But Sarah, who had not yet felt the birth pangs of legitimate children, lamented her childlessness, while Hagar bore Ishmael. With matters in the story standing so, God spoke to Abraham, saying: "I will shield you; your reward will be very great." And what does he say to this? "Master, what will you give me? I am departing childless; and the son of Masek my household servant, this is Damascus Eliezer." Note the precision of his words. "What will you give me," he says, "O Master?" You see how he says he has no further need at all of earthly possessions. Even if he became master of still more, he says, he would not count the thing a delight unless he had a legitimate heir sprung from a free marriage, a true son. Observe also that nature knows clearly what is good for us of its own accord, even without written laws. For although he had a son (I mean Ishmael), the inspired Abraham called himself childless. So nature knows quite clearly that one sprung from counterfeit and illegitimate unions could not reasonably be called a son at all. For, as it is written, he will not strike deep root. He further showed that even if a child should be born to someone from a maidservant, the thing is altogether cold and stale, and free people would not count it a delight, when he said: "And the son of Masek my household servant, this is Damascus Eliezer." That is: "What I will have left is the son of the household servant, a kiss of blood." For this is what "Damascus" means. "And he will be counted as help and aid from God." For that, again, is what "Eliezer" means. It is as if he said plainly: "In place of genuine blood and the love [?], my household servant will become, as though of necessity, a kiss of blood and help from God, and he will also be my heir. What then will you give me? If I have no legitimate successor, your Abraham, O Master, will be under reproach in every way. For he departs bereft of true children born of a free woman." But God did not let the righteous man grieve for long. At once he promised the offspring in Isaac, which he says will be as numerous as the countless multitude of the stars. And though Abraham was alarmed by fears of childlessness, God assured him that he would be called the father of countless nations. "And Abraham believed God," it says, "and it was reckoned to him as righteousness." So whoever honors the Master of all by faith has righteousness as his reward, for by this he has testified that God is able to accomplish all things. But the unbelieving and careless person will be a braggart and insolent, and for this reason he will in the end fall under judgment and have to give account. Abraham, then, believed God and was justified by him. But he further asks for a sign to confirm and verify that the things promised beforehand would come to pass. Then God, by his wise dispensation, puts forward the oath, so as not to let the believer be shaken into doubt. For it is written thus: "And he said to him: 'I am the God who brought you out of the land of the Chaldeans, to give you this land to inherit.' And he said: 'Master, Lord, by what shall I know that I will inherit it?' And he said to him: 'Take for me a three-year-old heifer, and a three-year-old ram, and a turtledove, and a pigeon.' And he took all these for himself, and divided them down the middle, and set the halves facing one another; but the birds he did not divide. And birds came down on the bodies, on their divided pieces, and Abraham sat down with them. Around sunset a trance fell upon Abraham, and behold, a great and dark dread falls upon him. And it was said to Abraham: 'Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land not their own, and they will enslave them and mistreat them for four hundred years. But I will judge the nation they serve. And after this they will come out here with many possessions. But you will go to your fathers in peace, nourished in a good old age. And in the fourth generation they will return here, for the sins of the Amorites have not yet reached their full measure.' And when the sun was setting, there was a flame; and behold, a smoking furnace and torches of fire, which passed between these divided pieces." But what exactly is it that took place? The lover of learning will consider this and investigate the manner of the oath-taking. He will ask what the divided pieces might mean, what the flight of the birds and their gathering upon the pieces mean, what again is meant by Abraham sitting with them, and what by the flame darting between the divided pieces. So we will explain.

Among the Chaldeans, passing between animals cut in two necessarily served as an oath. Through the very act one would, as it were, declare: "May I become like these." Since Abraham was a Chaldean by race and had only just come out of his native land, the Master of all, by his wise dispensation, ordered him to do what was customary for oaths, and elegantly wove the mystery of Christ into the sacrificed victims. When the divided pieces had been laid out in order on the ground, as though God were about to pass between them, "birds," it says, "flocked to them in numbers, and Abraham sat down with them." That is, he sat round about and guarded them, so that no harm might come and the things brought for the oath might not lie there as food for unclean birds. "Around sunset," it says, "a trance and dread fall upon Abraham." And I shall explain as best I can what the reason for this might be understood to be. Among the Chaldeans it was a custom, held in good and entirely blameless repute, to examine the flights of birds minutely. So the God of all, by his wise dispensation, allowed Abraham to be instructed about the future by means he knew, which some were accustomed to use. When the birds gathered on the divided pieces, then, the inspired Abraham was frightened, wondering perhaps where and upon whom the sign would fall. For it seemed to him an evil omen, and no small cause for concern, that the most loathsome of birds had flown down upon the sacrifices, since birds that habitually eat flesh are somehow always unclean. But when he feared for his own head, lest the thing should come upon him, God frees him from his anguish over these things. "What you suspect," he says, "will not come upon you. But know for certain that your offspring will sojourn in a foreign land." And very many indeed will be those who want to harm them; the birds that swooped down on the sacrifices laid out were a type of them. Yet after causing only a little grief, they will pay the penalty. "But you will go to your fathers, nourished in a good old age." Then it says that when the sun had reached the very point of setting, a flame of fire and a furnace and torches passed between the divided pieces. Here again the Deity is understood to fulfill the oath in the form of fire, in keeping with the Chaldean custom.
