Accordingly the inspired Paul also takes the event as having the force of an oath, and says: "For when God made his promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying: 'Surely I will bless you abundantly and multiply you abundantly.' And so Abraham, having waited patiently, obtained the promise. For people swear by someone greater than themselves, and for them an oath given as confirmation puts an end to every dispute. So when God wished to show even more clearly to the heirs of the promise that his purpose could not change, he guaranteed it with an oath. He did this so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled to him for refuge might have strong encouragement to lay hold of the hope set before us."

It was by a most fitting dispensation, then, that God made the promise under oath, although he does not know how to speak falsely. As the inspired Paul writes, he did this so that we might have strong encouragement and no longer doubt that it will come to fulfillment in every way. Now (for I shall take the discourse back a little), while Hagar was still pregnant with Ishmael, Sarah was vexed, perhaps unable to bear the servant woman's boasting over her pregnancy and her immoderate haughtiness. Then she drives her from the household and told her to go wherever she chose, for her lawful husband (I mean Abraham) had permitted her to do this. But as the sacred text says: "An angel of the Lord God found her by the spring of water in the wilderness, on the road to Shur. And the angel of the Lord said to her: 'Hagar, maid of Sarah, where have you come from, and where are you going?' And she said: 'I am running away from Sarah my mistress.' And the angel of the Lord said to her: 'Return to your mistress and humble yourself under her hand.'" So Hagar went back and put herself under the yoke of slavery. God now also gave Abraham the law of circumcision, saying: "You shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations. And this is the covenant which you shall keep, between me and you and between your offspring throughout their generations: every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you. Every male child among you shall be circumcised at eight days old, throughout your generations. The slave born in your house and the one bought with money from any foreigner, who is not of your offspring, shall surely be circumcised, both the one born in your house and the one bought with money. And my covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant. And any uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin on the eighth day, that soul shall be utterly cut off from its people, because he has broken my covenant." Since it was necessary to submit to the divine laws, the inspired Abraham was circumcised with all his household, and he circumcised Ishmael together with the others. After this the son of the free woman was born, that is, Isaac. And what came next? Ishmael, the illegitimate son, who played about the household and was perhaps honored on an equal footing with Isaac, could no longer be tolerated. "For Sarah," it says, "saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, playing with her son Isaac." Then she comes to him, in tears as is likely, and says: "Cast out this slave woman and her son, for the son of this slave woman shall not inherit with my son Isaac." "And the word," it says, "seemed very harsh to Abraham on account of his son. But God said to Abraham: 'Let the word not seem harsh to you concerning the boy and the slave woman. Whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice, for it is through Isaac that your offspring shall be named. And as for the son of this slave woman, I will make him a great nation as well, because he is your offspring.' So Abraham rose early in the morning, took bread and a skin of water, and gave them to Hagar; he put the child on her shoulder and sent her away. And she went off and wandered in the wilderness near the Well of the Oath. When the water in the skin was used up, she cast the child down under a fir tree. Then she went and sat down opposite him some way off, about a bowshot away, for she said: 'Let me not see my child die.' And she sat opposite him. And the child cried aloud and wept. And God heard the child's voice from the place where he was. And an angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and said to her: 'What is the matter, Hagar? Do not be afraid, for God has heard your child's voice from the place where he is. Get up, pick up the child, and hold him by the hand.' And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of living water. She went and filled the skin with water and gave the child a drink. And God was with the child, and he grew." The inspired Abraham, overcome by the laws of a father's love, wanted to keep Ishmael as his own. But since the divine oracle called on him to devote himself to Isaac alone, because the promise had been made in him, he let Hagar go and told her to leave the master's household with the infant. In this way the law was showing in advance the type of the mystery of Christ.

And now we must bring the discourse back to where it began. For here one could see most readily that what comes through Christ is older than what is in the law, and that justification by faith was shown forth earlier than circumcision in the flesh. For circumcision was given to Abraham as a sign of the faith he had while uncircumcised, as the most wise Paul says. Blessed Abraham, then, was distressed that he had not become the father of a free child. Though he had a son by the Egyptian woman (I mean Hagar), he remained utterly disheartened, counting illegitimate and unfree offspring as no better than childlessness. But when he received the promises concerning the legitimate child (I mean Isaac) and heard clearly that through him he would be the father of countless, innumerable nations, he believed and was justified. And when God told him that he would come into possession of the land God had shown him ("for to you," he said, "I will give this land"), he begged to be fully assured, saying: "Master, by what shall I know this, that I will inherit it?" For this reason God ordered him to take the animals to be divided: a three-year-old heifer, a goat along with it, a ram as well, a turtledove, and a pigeon. Abraham cut the four-footed animals in two and set the halves facing one another, that is, he arranged them in rows; but the birds he did not divide. He also drove off the birds that wanted to devour them. And when the sun was already going down to the farthest edges of the west, God passed between the divided pieces in the form of fire. What spiritual meaning, then, might we apply to such things? We will say, as best we can.

Israel according to the flesh was the first to become a son, so to speak, to the God of all. For he says, “Israel is my firstborn son,” but a son born, as it were, of a slave woman and redeemed out of Egypt. Yet God did not see fit to count him among his children in any real way, for his nature loves freedom and loves what is legitimate. Instead he sought the people who please him, that is, the people who come by faith in Christ according to the promise. In this people the divine Abraham and his line became fathers of many nations. They inherited the glory attached to this promise not in Israel according to the flesh, but in those from the nations who have been saved through faith. Paul will bear witness to this when he writes: “For the promise to Abraham that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.” We who believed while still uncircumcised claim Abraham as our father, and God justifies us just as he justified him. Paul, who was learned in the law, will make the divine mystery very clear to us. After he had been perfected in Christ he wrote as follows, rebuking the Galatians, who were going backward, as it were: “Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave girl and one by the free woman. But the son of the slave girl was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through the promise. These things are an allegory. These women are the two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai and bears children for slavery; this is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia; it corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children. But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written: ‘Rejoice, you barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor; for the children of the desolate woman are more than the children of the one who has a husband.’ Now we, brothers, are children of the promise, like Isaac. But just as at that time the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the Spirit, so it is now also. But what does the Scripture say? ‘Cast out the slave girl and her son; for the son of the slave girl shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.’ So, brothers, we are not children of the slave girl but of the free woman, by the freedom with which Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.” You see, then, how clearly he says that Hagar and Sarah are images of the two covenants. He likens the slave girl to the mother of the Jews, that is, the earthly Jerusalem, since she is subject to laws of slavery and is not marked by a free spirit. But the first and free woman, I mean Sarah, whose name is interpreted as “ruler” for this very reason, he says is bound up with the figures of the Jerusalem that is on high and above. He affirms plainly that she has become the mother of those who have been justified by faith and called by God’s promise to be children of Abraham. “For we,” he says, “are children of the promise, like Isaac.” We have been set free in Christ. Through him and in him we have been enriched with the divine Spirit from above. We have been enrolled among the children of God, we cry, “Abba, Father,” and we have become heirs of the good things promised to the saints, God having all but sworn by himself. For the Son, that is, the mystery concerning him, was brought in as the Father’s oath. It is the Father’s custom to swear by his own power, the Son, and this is what swearing by himself means. For the Son is not other than he, I mean in terms of essence and the identity of the Godhead. Indeed, when the divine Moses showed us God swearing, he presented him as saying quite plainly: “I will lift up my hand to heaven and swear by my right hand.” For the right hand of God the Father is the Son. By him the Father rules over all things and, as it were, grasps the whole universe. By him he works as befits God, calling into being things that do not exist and granting well-being to those that already exist. So the mystery of our Savior was brought in to serve as an oath, confirming the heirs in their faith in the promise. And Christ was prefigured, as it were, in a heifer, and also in a goat and a ram, and in two birds, I mean a turtledove and a pigeon. What this means I will explain as far as I can.

Sometimes, because of his exceedingly great strength and his invincible might (clearly the might that befits God), he is likened to a bull calf. At other times, because of his humanity and because he came under the law, he is called a heifer. For the female somehow always comes after the male and is lesser than him, since the male leads and is preeminent. The Son is beyond all creation, and with incomparable superiority he surpasses the nature and glory of all things that have come into being, for he has the highest root, I mean the Father and God of all. But since he was born as we are, he was placed under the law as under a superior. That is why he said: “I did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it.” If we choose to think rightly, we will attribute this too to the limits of his self-emptying. For this reason Christ is a heifer, while Moses, or rather the law laid down through him, plays the part of the male, the law. He is also likened to a goat. For what reason? Because he offered himself for our sins, according to the Scriptures, and under the law the sacrifice for sin is a he-goat. He is also compared to a ram, because he leads the rational flocks. For we have one guide, Christ. And we are “the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand,” as it is written. But since he was made like his brothers, that is, like us, in every respect, lowering himself into self-emptying, he is written of as a ram but understood to be the leader. For the rams are always at the head of the flock. So the same one is a heifer, because he is under the law; a goat, because he is a sacrifice for sin; and also a ram, because he is the leader. If we choose to follow in his footsteps as we must, and press on eagerly, we shall be “in good pasture and in a rich place,” as the prophet says, and we shall dwell in holy courts. For he will settle us in the dwelling places above. He himself is both ram and chief shepherd. He is under the law as one of us, and above the law as God, being himself all righteousness, even though “he was counted among the lawless” and endured slaughter for our sake. Again, he is pictured in a turtledove and a pigeon. For he is the only spiritual and most talkative turtledove, the truly sweet-voiced bird, the one who is from heaven and from above, who charmed the whole world under heaven with the proclamation of the gospel. The bride herself, that is, the Church from the nations, called out to him: “Show me your face, and let me hear your voice; for your voice is sweet and your face is lovely.” He is also the simple dove, innocent and without guile. For “no guile was found in his mouth,” as it is written. The heifer is three years old, and so are the other animals. For the Lord is perfect in every way, and the age of the animals neatly hints at the perfection of the Only-begotten as God. The animals are laid open, for they were cut in two, but the pair of birds remained undivided. What does this mean? Insofar as the only-begotten Word of God became flesh, he is in a sense divided in two, and our account of him broadens into a twofold contemplation. At one time we consider his divine and ineffable birth from the Father; at another we speak of the mystery of the incarnation, all but unfolding the depth of the divine plan and laying it out for those who do not know it, so that they may know. But even if our account of him has become twofold in a sense, he is certainly one and the same, and he is not divided into two after his union with the flesh, nor cut into a pair of sons. For Christ is one and indivisible. A clear type of this too would be the fact that the birds were not cut apart: “But the birds,” it says, “he did not divide.” He was signified as being from the earth, because of his humanity, in the calf, the goat and the ram. But he is understood, through the birds, as being from heaven and from above, because he is God. Though he willingly endured slaughter for us, “his flesh did not see corruption,” as it is written; and, as the Psalmist says, “The enemy shall gain nothing against him, and the son of lawlessness shall not harm him again.” The divine Abraham would show this very clearly, again as a type, when he drove away from the divided pieces the birds that wanted to devour them. And after it had been foretold to Abraham that his descendants, that is, Israel, would in time be oppressed in Egypt and would be marvelously redeemed, “About sunset,” it says, “a smoking furnace of fire and torches of fire passed between the divided pieces.” For the law given through Moses dawned before those who were born of the promise, bringing to its hearers long narratives about the slavery of the Israelites and also about their redemption. But in the last times of the age, toward evening as it were, “the Word became flesh.” This, I think, and nothing else, is what is meant by the divine and ineffable nature darting down, in the form of fire, upon the divided pieces themselves. But “there was,” it says, “a flame of fire, and a furnace of fire, and torches of fire.” For the venerable mystery of the incarnation truly became, for those who chose to disobey and turned to unruliness, a furnace and a flame and the most unbearable and final punishment of all. Indeed, concerning those of Israel who senselessly insulted the mystery of Christ and were shown to be malicious and arrogant, David says to the Father and God of all: “You will make them like a furnace of fire at the time of your presence; Lord, in your anger you will throw them into confusion, and fire will devour them.” The time of the Father’s presence may reasonably be taken to be the time of the incarnation, since the Son is both the face and the image of God the Father. So he is a fierce flame and a furnace to those who want to reject the mystery of the incarnation of the Only-begotten. But to those who have recognized his appearing he is, as it is written, “a lamp shining in darkness.” He thins out the thick mist of the devil and does not let the multitude of those who worship him stumble over the obstacles that lie in their path. In this way God the Father also named the Son for us through the voice of Isaiah, saying: “For Zion’s sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest, until my righteousness goes forth like light, and my salvation burns like torches.” For the Son has become salvation and righteousness for us from God the Father. It is true that in him we are justified, and that by conquering death, which long ago tyrannized over us, we return to incorruption and are reshaped into what our nature was in the beginning.

Once Emmanuel had appeared and the mystery concerning him had been revealed in the world, the types of the Mosaic worship had to be subordinated to the teachings of the gospel and to give way to better and more perfect commandments. This was again sketched out in a rough type. What this type is, I will explain. Since Sarah bore no child but Hagar conceived Ishmael, Hagar was then caught looking down on the free woman. Sarah could not bear her contempt and mistreated the Egyptian. Hagar fled the household and wandered in the desert. An angel from heaven asked her where she was going and where she had come from. She replied: “I am running away from my mistress Sarah.” What did the divine angel say? “Return to your mistress, and humble yourself under her hands.” For the worship under the law appeared first, in labor with Israel. But since she was a servant (for there was no free spirit in her), she bore the people that came out of Egypt, as it were, before the new teaching of the gospel. That is why she thought highly of herself and persecuted those who are in Christ, and was caught in many ways looking down haughtily on the decrees of the gospel. For the Synagogue of the Jews rebuked the holy apostles, saying explicitly: “We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name, and look, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching.” You see how the Egyptian exalts herself over Sarah, and the slave girl grows insolent toward the free woman. But in time she was defeated and ran away, in a sense prizing her unruliness. Yet she is commanded by the voice of an angel not to reject the free woman, that is, the teaching that calls us to the dignity of freedom, but rather to humble herself under her hands. For the worship under the law, which proceeds through figures and types, is in a sense a servant to the teachings of the gospel, showing in itself only a dim reflection of the beauty of the truth. The law given long ago through Moses was ordained through angels, and through the voice of an angel it is commanded, as it were, to bow its neck to the decrees given through Christ, to submit to the free woman, and to give way even against its will. This, I think, is the spiritual meaning of Hagar coming under Sarah’s hand. We must remember that the divine Paul also treated them as a pair of covenants: one bearing children for slavery and corresponding to the present Jerusalem, the other, I mean Sarah, bearing children for the dignity of freedom. The blessed Abraham was also plainly taught that once Christ had appeared, the time of circumcision in the spirit would surely dawn along with him. For God made it a law that circumcision must be carried out, foreshowing spiritual realities, I think, through bodily examples. “Every male among you,” he says, “shall be circumcised.” And he set ruin and destruction as the penalty for neglecting it, for he said: “And the uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin on the eighth day, that soul shall be utterly destroyed from among its people, because he has broken my covenant.” You see that a type in the flesh, so to speak, was shown beforehand of the circumcision in spirit and in truth. For it is performed on the eighth day, the day on which Christ came back to life from the dead. And then it was time to share in the Holy Spirit and to receive the circumcision that is in him, a circumcision that does not pain the flesh but cleanses the spirit, that does not remove bodily dirt but frees us from the diseases of the soul. For when Christ came back to life, having destroyed the power of death, then, at that very moment, he placed in the holy disciples a kind of firstfruits of the Holy Spirit. “For he breathed on them,” it says, “and said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit.’” The most wise John will also support this argument when he says: “For the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.” He was glorified when he was raised from the dead on the eighth day. Therefore the Spirit was sent to us, and in him we have been circumcised with a spiritual circumcision not made with hands. For this is the kind of circumcision that pleases God. Indeed, the divine Paul says somewhere: “For a person is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is true circumcision something outward in the flesh. Rather, a person is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter. Such a person’s praise comes not from human beings but from God.”

The worship under the law had ceased to function, and the new worship in Christ now prevailed. The peoples of faith had been revealed, and they were placed among the children of the free woman, not having a slavish spirit (for they have cried out, “Abba, Father”). So it was now time for the assembly and Synagogue of the Jews to be sent away, and for the people born of her to be disinherited, as it were, from the promise. Yet she will return in due time and be accepted, and she will receive kindness from above and from the Father when she recognizes the Savior and Redeemer of all. The sacred text again signifies all this. The boys were playing, jumping at each other, Isaac, that is, and Ishmael. The game, I suppose, was a chase: Ishmael was the one in pursuit, while Isaac was seen running away. But the free woman, I mean Sarah, was angered by this. And she said to the divine Abraham: “Cast out this slave girl and her son; for the son of this slave girl shall not inherit with my son Isaac.” These words troubled Abraham when he heard them. But he heard from God that he must do what Sarah said. So he gave Hagar bread and water for the journey and told her to leave her master’s household together with the boy. She went away distraught and in tears, and she wandered in the desert. When the child was in danger and crying out, “God opened Hagar’s eyes,” it says, “and she saw a spring of living water, and gave him a drink.” See, then, how even the children’s game may contribute something to our knowledge of the mystery. Ishmael chased Isaac. And the blessed Paul made it clear that in time the son of the maidservant, that is, Ishmael, would persecute the son of the free woman, namely the people who are in faith and in Christ. For he speaks about Ishmael and Isaac as follows: “But just as at that time the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the Spirit, so it is now also.” Since Ishmael made war on the children of the free woman, the Synagogue of the Jews is then sent away with grim and meager provisions, bread and water. That is, she was given a measured portion of knowledge and piety, enough that she would probably not depart altogether and die. For God says somewhere, having left in Israel a remnant, as it were, and a small seed of the goodness that comes from the law: “And I will be a little sanctuary for them in the lands to which they go.” He says that a little sanctuary would be left to the people of Israel after their dispersion among the nations because the Jews were not strong enough, I mean, to carry out even the law given through Moses. They would keep only very little of it, and that with difficulty: perhaps circumcision in the flesh and rest on the Sabbath. So she who bears children for slavery, that is, the Synagogue of the Jews, is barely supplied with water and bread. Abraham was distressed when Hagar went away, but he let her go all the same at God’s command. For admittedly the falling away of Israel grieved the holy apostles and evangelists. Yet they parted from Israel, though unwillingly, because of what pleased God and because of their love for Christ. Indeed, the divine Paul writes: “I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites.” Once she had been sent away, the mother of the Jews wandered for a long time, and she has been in danger of perishing altogether. But if they cry out and call aloud to God in due time, they will surely and in every way receive mercy. For he will open the eyes of their mind, and they too will see the spring of living water, that is, Christ; and when they drink, they will live in him. They will wash and become clean, as the prophet says. That Christ is the spring of life the Psalmist will make clear when he says to the Father and God in heaven: “How you have multiplied your mercy, O God! The children of men will hope in the shelter of your wings. They will be drunk with the richness of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight, for with you is the spring of life.” And this spring is none other than Christ, through whom and with whom be glory and power to God the Father, together with his holy, consubstantial and life-giving Spirit, for all the endless ages of ages. Amen.

“And it came to pass after these words that God tested Abraham and said to him, ‘Abraham, Abraham.’ And he said, ‘Here I am.’ And he said, ‘Take your beloved son, whom you have loved, Isaac, and go into the high land, and offer him up as a whole burnt offering on one of the mountains that I shall tell you.’” Such, then, was the message that came from God. So without delay the righteous man saddled his donkey, as it is written, told only two servants to follow, and taking up his beloved son set out for the sacrifice. When he reached that holy place, barely on the third day, he said to the servants, “Sit here with the donkey; the boy and I will go on as far as yonder, and when we have worshiped we will return to you.” He loaded his son with the wood for the burnt offering, persuaded him to walk on so, and followed behind. And when the boy asked his father, saying, “Here are the fire and the wood; where is the sheep for the burnt offering?” he said, “God will provide for himself a sheep for the burnt offering, my child.” Having built that divine altar, he heaped up the wood on it. And when he had bound the youth upon it and had already taken hold of the knife, an angel’s voice stopped him, saying that he must not slay the boy, for God already knew the good resolve that was in him. Then the righteous man, catching sight of a ram hanging by its horns in a sabek plant, completed the sacrifice, offering it up in place of the child. And so he went down to the servants, bringing his son back to them safe and sound. Having thus cut down the breadth of the story and gathered into a brief account what serves to show that through these events the mystery of our Saviour was prefigured, we shall not hesitate to set it forth again, taking it up as far as we are able. But if not everything set down in the narratives fits the interpretation, let no one find fault. For the spiritual meaning is often hidden in what is superfluous in the story, just as the most fragrant of the flowers in the meadows are wrapped on the outside in useless leaves; if one cuts these away, he will find what is beneficial and useful laid bare. So let the allegorical account now begin.

Blessed Abraham is tested and commanded to sacrifice his beloved son. As is natural, he is grieved as a father and pricked by the hot goad of nature toward fatherly affection, yet he nonetheless puts first the good that would come of the deed. This shows us again, and very clearly, what the Saviour said: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.” For if we must say something in human terms to make the thought plain, God the Father was in a certain way stung to the heart in sending his Son to death for us, even though he knew that he would suffer nothing painful, since he too was impassible as God. Nevertheless, considering the benefit of the death—I mean the salvation and life of all—he disregarded the affection that befits a father. That is why Paul marveled at him, saying: “He who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all.” For on what grounds could the love of God the Father for us rightly be a cause of wonder, unless he seemed to endure something against his will in giving up his own Son for us? This is what Paul persuades us to understand when he says “did not spare.” That expression would never be used of ordinary things, but only of those who boldly undertake some great deed, as in: “Enlarge your cords and strengthen your stakes; spread out still further to the right and to the left”; and further, “Drive them in; do not spare.” And again: “Rescue those being led to death, and ransom those being slain; do not spare.” So much, then, we have to say on “Take your beloved son.” The two servants who accompanied the old man and went along with him as far as the third day may be a type of the two peoples called into servitude through the law—I mean Israel and Judah. They thought they need follow only the commands of God the Father, just as those servants followed Abraham, not yet perceiving the Son through whom are all things, nor recognizing the Father’s heir. Of him Isaac would present a most beautiful image, being small and still lying in his own father’s bosom, and not yet bearing the authority befitting a master. For the Son was, and always is, Lord and all-perfect God. But because he was not manifest to all, and especially to the impious Jews, who looked only at the flesh, he was thought to be someone small and ordinary. Knowledge of him is in some way measured out in proportion to each person’s understanding: it is found small in the small, but great in the great. So the prophets say, “He is great and fearsome over all who are around him,” that is, over those who have come near him through very great sharpness of mind. And Paul is in labor for some “until Christ is formed in them,” that is, until the great and supernatural marks of his divinity are gradually molded into their minds. The servants followed as far as the third day, yet they were not allowed to be brought up into the high and holy land, but were rather ordered to sit with the donkey. This signifies the two peoples’ following of God through the law, which extended as far as the third time, that is, the last, in which Christ appeared to us. For the whole age is measured out in three times: past, present and future. So the end comes in the third. And the divine Scripture says that Christ came to dwell among us in the last times of the age. So Israel, having followed God through the law right up to the time of our Saviour’s coming, would not follow Christ through faith as he went up to the death he died for all; or rather, it was prevented by its many sins. For “a hardening has come upon Israel in part,” and this is signified by the donkey that was with the servants at that time. For the donkey is an image of the utmost unreason, and hardening is unreason’s child. Then the father parts from the servants and goes off with his son, yet says that he will come back again: “For I,” he says, “and the boy will go on as far as yonder, and when we have worshiped we will return to you.” This signifies God’s temporary withdrawal from the children of Israel, and his return to them that will come at the end of the ages, accomplished through faith in Christ. For “when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved.” Blessed Abraham does not say plainly that he is going up to sacrifice his son, but uses a pretext, as it were: “We will go on as far as yonder.” This would be a clear sign that the mystery of Christ was not entrusted to the peoples of the Jews. And what we say about this will prove true when we see Jesus speaking to the Jews as in parables and through riddles, while saying to his own disciples: “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables.” The boy, that is, Isaac, was loaded with the wood of the burnt offering by his father’s hand, and reaches the place of the sacrifice. For Christ, carrying his own cross on his shoulders, suffered outside the gate. He was not forced into suffering by human strength, but went of his own will and by the counsel of God the Father, as he himself said to Pontius Pilate: “You would have no authority over me at all, unless it had been given you from above.” Isaac, once laid on the wood, is stolen away from death and suffering, and a God-given ram goes up as the sacrifice. For it was truly the Word, who shone forth from the essence of God the Father, in his own temple—I mean the one born of the Virgin, which was also nailed to the wood. But being impassible and immortal as God, he withdraws himself from death and suffering. Yet he goes up as a fragrant aroma to God the Father through his own body, which he himself is said to have received from the Father, as it is said in the Psalms in his own person: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you took no pleasure. Then I said, ‘Behold, I have come; in the head of the book it is written of me; I desired to do your will.’” That the details of the story set before us will very fittingly be referred to Christ, he himself will testify again where he says: “In the head of the book it is written of me.” For the whole most wise writing of Moses is a single book in five parts. And the head, that is, the beginning, of the whole book is the part called Genesis, in which these things are written about Christ. That “head” means “beginning” in the divine Scriptures, you will be fully convinced once you understand what Paul says: “The head of every man is Christ; the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God.” For Christ is the beginning of the man, since he brought him from non-being into being. The man, again, is the beginning of the woman, because of what was said and truly done: “She shall be called woman, because she was taken out of her man.” And he says that the beginning of Christ is God himself, since the Son is from him by nature, and though without beginning he has the one who begot him as his beginning, while also coexisting with him eternally.

The mystery, then, has been fitted very well, I think, to the words of the story. But now, I think, we must adorn the divine Abraham with extraordinary admiration, and with the highest praise show him glorious and conspicuous to all people everywhere; and besides this we must see clearly the depth of God’s skillful design. For the divine Abraham was tested, not because God did not know what would happen; nothing could escape the all-knowing Mind. That is why he said: “Who is this who hides counsel from me, keeping words shut up in his heart, and thinks to hide them from me?” And again through the voice of Isaiah: “For I am God, and there is no other besides me, declaring the last things beforehand, before they come to pass, and at once they are accomplished.” If we think rightly, then, we shall count it utterly senseless, and among the most absurd notions, to suppose that the God of the universe did not know the future and tested Abraham for that reason. Rather, it was necessary that the righteous man’s head should not shine in God’s knowledge alone, but that he should be rich in a most glorious renown, attested in the knowledge of all, through the trial itself, for every excellence. It was necessary also that the holy Scriptures should proclaim how very great his obedience was, and how highly he regarded the divine oracles—or rather, that nothing ranked above them. He came to such a pitch of resolve and eagerness that he disregarded even his love for his child, and did not fear the charge of child-murder. And what is more astonishing, it was in this very child that he expected to become the father of many nations. But he knew that God does not lie in this. So he brought the boy to the sacrifice, not despairing of the promises, but leaving to the Master’s power the way in which he would know how to fulfil what he had sworn. Nor was the matter without profit for him, even though he passed through so bitter a trial. For he was taught, from what was about to happen, the marvel of the resurrection from the dead, which surpasses all speech and is well worth hearing, and besides this the august and great mystery of the incarnation of the Only-begotten. So the divine Paul says: “By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac; he who had received the promises was offering up his only son, of whom it was said, ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called,’ reckoning that God is able even to raise from the dead; from there he also received him back as a figure.” For since God the Father was going in due time to make him a root, as it were, and the origin of countless nations, once Emmanuel had died for the world, the righteous man was usefully taught through the trial itself the supernatural and inexpressible love of God the Father for us. For he did not spare his own Son, as we have already said, but gave him up for all of us who have been justified by faith and reckoned as children of our forefather Abraham. If one may draw some inference from human experience, I would say that God’s command to sacrifice Isaac was burdensome and hard to bear for blessed Abraham. How do you think the man ordered to do this felt at the time? A man who had come into deep old age, blessed with a single son born late, robbed by time of the ability to become the father of others, and with a wife who was herself past her prime (for Sarah too was an old woman)—he was ordered to slay without delay this thrice-longed-for son, his only one, so often prayed for. With what hand did the old man expect to be able to drive the sword into the youth, and to dare so pitiable a slaughter of his own offspring? Is it not reasonable, then, to think that a bitter and sharp crowd of thoughts ravaged the righteous man’s soul beyond endurance? At one moment nature forced him toward fatherly affection; at another the divine oracle put him to shame, and perhaps summoned him, as if by necessity, to an unwilling obedience. Great indeed, then, is the wonder of the righteous man, and his love for God is worthy of all praise. For he offered the rational victim, bidding farewell to the laws of nature, trampling on the goad of an inexorable affection, and setting nothing earthly against his love for God. Therefore he was glorified and called the friend of God. And what he had looked for, the object of his hope, came to fulfilment for him: he became the father of many, countless nations in Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father with the Holy Spirit to the ages of ages. Amen.

The wise Paul writes to those who have been justified in Christ, and who, by sharing in the Holy Spirit, have been enriched with unity with him through the good pleasure of the Father: "For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ." The blessed disciples have become something like the inviters to the wedding and the escorts of the bride. They brought near those who were still far off, all but joining them to Christ and binding them to him by the union of the Spirit. Christ will indeed present the Church to himself. It is God the Father who raises her up and, one might almost say, leads her forward and pledges her to his own Son. Yet no one would doubt that the saints act as go-betweens. The inspired David, announcing the mystery to us beforehand, says to her somewhere: "Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father's house, for the king has desired your beauty; for he is your Lord, and you shall worship him." And Paul too, as I said just now, has declared that believers are presented to Christ like a bride. But one may see this mystery, so venerable and truly worth hearing, no less clearly in the following passage as well. For it is written: "Abraham was old, advanced in days, and the Lord had blessed Abraham in all things. And Abraham said to his servant, the eldest of his household, who ruled over all that he had: Put your hand upon my thigh, and I will make you swear by the Lord, the God of heaven and the God of the earth, that you will not take a wife for my son Isaac from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell. But you shall go to the land where I was born, and to my kindred, and take a wife for my son Isaac from there." When Abraham had given these instructions, the servant swore at once, laying his hand on his master's thigh. From this we may understand that the oath was sworn, as it were, upon all the offspring that would come from him. Then, having loaded many of Abraham's goods on ten camels, he hurried to Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers. He came to the city of Nahor and made the camels kneel outside the city by the well of water, toward evening, when the women come out to draw water. Having arrived there, he then implored God to make his way prosper and to show him a maiden who was diligent and hospitable, one whom no hesitation would hold back from kindness. "Let it be," he says, "that the maiden to whom I say, 'Tip down your jar so that I may drink,' and who says, 'Drink, and I will water your camels until they have finished drinking,' is the one you have prepared for your servant Isaac." And before long the maiden came, beautiful in appearance and most comely; I mean Rebecca. When he asked for a drink, she readily offered it. She promised to water the camels too, and carried out what she had promised. From this the servant concluded that she was the one, and no other. So he took bracelets and earrings and brought them to the girl. She bade him come to her home and follow her at once. When this was done, he was given hospitality there, and he gave a glowing account of his master's wealth. He added that his master, having one beloved son, Isaac, had given everything to him, and that the young man was lord of all. And when the escort of the bride wished at last to hasten back with the girl, they asked Rebecca whether she would go with the one who had called her and would welcome the departure. She readily consented. When she had arrived in this way, Isaac now gladly took her into his home, and he was greatly comforted, although his mother had died. The narrative is long and full. But having shortened it as much as possible, we have told enough. Now let the power of contemplation turn to this most skilfully wrought account and show once more the figure of the mystery, still as in faint shadows, yet in labor with the truth.

Abraham did not think it right to join his beloved son, Isaac I mean, to a wife from the daughters of Canaan. Instead he told his trusty servant to hasten to the land of the idolaters to look for a wife as fitting for him as possible. For God the Father did not wish to join the synagogue of the Jews to Christ, who is signified in Isaac. Isaac was born late and was beloved. Christ too appeared in the last times, and he is the beloved, delight and exultation, for that is what "Isaac" means. That the Canaanites may be understood as a figure of those of Israel becomes clear, and very easily, from the meaning of the name. For "Canaanites" means "ready for humiliation." And to whom would it apply to be about to come into humiliation, or rather to have come into it already, if not to the Jews? For they have been humbled, having slipped from the glory that is in Christ and been cast down into every kind of outrage. So Isaac's bride comes not from Canaan but from Mesopotamia. For, as I said, the Church spiritually joined to Christ the Savior comes not from the Jews but from the Gentiles. Yet this happened by the Father's counsel, through the mediation of servants who were most faithful and trusty. By these we are to understand the disciples, who became stewards and managers of the mysteries of Christ our God, and held, as it were, everything in his house in their hands. They left Judea, just as Abraham's servant left the land of Canaan, and went down into the land of the idolaters. They had loaded up, in a manner of speaking, the good things from God the Father; their minds were full of the wisdom from above, and they were filled with the gifts of the Spirit. Notice too that Abraham's servant is nameless, so that the figure of this ministry may apply to every faithful and approved disciple. He lodged by the well of water toward evening, besought God in prayer to be his helper, and chose to test the maiden by means of water. The inspired disciples likewise, as I just said, came to the lands of the Gentiles toward evening, that is, in the last times of the age, and tested the spiritual virgin by the waters. For the Church is exceedingly well suited, and strong enough, to draw the life-giving word "from the springs of salvation," as it is written. Nor, as far as aptness of mind and understanding is concerned, is she incapable of supplying others too with what leads to life. For Rebecca gave drink both to the servant himself and to the camels. The servant may here be understood as a figure of those from Israel. For they are people who already had the law as their tutor and possessed the mystery of Christ, though still as in shadows; yet they were not entirely uninitiated. Those from the Gentiles, differing in no way from irrational beasts, might fittingly be likened to the camels, for under the law that animal is unclean. Such, surely, are those who do not yet know him who is God by nature and in truth. The Church, then, is most able to water with sacred and divine streams both those from the Jews who come to choose love for Christ and those called from the Gentiles. When the disciples saw that the maiden was such, they at once adorned her with bracelets and added the ornament for her ears. That is, they made her splendid and most distinguished with the glories of ready obedience, for an adorned hearing would signify obedience. They also made her conspicuous, so to speak, for her works, that is, for the achievements of her hands. This, I think, is what is meant by putting the bracelets on her very hands. Abraham's servant told the people of Haran about his master's wealth, and that he had a single, beloved heir. And the inspired disciples initiated the Gentiles, proclaiming the wealth of God the Father: the hope, the life, the sanctification. They announced plainly that Christ is the one and only Son by nature and in truth, who has also been appointed heir of all things. The maiden was asked whether she would willingly go with the servant, and she consented at once. For the Church from the Gentiles is exceedingly ready, all but burning with love for Christ. The inspired David will bear witness to this, saying of the flock from the Gentiles: "Your ear has attended to the readiness of their heart." And when Isaac was finally united to Rebecca, "he was comforted," it says, "concerning his mother." From this too we may understand that Christ grieved over the synagogue of the Jews, which had all but died through unbelief, and from which he himself was born according to the flesh. But when he became the bridegroom of the Church from the Gentiles, he in some way ceased from his sorrow over her. For it has been said somewhere to the Church through the voice of the prophets: "And it shall be that as a bridegroom rejoices over a bride, so the Lord will rejoice over you." Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

"These are the generations of Isaac son of Abraham: Abraham fathered Isaac. Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebecca as his wife, the daughter of Bethuel the Syrian of Mesopotamia and the sister of Laban the Syrian. Isaac prayed to the Lord concerning Rebecca his wife, because she was barren. God heard him, and Rebecca his wife conceived. The children leapt within her, and she said, 'If it is to be like this for me, why is this happening to me?' She went to inquire of the Lord. And the Lord said to her: 'Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly; one people shall surpass the other, and the elder shall serve the younger.' When the days for her to give birth were fulfilled, there were twins in her womb. The firstborn son came out red, hairy all over like a hide, and she called his name Esau. After this his brother came out, his hand grasping Esau's heel, and she called his name Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when Rebecca bore them. The young men grew up. Esau was a man skilled in hunting, a man of the field, while Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in a house. Isaac loved Esau, because his game was food for him, but Rebecca loved Jacob. Jacob boiled a stew. Esau came in from the plain, fainting with hunger. And Esau said to Jacob, 'Let me taste some of this red stew, for I am fainting.' That is why his name was called Edom. Jacob said to Esau, 'Sell me your birthright today.' Esau said, 'Look, I am going to die; what use is this birthright to me?' Jacob said to him, 'Swear to me today'; and he swore to him. So Esau sold his birthright to Jacob. Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew; he ate and drank, and got up and went away. Thus Esau despised his birthright." God, who cannot lie, promised that the inspired Abraham would be the father of many nations, and affirmed again and again that the multitude descended from him would prove beyond number. "For it will be," he says, "like the sand, beyond counting, and like the stars of heaven in multitude." But the fulfillment of so splendid a glory has come about not in Israel alone, but also among the flocks of the Gentiles. For they have been called in through faith, and such people belong rather "in Isaac," that is, to the promise. The most wise Paul will bear witness to this, writing: "The Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham: 'In you all the nations shall be blessed.' So those who are of faith are blessed with Abraham, the man of faith. For all who rely on the works of the law are under a curse, for it is written: 'Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all the things written in the book of the law, to do them.' Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for 'the righteous shall live by faith.' But the law is not of faith; rather, 'the one who does them shall live by them.'" It is settled, then, that the promises were brought to fulfillment, and certainly not through those who were being tutored under the law, but through those justified by faith. The commandment given through Moses was brought in as part of God's plan. It was not that the promise had been neglected. Rather, the law was to tutor people and bring them back little by little to the calling through faith. And by exposing the weakness of those who had entered before, it would at length show that the grace that comes through faith, and justification in Christ, were most needful and necessary for all. The inspired Paul again spoke thus: "Brothers, I speak in human terms: even a man's covenant, once ratified, no one annuls or adds to. Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say 'and to seeds,' as of many, but as of one: 'and to your seed,' who is Christ. What I mean is this: a covenant previously ratified by God is not annulled by the law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance comes from the law, it no longer comes from a promise; but God granted it to Abraham through a promise." He immediately adds the reason why the law was introduced first, saying: "Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made; and it was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator does not belong to one party alone, but God is one. Is the law then against the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would indeed have come from the law. But the Scripture has shut up all things under sin, so that the promise based on faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. Before faith came, we were held in custody under the law, shut up for the glory that was to be revealed. So the law became our tutor leading to Christ, so that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a tutor. For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus." No one, then, would doubt in the least that the law was an exposure of the weakness of those under its tutelage, and rather a means of pointing out failings and sin. For, he says, "where there is no law, there is no transgression either." And again: "I would not have known sin except through the law." And: "When the commandment came," he says, "sin came to life, and I died." And again: "Until the law sin was in the world, but sin is not counted where there is no law." "For the law brings about wrath." The law therefore served as a tutor leading to Christ. It convicted those who transgressed, and by experience itself taught those on earth that man, sick with a proneness to sin, cannot possibly escape the indictment of the law, but stands in absolute need of the salvation that comes through Christ, who justifies by faith and mercy.

It is clear, then, that the plan of God's dealings with us made the commandment given through Moses most necessary, as a kind of advance showing of the grace that came running directly afterward in Christ. That grace brought into view the seed announced beforehand by God's promise, that is, those who are in Christ through faith. For in this way the inspired Abraham became the father of countless multitudes. Observe, then, observe the shape of this plan, elegantly modeled once again, as in a figure, in the pair of brothers born of Isaac, namely Esau and Jacob. God had said to the inspired Abraham, "In Isaac shall your seed be called." And Paul, learned in the law, interprets the oracle, saying: "Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say 'and to seeds,' as of many, but as of one: 'and to your seed,' which is Christ." So the promises were fulfilled in Christ, and Isaac has been set, in a way, as his image and figure. This name means "joy and exultation." The inspired David too called Christ "exultation," speaking as if in the person of those who thirsted for the salvation that comes through him: "My exultation, deliver me from those who surround me." For in Christ we have swum safely through the assaults of murderers, in him we have trodden on scorpions and snakes, and we who have believed have set our feet on asp and basilisk. That Christ is called "exultation" in the divine Scriptures, a prophetic word will also convince us. It runs thus: "And the Lord will make righteousness and exultation spring up before all the nations." For Emmanuel became righteousness and exultation not only for those from Israel, but also for the nations and peoples throughout the whole world. We have been justified in him and have thrown off the disgrace of the ancient curse. We have changed our clothing, as it were, for gladness and joy, set free from death and sin. And what good thing from above and from God have we not been enriched with? Therefore we have been taught to give glory, saying: "Let my soul exult in the Lord, for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a tunic of gladness." And what this tunic of gladness is, the most holy Paul will make clear, saying: "For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ." And again: "Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh to gratify its desires." Isaac, then, as "exultation," has been taken, most usefully for the contemplations before us, as a figure of Christ. Rebecca became his wife. Her name might be interpreted as "great and abundant endurance." And we shall take her person, understanding it rightly, as that of the Church, whose good repute lies in endurance. Indeed, for her children, the children of salvation in faith and in the Spirit, I mean, endurance has proved to be the way.

For sacred words have addressed them, at one time: "By your endurance you will gain your souls"; at another: "For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive the promise." See then how Rebecca came to labor late and with difficulty (for she was barren), yet nonetheless, through God's generosity and Isaac's love, gave birth to Esau the firstborn and to Jacob, who came immediately after him. Through these the two peoples might very well be portrayed for us once again: Israel, and the people from the Gentiles. Israel is the firstborn, for it was called first, through the law; second and after it comes the people that is in faith through Christ. One may see the difference between the two peoples in mind and manners, I think, both from the very names the two bore and from the appearance, or build, of their bodies. Esau is interpreted as "oak," that is, harsh and unbending. And God said somewhere to Israel: "I know that you are stubborn; your neck is a sinew of iron, and your forehead is bronze." Jacob means "heel-catcher," that is, one who is skilful, or who knows how to win. For one catches by the heel whomever one overcomes. And it is certainly not the people under the law that wins, but the people that is in Christ through faith, which has escaped the charges arising from sin and has blunted the very power of death. Esau was red all over (for it is written thus: "and hairy like a hide"), but Jacob was a smooth man. The redness, then, is a riddle signifying anger and wrath, since those in a rage do indeed always turn somewhat red in complexion. And who could doubt that shagginess and hairiness are beastlike? Anyone, I think, would see that Israel had such ways: governed by anger rather than by proper reason, and strongly inclined toward rashness and savagery. That is why they killed the holy prophets, and in the last times committed impiety against Emmanuel himself. Smoothness, on the other hand, is a clear sign of a form befitting a human being. And the new people, the people of faith, is very gentle and much inclined toward mildness. For the comeliness of the mouth [?] will serve as a clear sign of the spiritual and inward beauty, just as in the case of Esau we have taken hairiness and redness as a sign of wildness. Yet the two had one mother, Rebecca. And our Lord Jesus Christ presented the Church to himself as a pure virgin, serving, as it were, for the spiritual rebirth of the two peoples. For as far as the purpose of his coming was concerned, he created them into one new man, making peace and reconciling both in one Spirit, as it is written. But Israel, though firstborn in time, was unruly and out of harmony with the new people. The babies' leaping in the very womb also signifies something of this, I think, hinting at the enmity that was to come. That the new people would be better, and of greater glory than Israel the firstborn, he who knows all things signified at once, saying: "And one people shall surpass the other, and the elder shall serve the younger." For the mystery concerning both was proclaimed beforehand through the voice of the saints as well, and it was foretold to us in many ways that Israel would come after the Gentiles. But God showed the matter even in the birth itself: Esau fell from the womb first, and Jacob followed, showing by his grasp on the heel that he would catch his brother by the heel and overcome him.

Let this much be said for now, since the discussion has taken its starting points from the appearance of their bodies and from the birth itself. But let us go by way of other considerations no less, and say, as best we can, what concerns the two of them. Their very manner of life will reveal the disposition of each. The young men were of the same age, but not of the same mind, nor alike in their aims. Esau loved to spend his time in the fields and in hunting; the other was a man of the town, that is, approachable and sociable, "a plain man, dwelling in a house." The one could not restrain his fleshly desires: he threw away, as it were, the finest of his own privileges for the very cheapest things, and took in exchange things of necessity, cold and cheap. The other was an insatiable lover of the best things, and sought out on every side whatever might make him illustrious. For he bought the birthright when Esau tossed it aside, having carelessly put a full belly ahead of his own dignities. This is why his name was called Edom, that is, "earthy." For it is a clear proof of a truly earthy and utterly lowly mind to disregard the glory that belonged to him, to count the privileges of knowledge as nothing at all, and instead to choose passing pleasure as better and more excellent, crowning the delight of the moment with the higher vote, even if it brings great loss. That is why the divine Paul rightly called one who chose to live so shamefully "immoral and profane." He set Esau before us as a kind of type of those who have slid into such baseness, and made his unbridled appetite for desires (fleshly, that is, and rather earthy) the charge in his indictment, saying: "See that no one is immoral or profane like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal." So then, let us set the darkness of the Jewish way of life and the sincerity and freedom of the multitude from the Gentiles carefully alongside the characters of the young men, and say what is fitting. Israel was rustic and had a rather earthy mind, arrogant and warlike, and greatly excited toward bloodshed, like the rustic, beast-slaying Esau. And so the prophetic word accused them: "They set snares to destroy men." And Christ himself cursed them, saying: "Without cause they hid for me the ruin of their snare; in vain they reproached my soul. Let a snare come upon them that they do not know, and let the hunt that they hid catch them." For they sent some of the Pharisees with those called Herodians (these were tax collectors) to test him, saying: "Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?" So Israel too is a hunter. But the new people, the people of faith, is like the divine Jacob: a townsman and fond of home, gentle and settled, simple and without guile, "dwelling in a house," as it is written. It is true to say that the most gentle multitude of those justified by faith enrolled themselves in the Church as in a splendid and well-governed city, and made the way of life and the life in Christ a house firmly founded and unshaken by those who tempt. Their mind is simple and free of all perversity, and they utterly detest seeming to be feigned in mind or manners. It was about them, I think, that the divine David said somewhere: "The Lord makes those of one way dwell in a house." For the one who is simple in Christ is "of one way," and he is made to dwell in a house. Yet one of the holy prophets cries out to Israel: "You have wearied yourself with your many ways." So those in Christ lodge in a way of life and conduct in holiness and sanctification as in a house. They would be found weaving this as a kind of crown about their heads, and indeed counting it a kind of good fortune. That is why they say at one time: "I was glad when they said to me, Let us go into the house of the Lord"; and at another: "One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek." And what is the request? What is this one favor? "That I may dwell in the house of the Lord," he says, "all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to visit his holy temple." Do you hear how he says that dwelling in the house of God and spending one's time in the divine courts is counted as a splendid and exceptional grace? Yet this dwelling is not bodily; it should rather be understood as steadfastness of mind and of virtuous life. But "Isaac loved Esau," it says, "because his game was food for him." For Israel the firstborn was counted worthy of love from above, because he brought to God, as a kind of food, the accomplishment of the way of life under the law and the labors it required. There were saints in Israel too, lovers of God and keepers of the law. And so the prophet Isaiah lamented over Jerusalem as one who had become a harlot, yet said that righteousness at times "lodged in her," that is, rested and stayed there, because many arose in her who had attained the glories of the way of life under the law. So Israel, being firstborn, was in glory with God, but he did not keep to the end the honor allotted to his seniority. He gave up the birthright, as it were, to the new people that came after, that is, to those from the Gentiles, having leaned far too much toward the things of the flesh and of the world. And so, as we read in the gospel parables, the king made a wedding feast for his son. Then those sent to summon the guests came, announcing to them the message from God, that is: "Behold, I have prepared my dinner; my oxen and fatted animals are slaughtered, and everything is ready; come to the wedding." "But they would not come," it says. Instead, each offered whatever excuse he saw fit. One said: "I have married a wife; please have me excused." Another: "I have bought a field, and I cannot come." You see, then, how they imitated Esau. They preferred the enjoyment of passing and fleshly things to glory with God, and all but laid the birthright before others for the taking. For at once those from the Gentiles who believed were invited in their place, and they won the glory owed to Israel, and indeed the blessing too, because they were ready to obey and were very prompt and alert to fulfill what pleases God. The divine David can be our witness to this as well, when he says of them: "You have heard the desire of the poor, O Lord; your ear has attended to the readiness of their heart." For the people of faith is somehow always readier to obey, even though those from Israel had long been enriched with instruction in the law. And even if the multitude of the Gentiles suffered from a poverty of divine teachings, it proved more ready in faith and lent a keen ear, as it were, to the oracles given through Christ, as he testifies with his own voice. For he spoke thus through the lyre of the Psalmist: "A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me." But of Israel, as one already fallen into estrangement, no longer counted worthy to walk upright but lamed, as it were, in the leg of the mind, he says: "Foreign sons lied to me; foreign sons grew old and limped from their paths." The straight and unerring paths that lead to Christ are the instruction given through the law and the foretelling of the holy prophets. But when they reached the goal of the law and the prophets, that is, Christ, they limped out of lack of understanding. They raged against him, not from a sound mind, and dared to bring death upon the Author of life. That the new people of faith snatched the blessing owed to Israel, since its disposition was more ready to yield to the divine commands, we may also understand from what follows. For it is written thus: "And it came to pass, after Isaac had grown old and his eyes had grown too dim to see, that he called Esau, his elder son, and said to him, 'My son.' And he said, 'Here I am.' And he said, 'Behold, I have grown old, and I do not know the day of my death. Now then, take your gear, your quiver and your bow, and go out to the field and hunt game for me, and make me savory food such as I love, and bring it to me that I may eat, so that my soul may bless you before I die.'" This, then, is what the father said to Esau. And he at once left home to carry out the labors of the hunt, and made ready with youthful vigor. And what happened next? Rebecca persuades Jacob to get ahead of Esau and to snatch the blessing. At first he was afraid to do it; but as his mother urged him on, he brought in two kids from the fields, fine and tender, and set about cooking. Then he put the skins on his shoulders and covered the bare parts of his neck, and so skillfully imitated Esau's shagginess and his very hairy body, in order to fool his father's hands if he happened to touch him. Then, taking the dish in his hands, he went in to his father and said: "Father." And he said: "Here I am. Who are you, my son?" And Jacob said to his father: "I am Esau, your firstborn; I have done as you told me. Get up, sit and eat of my game, so that your soul may bless me." And when the old man had eaten what was brought, he said to the youth: "Come near and kiss me, my son." And he came near and kissed him; and he smelled the smell of his garments, and blessed him, and said to him: "Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field that the Lord has blessed. May the Lord give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, abundance of grain and wine. Let nations serve you, and rulers bow down to you; be lord over your brother, and the sons of your father shall bow down to you. Cursed be whoever curses you, and blessed be whoever blesses you." So Jacob was the first to win his father's blessing; then Esau came second, afterward, from the fields with the game he had caught. But when he brought it to his father, he was now superfluous, and he was told what had happened. For at once he heard: "Your brother came with deceit and took your blessing." And when he said, not without tears, "Have you only one blessing, father? Bless me too," Isaac said again: "Behold, your dwelling shall be of the fatness of the earth, and of the dew of heaven from above; by your sword you shall live, and you shall serve your brother. But it shall be, when you throw off and loosen his yoke from your neck." Having gathered up the breadth of the story in very few words, we have set it out clearly for those who will read it. But I think we must now fit the spiritual meanings to the events that happened in the realm of the senses.

We say, then, that before the others (I mean those called in faith and in Christ) the Master and Father of all commanded Israel to hasten to bring him, as a kind of splendid gift, as fruits of goodness and as it were the finds of good labors, the way of life and conduct pleasing to him. This was sketched out for the ancients beforehand through the life under the law. It was all but hidden in the types, lurking as in a thicket behind the superfluity of the letter, yet not beyond capture for those who are willing to hunt eagerly by means of a precise and spiritual contemplation. This, I think, is what Isaac's desire for Esau's game means. Israel, as I said, was commanded, and indeed promised to carry it out. For when the assembly was gathered at Horeb and God had come down on Mount Sinai in the form of fire, he said: "All that the Lord God says we will do, and we will obey." But his deeds exposed him as very negligent, though he was quick to promise. For this reason the supplanter Jacob, that is, the new people, the people of faith, steps in between and so gets ahead. For he brought to God what was sought: while the firstborn people held back and delayed, he was the first to offer the fruit of faith, which the divine nature counts as food. And so the Savior foretold the conversion of the Samaritans to the holy apostles, saying: "I have food to eat that you do not know." And explaining what he had said, he says: "My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work." Their readiness to promise was of no use to those from Israel, since the matter never reached completion for them; but their hesitation about believing did the Gentiles no harm at all, for they recognized the Redeemer and from then on honored him by readily obeying in every good thing. Christ taught us this through a parable. For he spoke thus: "A man had two children. He came to the first and said, 'Child, go and work today in my vineyard.' He answered, 'I will not'; but afterward he changed his mind and went. And he came to the other and said the same. He answered, 'I go, sir,' and did not go. Which of the two did the will of the father?" Clearly the one who went into the vineyard, even if for a short while sluggishness crept in and persuaded him to shrink from what was asked of him. See, then, in these things: Esau goes most readily to the hunt and promises to do it, but Jacob gets ahead, and although at first he refused to do it, he is blessed by his father. So too the new people snatches the blessing, wearing as it were a counterfeit form of the Jewish way of life, just as Jacob cleverly imitated Esau's hairiness with the kids' skins. But he heard his father cry out at once: "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau." How, then, might we apply to the peoples of faith this being in the form and likeness of the Jewish way of life, while having a voice different from theirs? We say this: in the divine Scriptures the hand is always a sign of work and achievements, that is, of practical activity. So as far as sameness of activity and richness of achievement are concerned, those in Christ also fulfill the law. They offer worship in the mind and in the spirit, and present themselves to God the Father as a fragrant odor. And so Christ, plainly laying down gospel laws for us, says: "Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets. I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it. For truly I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the law until all things take place." You understand, then: those in Christ fulfill the law by receiving circumcision in the spirit instead of in the flesh, by entering into Christ's rest and keeping sabbath in Christ, and by showing forth the Jew who is one in secret and inwardly. This, I think, is having the hands of Esau but a voice different from his. For we do not use the unbridled tongues of the Jews, nor are we in the habit of denying and blaspheming the Master who bought us. Rather, we glorify the Son together with God the Father, and call him Lord, Savior and Redeemer.

I think it worthwhile also to examine the force of the blessing given to each of them, and to say what comes to mind. This will be of benefit to those who read it. Blessed Isaac, then, said of Jacob: "Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field that the Lord has blessed. May the Lord give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, abundance of grain and wine. Let nations serve you, and rulers bow down to you; be lord over your brother, and the sons of your father shall bow down to you. Cursed be whoever curses you, and blessed be whoever blesses you." Here the account of the story is somehow mixed, and through two persons it arrives at one truth, attested by the events themselves. These things are not fulfilled entirely in Jacob, but also in Christ and in those justified by faith, who have become children according to the promise in Isaac. The sense of the prophecy will therefore fit both the new people and Christ himself, who is its beginning and leader. He has been reckoned as a second Adam, and has sprung up as a kind of second root of humanity. For what is in Christ is a new creation, and we have been renewed in him for sanctification, incorruption and life. The words of the blessing signify, I think, the spiritual fragrance that is in Christ, like that of a field or a meadow in full flower giving off the lovely and pleasant scent of spring blossoms. For so Christ named himself to us in the Song of Songs, saying: "I am a flower of the plain, a lily of the valleys." He was a lily and a rose springing up from the earth because of his humanity. Yet he knew no sin; rather, he gave off to all throughout the inhabited world the most divinely fitting fragrance of his righteous deeds. So he likens Christ to a field blessed by God, and very fittingly, since he is the fragrance of the knowledge of God the Father. For again the divine Paul spoke thus: "But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ, and through us makes manifest the fragrance of the knowledge of him in every place." Our Lord Jesus Christ was made manifest through the holy apostles as the fragrance of the knowledge of God the Father. For if anyone has known the Son, he has surely known the Father too, because of the identity of their nature, which is equal and without difference in every respect. Such things, then, will fit Christ; but this would also rightly suit the new people: "May the Lord give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, abundance of grain and wine." For the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth, that is, the Word from God the Father, has been given to us, by participation, clearly, through the Spirit, and through him we have become partakers of the divine nature. And we have received abundance of grain and wine, that is, of strength and also of gladness, if the word is true that says: "Bread strengthens the heart of man, and wine gladdens it." So bread is a sign of strength, the strength of the mind and the spirit, and wine of the other, gladness. These have been given through him to those in Christ. How, or in what way? We have become firm in godliness and in a sense immovable, knowing how to think rightly and founded so as not to be shaken. For we have received authority to tread upon snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. This, I think, is the abundance of grain. But we have received wine as well. For we rejoice in hope and have been made glad, as it is written. For we await the dwelling places above, life in incorruption, the age-long life, reigning together with Christ himself.
