Let these things be said about us too, for the text rightly calls us to it. Then the force of the blessing passes over again to Emmanuel himself. For it says: "Let nations serve you, and rulers bow down to you; be lord over your brother." Emmanuel was called firstborn when he became like us, firstborn among many brothers. But that is no reason for him to slip from being God and Lord of all. For we worship him as Master, and as God he is lord over those called into brotherhood by grace. For "who among the clouds," it says, "shall be equal to the Lord? And who among the sons of God shall be likened to him?" So Emmanuel, as God, is lord over those brought into brotherhood, and to him every knee shall bow, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. And whoever curses him is cursed, and whoever blesses him is blessed. The meaning is plain. For those who blaspheme him are accursed and hateful to God; but those who bless him, that is, who proclaim his divine glory, are filled with the gifts from above and from God.

This, then, is Jacob's blessing, and its meaning applies to Emmanuel himself and to those who have been justified by faith. Let us look also at the other blessing, the one given to the firstborn, that is, clearly, to Israel, of whom Esau was a type. "See," it says, "your dwelling shall be from the fatness of the earth and from the dew of heaven above; you shall live by your sword, and you shall serve your brother. But it shall be that when you break and loosen his yoke from your neck…" For a blessing was given to Israel: the law through Moses. The law was the word of Christ, ministered through angels. That it was he who spoke to those of old, the most wise Paul will confirm when he writes: "In many and various ways God spoke of old to the fathers by the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son." And the Savior himself showed that the law was his own words, when he said: "Truly I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota, not one stroke of a letter, will pass from the law until all is accomplished. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." If, then, it is true that the law given through angels was also the word of Christ, it came to Israel by way of a blessing, and we are to understand that Christ is the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth. For just as the multitude of angels lives in abundance, watered by the spiritual dews from above, so too the earth, growing fat, delights in the spiritual rains and bears spiritual fruit. But we who are in Christ through faith have been enriched with bread and wine. Israel has no share in these, for this was not added to the blessings of Esau. And in another sense too the wretched Jews have no share in the mystical blessing, since this was not given to the worship under the law, but was kept rather for the peoples who are in Christ and in faith. We, moreover, live in peace through Christ, but Israel lives amid wars; and we have inherited [?] the land of promise in a perceptible way, a land that bears the type of the spiritual land above, which the Savior himself mentioned when he said: "Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth." We are counted among the children through the spirit of freedom, and we draw near to Christ as to one like us and as to a brother, rendering him a good and willing submission. Israel, on the other hand, has been put under the yoke and weighed down by the laws of Moses, suffering death as the penalty for transgressions. For Esau was told, "And you shall serve your brother," that is, you will be made subject, and not willingly, to one who shares your nature. Moses was a human being like us, with nothing beyond the measure of humanity, so to speak. Indeed, the Lord of all called Israel the people of Moses, when they had made the calf in the wilderness. God then said to Moses: "Go, get down from here quickly, for your people, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, have acted lawlessly." And the inspired Paul likewise ascribed the written law to the blessed Moses, for he said: "Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses." That Israel would throw off the yoke laid on it through the all-wise Moses, when Christ called it to the grace that comes through faith, he foretold in the words: "But it shall be that when you break and loosen his yoke from your neck…" For those from Israel who believed loosened from their necks the yoke of the law, which was very hard to bear, since through faith in Christ they have been called to the dignity of freedom. Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

It is true that all who wish to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted. For the sons of lawlessness leap on them like wild beasts. They treat the brilliance of those who are regularly held in honour as a kind of indictment and denunciation of their own perversity. Somehow the worse is always exposed when it is set beside the better, and whatever carries the winning vote all but files a charge of ugliness against those who are defeated. What follows from this? The arrows of envy, and the fire of jealousy that smoulders within the defeated, become the beginning of madness and the occasion of impiety against those who have chosen to live in the best way. Even if these people should happen to fall into struggles and hardships, they could never be wholly captured by those who make war on them. For he who presides over the saints will by no means overlook those who are in danger for his sake. Rather, he will rescue them, and very easily, and make them more illustrious, setting their sweat before them as a training in endurance. The inspired Paul also supports this argument, for he wrote: "God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide the way out, so that you may be able to endure it." And those who have known struggles, and who bore the hardships of persecution in no ignoble way, cry out themselves in the book of Psalms: "For you have tested us, O God; you have tried us by fire as silver is tried by fire. You brought us into the snare; you laid afflictions on our back; you set men over our heads. We went through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment." You hear how they have resolved not to chafe in the least at the things by which they are tested. Instead they rejoice, because they have been shown to be better, they have been known by experience itself for what they are, and through suffering they have been attested in their utmost love of God. For they said that they had gone through fire. Just as the choicest kinds of incense, I think, display the fragrance within them only when they come into contact with fire, so a holy soul, fired in a sense by being tested and by toiling, displays more clearly the manifold virtue within it. Moreover, the inspired David somewhere sings of every saint, saying: "The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him and will deliver them." And again the giver of help himself says expressly: "Because he has hoped in me, I will deliver him. He will cry to me, and I will hear him; I am with him in affliction; I will rescue him and glorify him; I will fill him with length of days and show him my salvation." What, then, is the salvation of God the Father? It is God the Word who is from him, who for our sake and in the divine economy became as we are, in the form of a servant. This is what the Father called him when he said through Isaiah: "And the nations will see my righteousness, and kings my glory. And my salvation will burn like a torch." For the Son has become for us righteousness and glory from God the Father, and salvation as well. In him we have been justified and brought up into the glory of adoption. And that we have also been saved, escaping the bonds of death and returning to incorruption, how or on what ground could anyone still doubt? For the Son appeared to us like a torch in the night and in darkness, and he kindles the divine light in the souls of those who believe. That is why he said: "I am the light of the world." So, in the words of the Saviour himself, blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake. They will have the inheritance in heaven, and as their defender they will have the very God and Saviour of all. They will also see the mystery of Christ itself, and one could learn it no less from the story of blessed Jacob. I think it is fitting to set out what is written about him, so that those who read may understand more exactly. It runs as follows: "And Esau bore a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him. And Esau said to himself, 'Let the days of mourning for my father draw near, so that I may kill my brother Jacob.' And the words of Esau, her elder son, were reported to Rebecca. She sent and called Jacob, her younger son, and said to him, 'Look, your brother Esau is threatening to kill you. Now therefore, my child, listen to my voice: get up and flee to Mesopotamia, to my brother Laban in Haran. Stay with him for some days, until your brother's fury and anger turn away and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send and bring you back from there. Why should I be bereaved of you both in one day?'" Then she contrived a plausible reason for her son's departure. She went to Isaac and said: "I am weary of my life because of the daughters of the sons of Heth. If Jacob takes a wife from the daughters of this land, what is life to me?" The woman skilfully persuaded the old man to allow his son to go away, so that blessed Jacob would not leave against his father's will and become the cause of grief and anger. For it says: "Isaac called Jacob and blessed him and charged him, saying: 'You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan. Get up, flee to Mesopotamia, to the house of Bethuel, your mother's father, and take a wife for yourself from there, from the daughters of Laban, your mother's brother. May my God bless you and increase you and multiply you, and you shall become assemblies of nations. May he give you the blessing of Abraham your father, to you and to your offspring after you, so that you may inherit the land of your sojourning, which God gave to Abraham.'"

As far as the letter and the events of the narrative are concerned, it would be fitting to hold both Rebecca herself and blessed Jacob in no small admiration. She brought her request, I mean the one about her son, to her husband as to her superior. He at once made the law of nature the judge of what was fitting, and ordered his son to decline a marriage his mother did not want. In a way he was coaxing the son he had fathered and piously raised to walk in the footsteps of his father's virtue. Everywhere we shall find the inspired Jacob yielding to the wishes of his parents, and making this a clear and indisputable sign of his piety toward God. As for spiritual contemplation, I think we must once again take the innermost path, and I believe something needs to be recalled first. In this way the meaning will become quite clear with little effort. Before the pains of childbirth, while Rebecca was still carrying the pair who were born of her, she suffered a distress that was very hard to bear. She was already in the very terrors of death, for the unborn children were leaping violently. Then, not wanting the matter to stay hidden from her, she asked God, saying: "If it is going to be like this for me, why is this happening to me?" And what did God say to this? "Two nations and two peoples will be separated from your womb, and one people will surpass the other," he says, "and the elder will serve the younger." Let us therefore take Esau and Jacob as a type of the two peoples: the one from Israel, and the one that comes through faith. "Esau bore a grudge against Jacob," it says, because he had been deprived of the rights of the elder, having sold his birthright and handed his own honour to another. Moreover, because he came second in bringing the game from the hunt, he missed the blessing. For this reason he was already full of savage thoughts and was plotting murder, the partner and brother of envy. In the same way the firstborn Israel bore a grudge and raged terribly against those who came after it in faith, that is, against the new people. For the new people had come to stand in the first rank before God, and was counted as the firstborn, and was full of the blessing from above, having been enriched with the grace that is in Christ through the Spirit. So Israel attacked those who are in Christ through faith. As far as its own intention and the power of its efforts went, it became a bitter murderer, inflicting persecutions and wounding them with the arrows of murder and envy. But Rebecca persuaded Jacob to leave home and keep away from his brother, and to go to Laban, an idolater. And Jacob's father, the inspired Isaac, likewise urged him to refuse a marriage from Canaan and instead to seek a wife from the daughters of Laban. For when the new people was in danger and being persecuted, the Church, of which Rebecca would be a type, wisely advised it to keep away from the rage of the murderous. Rebecca's bridegroom himself, that is, Christ, consents as it were that they should reject spiritual kinship with those who were inflamed with unholy rage and savagely bent on murder. For marriage is a sign of kinship. Instead they should choose the women of Laban's house, that is, those from the nations. We shall find that the holy apostles, who became the firstfruits of those in faith and of the new peoples, were eager to carry out what had been commanded to Jacob. They separated themselves from the herd of the Jews, since it was thirsting for their blood. Moving from land to land and from city to city, they were sensibly eager to escape the rage of their persecutors. For they remembered Christ's command: "When they persecute you in this city, flee to the next." And to those of Israel's blood who had chosen disobedience and were insulting them without restraint, they said: "It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, see, we are turning to the Gentiles. For this is what the Lord has commanded us." You hear how the bridegroom of the Church, that is, Christ, commanded his own to go out to the multitude of the Greeks, to beget children from among them, and so to become fathers of peoples, as it were. That is why the most wise Paul writes to those of the Gentiles who believed through him: "For though you have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel." The inspired Isaac could show quite easily that God will be with the peoples of faith and bless them richly. As Jacob left his father's hearth, Isaac crowned him with the blessings from above, saying: "May my God bless you and increase you and multiply you, and you shall become assemblies of nations. And may he give you the blessing of Abraham your father." For those in Christ have been blessed and greatly increased. They have become a multitude and assemblies of nations, and they have been made fellow heirs with the holy fathers. In the words of the Saviour himself, they will recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. And we have been blessed again by him, for he said on our behalf: "Holy Father, keep them in your truth." But if Rebecca is also understood as the mother of Esau, this does no damage at all to the interpretation. We took Esau as a type of those from Israel, and we gave Rebecca the role of the Church. But those from Israel have also become sons of the Church through faith in Christ. They are no longer counted as that former, ancient people. Rather, they have been transformed into a new people, mingled together with those from the nations. For if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. And as the Scriptures say, Christ created the two peoples into one new man, making peace, and reconciling both to the Father in one Spirit. For he has broken down the dividing wall of partition and abolished the law of commandments expressed in ordinances.

So Jacob, provided for the road with his father's blessings, set out on foot toward the goal of his journey. What happened along the way we shall learn from the sacred Scriptures themselves. It runs as follows: "And Jacob went out from the Well of the Oath and set off for Haran. He came to a certain place and slept there, because the sun had set. He took one of the stones of the place, put it under his head, lay down in that place, and dreamed. And behold, a ladder was set up on the earth, and its top reached to heaven, and the angels of God were ascending and descending on it. And the Lord stood firmly above it and said: 'I am the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac; do not be afraid. The land on which you are sleeping I will give to you and to your offspring. Your offspring shall be like the sand of the sea, and it shall spread out to the west and the south and the north and the east. In you and in your offspring all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed. And behold, I am with you, guarding you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done everything I have promised you.' Then Jacob awoke from his sleep and said, 'The Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.' He was afraid and said, 'How awesome this place is! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.' Jacob rose early in the morning, took the stone he had put under his head, and set it up as a pillar. He poured oil on top of it and called the name of that place House of God." Now we say that the Well of the Oath is the name of a city. For it is written about it as follows: "And on that day Isaac's servants came and told him about the well they had dug, and said, 'We did not find water.' And he called it Oath. That is why the name of the city is Well of the Oath to this day." And if anyone wants to know why it is called the Well of the Oath, our answer is this: there the leaders of the Gerarites, Abimelech and those with him, swore an oath of peace with Isaac. So the inspired Jacob left his father's hearth and the city itself, and was cut off from his kin. For this reason he began to be terribly distressed. He was probably thinking that he would be a wanderer and a stranger and would live in a foreign land. Perhaps he would also be subject to others and would have to bear the unaccustomed yoke of slavery. For even the very nobly born must yield to those in power. But God, who knows hearts and minds, at once came to his aid and did not allow the righteous man's soul to be choked by such bitter forebodings. He showed him that a multitude of angels, darting up and down, easily keeps safe those who are devoted to God. This, I think, and nothing else, was what he was being taught through the dream. He saw with his senses the ladder reaching upward, and it was a sign of descent and ascent, even if it was drawn, as it were, in coarse figures. And he heard the voice of the very one who commands the angels, saying that he himself would bring to fulfilment the blessing Jacob had been given by his father. "For your offspring," he says, "will spread out to east and west, north and south." He also told him that Jacob would have him as his defender and preserver everywhere. When he woke, the inspired Jacob was utterly amazed and said: "The Lord is in this place, and I did not know it." But what does he mean by this? Surely it is worth looking into. We shall find that the ancients had very small notions of God. They thought that the divine abandoned all the rest of the earth and was confined, as it were, to the one land to which he had called them when they left home and departed from the country of the Chaldeans. For the worshippers of idols, sick with the error of many gods, assigned to each of the demons a particular territory of its own, as it were, and all but set up the gods worshipped city by city as tyrants. So they supposed that not all of them had power everywhere, or ought to be honoured everywhere. Accordingly the blessed patriarchs too, who had only just been freed from the customs of idolatry and the error of many gods and had recently been persuaded to worship the one who is God by nature and in truth, did not think that he was present with them and helped them in every land and every place, for their understanding was still very small. So blessed Jacob was taught, and from his journey he gained as fruit what was lacking in his faith. He learned that the divine is in every place and every land. It dwells in heaven, yet it encompasses the whole earth and has filled the inhabited world. All things are subject to it, including the spirits in heaven, which are commanded to run up and down and have him as their head and overseer. That is why he marvelled, saying: "The Lord is in this place, and I did not know it." And supposing that the stone had been the cause of the dream itself, he honoured it with what he had at hand, anointing it richly with oil. He called the place House of God and gate of heaven, and he set up the stone as a pillar.

Let this, then, stand once more as our more literal account. It was necessary to smooth out what seemed to be steep and difficult in the narrative. But now, turning the passage to spiritual contemplation, we say again that the new people of faith, understood as having its firstfruits in the holy apostles, hastened to escape and steadily to avoid the rage of the murderous, I mean the Jews. Moving, as it were, from city to city, it wooed the flocks from the nations, and greatly longed to gather them to itself through a spiritual and intelligible communion. In just the same way Jacob hastened to Laban's daughters while Esau was terrifying him and savagely attempting to kill him. And because the people of faith rested on Christ, who is the chosen stone, the precious cornerstone (for this, I think, is what sleeping on the stone means), we have learned that they will not be alone on earth. They will have the holy angels as helpers and supporters, running up and down. For Christ said somewhere: "Truly, truly, I say to you, from now on you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man." This, I think, is the ladder: the coming and going, up and down, of the holy spirits who are sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit the kingdom. And Christ stood firmly above the ladder, because the holy spirits reach up to him and have him as their overseer. He is not one of their kind, but their God and Lord. David too said somewhere to every man who chooses to dwell in the help of the Most High: "For he will command his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. They will bear you up in their hands, so that you do not strike your foot against a stone. You will tread on the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon." For we have trodden on serpents and scorpions and on all the power of the enemy, since Christ gives us the authority. So those in Christ are worthy of the vision of God, and worthy to be confidently assured that he will be with them, help them, keep them safe everywhere, and make them fruitful. "For behold," he says, "I am with you always, to the end of the age." And everyone can see that the blessed disciples became rich and became fathers of countless nations, I mean in faith in Christ and as by a spiritual birth. For Paul says plainly to those who believed through him: "Though you have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel." Their offspring, then, has become as numerous as the sands. It has spread out to the sunrise and the sunset, and to right and left, I mean south and north. The stone, too, was honoured as a type of Christ, set up as a pillar and soaked in oil. For Emmanuel has been anointed by God the Father with the oil of gladness above his companions. And he has been raised from the dead, though he went down willingly into death. This, I think, is the setting up of the stone as a pillar. And our Lord Jesus Christ is proclaimed through the holy apostles as anointed by the Father in the Holy Spirit and raised from the dead. Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

Who could doubt that we ought to long for the divine words, and to thirst above all to learn what is good, since this is the best of all things and has been crowned by God with the highest approval? That the matter is worth every word, and will bring us to the end we need, the Savior himself has assured us, saying: "The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls, who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it." So we must first seek out fine pearls, for in this way we shall find the one pearl of great value, that is, Christ. And who might the fine pearls be, which are well worth acquiring, and whose search brings the one pearl to light? I would say that in every way they are the saints, of whom it is said through the voice of the prophet: "Holy stones are rolled upon the earth." We must therefore examine very thoroughly what was said and done in the case of each of them, especially the more ancient ones. For in them we shall see the deep mystery of godliness, that is, Christ, still sketched in types, but wisely and skillfully drawn. Besides this, we shall also find the plan of salvation that is understood in him: it is shaded by certain obscurities, yet it is not shown in a way that is wholly unclear. The subject of our discourse now will be the inspired Jacob, and we shall tell how and in what way he lived. We shall also show the shape of the whole plan of salvation, I mean the plan of the gospel, as it appears in him. Like bees, we shall fly about the most flowery parts of the history and gather from each what is useful for making the discourse clear. But if not everything written about him is brought into the spiritual interpretation, let no one be annoyed. Let him bear in mind that some things belong, in a sense, simply to what happened in history, while others pass on into the innermost meanings and are shaped to express the power of the mystery.

So it is written further on: "And Jacob set out on his way and went to the land of the east, to Laban the son of Bethuel the Syrian, the brother of Rebecca, the mother of Jacob and Esau. And he looked, and behold, there was a well in the field, and three flocks of sheep were resting beside it, for they watered the flocks from that well. A great stone lay over the mouth of the well, and all the flocks would be gathered there, and they would roll the stone away from the mouth of the well and water the sheep, and then put the stone back in its place over the mouth of the well. Jacob said to them, 'Brothers, where are you from?' They said, 'We are from Harran.' He said to them, 'Do you know Laban the son of Nahor?' They said, 'We know him.' He said to them, 'Is he well?' They said, 'He is well. And behold, Rachel his daughter is coming with the sheep.' And Jacob said, 'It is still broad daylight; it is not yet time for the livestock to be gathered. Water the sheep, and go and pasture them.' But they said, 'We cannot, until all the shepherds are gathered and they roll the stone away from the mouth of the well; then we will water them.' While he was still speaking with them, Rachel the daughter of Laban came with her father's sheep, for she pastured her father's sheep. And when Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of Laban his mother's brother, he went up and rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well and watered the sheep of Laban his mother's brother. And Jacob kissed Rachel, and lifted up his voice and wept. He told Rachel that he was her father's kinsman and that he was Rebecca's son, and she ran and told her father all these things. When Laban heard the name of Jacob, his sister's son, he ran to meet him, embraced him, kissed him, and brought him into his house. And he recounted all these things to Laban, and Laban said to him, 'You are of my bones and of my flesh.'" This came after that extraordinary vision of God and revelation. For Jacob had seen a ladder reaching to heaven, with the Lord standing upon it and the angels running up and down, and he had heard clearly that God would be with him and would spread his seed into a countless multitude of peoples. After he set up the stone as a type of Christ, then indeed, then with confidence, his hope for what was to come firmly fixed on God, he pressed on toward the goal of his journey and arrived in the land that lies toward the dawn. At once he made himself known to a good many shepherds as one who was himself highly practised in shepherding. He showed that he was experienced in the work by saying: "It is still broad daylight. Now then, water the sheep, and go and pasture them." He also made himself known to Laban's daughter. As a kind of first fruits and offering of the nobility of character within him, he thought the flock she tended worth his care, and he watered the sheep. For, having been brought up in the best of manners, he very likely reflected that it was most unseemly for Rachel, a virgin of marriageable age, to wait for the shepherds to gather so that she could water her sheep once the stone had been moved, giving way to the others because of her weakness and the modesty that befits a virgin. Besides this, the law of family affection also called him, since he now ought to show himself useful to his own blood and close kin. So he watered Rachel's sheep, rolling the stone away from the well by himself. Here we must recall that the inspired Moses too, when he fled from the land of the Egyptians, came to the country of the Midianites. There he fell in with shepherds, found Jethro's daughters being wronged, and made himself known by the same kind of zeal. What is written about him runs as follows: "Moses withdrew from the presence of Pharaoh and settled in the land of Midian. And when he came into the land of Midian, he sat down by the well. Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, who pastured the sheep of their father Jethro. They came and drew water until they had filled the troughs, to water the sheep of their father Jethro. But the shepherds came and drove them away. Then Moses got up and rescued them, and watered their father's sheep. When they came to their father Jethro, he said to them, 'Why have you come back so quickly today?' They said, 'An Egyptian rescued us from the shepherds, and drew water for us, and watered the sheep.' He said to his daughters, 'And where is he? Why have you left the man like that? Call him, then, so that he may eat bread.' And Moses settled with the man." You see, then, how the ideas are in a sense sisters, and how closely related are the things they hint at. There is this difference: the inspired Moses drove off the greed of the other shepherds and drew water and watered Jethro's flocks, while Jacob rolled away the stone by himself, though a great many were accustomed to do this only with much sweat, and likewise watered Laban's flocks. And just as Moses lodged at the hearth of an idolater, so did the inspired Jacob, for Laban was still a worshipper and servant of idols. Since the discourse has given Jacob the role and figure of the peoples who are in the faith, come, let us speak of the innermost and hidden meanings, opening up the dense surface of the history.

The people that is being created, in the words of the Psalmist, would be, I think, none other than the new people, the people in Christ. That is, it is the people brought by faith into the glory of the firstborn, after the first people, Israel, was thrust aside and fell. For the one who was the head, that is, the preeminent, has become the tail, and the one foreknown is now spoken of as following in the wake of the calling of others. They have been put at the back, and they come behind the Gentiles. So the people in Christ by faith is indeed the supplanter, and is reckoned as standing in the place of the inspired Jacob. The first fruits of such a race might be understood to be the company of the holy apostles. They were of the blood and race of Israel, but since they were enriched with faith in Christ and had put on, like a crown, the grace that comes from the Holy Spirit, they gave offence to their own kin. For this reason they left behind those who thirsted for their blood and raged savagely against them. All but departing from their ancestral hearths and from the very land that bore them (I mean Jerusalem, or the country of the Jews), they set out for the land of the Gentiles. They had Christ as their helper and partner in every good thing whatever, and the angels running alongside them. They were supported by hopes from above and expected to become fathers of many nations, so that their seed would stretch to east and west, to north and south. That seed is those who are reborn in the Spirit through faith and justified in Christ. To them the apostles also called out, saying: "You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession, so that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people in Christ." And who could doubt that divine Scripture calls those who are appointed to teach the peoples their fathers? So the apostles withdrew from the country of the Jews, left behind the arrogant and insolent people, and turned to the Gentiles, according to the commands of our Savior. But they showed at once that they are spiritual shepherds, skilled in the training that is according to God, for they would not stay idle in the work that most befits them. They immediately brought the word of the teaching of Christ and persuaded people to do what by its nature brings benefit. In just the same way the inspired Jacob made it plain to the shepherds from Harran that he too was a shepherd, saying: "It is still broad daylight; it is not yet time for the livestock to be gathered. Water the sheep, and go and pasture them." Do you hear how he instructed the shepherds to pasture the sheep? This is just what the most wise disciple commanded the elders of the people, that is, the bishops, to do: "So I exhort the elders among you," he says, "as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and also a sharer in the glory that is to be revealed: shepherd the flock of Christ that is among you." And as they went through country and city, they appointed countless other shepherds over the peoples and charged them to take care of the rational sheep. They were to feed them as in a good pasture and a rich place, and lead them, as it were, to the most flowery grass, the divinely inspired Scripture. For the word of God is the life-sustaining food of the soul. So let it be said to the spiritual shepherds: "Take care of the green things in the field, and you will shear the grass; gather the ripe hay, so that you may have sheep for clothing." In another way, too, the inspired disciples among the Gentiles proved to be leaders of the shepherds there, that is, of their wise men and teachers, for they brought a truer instruction to those who heard them. And that they were far stronger and better than those men, one could perhaps see quite easily by reflecting on this: a heavy stone lay on the well, which a great crowd of shepherds could barely shift, yet Jacob did this by himself. Come, then, let us say as best we can what the well signifies, and what the stone in turn signifies. In this way we shall learn both the difference in the shepherds' strength and how far the Savior's disciples excel and surpass them in understanding.

Scripture, then, is accustomed to liken the knowledge of God to water. The Savior testified that this knowledge is life-giving when he said to the Father in heaven: "And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." He also once said to the woman, I mean the woman from Samaria: "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water." Here, I think, he calls his own word and instruction life-giving. The Master also cried out: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." Moreover, through the voice of the prophet he accuses some who foolishly turned aside to take up other teachers after the instruction of the law, and had strayed into the teachings and commandments of men. He spoke as follows: "Heaven was astonished at this and shuddered greatly, says the Lord, for my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns, which cannot hold water." The life-giving water, then, would be the divine word. But it lies at a great depth, and I do not think anyone could ever obtain it without sweat, for it is not simply ready to hand for whoever wants it. Rather, the obscurity that surrounds it lies on top of it like a heavy stone that is hard to move, overcoming the weakness of our minds. And indeed those who pasture the spiritual flocks need toil and long sweat to free the word from its obscurity. Only then can they draw it up and bring it, as it were, from the depths to the surface where it can be seen, and set it out clearly for those who come to it to enjoy as food for life. Now the shepherds among the Greeks, that is, their wise men and learned elite, many as they are and crowding together, barely lever the truth of the doctrines about God a little way, as it were. For they do not hold right opinions about him: they confess the nature of God, but they share out the glory of the Godhead to whomever they happen to choose. But a single one of the shepherds in Christ is enough by himself to move the stone from the well, however hard it is to shift. That stone is the covering and obscurity cast over beliefs about God. So the shepherds in Christ make the truth plain to the Gentiles and have never ceased to point out the one God, who is God by nature and in truth. Indeed, when the blessed Paul came to Athens, he set the living water before the learned elite there, saying: "Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious. For as I passed through," he says, "and looked closely at the objects of your worship, I also found an altar with the inscription: 'To an unknown god.' What you worship, then, without knowing it, this I proclaim to you." You see how, though they were leaders of peoples and shepherds and guides of those among them, they barely lever the heavy stone a little way off the well. They suppose that they are being pious because of their reverence for the divine, but they have badly missed the truth. For they built an altar and carved on it the inscription "To an unknown god," that is, to the deity that had not become known. They thought they had attained the best belief about God. But the inspired Paul cleverly turns the inscription to his purpose and very skillfully leads it to a useful end, saying that the God unknown to them is Christ. "For what you worship," he says, "without knowing it, this I proclaim to you." You see how he uncovered the well, rolled away the stone, and showed them the life-giving knowledge. The difference in the shepherds' sharpness of mind is therefore beyond comparison. The Greek shepherds, though very many, lagged behind the true belief about God; defeated by the obscurity of the doctrines, they were carried away into mere opinion. But Paul, though he was alone, set forth the truth. For Jacob alone rolled away the stone and watered the sheep in Rachel's care. And indeed he thought the girl worthy of love, for he kissed Rachel, it says. He was at once recognized by Laban, who then took him into his home, thought his nephew worthy of love and embraces, and counted him among his close kin. For he said: "You are of my bones and of my flesh." The name Rachel means "sheep of God," and one might quite reasonably give her the role of the Church from the Gentiles. For she is the sheep of Christ, which has been mingled with the older flocks and penned within the Savior's folds. That is why he also said: "And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring those also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock, one shepherd." And the inspired disciples shepherded the Church of Christ, that is, the rational flock understood to be in her care. Indeed, they became her lovers and the ones who led her to her bridegroom, presenting her to God as a pure virgin, without spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind, but rather holy and blameless.

That the people of Israel had the beginning of their race, and as it were the first shoots of their root, from the Gentiles, we shall understand from Laban's words. For an idolater greeted Jacob warmly and said that he was born of his sister, clearly meaning Rebecca, and called him his own flesh and bone. The inspired Abraham was called while still uncircumcised, after being brought up in the land of the Chaldeans in pagan customs and laws. He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the faith he had while uncircumcised, as it is written. So Israel the firstborn is indeed akin to those from the Gentiles, even though the law set him apart so that he seemed to be different. But in Christ the two have become one. For he removed what stood between them, abolishing the law of the letter and the circumcision that divided. We were renewed into one new man, so that the Gentiles share one body and one soul with those from Israel. From now on they are seen to be all but brought into identity through their fellowship in the Spirit. For Christ said somewhere to his Father and God in heaven: "I desire that, just as you and I are one, so they too may be one in us." For he himself is our peace, who broke down the dividing wall of partition, as I said just now. He took away what divided us and bound us together, as it were, into unity through the Spirit. So it is a sign, and a very clear one, of the union of the two peoples in faith and in the Spirit, that Laban embraced Jacob and confessed that he was his bone and flesh. Come, now, let us add another point to these, taking it from the sacred Scriptures themselves. For it says: "Laban said to Jacob, 'Because you are my brother, you shall not serve me for nothing. Tell me what your wages shall be.' Now Laban had two daughters; the name of the elder was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel. Leah's eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in form and very lovely to look at. Jacob loved Rachel, and he said, 'I will serve you seven years for Rachel your younger daughter.' Laban said to him, 'It is better for me to give her to you than to give her to another man. Stay with me.' So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days, because he loved her. Then Jacob said to Laban, 'Give me my wife, for my days are completed, so that I may go in to her.' So Laban gathered all the men of the place and made a wedding feast. And when evening came, Laban took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and Jacob went in to her. Laban also gave his maidservant Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her maidservant. When morning came, behold, it was Leah. And Jacob said to Laban, 'What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve with you for Rachel? Why have you deceived me?' Laban said, 'It is not done this way in our place, to give the younger before the elder. Complete the week of this one, and I will give you the other also in return for the work that you will do for me for another seven years.' Jacob did so, and completed her week. And Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife. Laban also gave his maidservant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her maidservant. And Jacob went in to Rachel. He loved Rachel more than Leah, and he served Laban another seven years."

The historical part needs no explanation to make it clear, for there is nothing at all difficult in it. Unless, that is, one of those who make a habit of finding fault with such things should say: "Is it not counted among us as one of the most offensive things to enter at once into two marriages, and indeed to bring a pair of wives into one's house, and sisters at that?" To this we reply that for the ancients the whole aim of life was directed toward having many children, and the thing was even reckoned a share in the highest prosperity of all. It was also free of all blame to sleep not only with two women but with still more, extending one's family to a countless multitude. Indeed, they received the begetting of children from God as a blessing. The Lord of all himself promised to grant this gift both to the saints of old before Moses and to those who received the tutelage of the law. For he said, "There shall be none childless or widowed among the sons of Israel." We shall not take this saying as a law; rather, we say that it is a promise. For whatever lies within our power is subject to statutes, and quite rightly; but whatever matters do not lie within our power, but have their outcome in the laws of nature, do not have law as their arbiter. It is plain, then, and obscure to no one at all, that the Creator would not have commanded that there be no barren or childless person among the sons of Israel. Rather, he promised, as God, that if they kept the law he would make them fruitful. So for the ancients the having of many children was something eagerly pursued and reckoned a mark of glory. But we in Christ have been brought over to the duty of bearing fruit rather in the spirit. We do not dishonor marriage, but we choose what is far above it, which is crowned with the highest verdict in the divinely inspired Scripture: I mean, to wait upon God without distraction and not to be divided toward the things of the world. "For the unmarried man," says Paul, "cares for the things of the Lord; but the married man cares for the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided."

That is enough, then, of our discussion of these things. Come, let us now contemplate, turning our mind to spiritual contemplations, and bearing in mind, quite rightly, that the labor of the holy apostles in their preaching was not unrewarded, nor their sweat unhonored. For Laban said to Jacob, "You shall not serve me for nothing." And the inspired disciples made the multitude of those who believed at the beginning the ground of splendid boasting. Paul, at any rate, addressed them as "my joy and crown." But I think it necessary to remind you of something most useful that we set down at the beginning. I said that in spiritual contemplations the role of Jacob is sometimes taken by the company of the holy apostles, since they became the firstfruits of those sanctified in the Spirit and justified by faith; and at other times by Christ himself, as the firstfruits of humanity renewed to incorruption, as the firstborn among many brothers, as the second Adam and the second root of the race after the first. So the discourse always turns the aim of its contemplations in whatever direction it is fitting to go. For to miss the proper line of reasoning will make the working out of the contemplations less elegant. For the present, then, Emmanuel will wear the role of Jacob: the bridegroom from heaven, who took the daughters of Laban, as it were, not without sweat. For it is proper to the highest of all natures to accomplish without effort whatever it chooses to do. The blessed prophet Isaiah also said somewhere about it: "He will not hunger, nor grow weary, and there is no searching out of his understanding." For the Divine is in no way lacking, but is all-perfect in itself. It does not receive its strength as something acquired from another, nor is it invigorated by food or drink, as bodies are by their law; rather, it is power by its very nature. Therefore it establishes the heavens and distributes strength with authority to whomever it may choose. Yet though by nature it does not grieve, it is said to be grieved: for he says somewhere to the mother of the Jews, clearly meaning the Synagogue, "And you grieved me in all these things"; and the inspired Paul also writes somewhere, "And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God who dwells in you." In the same way, if it should be said to grow weary, we say such things not because it came to feel toil, but because, if toiling were natural to it, it would have toiled in accomplishing deeds surpassingly great and extraordinary, deeds for which any one of us would likely have had to endure terrible and bitter toils. So, passing from human things to the most exalted conceptions, we might see the pure nature's care for us as all but drenched in toil and sweat. Yet we must free it from toil, since it is not like us, but rather abides and is firmly established above all creation in its own preeminence. Not without wages, then, nor without sweat, did Christ first gather to himself the Synagogue of the Jews, which we shall take in the figure of Leah. For her name means "laboring" and "being renewed." She labored, burdened by the rapacity of the Egyptians and bearing the grievous yoke of slavery. And she was renewed to the worship of her fathers: she was refashioned, as it were, from frenzied idol-worship to knowing at last who is God by nature and in truth. For he called out to them through Moses, "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one Lord," and, "You shall have no other gods besides me." But at the beginning Christ desired Rachel, that is, the Church from the Gentiles. That is why he said of the Synagogue of the Jews to Moses, the revealer of sacred things: "I have spoken to you once and twice, saying, I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stiff-necked people. Let me destroy them, and I will blot out their name from under the firmament of heaven, and I will make you into a great and strong nation, far greater than this one." But those whose minds were still light and easily led astray could not rush at once to what is perfect, to the instruction that surpasses the mind and the understanding that comes from it, I mean the instruction of the Gospel. They had first to be taught through lesser things, and to make the life under the law a kind of preliminary exercise for the life in Christ. So the bridegroom from heaven desired the younger at the beginning, that is, the Church from the Gentiles; but first he takes the elder into his house, and that, so to speak, not without toil. For Jacob served for Leah. And it is plain to see that Israel was delivered from slavery in Egypt with many great labors, for the whole of creation went to war against the Egyptians. Jacob's service, then, which was surely not accomplished without hardship, is a sign that Israel was not redeemed without sweat, and so became God's own at last through worship under the law. When the week of the elder was completed, he took Rachel, that is, the younger, the one desired from the beginning. For the Church from the Gentiles was called in second, after the first, as God's sheep; for that, as I said before, is what Rachel means. And that Christ in a certain way toiled for her too, the inspired Jacob again showed us when he endured seven years of labor for Rachel as well. For if it were possible for the Son to grow weary, though he is God by nature, how could he not have done so here? At the beginning he endured Herod's persecution; then the plots of the Pharisees, the slanders of the rulers, the spitting, the blows, the scourging on his back, the drunken insolence of the soldiers, and at the last death itself on the cross. Leah and Rachel are daughters of Laban, a man who still worshiped idols. For both were called from the Gentiles: first the Synagogue of the Jews, since the inspired Abraham himself came of Greek root and stock; and second, after the first, the younger, that is, the Church. Leah's eyes were weak and feeble, but Rachel was beautiful in form and exceedingly lovely to look upon. And concerning the Jews Christ said somewhere to the holy apostles, "Let them alone; they are blind guides of the blind." But, "Blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear." So the feebleness of the Synagogue of the Jews in seeing God may fittingly be signified by Leah's eyes. But Rachel's beauty prefigured the wisdom and understanding of those who are in faith in Christ, their great beauty of comprehension, and indeed their distinction in works. Let the prophetic word cry out to the mother of the Jews, "Behold, your eyes are not, nor is your heart good"; but let Christ call the Church from the Gentiles and say of her, "Your eyes are doves." For he desired her beauty, as the Psalmist says. So Christ first took the Synagogue of the Jews as his wife, with Moses leading the bride and angels acting as mediators; and after her, as a second, the Church from the Gentiles, for whom the blessed Baptist was taken as a kind of mediator. That is why he said, pointing us to this spiritual and divine marriage: "He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. Therefore this joy of mine is fulfilled. He must increase, but I must decrease." And mercy and faith are the bride's wedding gift. For the bridegroom who came from above, from heaven, said somewhere to the Church from the Gentiles through the voice of the prophets: "And I will betroth you to myself forever; I will betroth you to myself in righteousness and justice, in mercy and compassion. I will betroth you to myself in faithfulness, and you shall know the Lord." For, as I said just now, he took the elder before the Church from the Gentiles. But the manner of that betrothal and the force of that union did not last forever. For again he said of her somewhere, "She is not my wife, and I am not her husband." And again: "I gave her a bill of divorce into her hands." For she was cast off as one who had played the harlot and was condemned for the most abominable things. He said of her somewhere: "If a man sends away his wife, and she leaves him and becomes another man's, will she ever return to him again? Will not that woman be utterly defiled? And you have played the harlot with many shepherds; yet return to me, says the Lord. Lift up your eyes and look straight ahead, and see where you have defiled yourself. You sat by the roadsides for them like a forsaken crow, and you defiled the land with your harlotries and your wickedness, and you had many shepherds to be your stumbling block. You had the face of a harlot; you were shameless toward all. Did you not call me your own, and father, and guide of your maidenhood? Will it endure forever?" Such is the state of the elder. But Rachel, the younger, that is, the Church from the Gentiles, he betroths to himself, and that forever. And let the words "to myself" be understood in this way. He betrothed the Synagogue of the Jews, but through Moses as mediator. But to the Church from the Gentiles he joined himself directly, calling her to this with his own voice and being seen as a man like anyone else on earth. For he granted the request of the bride who cried out, "Show me your face, and let me hear your voice." The people of old did hear him speaking, but through Moses or the prophets. But in the last times of the age the Son himself has spoken to us in his own person, as the wise Paul also testified.

Besides this, it is worth examining closely the birth of the sons born to Jacob, and seeing how many there were and from whom they sprang. First, then, Leah bore four: Reuben, Simeon, Levi and Judah. But since Rachel was still barren and childless, she was greatly distressed and at a loss, and she devised a clever remedy for her childlessness. She persuaded Jacob, saying: "Here is my maid Bilhah. Go in to her, and she will bear upon my knees, and I too will have children by her." When this was carried out, two sons were born to Jacob, Dan and Naphtali. Leah, for her part, put Zilpah her own handmaid in his bed and so made him the father of two more, Gad and Asher. And what happened after this? "Reuben went," it says, "in the days of the wheat harvest, and found mandrake apples in the field, and brought them to Leah his mother. And Rachel said to Leah her sister, Give me some of your son's mandrakes. And Leah said, Is it not enough for you that you have taken my husband? Will you take my son's mandrakes too? And Rachel said, Not so; let him sleep with you tonight in return for your son's mandrakes. And Jacob came in from the field in the evening, and Leah went out to meet him and said, You shall come in to me today, for I have hired you with my son's mandrakes." After this, Leah again bore Issachar, and after him Zebulun. When the number of the sons of Israel had reached this point, "God remembered Rachel," it says, "and the Lord heard her and opened her womb, and she conceived and bore Jacob a son. And Rachel said, My God has taken away my reproach; and she called his name Joseph, saying, God has added to me another son." After him she also bore Benjamin. And what is written about her runs again as follows: "And it came to pass, when she drew near Chabratha to enter the land of Ephrathah, Rachel was giving birth, and she had hard labor in the delivery. And as she labored hard, the midwife said to her, Take heart, for this one too is a son for you. And as her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Son of my pain. But his father called him Benjamin." So Rachel, after a hard labor at the last, departed from our world in those very birth pangs. Such, then, is the birth of Jacob's sons. But what the innermost meaning of what is written may be, he alone would know who knows all things, "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge," as it is written. Yet let us look with keen eyes, and, trying as far as we can to thin the thick mist that lies over these things, let us say to him who makes the blind wise: "Unveil my eyes, and I shall perceive the wonders of your law." So (for I will go back to the beginning and remind you again of what I said), Leah the elder may very well be likened to the Synagogue of the Jews, and Rachel we shall take to be the Church of the Gentiles. Having laid down our conviction on this point as a kind of foundation for our discussion, let us proceed to the rest.

Leah, then, bore four sons first; then, in between, four others were born of the two maidservants, Bilhah and Zilpah. But when Leah and Rachel divided between them the mandrakes that Reuben had found in the fields, both became mothers. In addition to her first four, Leah bore Issachar, which means "wage"; then Zebulun, which again, when interpreted, signifies "blessing" and "good journey." And Rachel bore Joseph, which means "addition of God," and after him, at the last, Benoni, which means "son of pain." For she who was elder in time, that is, the Synagogue, was the first to bear to God the multitude of the Jews. That God called those born of her his sons you will readily understand, since he says to Moses, "Israel is my firstborn son," and through the voice of Isaiah, "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I have begotten sons and raised them up, but they have rejected me." Yet they were born of free women on account of the fathers, on whom he did not lay the yoke of the law. For the inspired Paul himself showed us the freedom of the fathers when he said, "I was once alive apart from the law," referring the "I" to the root of the race and attaching it to the persons of the fathers. But that, though born of free women, they would come under the yoke of slavery under the law, the birth of the four sons born of the maidservants, which lies right beside theirs and is joined to it, would show us in a riddle. But there is a mystery in these too. Those born of Bilhah, Dan and Naphtali, were counted as Rachel's, while Zilpah's sons, Gad and Asher, were counted as Leah's and were born later than Bilhah's. But someone, I suppose, might quite reasonably raise this difficulty: how could the sons of a slave woman, I mean Bilhah, be counted as Rachel's, when Rachel fills out the type of the Church from the Gentiles? What, then, do we say to this? That the blessed prophets, in the early times, were numbered among the children of the Jerusalem that is in slavery, yet in a certain way were sons of the Church from the Gentiles. For they shared her mind: they said that the mystery of Christ would be revealed and would shine forth in due time, they prefigured it in countless forms, and they all but brought it before the eyes of the people of old. But those who came after them, born once more into slavery, did not accept Christ, the giver of freedom. And that the earlier ones were better than those who came after them is easy to see, since God says through the voice of Isaiah: "How has the faithful city, Zion, become a harlot! She was full of judgment, righteousness lodged in her, but now murderers." You see how he says that Jerusalem, or Zion, was full of judgment, that is, of uprightness, and was a lodging place for the righteous, but in later times was filled with murderers.

If one wished, one could see quite clearly from the names themselves that the sons born through Bilhah would be nurslings of the Church, while those from Zilpah would rather be its enemies. For Dan means "judgment," and Naphtali "enlargement." This was the message the prophets proclaimed. It is not hard to show, once again, that Christ was going to judge the world in righteousness. He would condemn Satan as the one who had defrauded and destroyed us, and he would save us and move us, as it were, out of very great constriction into breadth of heart. For the blessed Psalmist cried out, speaking as if in the person of those who are in Christ and sanctified in the Spirit: "I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart." And the most wise Paul writes to the believers of Corinth who were inclined to be unequally yoked: "Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections. In return (I speak as to children), enlarge your hearts too. Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers." That Christ made a right and just judgment, blessed David himself will again make plain. He takes on himself the person of those who had been wronged and says to Christ, the Savior of all: "Rouse yourself, O Lord, and attend to my judgment, my God and my Lord, to my cause." Indeed, the Savior himself makes this evident when he says: "Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself." Do you see that the prophets, when they spoke of the mystery of Christ, proclaimed beforehand that we would have a just judgment and an enlargement of heart? So Bilhah bore Dan and Naphtali, that is, judgment and enlargement. Zilpah, on the other hand, bore Gad and Asher. Gad means "trial," and Asher "wealth." Were not the later generations of the Jews, who came after the first, exactly like this? How then can it be disputed? For one could see it from the very things that happened to Christ. Some tested him together with those called Herodians, saying: "Teacher, we know that you are truthful and do not defer to anyone, for you do not regard people's standing but teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to pay tax to Caesar, or not?" They came testing him so that they might trap him. This is what the inspired evangelist has testified. Others, for the sake of gain and out of love of profit, did not receive the Son. For they said among themselves, it says: "This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours." Anyone who turns his mind to what is written about them could see very readily that the Pharisees and the unholy band of scribes were exceedingly fond of wealth and gain. Our Lord Jesus Christ said that those who have chosen to set their minds on things above must sell their earthly wealth and give what they have to the poor, so that they may gain the treasure above. But, as the evangelist says, the scribes and the Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard these things and sneered at him. They stooped even to the most trivial matters and busied themselves with great precision and hair-splitting. They would not let the smallest thing pass for those who did not bring the tithes appointed by the law, though they cared little for the law themselves. The Lord made this entirely clear to them when he said: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: judgment, mercy, and faith." So Gad is trial, and Asher is wealth. Both were born of the maidservant Zilpah, after Dan and Naphtali, who were Bilhah's. Let these things, then, describe for us the time before the coming of our Savior. During that time Rachel, that is, the Church from the Gentiles, was still barren. Yet Isaiah cried out beforehand that she would bear many and would nurse countless children: "Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and shout, you who are not in labor; for the children of the desolate woman are more than those of her who has a husband." The inspired David also made this plain when he said of God: "He settles the barren woman in a home as a mother rejoicing over her children." And the Master and God of all said to her somewhere: "Lift up your eyes all around and see them all." And again: "Behold, these come from afar, these from the north, and these from the sea, and others from the land of the Persians." Come then, if you please, let us consider when and how the barren woman gave birth. After the sons born of the maidservants, Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, finds the mandrakes in the field and brings them to Leah, his own mother. She gives them to Rachel when she asks for them. Leah, having received the mandrakes, again bears two sons, Issachar and Zebulun. Then God remembers Rachel, and her womb is opened. She too bears Joseph, and at her death Benjamin. Our discourse has already shown us many times that Leah signifies the synagogue of the Jews and Rachel the Church from the Gentiles. So let us leave aside further repetition as useless, and go on to explain what the mandrakes found by the firstborn Reuben might typify. We must also explain what is meant by their being shared between the two women, perhaps equally (for Leah gave some to Rachel), and also what is meant by the birth of the children itself, which holds the mystery within the meanings of their names.

Mandrakes, then, grow in fields, and their fruit looks like an apple. That the plant brings on sleep and makes those who take it drunk with a deep stupor needs no long argument to prove, I think. For the skill of physicians sometimes overcomes the sleeplessness of the sick by the natural power of mandrakes. These would point us in a veiled way to the mystery of Christ. In a sense he slept for our sake and lowered himself into self-emptying even to the point of death, though he came back to life. For he was God by nature, and he became flesh. And wherever death is taken entirely as a kind of sleep, we must look there for a return to life as well. The whole mystery of Christ lies, as it were, in these things. So the inspired Paul solemnly charges those who had been lightly moved to a heterodox opinion: "For I handed on to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures." And a little later: "Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?" For Christ was the first among human beings to show that death is sleep, since he was Life by nature. Through this, a door and a way, so to speak, has been opened for human nature to triumph over death itself from now on. For this reason the most wise Paul again and again calls those overtaken by death "those who have fallen asleep," since before long they will come back to life through Christ. For he said again: "For if we believe that Christ died and rose again, so too God will raise with Jesus those who have fallen asleep, and will present them with us." The mandrakes, then, are a sign of sleep. Reuben, being the firstborn, finds them and brings them to his mother, and she shares them with her sister. For those of Israel, the firstborn in time, were the first to understand the mystery of Christ and be enriched by it. They brought to their own mother, I mean Jerusalem, a splendid find of their own insight and persuaded her to rejoice. For before the calling of the Gentiles, the inspired disciples initiated people throughout all Judea into the mystery. Even if perhaps not all believed, they nevertheless [?] accepted the word about Christ. And the remnant has been saved, according to the Scriptures. That the Jews came to faith before the Gentiles is surely evident and unclear to no one. Leah, then, having received the mandrakes, bore two sons, Issachar and Zebulun. Issachar means "reward," and the other, Zebulun, means "a prosperous way" and "blessing." As I have already said, the synagogue of the Jews received the mystery of Christ through the holy apostles as if from its own children. It was then shown to be the mother of children whom God prospers with reward and blessings. The forgiveness of sins would at once show that faith in Christ is not without reward. Our Lord Jesus Christ himself confirms this when he says: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me has eternal life." No less does the blessed Paul: "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim). For if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved." What reward, then, is greater or more worth gaining than the saving of a soul? The Savior himself persuades us that this is something exceptional and worthy of all esteem: "For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world but forfeits his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?" Glorious, then, and saving is the reward for those who believe. And it would be beyond dispute that blessing must surely follow for those justified in Christ, for we have been sanctified in the Spirit. And blessed David says: "The blessing of the Lord be upon you. You are blessed by the Lord, who made heaven and earth." God also said somewhere through the voice of Isaiah to the mother of believers, I mean the Church: "I will put my Spirit upon your offspring, and my blessings upon your children." This is why the most wise Paul writes to those justified by faith: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing." And how could those who have richly shared in the blessing from above fail to prosper in every good work? For, it says, "the way of the godly has been made straight, and the way of the godly is prepared, for the way of the Lord is judgment." Concerning the synagogue of the Jews, God said somewhere: "Behold, I will block up her ways, and she shall not find her path." But when he sends us into the dwellings above along a smooth and, as it were, cleared road, he commands his holy ministers: "Open the gates; let a people enter who keep righteousness and proclaim truth, who hold fast to truth and keep peace." And again: "Make a road for my people, and throw the stones out of the way," so that they may not stumble over obstacles along the way and grow sluggish in their zeal for good things. So Leah bore those whom God prospers with reward and blessings, and Rachel likewise received the mandrakes and bore Joseph. For the Church received the mystery of Christ through the holy apostles, as if from a sister like herself, the synagogue of the Jews. She then became the mother of a people that is always increasing and growing into a multitude beyond measure (for Joseph means "addition of God"). The Church from the Gentiles has been added to the flocks of Israel. That is why Christ said: "And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice, and there will be one flock, one shepherd." So, as I have just said, the flock from the Gentiles has been added to the older flocks. It grows without ceasing, richer and richer, until Benjamin himself is born, as it were, in the last times. He is the people called "son of pain."

And who is this, at whose birth the very mother who bore him will cease and pass, as it were, into another life? For Rachel died in the very pangs of giving birth to Benjamin. To know these things with great exactness we shall again leave to God and to those wiser than we are. But there is no harm in saying what comes to mind. I think, then, that the people called "son of pain" may fittingly be understood as the multitude of believers in the last times of the age. For at that time the son of lawlessness will also appear, "who opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God as God, proclaiming himself to be God." He will set himself against the saints and will be no different from untamed beasts. For, as the Savior himself said, there will then be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world, nor ever will be. Christ himself made clear that the effects of that one's perversity and inhumanity will fall on the saints more than on anyone else, for he added: "And if those days had not been cut short, no flesh would be saved. But for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short." There will be persecution against everyone who is chosen and genuine in faith, a terrible and unbearable oppression, and some will even suffer torture. So the time will surely be shortened, since the compassionate God, I think, measures the trial to the strength of those who suffer. The most wise Paul also persuades us to think this: "God is faithful, and he will not let you be tested beyond what you can bear. With the testing he will also provide the way out, so that you may be able to endure it." When Benjamin is born, then, that is, the people at the end who are in pain, Rachel too will cease. For, as I have just said, the Church will pass into another life. By the Church I mean us, who through faith in Christ have been enriched with union with God through the Spirit. And do not be surprised that death removed Rachel from the affairs of this world. When some people are led to contemplate what happened long ago, the matter may sometimes trouble them: "Will the Church, then, cease at some time and in some way be extinguished by death? And is this the passage to better things?" To such questions we reply: when you hear "Church," know that it means the holy multitude of believers. For them, dying in place of the worldly, fleshly life is the way to progress in the life and conduct that are in Christ, and a means of passing into better and higher things. This is why the blessed Paul delivers a rather vehement rebuke to some, saying: "If you died to the elemental principles of the world, why do you submit to regulations as though you were still living in the world?" And again he writes to those who are shaking off the fleshly, pleasure-loving life: "For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, who is your life, is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory." And he said plainly that we must put to death our members that are on the earth, meaning fornication, impurity, and things akin to them. So the death of Rachel surely signifies, for the flock of believers, that is, the Church, the death understood in Christ, which carries them, as it were, into another life. For it is true that our condition will be changed from corruption to incorruption, from death to life, from weakness to power, from dishonor to glory, and from measured times to everlasting life. For in this way, in this very way, we shall be with Christ himself forever. Through him and with him be glory and power to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, for ages of ages. Amen.

In many parts and in many ways the divinely inspired Scripture proclaims beforehand the types of the salvation that comes through Christ, and so gives no small benefit to those who read it. Painters who are fully trained in their art adorn their panels with colours of every kind, bringing the shadows into clearer view and pouring great charm over the picture. In the same way the wisdom that crafted this universe, that is, God, subtly reveals beforehand the beauty of the mystery through all kinds of varied glories. He does this so that those being initiated may understand as if in riddles, and may take the matter as a kind of preliminary instruction and first step toward understanding, and so be somehow readier to receive the truth. We were living in this world, then, differing little from the irrational animals, or perhaps even falling below them, if God's rebuke against those of Israel was true when he said: "The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's manger; but Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood." And if the people of the Jews, who had the law as their tutor, were condemned for such dreadful ignorance, what could be said of the gentiles, on whom the deep darkness of polytheistic error had fallen? Always bent downward, as it were, and entangled in the desires of the flesh, they cared only to think of earthly things. They could not even lift the eye of the mind, so to speak, toward the glories of the love of God. For this reason the blessed prophets mourned over us and all but wept over us as we lay fallen, and they spent countless words on us. The blessed Isaiah says: "Hades has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without ceasing." For there was no turning away from evil. Weighed down by the unbearable greed, as it were, of Satan, who tyrannized over us, the wretched went down to Hades when they departed from here. Death swallowed them greedily, and the inventor of sin, as it were, herded us into it. And so, as I said just now, the divine David himself recalled such a calamity, and not without tears. He spoke about us once in this way: "Like sheep they are laid in Hades; death shall shepherd them." And again: "You who shepherd Israel, give heed, you who lead Joseph like a sheep; you who sit upon the cherubim, shine forth; stir up your might and come to save us." This is why we did not remain under death forever. For God the Father sent us from heaven the good shepherd, our Lord Jesus Christ.
