He does not shepherd those under him into Hades but carries them off to incorruption and life. For he pastures his flock among lilies, in good pasture and in a rich place, as it is written. He sets spiritual grass before us and gives us our fill of streams from above and from heaven. He makes us fruitful, and besides this he enlarges us into a countless multitude of peoples. As I said, one might again see this as if in shadows in the divine Jacob, when the word sets out what is written about him and makes clear, as far as possible, whatever in the story seems somewhat obscure. It is written as follows: "And it came to pass, when Rachel had borne Joseph, that Jacob said to Laban, 'Send me away, so that I may go to my own place and to my own land. Give me my wives and my children, for whom I have served you, so that I may go. For you know the service with which I have served you, and how your livestock fared with me. What you had before I came was little, and it has increased to a multitude, and the Lord has blessed you at my foot. Now, then, when shall I also make a house for myself?' And Laban said to him, 'What shall I give you?' And Jacob said to him, 'You shall give me nothing. If you will do this one thing for me, I will again shepherd your sheep and keep them. Let all your sheep pass by today, and separate from them every speckled and dusky sheep and every dark animal among the lambs. Every white-spotted and sprinkled one among the goats shall be my wages. And my righteousness will answer for me tomorrow, because my wages are before you. Anything among the goats that is not sprinkled or white-spotted, and anything among the lambs that is not dark, shall be counted as stolen if it is found with me.' And Laban said to him, 'Let it be as you say.' And on that day he separated the sprinkled and white-spotted he-goats, and all the sprinkled and white-spotted she-goats, and everything that had white on it, and everything that was dark among the lambs, and he gave them into the hands of his sons. And he put a three days' journey between them and Jacob. And Jacob shepherded the rest of Laban's sheep." We must again gather the breadth of the story briefly, and then say what meaning would fit our contemplation of it.

The blessed Jacob had served Laban for two daughters, Leah and Rachel. He spent long years at this, and when Joseph was born to him of Rachel, whom he loved far more than the other, he naturally grew restless and was eager to go home again. The reason he gives for leaving is not implausible. "If I am to go on pasturing your flocks endlessly and without wages," he says, "when shall I make a house for myself?" That is, when shall I gather a living for my own children and myself be called master of a household? This is what Jacob says. But Laban claims him as a good shepherd and says he has been blessed by his coming. He refuses to let him go, although the service for his daughters had reached its appointed end. Instead he promises to give whatever wages please him. Jacob, for his part, plainly affirmed that he had been kind, fair and exceedingly long-suffering, and indeed the one who had brought Laban the blessing from God. For he said, "God blessed you at my foot," putting "foot" in place of "coming," because Laban had said this first. He asks for wages and promises to pasture Laban's flocks, on condition that the sprinkled ones, that is, the white-spotted and ash-coloured, are assigned to him and set apart specifically for him. When this had been done, Jacob set apart the flock allotted to him along with his own children, while he himself went on pasturing Laban's flocks. Now we must say what the clear meaning of these things would be, refined to spiritual subtlety.

Let Jacob, then, take on the person of Christ himself, as we indeed said earlier. For Christ is the true supplanter, since he has trampled sin down completely. And as he is understood to have appeared also as a man, he is the youngest, born later than those who came before him, that is, the holy prophets and Moses himself. Yet he holds the rights of the elder and is the firstborn, because the Only-begotten came to be among many brothers. He is the one blessed by the Father with abundance of grain and wine. Nations have served him, and rulers have bowed down to him. Whoever curses him is cursed, and whoever blesses him is blessed, according to the blessing of Isaac. Like Jacob, he all but left heaven as though it were his father's hearth and came to Laban. Laban is to be compared to the world, which never knew who is God by nature and was gravely sick, as it were, with the error of polytheism; for Laban too was an idolater. The world is Christ's own, since he is understood to be God by nature and the Lord and Creator of all. Yet it is not his own, because of its apostasy and because through sin it seemed in some way to have come to belong to another; for it had enrolled Satan as its king. So the Word came down from heaven, as if leaving his father's hearth, as I said just now. And he was like a stranger in his own world. The wise John will bear witness to this when he says: "He was in the world, and the world came into being through him, and the world did not know him." But perhaps these words would more properly fit the time of his coming among us. That even before the incarnation he was among his own as God, and, though unknown to the world, cared for our affairs out of innate goodness and a gentleness befitting God, the divine Jacob at once shows as a type in his own person. For he shepherded Laban's sheep though he received no wages at all from him. He was led to it only by the hope of being joined to Laban's two daughters and of becoming the father of legitimate children. These daughters were Leah and Rachel. For the Son, who is God by nature, was in the world, and this is Laban. And in a certain way he shepherded it, providing as God the necessities of life. He gave the fruits of the earth, sent up springs of water and streams of rivers, made his sun rise, as it is written, sent down rains, and implanted in human nature its innate understanding. For he is "the true light, which enlightens every person coming into the world." He did all this, as I said, solely out of his innate gentleness. At that time he received no wages, as it were, from those in the world: no praise, no worship, no right belief, no unerring understanding of him. But he knew in advance that in due time he would have two wives who would be mothers of legitimate children for him, giving birth in a spiritual way. Who are they? The first is the elder, Leah, who fulfils the type of the synagogue of the Jews. The second, not long after and thrice longed for, is the younger, Rachel, that is, the Church from the gentiles. She bore Joseph, whose name means "addition of God." For the flock from the gentiles has been added to those from Israel. It can also be understood in another way, as the Church grows into a countless multitude through the additions of believers over time. But look closely, for precision in these matters is very profitable. Leah gave birth before Rachel, and in between them two maidservants, Bilhah and Zilpah, also gave birth. But Jacob remained quiet in the meantime and was not yet thinking of making a house of his own. When Rachel bore Joseph, then at last he longs for a house: "When shall I make a house for myself?" he says. The synagogue of the Jews bore those destined for slavery under the law. But Christ did not yet openly acknowledge that he had a house of his own. For he did not much approve of the temple of stone that Solomon built. Indeed, when the Jews were exceedingly proud of it, he once all but rebuked them, saying: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?" Nor did Israel become a spiritual house of God, for he did not dwell in them. But when the Church from the gentiles bore the new people, the people of additions, the Saviour at last prepared a house of his own for himself. And who is this house? It is we who have believed. Of us he says through the voice of the prophet: "Putting my laws into their minds, I will also write them on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people." He dwells in us through the Spirit, as I said just now, though he did not dwell in Israel. That those who lived before his coming had no share in the Spirit, in the way that we do, the most wise John will make clear when he says: "For the Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified." For after he had risen from the dead, refashioning human nature into the divine image, he first breathed on the holy apostles, saying: "Receive the Holy Spirit." And the divine Paul says somewhere: "For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, 'Abba, Father.'" So there was a spirit of slavery in Israel. But in us who are from Rachel, that is, from the Church of the gentiles, there is the Spirit of God for adoption, who makes us a spiritual house. For those born of Rachel are free, and Rachel's eyes are beautiful and lovely, though Leah's are not. For the synagogue of the Jews does not see soundly. The most wise Paul will bear witness to this when he says: "For to this very day, when the old covenant is read, the same veil remains unlifted, because it is only in Christ that it is taken away. Indeed, to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts. But whenever someone turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." But, as he says again, "we all, with unveiled faces, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Lord, the Spirit." Do you see that we behold the glory of the Lord with beautiful eyes and unveiled faces? For Rachel's eyes are bright, as I said just now. So when the youngest, Rachel, had borne Joseph, the divine Jacob at last hastens to go home. But Laban claims him and says he has been blessed, since his flock had grown to a great multitude. For the world greatly needs God, even if perhaps it does not say so, at least in knowing and confessing that everything it has, both the necessities of life and whatever makes for its well-being, comes from God. The blessed Jacob asks for wages, no longer willing to stay for nothing. And the wages he chose were not unwelcome to him: the sprinkled and ash-coloured ones. In earlier ages long past, God the Word, through whom all things exist, governed the world out of his innate gentleness befitting God, yet he let those in it go their own ways, as it is written. But when the Church bore the new people, the people that is always being added to, that is, those who have already received spiritual rebirth through faith in him, then he asks the world for a kind of wages for his care of it: those who are readier to believe. The ash-coloured and sprinkled ones would be a type of these. What does this mean? In flocks of sheep and goats, those of a single colour are always preferred by those who raise them. The sprinkled and spotted ones hold second rank and are not valued equally with the rest. For their wool is not of one colour; it changes in small patches, and is varied in colour and, as it were, mixed up. So Christ does not receive from the world what is held in honour in it and choice among men, but rather those who seem lower among them and of lesser repute. The divine Paul confirms this when he writes to those who have believed: "For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many of noble birth. But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong." If one wished to examine such things precisely, the ash-coloured and sprinkled one might also be understood in another way. For those who are in Christ have a comeliness that is varied, as it were, in both deeds and words. The dark, blackish colour might be taken as the riddle and shadow of the mystery of Christ, and might stand for the dark teaching about it, which is obscure to most people. For the divine David says somewhere in the book of Psalms: "He made darkness his hiding place; around him was his tent, dark water in the clouds of the air." Here he likens the doctrines about God, which are hard to grasp, to a tent, and calls them darkness and dark water in the clouds of the air. Wisdom too promises to grant some people richly the power to understand parables and dark sayings, the words of the wise and their riddles. So the dark colour hints to us at the depth and, as it were, the blackness of the doctrines concerning Christ. The other colour, white, will represent what is bright and, as it were, transparent, that is, works of piety. Accordingly the Lord of all foretells the cleansing that comes through faith in Christ when he says through the voice of the prophet: "Learn to do good, seek justice, rescue the wronged, defend the orphan, and vindicate the widow. Come, and let us reason together, says the Lord. Even if your sins are like crimson, I will make them white as snow; and if they are like scarlet, I will make them white as wool." So those who hold second rank in the world are chosen and held in the highest account by Christ, the Saviour of all. They are placed lower than others, as it were, and outdone in reputation. Yet they are spotted, as it were, having spiritually a varied colouring in the depth of their doctrines about God. They are rich in the teaching that is obscure to others, and they shine out brightly in the radiance of piety. So the spotted ones were Jacob's wages. But let us inquire, if you please, how he outwitted Laban and made the ones he had chosen very numerous, and let us learn it from the holy Scriptures themselves. The passage goes like this: "Then Jacob took for himself green rods of storax, walnut and plane. And Jacob peeled white strips in them, stripping off the green, and the white that he had peeled showed on the rods, making them variegated. He set the peeled rods in the troughs at the watering places, so that when the sheep came to drink, they would conceive in front of the rods as they came to drink. And the sheep bore white-spotted, variegated, and ash-coloured sprinkled young. Jacob separated the lambs, and he set before the sheep a white-spotted ram and every variegated one among the lambs. He set apart flocks for himself and did not mix them with Laban's sheep. Whenever the sheep were in heat and conceiving, Jacob set the rods in the troughs before the sheep, so that they would conceive at the rods. But when the sheep were giving birth, he did not set them there. So the unmarked ones became Laban's and the marked ones Jacob's, and the man became exceedingly rich." We say that it belongs to the shepherd's craft to know that sheep and goats will always give birth to young that resemble what they see. If they look at something while they are in heat, their offspring will take on the colours of whatever comes before their eyes. The thing seems somehow to be brought about by the laws of nature. Yet such matters are wholly beyond words and untrodden by our thoughts. Again, it was at a divine oracle that the divine Jacob chose the ash-coloured and spotted ones. For he said somewhere to Leah and Rachel: "And it came to pass, when the sheep were in heat and conceiving, that I saw in my sleep with my own eyes. And behold, the he-goats and the rams mounting the she-goats and the sheep were white-spotted, variegated, and ash-coloured sprinkled. And the angel of God said to me in my sleep, 'Jacob.' And I said, 'What is it?' And he said, 'Lift up your eyes and see the he-goats and the rams mounting the sheep and the she-goats: they are white-spotted, variegated, and ash-coloured sprinkled.'" This is what the holy Scripture says. But come, let us pass over the lowly ground of the story and climb up to spiritual things.

Once again the rod figuratively points us to Emmanuel, for he is called by that name in the divinely inspired Scripture. The divine Isaiah says: "And a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from the root." And the divine David, speaking in the person of believers, cried out to the Father and God in heaven: "Your rod and your staff, these have comforted me." For we have been comforted in Christ and have made him our support. For it is written: "The Lord upholds the righteous." To us, then, the rational goats [?] and flocks spread through the whole inhabited earth and the entire world, Christ sets himself before us as a kind of rod. And not just any rod, but one of storax, and of walnut, and as it were of plane. Each of these is a plant attested for its straightness. The storax rod is a sign of death. For a dead body is tended with spices, and the sweetest of spices is storax; and Christ died for us and was buried, according to the Scriptures. The walnut rod is a sign of watchfulness and wakefulness, for this is the effect such a plant has on us. And Christ was raised for us; for he was not held fast by the gates of Hades, nor was he wholly caught in the bonds of death. The plane rod, again, seems to hint at the rise to the heights and the course on high, that is, Christ's ascension into heaven. For the plane is a well-grown tree and among the very tallest, and the Son was exalted by the Father. Peter said of him: "Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God." And Paul says that he was highly exalted and received the name above every name and the worship of all. But if anyone wishes, he may take the plant in yet another sense. And what is that? Those who busy themselves with the etymologies of names say that the plane (platanos) got its name because its leaf spreads so very broad. For we too are broadened through faith and love, all but growing around Christ. For the law is very narrow, and the mind of idolaters is cramped. So God cried out to the flocks of the Gentiles through the prophet: "Learn to hear, you who are hemmed in." And to the Corinthians, who chose to slip back into their old error after the broadness of faith, Paul writes: "Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections. In return (I speak as to children), be enlarged yourselves too. Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial?" Indeed the Psalmist, speaking somewhere in the Spirit to Emmanuel himself and disparaging the narrowness of the law, says: "Your commandment is exceedingly broad." And again: "I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart." And besides: "And I walked in a broad place, because I sought out your ordinances." That the walnut rod, as I said just now, is by nature productive of wakefulness is shown when God says to the prophet Jeremiah: "What do you see, Jeremiah?" "And I said," he says, "a walnut staff. And the Lord said to me: You have seen well, for I am watchful over my words to perform them." So Christ, understood under the figure of the rod, sets himself before us, as it were, as one who died, was raised, and was exalted to heaven, and who spiritually broadens through the Spirit the hearts of those who receive him. But where did Jacob place the rods? In the troughs of the watering places. The troughs and watering places of the rational flock, that is, of us, may in turn be understood as the writing of Moses and the proclamations of the prophets, which all but pour out for us the word from above and from God. For it is written: "And you shall draw water with joy from the springs of salvation." There we shall find Emmanuel, the rod of power: as in death for our sake, as firstborn from the dead, as exalted in glory, and as broadening those who believe, as I said just now. For virtually the whole word of the holy prophets, and indeed of Moses, looks toward the mystery of Christ. That is why the wise Paul said that "Christ is the end of the law and the prophets." But Jacob peeled the rods in white strips, stripping off the green, and so the flocks conceived the variegated young by looking at them. For Christ strips away, as it were, the shadow of the law and what we might call the veil over the prophetic writings, and by showing us the word in them whitened and thoroughly clear to see, he works a spiritual charm. He all but persuades those who wish to be variegated in virtue to conceive, practising it in two ways, I mean in deed and in word. So the divine prophets, speaking in the person of those justified by faith, have cried out plainly: "Through fear of you, O Lord, we conceived and were in labour and brought forth the spirit of your salvation." And the same blessed Isaiah said again, in his own person: "Be strong, you slack hands and paralysed knees. Take comfort, you faint-hearted in mind; be strong, do not fear. Behold, our God repays judgment, and he will repay." And again: "Behold, the Lord comes with strength, and his arm with dominion; like a shepherd he will tend his flock, and with his arm he will gather the lambs, and he will comfort those that are with young." That is, there will be spiritual comfort for those already in labour with the divine word, since they will bear fruit and are on the very point of bringing forth the glories of the gospel way of life. For this is the fruit of a holy and genuine soul. "But Jacob," it says, "made flocks for himself apart, and did not mix them with Laban's sheep." For the profane is incompatible with the holy, the filthy with the pure. Christ's people are apart: they refuse to be mixed up with those in the world, they are freed from all love of the flesh, and they are not unmarked in their life but rather most conspicuous for virtue. For, it says, "the unmarked ones were Laban's, and the marked ones Jacob's." Yet Jacob did not escape envy. When Laban's sons saw him rich and prospering, they were bitterly stung, and so he planned to depart and go back again to his father's hearth. For it is written: "And the man became exceedingly rich, and he had many cattle, and oxen, and male and female servants, and camels, and donkeys, and mules. And Jacob heard the words of Laban's sons, saying: Jacob has taken all that was our father's, and from what was our father's he has gained all this glory. And Jacob saw Laban's face, and behold, it was not toward him as it had been yesterday and the day before. And the Lord said to Jacob: Return to the land of your father and to your kindred, and I will be with you. And Jacob sent and called Rachel and Leah to the plain where the flocks were, and said to them: I see your father's face, that it is not toward me as it was yesterday and the day before. But the God of my father has been with me. And you yourselves know that I have served your father with all my strength. But your father cheated me and changed my wages of the ten lambs." Then he says: "And God has taken away all your father's livestock and given them to me." For truly our Lord Jesus Christ has grown rich beyond all counting, gathering his own worshippers in the world, who make the confession of their service under him a splendid offering of a good mind, saying: "We are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand." But the children of the world cannot bear to stay quiet at this. Seeing their own father despoiled, as it were, and the most conspicuous of the sheep passing under the hand of the good shepherd, and those born under Christ variegated with virtues of every kind, they mutter, saying: "Jacob has taken all that was our father's, and from what was our father's he has gained all this glory." And they are not lying at all; what they say is true. For Christ has gathered to himself all who are in the world, and having folded the flocks of believers in his own courts, he possesses a wealth befitting God and a surpassing glory. For he himself said somewhere to the Father and God in heaven: "All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine, and I am glorified in them." Let us look at Jacob's wages themselves. He had, it says, many cattle and oxen, male and female servants, camels and donkeys. You see Christ too gathering from every kind, as it is written: "The kingdom of heaven is like a net thrown into the sea that gathered from every kind." For he receives the slave, to make him splendid with the glories of freedom. He receives those under the law as already holy and fit for spiritual sacrifice, as in the rank of sheep and ox, so that by moving them into the brightness of the gospel way of life he may make them holier still. Besides these he also receives the unholy and unclean race, as in the rank of the camel and indeed of the donkey, so that, having melted away the filth of polytheistic error, he may join them, clean and purified, to the choirs of the saints. So, when Laban's sons had been stirred to envy, and Laban himself showed an unsmiling, sullen brow not free from malice ("for his face," it says, "was not as it had been yesterday and the day before"), God commanded Jacob to return home. He sent for the women, I mean Leah and Rachel, and set out their father's injustice plainly. And he added: "God has taken away all your father's livestock and given them to me." "And Rachel and Leah answered and said to him: Is there still any portion or inheritance for us in our father's house? Are we not regarded by him as foreigners? For he has sold us, and has used up our money entirely. All the wealth and glory that God has taken from our father shall be ours and our children's. Now then, do whatever your God has told you." For while the world and its children scowl at Christ, comfort is given from above and from heaven, that is, from the Father, to the Saviour's brides, I mean the Churches. Yet this comfort comes through the Son, who ferries over to us, as it were, the words of the Father. For "he whom God has sent speaks the words of God," as John says. Notice how God spoke to Jacob, and Jacob to his brides, I mean Leah and Rachel. And the word of comfort was that they must depart from their father's hearth together with their own bridegroom. So too the blessed Psalmist says in the Spirit to the Church: "Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house; for the king has desired your beauty, for he is your Lord, and you shall worship him." So Jacob spoke to his brides what came from God. And what was it he said? A complaint against Laban: that he was unjust and wicked and slow to pay whatever wages he owed. Christ himself likewise charges the world with great insensibility: it will not bring itself to pay its Master the thanks due to him, nor is it willing to bring, as a debt and a wage, spiritual gifts in return for his care of it, I mean faith and love. Yet all things have come under him, as God the Father draws them in as with a net. For the Son said to him somewhere: "Those whom you gave me out of the world were yours, and you gave them to me." This, then, is the meaning of "God has taken away all your father's livestock and given them to me." The holy brides of the Saviour promise to follow readily, and they say that they have been sold, as it were, to him by the world. For Emmanuel bought the Churches with his own blood, and they have become estranged from their former father. They have no share or portion at all with the world, out of which they have been called. Rather, their wealth, and their children's, is beyond mind and word: he himself is their portion and their lot, their glory and their boast, and everything that makes for splendour and prosperity. The world, then, together with its own children, scowls at Christ and is consumed by the fire of envy, seeing him advanced so far in glory that he has brought the whole region under heaven under himself and mastered all that is on earth. Its madness reaches beyond muttering and abuse: it persecutes and thirsts for blood, and, so to speak, brings all its power to bear against the Saviour's glory, and it is caught out as the bitterest enemy of the Churches under him and of his children, that is, of the multitude of believers. Anyone who chooses to learn this can see it without trouble from what follows: "Jacob rose and took his wives and his children and put them on the camels, and he carried off all his possessions and all his baggage which he had acquired in Mesopotamia, and all that was his, and went away to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan. Now Laban had gone to shear his sheep. And Rachel stole her father's idols. And Jacob hid from Laban the Syrian, so as not to tell him that he was running away. And he fled, he and all that was his, and crossed the river, and set out for Mount Gilead. On the third day it was reported to Laban the Syrian that Jacob had fled. And taking all his kinsmen with him, he pursued him for seven days' journey and overtook him at Mount Gilead. But God came to Laban the Syrian in his sleep by night and said to him: Take care not to speak evil to Jacob. And Laban overtook Jacob. Jacob had pitched his tent on the mountain, and Laban stationed his kinsmen on Mount Gilead." So Laban comes upon him and sharply accuses the divine Jacob of slipping away in secret, all but stealing his daughters and his household gods. For he spoke thus: "Now you have gone off, for you longed greatly to go away to your father's house. Why," he says, "did you steal my gods?" "But Jacob did not know," it says, "that Rachel his wife had stolen them." Laban searched for his gods, but did not find them with Leah, nor in the dwelling of the maidservants Bilhah and Zilpah. And since Rachel expected to be searched by her father, she contrived a rather clever ruse. "She took the idols," it says, "and put them in the camel's saddlebags and sat on them, and said to her father: Do not take it ill, my lord, that I cannot rise before you, for the way of women is upon me. And Laban searched her whole dwelling and did not find the idols." Then, when Laban was now at a loss and, naturally, lamenting the loss of his own gods, the blessed Jacob in turn rightly accused him of having chosen to pursue him for nothing, when he had no charge at all to bring. After that they began to talk of an agreement, and the two of them reached an understanding for peace. "For Laban answered," it says, "and said to Jacob: Your daughters are my daughters, and your sons are my sons, and your livestock is my livestock, and all that you see is mine and my daughters'. What shall I do today to these, or to the children they have borne? Now then, come, let us make a covenant, you and I, and it shall be a witness between me and you. And he said to him: Behold, no one is with us; see, God is witness between me and you. And Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar. And Jacob said to his kinsmen: Gather stones. And they gathered stones and made a heap, and they ate there on the heap. And Laban said to him: This heap bears witness between me and you today. And Laban called it Heap of Testimony, but Jacob called it The Heap Is Witness."

In all this we have narrated the story briefly, taking pains to cut it short as far as possible. But now it is necessary to bring out its innermost meaning. That the world raged against Christ as he grew rich in flocks of believers, and that it springs at him in its frenzy, would need no long argument for a clear demonstration. Just see how, when Jacob departs, Laban pursues him, raging, together with his own children. For Christ too departs, as it were, from the world together with his brides, that is, the Churches, and moves away with his whole household, so to speak, spiritually calling to his own: "Rise, let us go from here." But this departure does not take place in a way the senses can perceive, nor bodily from place to place; it would be quite absurd to think or speak like that. Rather, it is profitably accomplished when we pass from minding the things of the world to wishing to do what pleases God. For as the blessed Paul writes, "we have no lasting city here, but we seek the city that is to come, whose architect and builder is God." And another of the holy apostles writes: "I urge you as aliens and exiles to abstain from the desires of the flesh, which wage war against the soul." Though we walk on earth, let us live as citizens of heaven, striving to live no longer according to the flesh but rather in a holy and spiritual way. Paul rouses us to this when he writes: "Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, so that you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect." But since we have not been conformed to the world, having escaped worldly deceit, we shall be imitated by it [?]. Knowing that this is so, the Saviour said: "If you were of the world, the world would love its own; but because you are not of the world, therefore the world hates you." So it pursues out of hatred. But when it thirsts for blood and glares like a bull in uncontrollable rage, God reins it in, not allowing it even, so to speak, to wound with harsh words. For God said to Laban, it says: "Take care that you do not speak evil against Jacob." Yet the world accuses, as though it had been robbed and its gods had been lost to it. And Rachel had in fact stolen them. But notice what happens. Laban searched for the gods with Leah, and also with the two maidservants, and did not find them, it says. Rachel was sitting on them, pleading the way of women. What, then, does this mean? The overthrow of the idols was not the achievement of the Jewish Synagogue, nor of those born into slavery, but of the youngest, Rachel, that is, of the Church, which has heaped dishonour on things made by hands, and all but fulfils in their case what was spoken through the prophet: "And you shall remove the idols overlaid with silver, and those overlaid with gold you shall grind to powder, and scatter them like the water of a menstruous woman, and thrust them out like dung." Since Laban did not find his gods, he then made terms of peace with the divine Jacob. For once the world no longer has its falsely named gods, it will be a friend; or rather, Christ has already become the bond of peace. He again is the most approved stone, the precious, the chief cornerstone, the honoured one, the head of the corner, the one laid in the foundations of Zion. For Jacob, it says, set up a pillar, as a figure of Christ. And other stones are heaped together, those of the holy apostles, or of those justified by faith and sanctified in the Spirit, elegantly prefiguring the coming together around Christ. For of the holy apostles the prophetic word said: "For holy stones are rolling upon the earth." For the divine disciples ran through the whole earth, carrying the gospel proclamation to the nations. And to those justified by faith the wise Paul writes: "In whom you also are built together into a dwelling place of God in the Holy Spirit." So the gathering of stones is called Heap of Testimony by Laban, but the divine Jacob carries the meaning up to something still greater and incomparably superior, that is, to Christ, naming what had been made The Heap Is Witness. For Christ himself is the head of those who believe. And that, when Christ the Saviour of all saves his own and leads them out of the wickedness in the world, the multitude of angels will be present to minister, plainly fulfilling the service assigned to them, one may easily learn from these words too. For when Laban had now withdrawn and gone back home in peace, "Jacob," it says, "looked up and saw a camp encamped, and the angels of God met him. And Jacob said, when he saw them: This is the camp of God. And he called the name of the place Camps." And it is written: "The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will deliver them." And again: "He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways." Truly our Lord Jesus Christ saves all who love him; through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

The way of life of the saints is not unadmired, at least among those who have chosen to live in the best way; yet the glory of their conduct will surpass all speech. Still, it can become a good model for those who wish to live devoutly, showing in many ways how one ought to make one's way straight toward what is fitting and pleasing to God. For I say, or rather the word of divinely inspired Scripture itself says, that we must rightly consider the outcome of the conduct of the saints of old and imitate their faith, and all but walk in the footsteps of the virtue that was in them. For it would be absurd if those who have become skilled in the royal arts take those before them as their teachers in this, and hasten to emulate those who have most precisely mastered what is excellent in them, while we ourselves, whose aim is to achieve virtue, do not fix the eye of the mind on the excellences of the ancients and in some way take from them an impression of the things by which one may become most approved before God, and make one's own mind skilled in holy conduct. Let the divine Jacob, then, be set before us, no less than anyone. As far as was possible, he walked blamelessly the road of life in his conduct, in a manner suited, I mean, to the time in which he lived. He had the God of all as his helper and protector, who sometimes allowed him to meet with toils for his good (for no one could win the glories of virtue without sweat), but who after the training crowned him with joys and, as with one of the strongest of contestants, enriched him with an abundance of prizes. Do not say to yourself, 'Why did God not grant the saints gladness [?] free of toil?' For that would have been to leave them untrained, and by no means to grant them well-being as a reward for virtue, but rather to make his kindness toward them, and the splendid and most desirable generosity of his gifts, the fruit of an untested inclination of the will. Rather, they had to be seen to be approved, and to show themselves beforehand by their very deeds worthy of what comes from God, and to be set before those who came after them as an example and a clear model of the need to choose to be most industrious and vigorous, bearing in mind that for those who live a life without toil and worthy of condemnation there will be no reward, but that the most excellent things of all will surely follow those who are most hardworking and who have valued sweat for the sake of good things above the sweetest things in life. So one of the wise said: 'My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for trial; set your heart straight and endure.' For endurance produces proven character, and proven character hope, and hope does not put to shame, as it is written. But let us pursue the purpose set before us.

After Laban's departure from Mount Gilead, then, the divine Jacob was hurrying toward his homeland and wanted to make haste. But scarcely had he been freed from Laban's attack and caught his breath a little when he immediately fell into worse fears. For since, departing from Mesopotamia and returning to the land of Canaan, he had to pass through the middle of Seir, where Esau lived, he was very much afraid. He knew well that he had grieved him over the blessing and over the birthright itself. How he removed his grief over these things and brought his brother to love and gentleness, how is this not worth seeing, and admiring besides? It is written, then: 'And Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to Esau his brother, to the land of Seir, to the country of Edom, and he commanded them, saying: Thus you shall say to my lord Esau: Thus says your servant Jacob: I have sojourned with Laban and stayed until now; and I have oxen and donkeys and sheep, and menservants and maidservants. And I have sent to tell my lord Esau, so that your servant may find favor before you. And the messengers returned to Jacob, saying: We came to your brother Esau, and he is coming to meet you, and four hundred men with him. And Jacob was greatly afraid and at a loss. And he divided the people who were with him, and the oxen and the sheep, into two camps. And Jacob said: If Esau comes to one camp and cuts it down, the second camp will be saved. And Jacob said: God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, Lord, you who said to me, Return to the land of your birth, and I will do you good: let it be enough for me, of all the righteousness and all the truth that you have shown to your servant. For with this staff of mine I crossed the Jordan, and now I have become two camps. Deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau, for I fear him, lest he come and strike me down, and the mother with the children. But you said: I will surely do you good, and I will make your offspring like the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted for multitude.' Do you see how he approaches Esau with flattery, all but fawning on the aggrieved man, and tries by kind speech to steal away the unchecked force of his anger? For although by his father's blessing he had been allotted the better place, and had been preferred with the honor of the firstborn, and had God as his helper, he yields in a manner befitting a saint, plainly choosing to fulfill that saying: 'If possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people.' For a word that is sometimes harsh and hard and full of arrogance will be unbearable to some. But as the wise writer of Proverbs wrote, 'A submissive answer turns away wrath.' And observe, I pray, the righteous man's skill in piety. He sends messengers to ask for peace and to carry the most tender words to Esau, for he instructed them to say again and again, 'Thus says your servant Jacob.' And he himself turns again to prayer and does not let go of the help that always saves. And he confirms that the experience of what had already passed made clear his hope for what was to come, saying: 'With this staff of mine I crossed the Jordan, and now I have become two camps.' For he meant: 'With nothing but the staff I had from home I crossed the Jordan, and I have become master of many things, because I had your favor, O Master.' From this, then, we too shall learn that we must be meek and peaceable, and seek by every means to live without strife. For 'the servant of the Lord,' it says, 'must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all,' as it is written. Nothing prevents us from also making use of human skill for good ends; indeed, I think this would be most praiseworthy. But even if we do so, we must seek God's care and the help that comes from above, not thinking lofty thoughts, but rather pondering what is written: 'The greater you are, the more you should humble yourself, and you will find favor before the Lord.' If we choose to think and act in this way, we shall gain the goods that come from peace, and shall turn those who rage against us to gentleness. For 'wild beasts,' it says, 'will be at peace with you.' This is what Jacob did. For he not only softened his brother with winning and gentle words, but also made him a sharer in gifts and in his possessions, allotting him a very rich portion: sheep and oxen, goats and donkeys, camels and calves. For peace is better than money, and the possession of passing things should give way to love toward one's brothers. And so the divine Jacob feared his brother Esau, as I said, and was downcast, as if he were about to suffer the effects of his anger at any moment. But Esau, trampling down the envy he had at first, embraced Jacob and greeted him with tears, and yielded to the laws of nature the claims of love that he had been able to delay [?]. For it is written: 'And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him and kissed him, and fell upon his neck, and they both wept.' And all these achievements of meekness are the fruit of a humble and unboastful mind, and a gift of God's kindness to those who love him, who levels what is steep, smooths what is rough, and enriches with joys those who are eager to cleave to him. But I think we must now recast the narrative as spiritual contemplation. Come, then, let us speak, going back and returning to the beginning of the whole account. For so the mystery of Christ will become clear to those who choose to learn what is good.

Fearing, then, as was natural, his brother, who was murderous and raging like a wild beast, the divine Jacob set out on the journey to Haran and to Laban, his father, that is, Isaac, approving his flight. For it seemed to him that in this way he ought to evade the attack of the aggrieved man. Having come to Laban, he was betrothed to the man's daughters, Leah, I mean, and Rachel, and became rich in the birth of children and in herds of livestock, and besides these in other property as well. When at last he had come to this degree of prosperity, he thought of having a house of his own, and departed from Haran and from Laban's hearth together with what he had acquired, and indeed along with his wives and children. When Laban pursued him he was overtaken, but he made terms of peace, and Christ confirmed the bond of love; for the stone set up as a pillar was a type of him. Then after this, when Laban had at last hurried back home and gone away, he came to peace also with the one who had long been murderous and raging, that is, Esau. For they embraced one another, burying, as it were, their ill feeling over what had happened before by coming together in mutual love. With these events the whole account of the history was completed. We remember that we assigned to Jacob the person of Christ himself, and in some places also that of those justified by faith; and we said that Esau represents in himself the people of the circumcision and under the law. This is especially so since the God and Master of all himself says to Rebekah, while she was still in labor with the pair of youths: 'Two nations and two peoples shall be separated from your womb, and one people shall surpass the other people, and the elder shall serve the younger.' And this has indeed been fulfilled through Christ. For those from Israel, being first in time, and for this reason called firstborn, have come to be behind, and have been put at the back of those who are through faith in Christ. These have inherited the glory of the firstborn on account of the Firstborn who is among them, even though he is also the Only-begotten, to whom they have been conformed, having rebirth through the Spirit to incorruption and sanctification. Burning with envy, then, Esau, that is, Israel, persecuted Jacob, I mean Christ. But, as I said, our discussion does not draw a strict distinction in these matters, always seeking what is fitting, and sometimes referring Jacob to Christ, sometimes to the new people in faith. And Christ, persecuted in a way and not of his own will, departed to the land of the gentiles, crying aloud: 'I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my inheritance, I have given my beloved soul into the hands of her enemies. My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; she has raised her voice against me; therefore I have hated her.' Yet after the resurrection from the dead, out of gentleness and love for humanity, he also showed himself to the women in the garden, saying: 'Go, tell my brothers to go away into Galilee, and there they will see me.' Having come, then, into Galilee, as the divine Jacob came to Haran, he shepherded the sheep of Laban, that is, of the world, which had worshiped the creation and gone astray, just as Laban had. Once there, like a bridegroom he spiritually takes into his house a pure virgin, the Church from the gentiles, that is, Rachel, bringing in with her also the one already joined to him beforehand through the law, the synagogue of the Jews, of which Leah is a type. For the remnant of Israel has been saved, according to the prophet's word, even if perhaps not the whole multitude has honored the grace that comes through faith in Christ. Christ, then, having been revealed as bridegroom among the gentiles, and having by grace regenerated a great many to adoption in the Spirit, and having gathered a truly countless flock of rational sheep, was persecuted by the world. For some in the world who had been raised to the highest honors and held on earth a power hard to overcome made war on the glory of Christ. But divine grace won over even the world, and the world too came to peace with Christ, as Laban did with Jacob. But in later times our Lord Jesus Christ will also make his own Israel, the persecutor of old, just as Jacob, after his return from Haran, embraced Esau. For that Israel too will in due time be received into love for Christ through faith, we can hardly doubt if we yield to the words of the divinely inspired Scripture. For the Master of all said somewhere through one of the holy prophets: 'For the sons of Israel shall sit many days without a king, without a ruler, without sacrifice, without an altar, without priesthood, without oracles; and after this the sons of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God and David their king, and they shall hope in the Lord and in his good things in the last of days.' For while Christ, the Saviour of us all, is still gathering those from the gentiles who have believed, Israel has in a way remained idle, not having the law as arbiter of what must be done, not offering the prescribed offerings at the divine altar, but waiting for Christ as he returns, so to speak, from the calling of the gentiles, so that at last he too may be brought into the house through faith and all but bound together with the others by the law of love. Notice that Jacob returns from Haran rejoicing in the birth of children and in many herds of livestock, and only then receives Esau too into love. Israel, then, will return in due time, after the calling of the gentiles, and will marvel at the wealth that is in Christ. For those who wish can easily discern this very thing also through the events of the history. Jacob sent gifts to Esau, winning him over to love by the generosity of his gifts as well. And he also sent messengers of peace to speak to him. And Christ makes plain that in due time this too will come about: that one will come before long who will establish their friendship. For he said somewhere to the Jews through the voice of a prophet: 'And behold, I will send you Elijah the Tishbite before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes, who will restore the heart of the father to the son, and the heart of a man to his neighbor, lest I come and strike the earth utterly.' When he comes, he will, as is fitting, bring my intractable Israel to shame, turn him away from his ancient anger, and make him friendly and peaceable toward Christ, all but showing him, as already present, the gifts of Christ's generosity, that is, the hope of those who believe. For the things of the promise will no longer stretch out over a long span of time for those who believe then; rather, the gift is near and grace is close at hand. For the son of sin will at once be destroyed, and Christ, the Saviour of us all, will come down from heaven with the holy angels; through whom and with whom be glory to the Father with the Holy Spirit to the ages of ages. Amen.

Through sin, human nature had gone down to death. Since it was entirely cut off from the One who knew how to save, the being fashioned in the divine image was all but a prisoner taken at spearpoint, and was weighed down with the burden of slavery. For it bowed its neck, though not willingly, to Satan, who had got the upper hand. In his overweening arrogance (for the evil spirit is haughty), he was emboldened against practically everything on earth, saying: “I will seize the whole world in my hand like a nest, and I will carry it off like abandoned eggs, and there is no one who will escape me or speak against me.” For he had made himself king by usurpation, as I said, and had been named the god of this age. The world worshiped him and served the creature rather than the Creator. But since God took pity on us, brought to such a depth of misery, he promised to send us his Son from heaven, to restore human nature once more to what it was in the beginning. “The things in Christ are a new creation,” according to the Scriptures. The blessed prophets became the bearers of these good tidings meant for us, “who prophesied of the grace that was to come to us, searching out to what or what kind of time the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing, when it testified in advance to the sufferings of Christ and the glories that would follow them. It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but us in these things.” So the Savior's disciple writes. Much is said among the prophets about the incarnation of our Savior, and about how a redeemer would come in due time. To help those who will read this understand more easily, there is no harm in bringing forward a few passages. It would be fitting to make the matter a charge against the Jewish people, as one can see from the facts themselves. Although it was possible to discern the Savior's coming from the words of the prophets (or rather, the wretches perhaps even understood it from the very shadow in the law), they perversely opposed the oracles delivered by God, and Christ himself. Or else it was as our wise Paul told us: “A hardening has come upon Israel in part, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not hear or understand.” The Savior himself said the same. So the inspired Isaiah spoke, or rather, in his own writings he brought Emmanuel himself before us, plainly saying: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me. He has sent me to bring good news to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense.” These were the splendid achievements of his sojourn among us. Hosea, too, says of him somewhere: “And the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel will be gathered together, and they will appoint for themselves one head, and they will go up from the land, for great is the day of Jezreel.” At various times a great many teachers among the Jews persuaded the peoples in their charge to honor the God of all with their lips only, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men. But Christ has been set as the one head over all and for all, and we have gone up from the land; that is, we have been taught to set our minds on things above. For truly great is the day of Jezreel, that is, of God's seed, namely the Son. The inspired David also reminded us of this day, saying: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.” And our most wise Paul says besides: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” On this day, clearly, we have been saved, with Christ calling us to it. As the wise disciple said: “There is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” You will also hear Jeremiah plainly saying: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will raise up for David a righteous dawn. A king will reign and will understand, and he will execute judgment and righteousness on the earth. In his days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell in confidence. And this is his name, by which the Lord will call him: Josedek, among the prophets.” For Christ has reigned over us as a righteous king. He has executed judgment and righteousness, freeing from their sins those who had been deceived and condemning the enemy, Satan the usurper. His name is Josedek, that is, “righteousness of God.” For we have been justified in him, “not by works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his great mercy.” That is why God the Father also said: “My righteousness draws near swiftly, and my mercy will be revealed.” Christ has become mercy and righteousness for us from God the Father, and the splendid choir of the saints called him by this very name, “Christ.” For the blessed Samuel, renowned among the prophets, addressed the people of Israel, saying: “Behold, I have walked before you from my youth until this day. Here I am; testify against me before the Lord and before his Christ.” And again: “The Lord is witness among you, and his Christ is witness this day, that you have found nothing in my hand.” The blessed David speaks more clearly still. He all but accuses the madness of the Jews, their unbridled audacity against Christ, their futile schemes and childish reasonings, when he says: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things? The kings of the earth took their stand, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.” For the plans that Jewish ignorance laid against Christ were truly vain. Life could not have died, nor could he be held fast at the gates of Hades who said to the spirits below, “Come out,” and to those in darkness, “Be revealed.” The prophet Jeremiah lamented over Jerusalem as unholy, as the slayer of the Lord, as profane and ungrateful. This is what he said: “The breath of our face, Christ the Lord, was taken in their corruptions, he of whom we said, ‘In his shadow we shall live among the nations.’” When they ought to have chosen the grace that comes through faith as the way of salvation, they were caught fighting against God. So the Maker of all things, the only-begotten Word of God, lowered himself into self-emptying, was anointed by the Father, and became as we are. The purpose of his self-emptying was to save those on earth. And so the prophet Zephaniah announced the good news, saying: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem! Be glad and delight with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem! The Lord has taken away your iniquities; he has redeemed you from the hand of your enemies. The Lord, the King of Israel, will reign in your midst; you will see evil no more.” But the disobedient and unyielding, going beyond all audacity, committed against him the most shameful outrages of all. They acted lightly and deliberated rashly. So they have paid the penalty for their offenses: the wicked have perished wretchedly. Yet not entirely, for a remnant has been shown mercy and saved, as the prophet's words say.

The inspired Jacob was taught that these things would turn out this way in due time, as God gracefully gave the matter shape. I will explain how, first setting out, as I must, what the sacred Scriptures say. It runs as follows: “That night he rose and took his two wives, his two maidservants, and his eleven children, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok. He took them and crossed the brook, and brought across everything that was his. And Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him until morning. When the man saw that he could not prevail against him, he touched the broad part of his thigh, and the broad part of Jacob's thigh went numb as he wrestled with him. Then he said to him, ‘Let me go, for the dawn has come up.’ But Jacob said, ‘I will not let you go unless you bless me.’ He said to him, ‘What is your name?’ And he said, ‘Jacob.’ Then he said to him, ‘Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name, for you have prevailed with God, and you are strong with men.’ Jacob asked him, ‘Tell me your name.’ And he said, ‘Why do you ask my name?’ And he blessed him there. Jacob called the name of that place ‘Form of God,’ for ‘I have seen God face to face, and my life was preserved.’ The sun rose upon him as the Form of God passed by him, and he was limping on his thigh.” The inspired Jacob brought everything that was his across the Jabbok, that is, the brook, and he himself remained alone. How could the matter not be worth looking into? Come then, let us examine the reason, for this discussion will lead us straight on to spiritual matters.

Esau lived in Edom and Seir. He held sway over that land, and his power was beyond Jacob's control. Jacob was leaving Mesopotamia and Laban's household and hurrying to reach his father's land, and he had no choice but to make his return through Edom. So he very prudently sought peace with his brother. He told messengers to go ahead with splendid gifts of hospitality, and ordered them to announce in advance that he himself would come to see and greet him. By gifts and words he set out to tame the man who had long been murderous and savage. When the men he had sent ahead returned, they said: “We came to your brother Esau, and behold, he himself is coming to meet you, and four hundred men with him.” The inspired Jacob was terribly afraid. He could not know for certain which Esau he would meet: one friendly and peaceable, or one no less aroused to his usual audacity and bent on acting out of envy. Jacob brought everything that was his across and remained alone. I suppose he had certainly reasoned this out to himself: if Esau proved kind and gentle, there would be no difficulty in bringing his wives and children back across to be present and greet him. But if he came still harsh and quarrelsome, and no less bent on murder, he would spare the little ones and pity the women's tears. Finding Jacob alone, he would vent his rage, and the death of the man who had wronged him would be enough to satisfy him. But by the power of God, things turned out for him beyond all hope, as we have already said, for they embraced each other. From what happened, then, Jacob was taught the power of the mystery. How, or in what way? I will tell you again. He brought all his household across the brook, and when he remained alone, a man wrestled with him until morning. We say that the one who wrestled with him was a holy angel, a type of Christ, who became like us, because of his human form. Because Jacob did not cross the brook along with the others (that is, the Jabbok, whose name means “wrestling”), the apparent fight took place between them. And how might the meaning of this be understood, its innermost sense? Christ does not wrestle with those who cross the Jordan, of which the Jabbok is a type, nor does he count those who honor his mysteries as enemies or adversaries. Rather, he saves them, and when they have conquered the world, as in a contest (a spiritual one, I mean), he crowns them and makes them radiant with the highest honors. The river's name is “wrestling,” for “the kingdom of heaven is taken by force, and the violent seize it.” And: “Very narrow is the gate and hard the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it.” So the event intimated that those who in time would be descended from Jacob would not cross the Jordan, that is, the grace that comes through holy baptism, but would impiously dishonor it, and would then have Emmanuel himself as their adversary. That those who do not honor him with faith will in every way and without doubt be counted among his opponents, the Savior himself assures us, saying: “Whoever is not with me is against me.” May those who have believed be with him! And who could doubt that the reverse is also true? In any case, it says: “The man wrestled with Jacob until morning, and he saw that he could not prevail against him.” Do you hear how the wrestling took place at night? And Jacob was shown to be falling and beaten, because he was seeking the impossible: he had chosen to fight against God and to overpower the God who can do all things. This, I think, is what the inspired David also said in his psalm about the people of Israel, that they were plotting terrible things against their own head (not to say against Christ): “They devised a plan that they cannot establish.” So Israel fought against Christ while in darkness. That is, it did not have the divine mind to give it light, nor the dawning day, nor the morning star that rises spiritually in the hearts of believers. For it remained disobedient, and as the prophet says: “While they waited for light, darkness came upon them; while they waited for brightness, they walked in the dead of night.” But the inspired Paul writes to those who have been justified in faith and enriched with the riches of the Spirit, saying: “We are not of night or of darkness, but sons of light and of day.” He indicated that they had risen above the ignorance of the Jews and had left behind the darkness that suits them, when he added: “The night is far gone, and the day has drawn near. Let us then cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk decently, as in the day.” So believers are in the day, while the disobedient fight against Christ as in the night and in darkness. This is what the descendants of Jacob did, but they were weakened and beaten, and they cannot walk straight. For the man who wrestled with Jacob, it says, touched the broad part of his thigh, and the broad part of Jacob's thigh went numb as he wrestled with him. Come, let us say what we will learn from this as well. In the divinely inspired Scripture the thigh generally hints at the parts of the body needed for begetting children, and so by extension at offspring itself, for in everyone the generative members lie near the thighs. So when the blessed Abraham sent his trusted servant to Mesopotamia to take a wife for Isaac, he ordered him to swear an oath, saying: “Put your hand under my thigh.” That is: “Swear by God, and by those who will come from me, and by the Lord's descent.” The thigh, then, signifies those who come from the thighs. So Jacob's thigh went numb, for those born from his thighs, that is, the people of Israel, became lame. The Savior himself bears witness to this through the voice of David, saying: “Foreign sons lied to me; foreign sons grew old and limped away from their paths.” Wise Paul also knew that Israel had suffered a spiritual lameness. He writes: “Therefore lift up your drooping hands and paralyzed knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be turned aside but rather be healed.” Such lameness could never be healed in any other way than through faith in Christ and love for him alone. Those who did not accept the faith have remained lame and turned aside by their affliction, as the blessed Paul says. So the injury Jacob suffered to his thigh while he wrestled is a riddle pointing to Israel's spiritual lameness. Further, we would not be speaking falsely in affirming that Christ in some way opposes and wrestles with those who are in night and whose minds are darkened, disabling them with spiritual lameness. One could learn this no less easily from what follows. For the man who wrestled with Jacob said to him: “Let me go, for the dawn has come up.” Do you see how he will not keep wrestling once day is dawning? He does not fight with those who have come into the light. Those who have passed into this most brilliant state can fittingly say from then on: “O God, my God, I rise early to seek you.” And in addition: “In the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you, and you will watch over me.” For when the light of righteousness, that is, Christ, rises in our minds and sends a spiritual radiance into our hearts, then indeed, then we will stand before him shining brightly through our goodness in every respect, and we will show ourselves worthy of his watchful care from above. “For the eyes of the Lord,” it says, “are on the righteous.” So when dawn is already rising, he ends the wrestling. See how wisely and with what great skill he teaches Jacob, by wishing to leave, to cling to him and to long earnestly for him to grant what Jacob needed for salvation. The one who had won outright and was able to leave even if the loser would not let go says, “Let me go,” as though giving Jacob the power to hold on tight if he chose. We will find something like this in what God said, wisely and with a purpose, to Moses. God wanted to punish senseless Israel for its idolatry in the wilderness, for it had made the calf. But as if allowing the blessed Moses to restrain his anger if he wished and to make supplication for the sinners, he says: “I have spoken to you once and twice, saying: I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stiff-necked people. Let me alone, and I will destroy them and blot out their name from under heaven, and I will make you into a great nation.” When Moses understood the purpose of God's gentleness, he set about restraining him and said: “If you will forgive their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me also out of this book that you have written.” It was in this same way, then, that the one wrestling with Jacob said to him, “Let me go.” And Jacob, quickly understanding who the wrestler was and now grasping the whole matter, holds on to him tightly and says: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” He was blessed, and the form his blessing took was the change from his first name to another. For it says: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.” Jacob means “one who grasps the heel,” that is, one who is energetic and sober enough to accomplish what he must, while Israel is interpreted “a mind seeing God.” Come, then, let us say what this means, drawing the narrative back a little.

Jacob wrestled and was defeated, and in the dark he suffered the numbing, in the thigh, that is. After that he holds on to the one wrestling with him, now peaceably, since the light was dawning and it was already daybreak. He pressed him, as it were, to bless him, and indeed he was blessed, for he was renamed Israel. Israel, as it were, set his disobedience and stubbornness against Emmanuel, but did so in ignorance and darkness, the darkness of unlearning, I mean. For he had been hardened, and he recognized him only with difficulty, when the divine light rose in his mind too. And he was blessed by Christ, perhaps not as a whole, but at least in the portion of those who believed. For there came to be in Israel a remnant chosen by grace, as it is written, and not a few of the Jews believed. Foremost among these were the holy disciples. They were once Jacob: they had the weakness that belongs to the law, and they were supplanters, as it were, briskly [?] and doing all they could to avoid offending God, for they were blameless as to the righteousness that is in the law. But afterwards they became Israel too, that is, they passed over at last to a mind that sees God. To know Christ, who he is and from where he came among us, and the manner of his economy in the flesh, is, I say, to receive into the mind the light of the true vision of God. That knowledge of God is greater, more excellent and incomparably better than the way of life under the law, he himself will assure us when he says through one of the prophets: “For I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and knowledge of God rather than whole burnt offerings.” And Paul, though he had been brilliant and blameless as to the righteousness that is in the law, “counts such things as loss because of the surpassing worth of the knowledge of Christ.” Paul will make it clear again that a pure knowledge of Christ ranks even above splendid works, when he writes to Timothy that he should train himself in godliness: “For bodily training is of little benefit, but godliness is beneficial in every way, since it holds promise for the present life and for the life to come.” As the Savior himself said to the Father in heaven: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” So even if someone happens to be Jacob, that is, if he can supplant, and can deftly and vigorously escape everything that tends to weaken him and draw him into sin, he will advance through Christ to an understanding fit for the saints. He will also be called Israel, that is, “one who sees God.” Then, yes then, he will be strong with men too, because he has prevailed with God. To know God and to attain knowledge of him, even if one sees in a mirror and in a riddle, cannot be the work of someone feeble and sickly. It belongs to one who has been raised above weakness in this regard, so that he makes no account of fleshly and worldly things and can dart toward what pleases God with a quick and almost unstoppable mind. It is this person who will be strong among men and will prevail with God. So the holy Jacob is blessed, but he presses further, saying: “Tell me your name.” “And he said,” it says, “Why do you ask my name?” God does not tell his name, and by this very fact he shows that he is God by nature. For God would have no name of his own, as a man does; rather, he is named in many ways from what he is. He is light and life and power and truth, the Only-begotten, the radiance and imprint of the one who begot him, mercy and wisdom and righteousness and redemption. The blessed Jacob understood, then, that this must be God, to whom no name of his own could belong, and he called the name of that place “Form of God.” “For I have seen God face to face,” he says, “and my soul was saved.” Notice how he became Israel, that is, “one who sees God.” Though it was a man who wrestled with him, he says that he saw God face to face and that his own soul was saved. For the knowledge of Christ is a thing that saves. The Word, then, is God even in the flesh, for the patriarch Jacob says that he has seen God face to face. “And as the sun rose,” it says, “the form of God passed by, and he was limping on his thigh.” As I have already said, once the Jews were enlightened the wrestling ceased. And the form of God passed by, that is, Christ ascended into heaven. But Israel has not been freed from lameness, for not all of Israel has been saved. Through those who disobey, it suffers so that it cannot walk wholly upright. So he was renamed Israel, and the supplanter was enrolled anew as a mind that sees God. And what comes after this? “And Jacob set out for Tents,” it says, “and made himself houses, and he made tents for his cattle. Therefore he called the name of that place Tents.” You hear how he dwelt in tents. This too would be a clear sign that Israel's way of thinking had changed for the better. For once he had pitched tents, he also lived in them. When the mind already sees and has been granted the vision of God, and has been nurtured and is running onward to perfection by progress toward what is better, it would bear a fruit precious to God: it would no longer make any account of the affairs of this world, but would regard life in the body as a sojourn. Such a mind befits the saints and is an exact indication of an exceptional and elevated way of life. You would be convinced of this by the blessed David, who had reached this height and sings: “Spare me, for I am a sojourner on the earth and a stranger, like all my fathers.” And Paul writes to those who have come to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ and have reached mature manhood: “For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come, whose craftsman and builder is God.” So when the holy Jacob, or Israel, chose to live in tents, it would be a sign, and one not obscure to anyone of sense, that those who already open their eyes toward God and have minds made radiant ought to regard the affairs of this world as a sojourn. Then he moves on to Salem, a city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan. There the righteous man was tested again, when he suffered the wrongs done to his daughter Dinah. She was a young girl, a maiden still in her youth, and she ran out of her father's tent to look at the daughters of the local people. For the female sex is always eager to hasten to the company of those its own age. So the girl ran out, and Shechem the son of Hamor shamefully violated her. He took her virginity, and then, gripped by an uncontrollable desire, he asked to make the girl his wife. Then, yes then, Simeon and Levi, the girl's brothers, were whetted to anger. They found the outrage unbearable and plotted to do unholy things to the wrongdoers. They persuade the men of Shechem to adopt their ancestral and customary circumcision, and then they killed them, having cast off all mercy and pity entirely. The holy Jacob was greatly indignant at this and rebuked them, saying: “You have made me hateful, so that I am evil in the eyes of those who live in the land.” Those who did the killing set no limit to their anger, nor did they think anything that was not wholly perverse, as one might expect from men raised by a righteous father. For they plundered and killed men who had chosen to think as they did and who had trusted them in good faith. What benefit, then, might come to us from this? For divinely inspired Scripture never speaks idly. Come, let us say as well as we can.

We have been born with a spiritual birth and are counted among the children of God through Christ. Suppose, then, that a soul already reborn through holy baptism and made a daughter of God should be corrupted by those who make a practice of this. She might be led astray into choosing to think fleshly things, or as it were into twisted notions about God, for such truly are the paltry opinions of the unholy heretics. In that case her brothers in the faith may hold priestly rank, as Levi did, or perhaps they may be understood as Simeon, that is, those who stand in the rank of the obedient, for Simeon means “obedience.” Let them be indignant that someone close to them in the faith has been wronged, but let them not go as far as bloodshed or exact savage punishment from the corruptors, lest they hear Christ say to them: “You have made me hateful, so that I am evil in the eyes of those who live in the land.” We must remember that the Savior himself once rebuked the holy Peter when he drew his sword, saying: “Put your sword back into its sheath, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword.” We who have chosen to contend on behalf of piety toward God ought not to arm ourselves with swords against our enemies. We ought rather to endure suffering, even if some choose to persecute us; to bless when we are reviled; and when we suffer, not to answer back, but rather to hand ourselves over to the one who judges justly. Those who wish to avoid being corrupted must take care not to wander away from their father's tent, that is, the house of God, and not to approach the flocks of foreigners, that is, of those who think otherwise. For when Dinah left her father's tent, she was carried off into the house of Shechem. But she would never have been outraged if she had been glad to stay in her father's rooms and had lived in the tents of the saints. The blessed David will convince us that this is a good thing and contributes not a little to our benefit, when he sings: “One thing I have asked of the Lord, and this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to visit his holy temple. For he hid me in his tent; in the day of my troubles he sheltered me in the secret place of his tent.” So when Jacob had become thoroughly fearful and disheartened, God ordered him to set out. The passage runs as follows: “And God said to Jacob: Arise, go up to the place Bethel and live there, and make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you were fleeing from the face of your brother Esau.
