And Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him: Put away the foreign gods from among you, and purify yourselves, and change your garments, and let us arise and go up to Bethel, and let us make an altar there to the God who heard me in the day of affliction, who was with me and kept me safe on the road on which I travelled. And they gave Jacob the foreign gods that were in their hands and the earrings that were in their ears, and Jacob hid them under the terebinth at Shechem, and they did away with them until this very day.” The God of all summoned the righteous man from Shechem to Bethel, and he did not disobey. On the way he came to Luz, where he was granted a vision of God and was confirmed by promises that he would be the father of many nations. Then he goes up to Bethel, “and there,” it says, “Jacob set up a pillar in the place where God had spoken with him, a pillar of stone, and he poured a drink offering on it and poured oil on it. And Jacob called the name of the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.” Many things together offer clear proof that Jacob had turned toward the land of Israel and had made an incomparably better change. He lived in tents, all but showing by this that the race of the saints are sojourners in the world. Then, in the meantime, he suffered what befell his daughter. He was grieved beyond measure at those who had been basely overcome by anger, Simeon and Levi, I mean, and he rebuked them sharply, showing us by his actions that forbearance and endurance in trials befit the saints. And when he was called by God and went up to Bethel, that is, to the house of God (for this is what Bethel means), he offers sacred worship to God and shows himself to be a guide into the mysteries. He makes plain to those who follow him how one ought to enter the house of God. For he ordered them to throw away the foreign gods as so much refuse and uncleanness, and to change their garments. This is just what we are accustomed to do when we are called into God's presence and enter his divine temple, especially at the time of holy baptism. We must put the foreign gods out of our midst, as it were, and as we depart from such error we must say: “I renounce you, Satan, and all your pomp and all your worship.” We must all change our garment too, stripping off, as it were, the old man, who is corrupted by deceitful desires, and putting on the new man, who is renewed after the image of his creator. The women with Jacob also cast off what was in their ears. For when women too enter the house of God, they wear no fleshly adornment and even let down their hair, freeing their heads, perhaps, from the charges that arise from braiding. This, I say, is what the women's removal of the ornaments from their ears means. So when we go up to Bethel, that is, to the house of God, there we will recognize the stone, the chosen stone that has become the head of the corner, that is, Christ. And we will see him anointed by the Father for the gladness and rejoicing of all the world under heaven. For the Son has been anointed by God the Father, as I said, “the gladness of us all, the joy of the whole world,” in the words of the Psalmist. You can see this too foreshadowed in what we have just said. For Jacob set up the stone as a pillar and poured oil and wine over it. What he did was a type of the mystery of Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

Great indeed, beyond dispute, is the mystery of godliness, that is, Christ. Very deep is the account concerning him, and the purpose of his dispensation in the flesh. Those who approach it carelessly will hardly grasp it. To the sound-minded it will become clear, though not without sweat, since they are lit by divine grace, wise and quick of understanding, and learned in the writings of the law and the prophets. So the divine Peter, foremost among the disciples and set above the others, confessed the faith rightly, and he heard from Christ: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." For God the Father initiates us into the account concerning the Son, and in this way he saves us, bringing us to him as Savior and Redeemer. "For no one comes to me," he says, "unless my Father who sent me draws him." We should understand the account concerning him through the whole of holy Scripture, so to speak, and gather an unerring faith. Then our hearts will not be shaken by accursed double-mindedness, as though drunk, and we will not fall into the tossings that come from ignorance. So let us hear God speaking through the voice of the prophets: "They loved to move their feet, and they did not hold back, and God took no pleasure in them." This is why he establishes us in the truth through countless images. Through the events that happened in their own times he usefully laid down faith in him beforehand, setting up brilliant images, as it were, of the knowledge of him. Let us see, then, whether what I have said proves true once again in the story of the divine Joseph. The account concerning him runs as follows: "These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph, when he was seventeen years old, was shepherding the sheep with his brothers. He was young, and he was with the sons of Bilhah and the sons of Zilpah, his father's wives. And Joseph brought an evil report to Israel his father. Now Jacob loved Joseph more than all his sons, because he was the son of his old age. And he made him a coat of many colors. When his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his sons, they hated him, and could not speak a peaceable word to him."

The writer of the book has given an exact list of those descended from Esau. The sacred Scripture has taught us who was born of whom, where on earth each of them settled, and over whom each gained rule. Yet not one of them did anything noble, or even worthy of remembrance. The narrative all but swims past those it names and puts in, as it were, at the divine Joseph, and it makes a splendid narrative of those of Jacob's blood. Joseph was the youngest of them (for he was seventeen years old), yet he did not shirk a shepherd's sweat. Together with his other brothers he took his share in the same labors. He did not prize the ease that is so delightful to the young and somehow always dear to them. He did not refuse the cares of life that came to him early, nor did he prefer to take his leisure, as one still counted among boys might have done. Instead, like an old man, he had already reached calm in his reasoning and had a firmly settled mind. He spoke with grey-haired wisdom and showed in advance the beauty of his future splendor. So he was naturally admired by his blessed and affectionate father, and was thought worthy of special love and tender care. "For he was," it says, "the son of his old age." What does this mean? The text is examining the dispositions within us. In some parents, affection for their children is entirely equal and in no way less toward any of them. But nature often prevails and overpowers the mind, persuading it to give a little more than to the others to those who are weaker, since they need more pressing care. Besides, when many children have been born, affection somehow tapers off, and the surplus of love comes at last to anchor in the youngest, who somehow snatches to himself the affection meant for those who came before him. For the human mind loves novelty. It does not shake off its weariness with what it already has, but it grasps eagerly at what is not yet present or has only just been acquired, and feels a keener desire for these things. So the divine Jacob loved Joseph more than the others, "because he was the son of his old age." But we should note that, although he had first taken Leah into his house in Haran, he loved Rachel, who bore Joseph and, as she was dying, Benjamin. To this we reply that both were sons of his old age. But Joseph's natural gift for everything was not shared equally by all, and it showed the old man leaning, as it were, the other way, toward him. For he probably reasoned that Joseph would be illustrious and celebrated. A youth who paid no heed to the frolics of his age and was already becoming a man, how could he fail to become one of the admired? The blessed Jacob also did something new for him beyond the others: he wove him a coat of many colors and honored him with the finest clothing. What followed from this? The sons of Zilpah and Bilhah were whetted to anger. Along with them the sons of the free woman, I mean Leah, were carried away into extraordinary resentment, and from then on they harbored envy against the boy. The youth had done them no wrong. But the father's love and the boy's fine nature kindled in them the fire of unjust spite. For a while they shot at him with their tongues, reviling and disparaging him in the ways one might expect enemies to reproach a young man. This, I think, is the meaning of "They brought an evil report about Joseph to Israel their father." So skirmishes, as it were, were the first-fruits of their unholy designs: fault-finding and jibes from an unbridled tongue that was now set to serve envy. Their hostility was inflamed to a greater intensity by a cause of this kind. God showed the youth in advance that in due time he would be illustrious and admired, set above his brothers, and crowned with glory at the last. This, I think, was a challenge, sharpening the youth's desire for virtue. Trainers anoint the young and spur them on to the boldest feats. They persuade them to choose endurance and to value it, announcing in advance the prizes that go with the glory of victory: the generous gifts of those who preside over the games, the acclamations of the spectators, the praises, the applause. In the same way the God of all, when he sees a well-endowed soul that is distinguished by a tested and unalloyed mind and well suited to everything excellent, calls it to choose to do good. He shows it beforehand what is to come and providentially rouses it to eagerness, clearly an eagerness for virtue. So a vision and a voice from above once came to the young man, I mean Joseph. Marveling, I suppose, he shared it with his brothers, saying: "Listen to this dream that I dreamed. I thought we were binding sheaves in the middle of the field, and my sheaf rose and stood upright, and your sheaves gathered around and bowed down to my sheaf." His brothers said to him: "Are you really going to reign over us? Are you really going to be lord over us?" And they hated him even more because of his dreams and because of his words. Observe, then, that their spite keeps growing, and they turn what the dreams hinted at into a kind of food for envy. From the start they had been grieved beyond measure, especially because he had been honored. How could they have borne it, then, to bow down to him by choice and to accord him so august and so greatly exalted a rank? But it is worth seeing how envy always attacks in an unholy way and advances through the same evils. We shall find this beast to be, above all, blind and at war with God. Look: when God foretold to Joseph the splendor of the glory to come, they ought to have reflected clearly that God, who judges justly, would not bestow the highest honors on those unworthy to receive them. Then they ought to have rejoiced in a brother whose hope was so plain and who had been honored by divine decree. This they did not do. Instead they drove the sting of envy in harder and raged like wild beasts, all but rebuking God, who had promised him glory and foretold that he would be renowned. We shall find that this also happened with Cain and Abel. The God of all judged Abel's sacrifice worthy of praise and accepted his offering by sending fire down from heaven, but he paid no regard to Cain's. At once Cain took murderous envy into himself. Setting his own anger, as it were, against the decrees from above, he pursued his brother with treachery and actually killed him. For envy always ends, somehow, in things like this. But what is the meaning of the visions? We shall take the sheaf as a sign of a season. The raising of the one sheaf would indicate renown in glory. So a time would come when the divine Joseph would be glorious, and the whole crowd of his brothers would fall down before him, as it were, and be brought under him. This was shown beforehand in a riddle by his sheaf, which received homage from the others. But Joseph's dreams did not stop there. He saw something else after this, and again he told it about himself to his blessed father and his brothers. "For he saw," it says, "another dream, and told it to his father and to his brothers, and said: 'Look, I have dreamed another dream: it was as if the sun and the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me.' And his father rebuked him and said to him: 'What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers really come and bow down to the ground before you?' And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the matter in mind." The old man was skillful and distinguished by the highest shrewdness. He understood the force of the visions, yet he rebuked the boy, saying: "Shall I and your mother and your brothers really come and bow down to the ground before you?" How should this be understood? The manner of the rebuke was wise and necessary. He cleverly checked the envy of those who were listening. In a way he also tamed the youth, who was being swept along by insufferable boldness, and called him to gentleness. He did not allow the boy to vaunt himself over his brothers because of what the dreams promised, nor to slight the honor due to his father without thinking, all but snatching for himself ahead of time the preeminence of his future splendor. See how cleverly he turns the force of the visions toward an impossible outcome. Rachel, who had borne Joseph, was already dead, and yet he says: "Shall I and your mother bow down to you?" As I said just now, he did this both to pull down the pride of the young man's heart and to lull to sleep the envy his brothers had stirred up against him. Yet he himself expected the thing to happen. He did not listen carelessly, nor did he think the words fit to be forgotten, even though he wrote them off as idle. For he kept them in mind, confident, perhaps, that they would come to fulfillment. After the dreams had been told, the brothers went off together to pasture the flocks of goats in Shechem. Then, after a short time had passed, the father urged the boy to go and visit his brothers. "Are not your brothers," he says, "pasturing the flocks in Shechem? Come, I will send you to them." And he said to him: "Here I am." And Israel said to him: "Go and see whether your brothers and the sheep are well, and bring me word." He promised most eagerly to go. He set out and left the valley of Hebron. As he was wandering about the wilderness, someone met him and asked why he had come, where he was going, and whom he was looking for. He answered at once: "I am looking for my brothers. Tell me where they are pasturing their flocks." "And the man said to him," it says, "'They have left here, for I heard them say, "Let us go to Dothan."'" When he arrived there, he was unexpectedly plotted against. Envy, as if it had found its moment, carried out what it had long intended. The sons of the maidservants Bilhah and Zilpah wanted to do away with him entirely, for they were saying: "Look, here comes that dreamer. Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits, and we will say, 'A wild beast has devoured him.' Then we shall see what becomes of his dreams." But when Reuben heard this, he rescued him from their hands, saying: "Let us not take his life." And Reuben said to them: "Do not shed blood. Throw him into one of these pits in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him." He said this so that he might rescue him from their hands and restore him to his father. So they stripped him of the coat of many colors and let Joseph down into a pit, not dead, but as one who would die before long. Then some Ishmaelites, spice merchants, came hurrying on their way to Egypt. On the advice of Judah, who had plainly cried out that they must not destroy their brother, they sold the boy to those who wished to buy him, and the buyers paid twenty gold pieces for him. So Joseph was carried off to Egypt. Reuben, for his part, did not know what had happened and came to the pit. When he did not see the boy, he supposed that some harm had come to him. He tore his garment and laid the charge of Joseph's loss against the others, saying: "The boy is gone, and I, where shall I go now?" It is as if he were saying: "How could I go back to our father? How would he receive us at all, when we do not have his beloved son? What shall we say to our father when he asks for the boy?" But they soaked the coat of many colors in goat's blood and brought it to their father, composing a speech drunk with deceit and trickery. "We found this," they say. "See whether it is your son's coat or not." The father wailed aloud, and perhaps he was crying out against the spite of his sons and their unholy designs when he said: "A wild beast has devoured Joseph." Over the boy's misfortune he sank into a despondency that nothing could lull and no counsel could reach. "For he would not be comforted," it says, "but said, 'I will go down to my son in Hades, mourning.'" Now that the historical narrative has reached its end, the mind will turn again to search out the innermost meanings. Coloring the truth, as it were, with the shadows of things that happened in the world of the senses, it will bring out the beauty of contemplation as fittingly as it can.

Joseph, then, was born to the younger sister, Rachel, who was beautiful in form and shone with charm in the bright glances of her eyes, though Leah was not like that. How do we know? It is written that "Leah's eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in form and exceedingly lovely to look at." But we said that Leah was the mother of the Jews, that is, the Synagogue, and we gathered proofs of this from her eyes and from the meaning of her name. For the inward and spiritual sight of the Synagogue of the Jews is truly without beauty and badly afflicted with weakness. "For they have eyes and do not see," in the words of the prophet. They did not understand the writings of Moses, nor were they able to perceive the mysteries in them, through which Emmanuel was portrayed in many ways. Leah means "laboring," as we have also said elsewhere. For the Synagogue of the Jews has labored, carrying the law given through Moses as a heavy burden, hard to bear. That is why Christ too, seeing them laboring and weighed down, called them to the relief that comes through faith, saying: "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." So much for Leah. Rachel's eyes, however, are perfectly clear. For the Church from the Gentiles has beheld the glory of Christ, and the Father in him. She has been called, after the first, into union with the spiritual bridegroom, that is, Christ. For she is the youngest, without wrinkle, while the first had grown old and, having aged, was close to vanishing. Rachel also means "God's flock." For the Church is the flock of the Savior. To the Jews he said through one of the holy prophets: "And I said, I will not shepherd you. Let what is dying die, and let what is failing fail, and as for the rest, let each devour the flesh of his neighbor." But concerning us he says: "My sheep hear my voice, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life." He is, then, the good shepherd, and he himself holds first place in everything. But he was also called a sheep, since he became like us. So the wise John pointed him out to the crowds of the Jews, saying: "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." Countless animals were slaughtered according to the type of the law, but none of them wiped away the sin of the world. "For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sin." But the spotless Lamb, the true one, the unblemished victim, has taken away the sin of the world. So he too has been counted as a sheep among us. For this reason he might also be called a son of the Church, as the firstborn among brothers. We should also know that Joseph means "addition and increase of God." For the holy multitude keeps growing, increasing the number of the Church's children. That is why it was also said to her: "Lift up your eyes all around, O Zion, and see them all. Look, they have gathered together and come to you." And again: "Look, these come from afar, these from the north, and these from the sea, and others from the land of the Persians." And it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, in one place, that "the Lord added day by day those who were being saved"; and again in another: "And more and more believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women." For this reason, as I said before, the spiritual Joseph, that is, those who are in Christ, may fittingly be understood as "God's addition." Nor would our account be off the mark in naming those who have believed in him as though they were he himself, in keeping with the divine plan. For he himself is the head, and we are the body and its individual members. He himself is the vine, and we have grown into him like branches, bound together through sanctification by a spiritual union. But "Joseph," it says, "was seventeen years old." That he was very young Scripture shows us, I think, through these words as well. We also say that Emmanuel himself is the youngest of the others, granting seniority in time to those who came before him, such as Moses and the prophets. But when we examine the force of what is written closely, we shall find that something else is also signified here. For perhaps the number of years will in some way portray for us the deep mystery of the dispensation in the flesh. I will try to make the way it does so as plain as I can. For, as I have already said elsewhere — and I will recall it —

It is the custom of divine Scripture to treat as symbols of perfection those numbers which, once they have reached their appointed completion, turn back again. I mean something like this. If someone counts up to ten and then decides to go beyond it, he begins again from one, as if ten had brought him to the end. The same holds for the week. Starting from the first day, one goes up in order to the seventh; then, having closed the count of days at its end, one comes back again to the first. In this way, then, our sacred word makes numbers of this kind signs of perfection. So in the distribution of the talents, the one who had reached the full measure of diligence in God's service is said to have received ten talents, and indeed to have been set over ten cities. By this the one who distributes them, that is, Christ, shows that the rewards will in every way and entirely match the perfection of good deeds. And one of the saints said that the barren woman bore seven, using seven, I suppose, in place of "many," or of as many as anyone who chose to count them might reckon a perfect number. So when it is said of Joseph that he was seventeen years old, we will take it that Emmanuel is composed into one Christ and Son out of two perfect things, divinity and humanity. For we will not accept what some people hold, who think that the divine temple which God the Word bore from the holy Virgin was empty of a rational soul. Rather, just as he was perfect in divinity, so also in humanity, though he was composed into one ineffably and beyond understanding. The number ten, then, signifies his perfection in divinity and in some way hints at it to us. The seven, in turn, might suggest the same perfection in humanity. It falls short of ten by a triad, so to speak, yet it is added to ten and, as it were, attached to it. For in seventeen the seven comes after the ten. God the Word, who is from the Father, stands in the pre-eminence of the Triad, that is, of the Godhead; the human stands lower and is less than the glory of God. God the Word is understood as existing beforehand, and the human was added to him. So the number ten is necessarily placed first, and the seven is added. For Joseph, it says, was ten and seven years old. Notice also, please, that Emmanuel is both temporal and without beginning, with respect to time, I mean. For a count of years was given to Joseph, as in an image; but the word "was" is added. For although the Word is God, he was called to a birth such as ours, and to a count of years because of his humanity. But the "was" will certainly go with him. For he is understood to be, and truly is, coeternal with God the Father, and, as the inspired John says, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." So I will say it again: the inspired Joseph was seventeen years old, and he shepherded his father's flocks together with his brothers, the sons of Zilpah and Bilhah, I mean, that is, the sons of the maidservants. For when the Word from God became man, he went up and down through the land of the Jews, gathering the lost sheep of the house of Israel, as it were, into love for God the Father. For as blessed Paul writes, "God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself." So Emmanuel shepherded together with those born into slavery, those who had, in a way, a bastard and not a free birth from two slave girls. For after the reign of Jeroboam the ten tribes broke away from Jerusalem and went off and settled in Samaria, Jeroboam leading them astray into this. There they went astray and worshipped the golden heifers. That is why God, through the voice of Ezekiel, accused them as two women who had played the harlot, saying: "Son of man, there were two women, daughters of one mother, and they played the harlot in Egypt; in their youth they played the harlot, and their breasts fell. There they lost their virginity. Their names were Oholah the elder and Oholibah her sister. And they became mine, and bore sons and daughters. As for their names, Oholah is Samaria and Oholibah is Jerusalem." So the Son, having become like us, shepherded together with those born of slavery and of harlotry alike. For those set over Israel under the law were still leading them, even though Christ was already teaching and initiating those who came to him and bringing them onto the path of truth. That path was himself. That is why he said, "I am the way." But the scribes and Pharisees, and those who had a reputation for the law, led the flock to graze among thistles and thorns, into wandering, into the teachings and commandments of men. He, however, led them into good pasture and, as it were, into grass full of flowers: the rich and admirable knowledge of the gospel teachings. They were lazy and slack shepherds, and besides this they were slaves to gain and sick with the worst love of profit: eating the milk, clothing themselves with the wool, and slaughtering the fat, as the prophet says. They were hirelings and arrogant, and they thought very little of the duty to labor for the sheep. Just as the sons of Zilpah and Bilhah brought an evil report against Joseph, so too the most perverse crowd of the unholy Pharisees slandered Emmanuel and dared to malign his glory. They impiously called him a Samaritan and a wine drinker, and on top of that possessed by a demon and helped by the workings of Beelzebul, so that he could, I mean, drive the evil spirits out of the sick. That is why Emmanuel himself, through the voice of a prophet, cried out against the unbridled tongue of the Jews, saying: "Woe to them, for they have leapt away from me. They are wretched, for they have acted impiously against me. I redeemed them, but they spoke lies against me." And again: "Their rulers will fall by the sword because of the coarseness of their tongue." So the bold and churlish gang of Pharisees babbled against Christ. And this, I think, is what is meant by the brothers bringing an evil report against Joseph. But he was loved, it says, by his father, because he was the son of his old age. For before our Savior appeared in the world in the flesh there were other shepherds too, fine and good men, and above all the others the inspired Moses, and those who shepherded the rational flocks after him. But the Father loved the Son above all, even though he came last, after the others, and appeared in the final times of the age. Now it fits Jacob to have Joseph as the son of his old age. God, however, does not age; he is without beginning and without growth, and always perfect in every way. So, wisely keeping our discourse from missing what is fitting, we say that Emmanuel was born to God the Father as a son of old age in this sense: he came in the last times of the age, clearly the present age, and after him there is no other. For we do not expect to be saved in anyone else. He alone will be enough, since we say that the salvation and life of the world lie in no one else. He, then, will shepherd us forever, as the Psalmist says, and we will be placed under him, the beloved, who appeared in the flesh in the last times of the age, as I have just said, but who existed beforehand as God. For we say that he is coeternal with the Father. So Joseph was especially loved by his father, and his father gave him a many-colored tunic as a special gift, making it a clear sign of the affection he had for him. But this too provoked envy in the brothers and gave them a reason for jealousy, as the outcome of events itself will show. The Pharisees likewise raged against the beloved, that is, Christ, because God the Father had clothed him with a glory of many kinds. For he was admired, I think, in many ways: as giver of life; as light, able to enlighten those in darkness; as cleansing lepers and easily raising the dead, even those who already stank; as rebuking seas and riding on the very waves with authority. So the Jews, already at a loss and unbearably consumed by the fire of envy, said to one another: "What are we doing? This man is performing many signs." The many-colored tunic, then, is a figure for us of the varied glory which God the Father is said to have put on the Son when he became like us, because of his humanity. For as far as his own nature is concerned, he is himself the Lord of glory, even if, by way of the divine plan and because of his likeness to us, he says, "Father, glorify your Son." So the sons of the maidservants were provoked to grief by the things I have just mentioned. Besides this, they grew suspicious because of the telling of the dreams. For they learned in advance that in time they themselves would be under his feet and would bow down to him, while he would be far above them and would rise to such glory that even his own parents would bow down to him. So they were already gnashing their teeth and entertaining thoughts of murder. The Jews too were provoked and grieved no little when they learned that Emmanuel would be above even the holy Patriarchs and would be worshipped by all the people, or rather by the whole earth. Understanding this, they said, "This is the heir; come, let us kill him and take his inheritance." Yet blessed David plainly says to the Only-begotten made man, "All the nations you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord"; and elsewhere he makes plain the envy and unholy anger toward Christ of the people of Israel themselves, saying, "The Lord has become king; let the peoples rage." Now that we have sufficiently shown the harsh and untamed envy of the Jews, let us speak in due course of their grievous and bloodthirsty outrages, condensing the narrative of the story throughout and running back to the very purpose of the Only-begotten's incarnation. For the discourse brings us back to this again.

His father's command persuades the inspired Joseph to go to Shechem, to see whether his brothers are well, and where and how they are pasturing the flocks. He goes, but finds them only with difficulty. They are not in Shechem at all; they have gone off to Dothan. When they saw him approaching, they smiled a bitter and hateful smile and said, "Look, that dreamer is coming." They wanted to kill him, but Reuben held them back. Still, they let him down into one of the pits, disregarding Reuben's counsel. Not long afterward they drew the young man up out of the pit and sold him to the Ishmaelites, who were going down to Egypt. When Reuben came back to the pit and did not find the lad, he thought he was already dead, the victim of the murderers' wickedness, and he was greatly distressed. Joseph was carried off to Egypt, and his father mourned and went on lamenting for a long time. Our Lord Jesus Christ himself was likewise sent by God the Father to visit the people of Israel, to see whether they were still well (spiritually well, clearly) and whether the flocks in their care had fared well and had not lacked the kindness of shepherds. But they were found not in Shechem but in Dothan. Shechem means "shoulder," and that limb would be a sign of diligent labor. For inspired Scripture is in the habit of making the shoulder a figure sometimes of strength and sometimes of work. An example is the saying, "Set your heart to your shoulders," that is, to diligent labor. Dothan, in turn, means "sufficient failing." So the people of Israel were caught not in diligent labor toward virtue, nor in the good deeds of the law, but in great failing, plainly of righteousness and of all decency. For there was no one righteous, not even one; there was no one doing good, not even one. Instead, as God says somewhere through the voice of the prophet, they offered him only the honor of the tongue, having moved their minds elsewhere and moved their hearts far away from fulfilling what was laid down through Moses. For they held fast only to the teachings and commandments of men. Yet they recognized the beloved, the spiritual Joseph, when he was present in the flesh. For the blessed evangelist John said that many even of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him. So, having recognized him, they treated him with outrage. They killed him, and the wretches let him down, as into a pit, into the deep, dark chasm of death, that is, Hades. This is how the inspired David signified it to us, speaking to the Father and God in heaven as if in the person of Christ: "Lord, you brought up my soul from Hades; you saved me from those who go down into the pit." Notice, please, the force of the holy Scriptures and how very finely polished they are for precision. "The pit," it says, "was empty; it had no water," so that Hades might be clearly and vividly signified to us by this. I will explain how. Water would be a symbol of life, since it gives life. But it says there was no water in the pit. For Hades may fittingly be understood as the house and dwelling place of those deprived of life. Yet the boy was brought up. And Christ too came back to life from the dead. For Joseph was not held fast by the pit. Nor did Christ remain in Hades; rather, he emptied it. For he said to those in chains, "Come out." After he was brought up, before long the inspired Joseph went off to Egypt, the Ishmaelites having bought him; and they were spice merchants. For Christ too came back to life and came up from the pit. He left Judea and passed over into the land of the Gentiles, carried about by the spiritual Ishmaelites, that is, those who live in obedience to God, for that is what the name means. Who would these be? Again, the blessed disciples, who gave ear to the teachings of Christ and became the firstfruits of those who excel in obedience and faith and in glories beyond the law. Such people may fittingly be understood as spice merchants too, since they spread the fragrance of the mystery of Christ and impress on their own souls the form of every virtue in general. In a sense these bought Jesus, giving up all the splendid things of the law and acquiring by trade the one pearl of great price, as in the Savior's own parable. These carried Christ to the Gentiles, serving the gospel as priests and proclaiming him throughout the whole world under the sun as God and Lord, and as the chosen stone, rejected by the builders under the law, builders in a spiritual sense, but chosen and precious in God's sight and set as the head of the corner. Note, however, that Reuben kept his brothers from murder, and Judah too was distressed. Reuben was the firstborn, and Judah was of the tribe called to kingship. So all those among the Jews who were rich in conformity to the Firstborn, and all who were called to the kingdom of heaven by accepting the preaching that came through Christ, were greatly distressed at the outrages committed against him. For there were indeed, at that time, a great many people in Jerusalem and throughout the rest of the land of the Jews who grieved and suffered with Christ when he was dishonored. The father mourned Joseph: "For he would not be comforted," it says. Here too, then, we can see that the drunken violence against Christ and the murderous undertakings of the Jews grieved the Father and God in heaven beyond measure. They gave such terrible offense that he refuses comfort and will scarcely bear with anyone who chooses to make supplication on their behalf. For the prophets often pleaded and begged that Israel be saved, even though Israel had done things beyond all words against the prophets. And God often turned his mind to gentleness, for those who had been endangered were servants. But since they treated Christ himself with outrage, the Father cannot be comforted, and his wrath is hard to turn back. For it is no longer some prophet who has been insulted, but the Savior of all, the Master of the prophets, that is, Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father with the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

The aim of the divinely inspired Scripture is to signify to us the mystery of Christ through countless things. One might compare it to a splendid and admirable city that has not just one image of the king but a great many, set up conspicuously in every place. See how it passes over none of the narratives that serve this end, but goes through them all. And even if the account contains something unseemly in the story, it may well treat such things as of no account, so long as its purpose is woven well. For its aim is not to expose the lives of the saints (far from it), but rather to give shape to our knowledge of the mystery, through those things by which the account of it might become clear and true, and in no way deserve censure for having missed the truth. So once again the mystery of the Savior's dispensation is written for us, this time in Judah and also in Tamar. For it says: "It came to pass at that time that Judah went down from his brothers and came to a certain Adullamite named Hirah. And Judah saw there the daughter of a Canaanite man, whose name was Shua. And he took her and went in to her, and she conceived and bore a son, and called his name Er. And she conceived again and bore a son, and called his name Onan. And once more she bore a son, and called his name Shelah." So these three sons were born to Judah. When the young men had come of age, he takes Tamar and joins her to the firstborn, that is, Er. But since Er was wicked in the sight of God, he departed this life before begetting children. "For God killed him," it says. Then the father urges Onan to lie with his brother's wife and raise up offspring for the dead man. But Onan, since what was born, it says, would not be his, violated the law of union, spilling his seed on the ground instead of giving it. And he too perishes at once by divine wrath. After this had happened, Judah was afraid to give his third son to live with her, I mean Shelah. The reason for this fear was, "Lest he too perish," it says. And as his pretext for not having to complete the marriage he gave the boy's very young age. "For he said," it says, "to his daughter-in-law, 'Remain a widow in your father's house until Shelah my son is grown.' For he said, 'Lest he too die like his brothers.' And Tamar went away and lived in her father's house." Then, after time had passed, Tamar grew vexed at the delay of the marriage. She now somehow understands that her father-in-law would not carry through what he had promised her, but was rather making excuses, deferring what she had expected and turning it into hopes that would never be fulfilled. And what, then, does she contrive about this? "It was told," it says, "to Tamar his daughter-in-law: 'Behold, your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep.' And she took off the garments of her widowhood, put on a veil, adorned herself, and sat at the gates of Enaim, which is on the way to Timnah. For she saw that Shelah his son had grown up, yet he had not given her to him as wife. And when Judah saw her, he thought she was a harlot, for she had covered her face, and he did not recognize her." Then he was carried away by desire. When the woman asked for payment, he promised to send a kid, and when she asked for pledges of the promise, he gives her the staff, the ring and the necklace, that is, an ornament worn about the neck. (One might suppose, and very reasonably, that Judah, being a Chaldean, had not fallen into such slackness as to love reclining at ease.) For the Chaldeans are fond of adornment; they make both their hands and their necks splendid with gold, and sometimes even crown their very hair. Among them this is considered manly too, a mark of the highest nobility, and not without a share in the praise given to courage. When these things had been done in this way, Judah went on to where he had been heading in the first place. She returned to her father's hearth, and now she was with child, in good hope. When Judah learned of this, he said the woman must die for having played the harlot. But when she was at the very point of death, she showed him the staff and the rest, saying, "By the man to whom these things belong I am with child." And she said, "Recognize whose are this ring and necklace and staff." And Judah recognized them and said, "Tamar is more in the right than I, because I did not give her to Shelah my son." And he did not know her again. "And it came to pass," it says, "when she was giving birth, that there were twins in her womb. And as she was giving birth, one put out his hand first. And the midwife took a scarlet thread and tied it on his hand, saying, 'This one will come out first.' But when he drew back his hand, at once his brother came out. And she said, 'Why has the barrier been broken through on your account?' And she called his name Perez. After this his brother came out, on whose hand was the scarlet thread; and she called his name Zerah." This much I have set out according to the letter. But the meaning of what really matters lies hidden once more. We will examine what it is, and before long.

But before anything else I think it necessary to say this. Even if those who enjoy a shining reputation in the divinely inspired Scripture should somehow be found in conduct that is not altogether seemly, while God is arranging very well something needful for our benefit, we will drive far from us the harm of taking offense, if we care to be wise and shrewd and not ignorant of what is done, most usefully, by divine dispensation. Let us recall that the blessed prophet Hosea too once hired a harlot for himself, did not refuse a marriage so ill-reputed, and became the father of hated children, whose names were "Not My People" and "Not Pitied." What this was and why it was done we will not hesitate to explain. Since those of Israel who seemed most distinguished resisted the preaching of the prophets, and the divine word was unacceptable to them, such things were done from time to time through the saints. The purpose was that, at least by seeing the future in the very actions, written as it were brightly and openly on a tablet, they might set their minds on finding what was to their advantage, might themselves turn over to choosing what is beneficial, and might persuade others as well. For they were learning that in time they would be "not a people" and would be ranked among the "not pitied," hard and unwilling to listen. And indeed, what failing of this kind were they not sick with, and convicted of utterly? As for the prophet's living with a harlot, that was a type of God, who in a way lived with the synagogue of the Jews as with a harlot and a most abominable woman, and chose to beget from her children who were hateful. So, keeping in mind the various modes of the dispensation at various times, we shall rightly free both Tamar herself and Judah from blame and outcry over fornication, I mean. Rather, we say that this was a union brought about by dispensation. For she longed for freeborn offspring, having been deprived of her lawful husband; and he, for his part, was hardly much to blame if he chose to unite with another woman, since his first wife had died. Surely a bodily union and childbirth would sketch for us in themselves the types of spiritual fellowship and of spiritual birth. For in this way, and in no other, would the human mind be led by the hand to the truth.

So Judah went down and came to a man named Hirah. This man was a goatherd and skilled in the shepherd's craft. And seeing Shua there, Judah made her his wife and made her the mother of three children: Er, I mean, and Onan, and also Shelah. Er is interpreted "made of skin," that is, "fleshly"; Onan, "stricken in heart"; and the third, "drawing out," or "release" and "making peace." Now the only-begotten Word of God also came down from heaven, as from a kind of holy land, he who is truly praised and by nature possesses the glory of the kingdom. For the figure of Judah would hint at this to us: the meaning of the name signifies "praise," and the tribe of Judah is the most royal of all and has been set in the highest preeminence. That is why the inspired Jacob, in giving his blessing to him, says, "Judah, may your brothers praise you." And the most wise Paul too has testified that Christ, who is praised by all creation, sprang from the tribe of Judah. So the only-begotten Word of God came down and visited the wilderness of Midian when the blessed Moses was tending sheep there. For he appeared to him in the form of fire in the bush, and through him was in a way joined, as to a foreign Canaanite woman, to the synagogue of the sons of Israel in Egypt, just as Judah was joined to Shua through the shepherd. Shua is interpreted "exaltation" and "lifting up." For the synagogue of the Jews, once it had been called, as it were, into kinship with God, was no longer lowly and trampled underfoot, bearing the meanness of slavery, but became lofty and illustrious. For it was redeemed as from an iron furnace and from the house of slavery, as it is written. Then from the synagogue in Egypt, which had once been foreign, as it were, and idolatrous, came three peoples, who filled the rank of sons to God. They sprang, as it were, from one mother, but their births were spread out over time. In what way, we will explain before long. Next, Judah joined Tamar first to Er, who was the firstborn. But when God destroyed him for being wicked, Onan, who was second both in birth and in time, at once succeeds to the marriage. But since he would not raise up offspring for his brother, he perishes along with the first, divine wrath bringing him too to this end. Then the father does not allow the third, that is, Shelah, to take up the marriage, fearing that he might perish along with the first two. What this means I will try to explain, God granting wisdom. The first synagogue, the one in Egypt, which we have granted was foreign, because at that time it had become thoroughly savage in pagan ways and customs, God reshaped through a way of life under the law, and showed it to be, as it were, a new synagogue, in a sense different from the first. And this is Tamar. See how the mystery is found even in the interpretations of the names. Tamar is interpreted "failing" or "shaken." And the synagogue of the Jews has truly been shaken and has failed. How, and in what way? The worship according to the law did not remain entirely unshaken, but gave way to the worship in spirit. Then the worship through Christ was brought in, accusing the first as not being blameless. And Christ betrothed to himself the Church as a pure virgin, letting go of that ancient and first one. So it is with good reason that the synagogue of the Jews is understood as "failing" and "shaken." That no one is justified by the law before God, and that in the synagogue of the Jews there was no share in God's serenity (for the law brings about wrath, as it is written), the birth of Judah's sons, who were married to Tamar, would show in riddling form. For Er, the firstborn, is "made of skin," that is, "earthly." And since he was wicked, he was condemned to death. And truly the first people proved wicked, grumbling against God and saying, "Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? Since he struck the rock and waters gushed out and torrents overflowed, can he also give bread?" And again, when the men sent to spy out the land of promise returned, the people wailed like children, as though they were about to perish then and there, insulting the all-powerful God with their disobedience. That is why they perished, and none of them entered the land of promise, but their corpses fell in the wilderness, as it is written. So the firstborn Er, that is, the wicked and fleshly one, perished first, having no fruit of godliness. For childlessness would hint at this to us, again as in a type, since things perceived by the senses are like images of things perceived by the mind. Then after him came, like a second son of the God who redeemed them and brought them out of the house of slavery, the people that followed them. This people crossed the Jordan under the command of Joshua and inherited the land of promise. After this it came under judges, but it too fell under the indignation from above. For it was truly Onan, that is, "stricken in heart." For it turned outrageously to polytheism, having forsaken the one who is God by nature and in truth. So it was destroyed and became the slave of foreigners. The book of the so-called Judges has taught us this. This one too, then, died childless, like Er, sowing to no purpose, that is, on the ground. Hence, as was to be expected, it gained no fruit at all, nor did it raise up offspring for its brother. For the middle people, second in time, shrank from raising itself up to God, as it were, in place of those who had disobeyed, through the uprightness that the law requires, and from showing by its deeds a new people grown up in their stead. For this, I think, is the riddling sense of "to raise up offspring for his brother." Now that both had been removed, for good reasons (the one was wicked, the other stricken in heart), the father keeps the third from union with Tamar, fearing that he too might somehow be destroyed along with those already dead. For the third and, as it were, youngest people, the one belonging to the last period of the holy prophets (with whom the inspired Baptist is the immediate neighbor, pointing to the one from heaven, Christ, as already present), God did not allow, as it were, to be held in the arms of the synagogue of the Jews, nor does he wish it to have fruit from her, lest it too somehow perish. For the law brings about wrath, and no one at all is justified by it. See how well Shelah would show in himself the type of the last people, the people of faith. For his name is interpreted "drawing out" or "release." When divine wrath was, as it were, consuming those of Israel's blood, because of their impious crimes against Christ and their intolerable outrage, those who believed were drawn out as from a wild beast, and in a way released from the bonds that had seized them for punishment. For the remnant has been saved, according to the Scriptures. Indeed, God said somewhere through the voice of the prophet: "As when a shepherd draws out of the lion's mouth two legs or the lobe of an ear, so shall the sons of Israel be drawn out." That is why Shelah is called "drawing out." That the believers, who have been drawn out of the multitude of those who perished, refuse union with Tamar, that is, bearing fruit under the law, you can learn without any trouble from the blessed Paul, who says of the boasts that come from the law: "But whatever gains I had, these I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ." For he desired not to have a righteousness of his own, I mean again the righteousness that is in the law, but the righteousness that comes from faith in Christ Jesus. So Shelah, the youngest, is not joined to Tamar. For this reason she remained a widow and spent a long time in that state. Since God no longer allows the synagogue of the Jews to bear fruit, it has truly been, and been called, a widow, childless and without a husband, the spiritual bridegroom. For Christ said somewhere, "She is not my wife, and I am not her husband." Is there, then, no regard for her at all after this? Is she not thought worthy of God's care? Do not suppose so. For although she stands condemned for the worst impieties of all, God in his innate gentleness will have mercy on her in the last times of the age, and she too will bear as fruit the marks of Christ. That she will walk behind the nations we will learn no less from what is written. For Judah, going up to shear his sheep, made his union with her a side matter of the journey; and he lets her keep the staff, the ring and the necklace, promising also to send a kid. For Christ, whose own and most pressing concern is to receive the fruits of his rational flock, clearly meaning those who have believed and been sanctified in the Spirit, will at the appointed time make his spiritual fellowship with the synagogue of the Jews something done in passing, as it were, and not his chief concern. Yet he will make her fruitful, as it were, so that she is in labor with the wisdom that comes from him. And he will entrust himself to her, as he has to us, as a rod of power, as the image and likeness of God the Father (this is the ring), as fairer in beauty than the sons of men. For this, I think, is what the necklace signifies; any object that serves as an ornament may be understood as a sign of beauty. And he also sends her the kid, that is, he will grant her forgiveness of her sins. For under the law a kid was slaughtered for sin, and it hints at forgiveness of offenses. And Tamar is saved, although she had received the sentence of death and was already facing the extreme penalty. For Tamar had been condemned as a harlot. Nevertheless she is saved, for she showed the staff, the ring and the necklace, and declared plainly that she had conceived by Judah and carried his fruit. So too Christ will in due time free the synagogue of the Jews from the punishment she would otherwise suffer, when she bears the tokens of her fellowship with him and shows clearly that she has conceived what is his. For this is how those who have chosen to win approval through faith in Christ speak somewhere: "Because of the fear of you, Lord, we conceived in the womb and were in labor and gave birth to the spirit of your salvation, which we brought forth upon the earth." And Tamar, in labor with a pair of babies, at last came to the birth. Then the firstborn puts out his hand; but when he draws it back again, though it has already received the scarlet thread, the second springs out ahead, as though a barrier had been broken through, and then the first comes out last. This too would be a sign, by no means obscure, that the nations have been called before those of Israel's blood, and that those honored in later times have taken the glory of the firstborn. That the first too will follow, having accepted the sacrifice of Christ, is beyond doubt; for the scarlet would be a type of the holy blood. Who, then, is the one who broke down the dividing wall of the barrier, called the second into the rank of the firstborn, and placed the first behind? Clearly it is Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

We must now go on to the rest of what we had already begun to say about Joseph, since the story inserted in between, I mean the one about Judah and Tamar, has now come to a fitting end. Applying the story of the divine Joseph to the person of Christ, we said that his brothers threw him into the pit, and that he was then brought up again and sold to the Ishmaelites, who traded in the most fragrant spices and carried them to people who had none. We added that they took him away into the land of the Egyptians. For the Only-begotten lowered himself to the point of self-emptying and took on our condition. He was called brother to those on earth, and above all to the people of Israel. He endured death, submitted to the cross and went down to Hades, which the pit prefigures. Yet he came back to life, and was taken away from those of Israel's blood. He was handed over, as it were, to traders in spiritual spices, that is, to the holy apostles. Fragrant with his ointment, they came to the land of the Gentiles, and through the preaching of the gospel they carried him, clothed in the form of a servant, to those who did not know him. For he is preached as having come in the flesh for our sake, in the form of a servant. This, I think, is what Joseph's being carried into Egypt by the Ishmaelites means. Let us now consider, if you please, what happened to him once he was there, and what he had to do in the face of it. While he was still young, hardly more than a youth, he overcame the lewdness of the Egyptian woman, though she all but forced him, with great violence, to consent to what is unlawful. She clung to his garments tightly and shamelessly, and pressed him hard toward a sin he did not want. But he left the very garment behind, escaped the savage, lustful woman, and was not caught by the passion. After this he was slandered. The woman turned the charges back on him, and the chaste man of free spirit stood accused of indecency. Yet, it says, he was put in charge of the prison. Christ too came among the Gentiles, in the person, I mean, of the holy apostles, who said that they carried his marks in their own body. They refused to be conformed to those who had chosen to set their minds on the things of the world, and they kept far away from fleshly desires. For such is always the life of the saints. But they were plotted against for this. Slandered by people who habitually regard those who wish to live in Christ as tiresome, they fell into trials and became prisoners. Yet they remembered Christ saying, 'If you were of the world, the world would love its own; but because you are not of the world, the world hates you,' just as the lustful woman hated Joseph. Yet even in these hardships they found room to breathe, for the grace of God tamed those who were most likely to wear them down. For, as I said, the jailer took delight in Joseph. Then, when Pharaoh's eunuchs, I mean the cupbearer and the baker, were imprisoned, he interpreted their dreams. And for this reason, it says, the divine Joseph was greatly admired. Then Pharaoh himself dreamed of the abundant harvests that were soon to come and of the hardship of the famine, seeing them first as fat and lean cows and afterwards as ears of grain. The wise men of Egypt had nothing to say and had given up entirely on explaining what the visions signified. Then Joseph was spoken of as able to do this, and he came forward and explained them. Pharaoh was amazed and appointed him steward and governor over his realm. Christ was persecuted, as I said just now, in the person of the holy apostles. But in the very midst of their hardships the men we are speaking of, being very wise and able to explain what is hidden from the many, became known first to certain people in authority in the world, and then to the very rulers of the earth. These believed that the apostles had knowledge even of things to come, by revelation from God in the Spirit, and allowed them to become stewards and rulers of the nations, and to distribute to those starving for teaching the lessons that sustain them for undefiled life, that is, the divine and heavenly word and the instruction that leads to everything that is best. These men won the land of the Gentiles for God the Father, or rather Christ won it through them, just as Joseph won the land of the Egyptians for Pharaoh. Two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, were born to Joseph from their mother Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, who was a priest. Manasseh is interpreted 'forgetfulness of the evils that had happened', and Ephraim 'increase and progress toward what is better'. For fruits have come from a holy mother, as it were, I mean the Church, and those called from the Gentiles may be counted among the sons of God through faith in Christ. They will also be brought to forget their troubles. For, it says, 'They will forget their former affliction, and it will not come up into their heart. For on their head will be praise and gladness, and joy will overtake them. Pain, grief and sighing have fled away.' So in due time they will come to forget their evils, and they will advance in growth, running toward the sweet goal of their hope. For they will move from earthly things to heavenly, from what is measured by time to what lies beyond time, from corruption to incorruption, from dishonor to glory, from weakness to power. While the famine still pressed on them and dragged on, the sons of Jacob went down to Egypt to buy food. A short exchange followed, in which Joseph all but played with them, for he said they had come not for grain at all but rather to spy out the land. He also demanded Benjamin, who was his brother and the youngest, and insisted that they would not get away from Egypt unharmed unless they brought the boy. So the boy was brought, their father reluctantly letting him go. When they came with the boy, Joseph invited them to his hearth, and when they had washed in water he filled them with bread and wine. In the same way the Jews, afflicted and crushed, as it were, by an unbearable famine (clearly a spiritual one), will in due time drop their lofty and arrogant brow and come to Christ, longing for the food he gives, food that is holy and spiritual, I mean, and life-giving. He will not receive them, however, without the new people, of whom Benjamin would be a type. But when they come in one soul, as it were, and with one mind, he will receive them gladly and bring them as into his own house, that is, the Church. Then he will wash them in pure water, the washing of regeneration, and nourish them with bread and wine. The meaning here is mystical. But let us add this as well. Joseph made himself known to his brothers when they had come with Benjamin, and he even welcomed them to his table, as I said just now. But he gave them no allotted land at all. Instead he told them to hurry back and bring their father, I mean Jacob, to him. When Jacob had come down and Joseph saw him there together with his children, then, and only then, he gave him the best land of all. This too would be a clear sign that Christ will receive those of Israel who turn back in the last times of the age, evidently with the new people joined to them in unity of soul. For that, as I said, is what Benjamin signifies. Yet the inheritance laid up for us in hope will not be given apart from the holy fathers. For they died in faith, as the wise Paul said, but 'did not receive the promise, since God had foreseen something better for us, so that they would not be made perfect apart from us.' In the same way we too shall wait for the fathers, so that we may not be made perfect apart from them. So together with the holy fathers, we, the first, the middle and the last peoples, shall receive in Christ the best and inalienable inheritance of the kingdom of heaven. Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

Every good gift and every perfect present is from above, coming down from the Father of lights. And I say that there is not one of these venerable and exceptional goods that we do not gain through Christ. For, it says, he became the mediator between God and human beings, and through him we have access in one Spirit to the Father and God in heaven. That is why he said, 'No one comes to the Father except through me.' In him and through him are all the fullness of grace and a splendid inheritance. For though God was rich, he became poor for our sake, so that we might become rich by his poverty, and, rising up to the glory of the holy fathers, might be able to share in the hope that most befits them. Now look at the true account of these things, fixing the eye of your mind on the sacred Scriptures. For it reads as follows: 'After these words, Joseph was told, "Your father is ill." And he took his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, and came to Jacob. And Jacob was told, "See, your son Joseph is coming to you." And Israel gathered his strength and sat up on the bed. And Jacob said to Joseph, "My God appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and blessed me, and said to me, 'See, I will make you grow and multiply you, and I will make you into assemblies of nations, and I will give this land to you and to your seed after you as an everlasting possession.' Now therefore your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, are mine. Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are. But the offspring you father after them shall be yours; they will be called by the name of their brothers in their allotments. As for me, when I was coming from Mesopotamia of Syria, Rachel your mother died in the land of Canaan, as I was drawing near the racecourse of Chabratha in the land, on the way to the land of Ephrath, and I buried her by the road of the racecourse; this is Bethlehem."' The blessed Jacob had been sustained to a good old age, as it is written. When he was about to depart from our affairs, he set his mind on blessing Joseph's sons. Since they were born of a foreign mother, Asenath, daughter of the priest Potiphera, the divine Jacob wisely and prudently tried to teach Joseph himself and his other sons that, in following the divine decrees, he was claiming as his own all who had been born of them. He did this so that none of the Israelites would despise the boys or regard their line as alien and foreign. 'For God appeared to me,' he says, 'in the land of Canaan,' and openly promised that I would be the father of very many peoples, and that I would spread out into nations and assemblies of nations. At the same time, then, he urges them to honor God with true beliefs, and teaches them to regard their near kin as their own, or rather those sprung from themselves, even if they happen to be born of a foreign mother.

Going a little beyond the bare substance of the history, we say this. In the same way we too, who have been justified by faith, have become in Christ sons of God and members of the household of the saints. He acts as mediator, and through himself he binds us to himself, to the Father and to the choirs of the saints. In just this way Joseph, standing in between, as it were, made Ephraim and Manasseh sons of his own father and had them enrolled in the very list of the patriarchs. 'For now,' he says, 'your two sons who were born to you in Egypt are mine, Ephraim and Manasseh; they shall be mine as Reuben and Simeon are.' That is, they will be among the firstborn, and they will be ranked with those who obey. For Reuben was the firstborn, and Simeon is interpreted 'obedience'. Through faith we who were last have become first, and the people from the Gentiles has inherited the glory of the firstborn. They have been honored because of their obedience and readiness to comply. For Christ himself has borne witness to them, saying, 'A people I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me.' For even if we were born, as it were, of a foreign mother, because the Church has been called from the Gentiles, Emmanuel standing between will be enough to join us through himself to God the Father, to enroll us in the inheritances of the saints, to raise us to the glory that befits them, and to make us a holy race. Observe how, out of love for the blessed Joseph, Jacob ranks Joseph's sons among his own sons. For we too are loved in Christ, and since through him we have been born in the Spirit with the spiritual birth, we have become worthy to be received by the Father, as I said just now, and have been ranked with the saints who came before us. Yet even if we have been called sons of God the Father, we shall still be under the hand of the one who brings us near and unites us to him, that is, Christ. For see how the blessed Jacob, after enrolling Ephraim and Manasseh among his own children, says, 'But the offspring born to you after them shall be yours.' So you understand that even though we are called sons of God the Father, we shall belong no less to Christ. And this, I think, is what he said to the Father: 'Those whom you gave me out of the world were yours, and you gave them to me; and I have been glorified in them.' Jacob also said that Rachel was buried in Bethlehem. We have often recalled that we treated Rachel as an image and type of the Church from the Gentiles. One would not speak falsely, I think, if one wished to say that the Church has passed over to another life, one that is clearly better and superior to life in the world. She has died to the world, because she will not consent to think its thoughts, but she lives to God spiritually in Christ through the way of life of the gospel. For even if she is in the world because of life in the flesh, she is hidden, as it were, since she does not have the world's splendor, and she has all but been buried with Christ. And this, I think, is what the most wise Paul told us: 'For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.' Notice that while Rachel was buried in Bethlehem and no longer seen, Emmanuel himself was in a way hidden with her. For he had not yet been born through the holy Virgin. Let us therefore praise such a death of the Church, which leads up to the beginnings of the holy life in Christ. I think it necessary to add this as well. When the father had received Joseph's sons as his own children, their mother being dead, he also gave instructions about her. So by marking out the place where she was buried he would be urging nothing other than that due care should be taken for her. God the Father likewise gave instructions to the Son concerning the Church, and urged him to count her worthy of care, overcome as she was by death because of the ancient curse. That is why the divine David cried out for us to the Father and God in heaven: 'Command, O God, your power; strengthen, O God, what you have accomplished in us.' For he all but pointed to the body held fast by death, and he begged that through the Power of God the Father, that is, the Son, it might be freed from corruption and return again to what it was in the beginning, that is, to the blessed and undefiled life in Christ.

Israel was the firstborn and had been honored with the privileges that go with it. Yet he slipped from the glory he had, and the grace of such splendid renown passed to the new people that came from the Gentiles. We shall learn this no less from what follows. 'When Israel saw the sons of Joseph,' it says, 'he said, "Who are these to you?" And Joseph said to his father, "They are my sons, whom God gave me here." And Jacob said, "Bring them to me, so that I may bless them." Now his eyes had grown dim with age, and he could not see. And Joseph brought them near to him, and he kissed them and embraced them. And Israel said to Joseph, "See, I have not been deprived of your face, and see, God has shown me your seed as well." And Joseph brought them out from between his knees, and they bowed down to him with their faces to the ground. And Joseph took his sons, Ephraim in his right hand, at Israel's left, and Manasseh in his left hand, at Israel's right, and brought them near to him. And Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it on the head of Ephraim, who was the younger, and his left hand on the head of Manasseh, crossing his hands. And he blessed them and said, "May the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac were well-pleasing, the God who has fed me from my youth to this day, the angel who rescues me from all evils, bless these boys."' The boys were standing beside him, and the old man asked whose they were. To this Joseph replies, 'My two sons.' Then, when they had been brought forward and were close to him, he honored them with kisses and embraces. Understand, then, how we, who were in a way unknown to God the Father, have become known to him and near to him in Christ. He receives us very gladly, since the Son testifies to our kinship with him. In this way he counts us worthy of love and calls us to union, clearly a spiritual union, in the Spirit. A kiss would be a very clear type of love, and a clasp or embrace a type of union. That is why the most wise Paul writes to those who have believed in Christ, at one point, 'But now you who once were far off have been brought near,' evidently because Christ brought them, and at another, 'But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God.' For God the Father watches over and recognizes only those who have a spiritual kinship with the Son, and who have been enriched with rebirth through the Spirit under him and through him. In the same way, in Egypt, he acknowledged those who were smeared with the blood of the lamb, saying, 'And I will see the blood and protect you, and no plague will be among you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt.' Jacob, greatly cheered, said to his son, that is, Joseph, 'See, I have not been deprived of your face, and see, God has shown me your seed as well.' As far as it lay with the Jews, the Father was deprived of the Son. For they surrounded him with death, thinking that he would be held fast by the gates of Hades and lie dead with all the rest. But it was not possible for the author of life to be held in the grip of death. So he came back to life, and the Father saw him again, and with him the race that comes from him and exists in him, that is, those who have believed, the holy nation, the royal priesthood, the people for his own possession. In them Christ himself rejoices, saying, 'Here am I and the children whom God has given me.' Joseph brought them to his father, and they bowed down. Then, with Manasseh, who was the firstborn, standing on the right, and Ephraim, the youngest, on the left, Jacob crossed his hands as he laid them on the boys. He honored Ephraim by laying his right hand on him, and assigned second place, as it were, to Manasseh by giving him the left hand, and so he began his blessing of them. For we have been received as worshipers, both the first peoples and those who came after them. We were not brought by Moses or by the prophets, for the law was too sluggish to bring salvation, but by the Son himself. For through him, as I said, we have access. His aim was to put Israel ahead of the flock from the Gentiles, for Joseph placed Manasseh at his father's right. But since they behaved with unspeakable impiety toward him, the Father gave preference to those who came second in time, that is, the Gentiles, and the last became first and the first last. Jacob blessed the boys, calling God the one who fed him and an angel the one who rescued him, and so joining the Son to God the Father in everything. For the Son is also called the Angel of Great Counsel by the voice of the prophets. So every grace, and every kind of blessing and help that comes to us, can come in no other way than from the Father through the Son. Indeed the divine Paul says, 'Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.' The divine Joseph, however, was displeased to see the firstborn placed, as it were, behind the younger. Then the father made clear the force of the mystery, saying, 'This one too will become a people, and this one too will be exalted; but his younger brother will be greater than he, and his seed will become a multitude of nations.' Then, after some other words, it says, 'And he set Ephraim before Manasseh.' As far as it depended on Christ's will, Israel would not have slipped from its own glory. Indeed he said plainly, 'I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.' But since Israel was hardened, as it is written, and remained disobedient, treating with contempt the call to salvation from the one who called it, it was placed on the left and holds the lesser glory. It too is blessed and exalted, in the part of it that has been saved; and this is the remnant, as the prophet says. But the people from the Gentiles stands far above it, spreading out into assemblies of peoples. It is greater than Israel, and its preeminence lies in the immeasurable multitude of those who have believed. For we have been crowned with one and the same grace for sanctification, both those from Israel and those from the Gentiles who have believed and been justified in Christ. Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

The aim of this discourse is to set out each of the things said by the forefather Jacob about what would happen in due time to the sons born of him. But it gives clear warning in advance that the meaning of these sayings is extremely hard to reach. Most people cannot get to it, because it is expressed in riddles and obscurely. Mixed in with the form of blessing is something that is not blessing at all, and this is harder still to grasp. The inspired Jacob promises to foretell to his children what will happen in the last days. Yet he recalls things already past and takes the measure of their offenses: first that of Reuben, then straight after it, as its neighbour, that of Simeon and Levi. Who, then, would dare to say that recalling sins already committed will be a form of blessing for anyone, without being thought to speak falsely and to have run aground far from the proper sense? The account of this matter is deep, then, and not easily within reach of those who wish to grasp it. So what interpretation shall we say fits the passage before us? To put it briefly, the narrative of the prophecy will surely bring before us a type of the whole race, or of each tribe: what sort it will be in due time, for what things it will be condemned, how it will win good repute, or perhaps in what matters, and how its affairs will finally turn out. Observe how in some cases he paints what will come later from what has already happened, while in others he makes the account of the names, that is, their interpretation, a kind of disclosure of what is to come and a clear foreshowing. So it is written: "And Jacob called his sons and said: Gather together, so that I may tell you what will befall you in the last of the days. Assemble and listen, sons of Jacob; listen to Israel your father."

"Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the first of my children, hard to bear and harshly headstrong. You were insolent like water; do not boil over.
