For you went up onto your father's bed; then you defiled the couch you went up to." Reuben, then, stole his father's marriage bed. He was caught, quite openly, having done what is forbidden, and the deed was condemned as wicked by Jacob's own verdict, for, it says, "it appeared wicked in the sight of Jacob." But I do not think anyone would suppose that what is already past will take place in the last times. To understand it that way would be utterly foolish. Instead, if we recast the type of the offense into something resembling it, we shall see the sin of the firstborn people, I mean Israel. God took to himself the synagogue that came out of Egypt as if she were a wife, through the spiritual communion of the law. He received her and counted her worthy to belong to him, and so made her fruitful and a mother of children. The all-wise Moses all but led the bride to him, and angels acted as go-betweens in the union. But the Synagogue, brought to this by God, offended against the law of faithfulness. In a way she joined herself to the sons of her husband and played the harlot under them. She no longer bore fruit to the one who had lived with her through the law, but rather surrendered her own mind to the seed of others. Clearly I mean spiritual seed, the seed of teaching. For she despised as stale what had been set before her by God and turned to the commandments and teachings of men. Disregarding the lessons from above, she simply made a law of whatever she saw fit. That is why the prophet Isaiah says: "How has the faithful city Zion, once full of justice, become a harlot? Righteousness lodged in her, but now murderers. Your silver is debased. Your tavern-keepers mix the wine with water." Righteousness, that is, God, lodged with her and made his stay there. But she took in murderers, adulterers and corrupters, who gave her debased silver and mixed the wine with water. Truly debased is the word of those who persuade her to honor the teachings and commandments of men. Their teaching is adulterated, as it were, and not free of admixture with what is worse. This, I think, is what it means to say that the wine is mixed with water. And to see that the thing grieved the God of all, and that he rightly accused Jerusalem of harlotry, listen to him speaking plainly at one point through the voice of Jeremiah: "Lift up your eye and look straight ahead, and see where you have been defiled. By the roadsides you sat like a deserted crow, and you defiled the land with your harlotries, and you had many shepherds as a stumbling block for yourself. You had the look of a harlot; you grew shameless toward everyone. You did not call me your husband, and father, and guide of your virginity." And again at another point: "If a man sends his wife away, and she leaves him and becomes another man's wife, will she ever return to him again? Will not that woman be utterly defiled? And you have played the harlot with many shepherds, and yet you were returning to me? says the Lord." The Savior himself also showed us clearly what form this harlotry took. The Pharisees, always fault-finding and without understanding, came to him and said: "Why do your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread." And Christ said to them: "Why do you also transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? For God said: Honor your father and your mother, so that it may go well with you. But you say," he says, "Whoever says to his father or his mother, 'Corban,' that is, 'a gift,' whatever you might have gained from me, need not honor his father or his mother. And so you have made void the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition." Do you hear how, having come under other teachers and having chosen to think and do things contrary to what the lawgiver wished, they are caught out with very little effort? So the Synagogue of the Jews has played the harlot. But the pure and blameless virgin, free from every spot and wrinkle, that is, the Church, promises to keep the bond of marriage with Christ revered and unbroken, saying: "My beloved is mine, and I am his." Let us therefore take Jacob's concubine Bilhah as an image of the Synagogue of the Jews. Reuben, that is, the firstborn people, had relations with her. This is all the more fitting because Bilhah is interpreted "grown old" and Reuben "son of profanation." For the Synagogue of the Jews has grown old and indeed wrinkled, and in its place the new people, the people of faith, has sprung up. Over this people let David sing for joy: "A people being created shall praise the Lord." For according to the Scriptures, what is in Christ is a new creation. Israel, on the other hand, would rightly be considered profane and filthy, because it did not receive the cleansing that comes through Christ. And why do I say this? It even laid hands on the very one who spoke to it about cleansing. For this reason it was said through the voice of the holy prophets themselves, at one time: "If the Ethiopian can change his skin and the leopard her spots, then you too will be able to do good, though you have learned evil." At another time it was said to Jerusalem, as to a woman: "Even if you wash yourself with lye and use much soap, you are stained before me in your iniquities, says the Lord." So Jacob says: "Reuben, my firstborn; you are my strength and the first of my children." For in the case of the firstborn people that came out of Egypt, God made a display of great strength. The land of the Egyptians was punished in a great many ways, all of them marvellous: water was changed into blood, gnats were stirred up, frogs were brought up, hail was sent down, the firstborn were slain, and on top of this the redeemed passed through the midst of the sea as if over dry land. That is why Reuben is called the strength of God. But he was hard to bear and harshly headstrong, that is, unchangeable, unbending, savage and aggressive. For the Jews are truly impetuous and quite unruly. So they rightly hear: "Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit." And Christ himself says somewhere: "Which of the prophets did your fathers not kill? And you have filled up the measure of your fathers." Israel, then, is reckless, quick to anger and fierce in its attack. It is insolent like water, that is, its onrush is irresistible against whomever it chooses, for such somehow is the rush of waters. "But do not boil over," he says. What does this mean? Boiling water rises upward, overflows the cauldrons, and somehow seems to be a great quantity. Since he has given Reuben the rush of water, he keeps to the metaphor and says: "Do not boil over," that is, do not swell into a multitude and do not become numerous. For compared with the great number of the Gentiles, those of Israel's blood who have been saved through faith in Christ are few. Then he adds the reason for what will happen, saying: "For you went up onto your father's bed; then you defiled the couch you went up to." As I said before, they no longer search out what is in the law and the oracles from above, but [?] the commandments of men, and for this reason they have missed the knowledge of Christ. That is why he himself says: "You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life. And it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me so that you may have life." And again: "If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me." He also sharply rebuked the teachers of the Jews, saying: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces. For you do not enter yourselves, nor do you allow those who are entering to go in." And again: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you travel over sea and land to make a single proselyte, and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves." But he would not have become a son of Gehenna if he had not attached himself to the words of the adulterers. Those of Israel's blood, then, have gone up onto their father's bed. They thrust aside what the lawgiver wished as stale, brought in their own words for those they taught, and planted seeds of uncleanness in them.

"Simeon and Levi, brothers, carried out injustice by their own choice. Let my soul not enter into their counsel, and let my inmost being not be joined to their gathering. For in their anger they killed men, and in their desire they hamstrung a bull. Cursed be their anger, for it was headstrong, and their wrath, for it was hardened. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel." Jerusalem had played the harlot and had surrendered her mind to the unholy deceptions of those who make a habit of teaching otherwise. The God of all was rightly angered, and he said very plainly through the voice of Isaiah: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men." Profane Jerusalem was, as it were, drunk with her waywardness and negligence in these matters, and God the Father planned to reform her for the better. So he sent his own Son from heaven, made like us, that is, made man. The great number of the holy prophets had ended in futile labor, for they said: "Lord, who has believed our report?" So he sent the Son in order that they might at least respect him when he finally came. But they sank to such depths of bad counsel as to think they could even seize the Lord's inheritance. Having killed the saints, they went beyond the very limit of impiety and raged outrageously against the Son himself. For they said among themselves: "This is the heir; come, let us kill him and take possession of his inheritance." Nor did their impiety stop there. To the holy prophets they added a second group, I mean the holy apostles, and did not spare even their blood. This is the kind of meaning that the intent of the prophecy before us is laboring to bring forth. The inspired Jacob seems to be recalling once again what was done at Shechem. But the righteous man's real intent is this, for how could anyone accept what had already happened as something that would happen in due time? So, starting from what happened at Shechem, he applies it to what was done to Christ as a sin of the same kind, just as he did in the case of the firstborn Reuben. What, then, did Simeon and Levi do at Shechem? Dinah, the sister of Levi and Simeon, went out of her father's tent to see the daughters of the people of the land, and Shechem the son of Hamor took her by force. For he deflowered her. Her brothers were enraged at this and plotted to kill the men by deceit. First they persuaded them to adopt the circumcision of their fathers, saying that they would at once become their kinsmen by race too if they chose to do this. But when they had done it, the brothers killed them without warning, thinking it would be enough to defend themselves by saying: "Should they treat our sister like a harlot?"

We must now go on to what corresponds to this, and shape the contemplation as well as we can, gathering from every side whatever helps to make it clear. When we were expanding on the account of Jacob, we described how and in what manner he lived, which wives he took into his house, and how many children he fathered. We said that he married Leah, the eldest of Laban's daughters, and second after her, not long afterward, the youngest, Rachel. We also affirmed that for us Leah will be a type of the Synagogue of the Jews, and Rachel of the Church from the Gentiles. For Leah is interpreted "toiling," and her eyes were rather weak and less beautiful. The Synagogue of the Jews has toiled hard, burdened by the law given through Moses, and it looks upon the mystery of our Savior with eyes that are not strong. But Rachel was beautiful in form and very lovely, and the Church from the Gentiles is surpassingly distinguished. Now Leah's last daughter was Dinah. She too could be a type, of the multitude from the circumcision that arose in the last times, when the Only-begotten became man. That last multitude from the circumcision went a little outside the ancestral tent, that is, outside the customs of the law, and came into contact with the people of the land. In other words, it mingled with them in learning. I mean the holy apostles, who no longer lived in the Jewish way and were regarded, as it were, as foreigners. Then, at that very time, she was spiritually deflowered, receiving from them the seeds of the gospel and of the life in Christ. But some of Jacob's sons, Simeon and Levi, were indignant at this, that is, those ranked as subjects, and with them the sacred and chosen race. For Simeon is interpreted "obedience," and Levi "taken up" or "chosen." Those who had been allotted the honors of the priesthood under the law attacked the holy apostles fiercely, and the people ran along with them. How can anyone doubt this? They gnashed their teeth and called the conversion of those under their charge a corruption, bringing it as though it were one of the most outrageous charges: "Look," they said, "you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching." And since they reproached the apostles for no longer living like Jews, they were taught that circumcision was honored among them, and that nothing at all walled them off into difference, if only they chose to understand the writings of Moses in the proper way. For it says: "He is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision something outward in the flesh. Rather, he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter." You see how those who were reputed to be foreigners were conformed to the Jews, for they bore the circumcision of the spirit and were Jews inwardly. Yet even so they killed them, having already done away with the prophets, and Emmanuel himself. So, it says, "Simeon and Levi carried out injustice by their own choice." For Simeon, and Levi too, agreed and joined together in injustice against the saints, that is, the people and the priests. "By their own choice" means by deliberation and intent. The sufferings of the victims were not simply improvised by chance, nor were the outrages and the monstrous audacity unpremeditated. They came straight from their councils to do things beyond every evil. So the inspired Jacob rejects their compact in this matter, their joint counsels, their deliberation. "Let my soul not enter into their counsel," he says, "and let my inmost being not be joined to their gathering." It is as if he said: "May I never fix the eyes of my mind on such counsels, nor ever admit into my heart these grievous schemes of the impious." So too the prophet Isaiah bewails the Jewish crowds, saying: "Woe to their soul, for they have plotted an evil plot against themselves, saying: Let us bind the righteous one, for he is troublesome to us." And David sings: "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners." And again: "I have hated the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the ungodly." So the inspired Jacob distances himself from the Jewish schemes. He then adds the reasons, saying: "For in their anger they killed men, and in their desire they hamstrung a bull." As I said, they killed saints, driven by unholy anger to cruelty and inhumanity. And the wretches conceived an utterly futile and ill-considered desire and hamstrung a bull, that is, Christ. We have already said what that desire was: recognizing that he is the heir, they desired to have his inheritance.

Notice how precise the wording is. They killed the men, but they hamstrung the bull. They put the saints to death, and these remained dead, awaiting the time of the resurrection. But Christ, like a calf hamstrung by an eagle, sank down to the ground, as it were, willingly enduring death in the flesh. Yet death could not hold him fast. Although he died as a man, he remained alive in the nature of his Godhead. Christ is a bull, for this animal is exceedingly strong, clean and most sacred. And the Son is Lord of hosts. He committed no sin, but rather offered himself up for us as a fragrant aroma to God the Father. So let those who hamstrung such a venerable bull hear this: "Cursed be their anger, for it was headstrong, and their wrath, for it was hardened." What, then, has happened to them? They went out from their own land and left the country that bore them. They were scattered and became strangers everywhere, aliens living in fear. For it is true that "as a bird is when it flies from its own nest, so is a man when he is torn from his own places." I think it fitting to add this too. For those who hamstrung the bull the deed will be a curse. But for those who have grieved over it and shake off so terrible a charge, it will be a ransom, a cleansing and a putting away of sins. We shall find what I have said written in the shadow of the law. For in Deuteronomy it reads as follows: "If someone slain is found in the land that the Lord your God is giving you to inherit, lying in the open field, and it is not known who struck him, your elders and your judges shall go out and measure the distance to the cities around the slain man, and it will be the city nearest to the slain man. And the elders of that city shall take a heifer from the herd that has not been worked and has not pulled in a yoke. The elders of that city shall bring the heifer down into a rugged ravine that has not been worked or sown, and they shall hamstring the heifer in the ravine. And the priests, the Levites, shall come forward, for the Lord your God has chosen them to stand in his presence and to bless in his name, and by their word every dispute and every case of injury shall be settled. And all the elders of that city, those nearest to the slain man, shall wash their hands over the head of the heifer that was hamstrung in the ravine, and they shall answer and say: Our hands did not shed this blood, and our eyes did not see it. Be merciful, Lord, to your people Israel, whom you redeemed from the land of Egypt, so that innocent blood may not remain among your people Israel. And the blood shall be atoned for them. So you shall remove the innocent blood from among yourselves." Each of these points will be discussed in detail at the proper time, but for now we say this. Understand how certain people clear themselves of the charge of bloodshed, while the heifer represents Emmanuel for us in her own person. Those who clear themselves must, I think, say: "Our hands did not shed this blood." But the people of the Jews will never be found to have cried this out. Rather, as they hamstrung the calf, they dared to say: "Our hands shed this blood." For this, I think, is no different from what they said so senselessly about Christ: "His blood be on us and on our children."

Judah, your brothers will praise you. Your hands will be on the back of your enemies. The sons of your father will bow down to you. Judah is a lion's cub; from a shoot, my son, you have gone up; you lay down and slept like a lion, and like a cub. Who will rouse him? A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the things laid up for him come; and he is the expectation of the nations. Binding his colt to the vine, and the foal of his donkey to the tendril, he will wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape. His eyes are cheerful with wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.

The character of the blessing shows itself very clearly to us in these words, for it sets before its hearers the prediction of our Savior's dispensation. As a beginning for its praises it lays down first the meaning of the name, and then also the pre-eminence in glory of the tribe of Judah over the others. If anyone chose to explain the word or name "Judah," he would interpret it as "praise," or "hymning," or "one who is hymned." The saying refers to Christ, who according to the flesh is of the tribe of Judah. For he appeared from Judah, and Jesse, and David, and from the Virgin who was taken up for the birth of the flesh. So the prophet, looking ahead to the one from the tribe of Judah, says: "Your name is true, as the very force of events will show. For you will be hymned, and you will receive the glory that befits God. For being glorified would suit no other, but only the one who truly is and is known to be God. Even if you have appeared as a man and have emptied yourself, you will nevertheless be known as one to be revered and celebrated in song. And your brothers will not attach themselves to you as to a mere man because of your humanity; rather, though you have been placed among brothers, they will acclaim you as Master and hymn you as Creator; and though you are counted with them among created things, they will acknowledge you as King and Lord of all, even though you are veiled in the form of a servant."

That Emmanuel will prevail over all who oppose him and will easily overcome his enemies, he proclaimed beforehand, saying: Your hands will be on the back of your enemies. Christ himself also foretold this through the voice of David. For he said: I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they are consumed. I will crush them, and they will not be able to stand; they will fall beneath my feet. So the hands will be on the back of the enemies, he says, as of one who pursues rather than flees; not as of one who is struck, but as of one who strikes them down. For what is sung in the book of Psalms is true: The enemy shall gain no advantage over him, and the son of lawlessness shall not again harm him. If he himself grants us to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy, how can we not confess that he himself, before us, will hold under his hand those who wish to march out against him and who rise up against him impiously? That he does not know how to flee, but rather how to pursue, and how to conquer whomever he wishes, and that without effort—for he has overcome the world—the inspired Jacob declared beforehand, saying: Your hands will be on the back of your enemies, and the sons of your father will bow down to you.

Again, what is to be understood as the difference between the brothers who praise and the sons of the father who will be ranked with those who worship? This must certainly be explained. The blessed Joseph was registered as Christ's father, although he was not truly his father. He had sons and daughters from a first marriage. Since these perhaps shared a home with Christ, and saw him working signs and yet not altogether yielding to the requirements of the law—because of his indifference regarding food and his not choosing to honor the Sabbath rest very strictly, for he said, It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a man, and, The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath—they were divided in mind. They did not wish to honor him wholeheartedly, since he seemed not to be blameless in matters of the law, nor did they think it right to leave one so illustrious unadmired. And so they once came to him and said plainly: If you do these things, show yourself to the world. For no one does anything in secret while seeking to be known openly. And the evangelist added to this: For not even his brothers believed in him. But those who said these things at first came to believe as time went on. For they became fully convinced that he is God by nature, even though he came in the flesh and appeared as a man. The blessed prophet Jeremiah, foreknowing this in the Spirit, says to Emmanuel himself: For even your brothers and the house of your father, even they have dealt treacherously with you, and they have cried out behind you. They have gathered together; do not trust them, for they will speak evil to you. For those who once cried out against him together with the others were brought together in faith and spoke good things about him. Thus the blessed James writes to the twelve tribes, saying: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ. So then, those who have been called to brotherhood through faith and through the sanctification that comes by faith will praise him as God; and no less will the sons of the father worship him. And it is clear that those who worship will also praise, and those who weave the praise will no less be worshipers.

For Christ is a lion's cub from Judah, being the Son of God the Almighty, to whom it belongs to conquer without a fight and to be able to strike down his opponents with a mere word; for, as the prophet says, A lion will roar, and who will not be afraid? Christ, then, is a lion's cub, springing up as from a shoot and from a noble root, the holy Virgin. For he himself is the rod of power which God sent us out of Zion, the staff that comforts and upholds all, the staff of uprightness and of kingship, which shepherds the flocks of the saints rightly and gently, but shatters like a potter's vessel those who will not endure to be pastured under it. He is the rod of Aaron, which had its place in the divine tabernacle and was carried into the Holy of Holies, and which blossomed with almonds—a symbol of the resurrection. For the wood of the almond tree in some way produces wakefulness. And the mystery of the resurrection is held in high honor in the churches of God. For this reason the blessed Jacob, having named the shoot, at once recalls what came at the end of the dispensation, and says: You lay down and slept like a lion. That is: you underwent death not unwillingly; though you were able like a lion to seize and terrify all and to escape the hand of the hunters, you lay down of your own will, not overpowered by death, as those who chose to crucify you supposed, but as though taking sleep and closing your eyes for a little while. Who then will rouse him? he says. It is as if he said: He lay down willingly, but he will need no one else's help for his resurrection. For he is all-powerful, as the power of the Father, and not at all lacking the ability to give life to his own temple, and that very easily. This indeed is what he said when speaking to the Jews: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. That no one would be his helper in this, but that he alone, as the strength of the one who begot him, would suffice, the saying indicates quite plainly.

But what the time of his coming will be, he makes plain, saying: A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes for whom it is laid up; and he is the expectation of the nations. For the Jews ruled, and their leaders were of the blood of Israel, until Herod son of Antipater, a Palestinian, was named tetrarch and seized the rule; and under him Christ himself was born, the expectation of the nations. That the multitude of the nations was saved when he was born will need no long arguments to prove, since the fact itself proclaims it aloud. But that the newborn and new people from the nations entered first through faith, and that Israel will be called in after it, he taught at once, saying: Binding his colt to the vine. For the true vine, that is, Christ, bound to himself, as it were, through faith the people from the nations, whom he likens to the colt. And that he bound to the tendril of the vine—that is, by his own love—the foal of his donkey, I mean the people who believed from the older mother of the Jews, that is, the Synagogue: how could anyone doubt this, when practically the whole of divinely inspired Scripture speaks to us of this mystery?

That he would redden his own flesh with his own blood, when he was nailed to the wood and pierced by the lance, he showed by saying: He will wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape. Indeed the inspired Isaiah, recounting Christ's ascent into heaven, says that the holy angels, that is, the powers above, said: Who is this who comes from Edom? The red of his garments is from Bozrah. And again: Why are your garments red, and your clothing as from a trodden winepress? And that, even though he was among the dead and endured the drunken outrages of the Jews, their blows and reproaches, he takes little account of such things, since he suffered for us and saved the whole world under heaven, but rather abides always in the gladness that is most dear and natural to him, he shows by saying: His eyes are cheerful with wine. For in these words, I think, one may understand the, as it were, smiling, ever glad and gracious character of his divinity. For the mind of those who have drunk is somehow always cheerful, and utterly scornful of the things that usually cause grief. And since speech comes forth, as it were, from the teeth, he says that they too are white, as sending forth from the tongue a word that is pure and bright. For Christ in no way errs in speech, but rather speaks uprightly and truly; and whatever he utters is fitting for the holy, wondrous, and produces in those who hear it the greatest brightness of soul and mind.

Zebulun shall dwell by the sea; he too shall be by a harbor of ships, and shall extend as far as Sidon. We have already said earlier that, in examining the sense of the prophecy before us and striving to see how it stands and how it may be properly worked out, we proceed partly by analogy with what has already been treated; and partly, I think, anyone with sense could show that it is shaped almost entirely by the very interpretation of the names, and that it reveals beforehand the form of things to come. This can be seen especially, once again, in the case of Zebulun and those that follow. For the name is interpreted as "good journey" and "blessing" by those well accustomed to explaining such things. We shall find, then, certain blessed ones among Israel, rich in good success in all that pleases God—namely, those who have been justified through faith in Christ and made radiant by the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that at last they can cry out without falsehood: We are blessed by the Lord who made heaven and earth. I think the words of the blessed prophet Isaiah would also fit them: The way of the godly has become straight, and the way of the godly is prepared. For the way of the Lord is judgment. The God of all has commanded that those who are thus illustrious and blessed be called into the sacred and divine court, saying: Open the gates; let a people enter that keeps righteousness and keeps truth, that lays hold of truth and keeps peace. But so that they should not stumble on the obstacles along the way and grow hesitant about good things, he commanded that there be, as it were, a smooth road and that the entrance be cleared, saying to the holy priests: Go through my gates, and throw the stones out of the way. So those of Israel who have honored faith in Christ would be both blessed and prospered on their way.

He clearly affirmed that they, that is, Zebulun, would dwell in the region next to the sea. It is as if he were saying that Israel would henceforth be mingled with the nations, since the two peoples have been brought together into one flock and have come under the hand of one chief shepherd, who is good by nature, that is, Christ. That this riddle is true, the word of inspired Scripture will easily confirm, for it assigns the land bordering the sea to those of the nations. It says: Land of Zebulun, land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, and the rest who dwell along the coast, Galilee of the nations: the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light. Do you see how it called the land of Zebulun the land of the nations, who also beheld a great light—clearly through Christ? So Israel, dwelling with those who inhabit the coast, was enlightened together with them. And this, I think, is what it means to be prospered by God. For that being prospered must altogether and in every way follow upon being enlightened, we shall learn once more from the Savior, who says to the crowds of the Jews: While you have the light, walk in the light, so that darkness may not overtake you. So the people that formerly dwelt alone and refused to mingle with the nations will dwell together with them, with nothing standing between them to divide them, because Christ has broken down the dividing wall of the fence, abolished the law of commandments in ordinances, and at last made the two peoples into one new man in Christ through the Spirit. And he will be, he says, by a harbor of ships; that is, as if in a safe and calm harbor, fastening the cables of his hope to Christ. For, as though he had come out of a great storm, he will henceforth lie at anchor in Christ's grace, just as merchant ships do in harbors. And the statement that he extends even as far as Sidon seems to indicate that the two peoples will come together in such spiritual union that those of Israel's blood will fill even those cities which had incurred great blame and reproach before God, as having once led astray and, in a way, plundered those who worshiped him. For he said somewhere through the voice of the prophets: And what are you to me, Tyre and Sidon and all Galilee of the foreigners? Are you paying me back a recompense, or do you bear a grudge against me? Swiftly and speedily I will return your recompense on your own heads, because you took my silver and my gold, and carried my choice and beautiful things into your temples, and sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel to the sons of the Greeks, to drive them out of their borders. See, then, how the cities that were once dreadful and most hostile, bringers of destruction to those of Israel, will receive those who believe, free from all fear, as our Savior Christ binds the two peoples together in peace into one mind, abolishing the enmity and settling Israel among the nations in love. In this way, then, and in no other, I think, Zebulun will dwell by the sea.

Issachar desired what is good, resting among the inheritances. And seeing that rest was good, and that the land was rich, he set his shoulder to labor and became a farmer. Issachar, again, is interpreted as "reward." From what the name signifies, it would be a type, a clear image, as it were, of those whom God the Father allotted to Christ as a kind of reward. For, Ask of me, says David, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession. And again, I think, he sings of those given to Emmanuel, all but pointing them out: Behold, the inheritance of the Lord is sons, the reward of the fruit of the womb. For those who have believed, he says, both of Israel's blood and of the other multitude, I mean the one from the nations, have been given to Emmanuel as a kind of reward. Having named Jesus Lord, he said that he became the fruit of the womb because of his likeness to us. For he was born of a woman and shown to be the fruit of a virgin womb. So Christ has gained the believers, and it is perhaps about them that he says to his Father and God in heaven: Those whom you have given me out of the world were yours, and you gave them to me. These, then, desired what is good, that is, everything that is called, and truly is, excellent and most dear to God. This they hold of great account and strive to accomplish, crying out from a good heart: The judgments of the Lord are true, altogether righteous, more to be desired than gold and much precious stone. Good, besides this, is the desire to be under Christ himself. This is what the bride says in the Song of Songs: In his shadow I longed to be, and I sat down. The people who have advanced to this disposition will look carefully on the portions allotted by God, that is, the good things promised in hope to the godly. Of these the divine David also said: My lots are in your hands. It will lodge in them, as it were, and rest entirely and completely, because it will attain what it hopes for. Having then approved its own counsel and judgment, and having judged the rest found in these things worthy of no small admiration—that is, eternal honor, life in perfect holiness, endless glory, a kingdom that cannot be lost, and all that is beyond mind and tongue—it will henceforth be steadfast in hardship. For having seen that the land is rich, it will set its shoulder to it, he says, and love the labor. He takes the example from those who are accustomed to farm best, who are most industrious and fond of the mattock, and are eager to sweat at the plough if they get hold of rich land, thinking, I suppose, of the abundant fruit and what it will yield. The wise Hosea also urges us to this, saying: Sow for yourselves unto righteousness, gather the vintage for the fruit of life; kindle for yourselves the light of knowledge. Seek the Lord until the fruits of righteousness come to you. And the blessed Paul also prayed, saying: He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed and increase the harvest of your righteousness, so that, always having all sufficiency, you may abound in every good work.

“Dan shall judge his people, as one tribe in Israel. And let Dan be a serpent lying in wait on the road, on the path, biting the horse’s heel, and the rider shall fall backward, waiting for salvation from the Lord.” Once again the passage follows the etymology of the name, for Dan means “judge” or “judgment.” He, too, would represent in his own person the glorious and illustrious company of the holy apostles. They were set as rulers over the believers and were given the office of judging, Christ assigning it to them. The divine Paul says as much: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more the affairs of this life!” According to the Scriptures there is one judge and lawgiver, Christ. But if the apostles are ambassadors on Christ’s behalf, and the word of reconciliation has been entrusted to them, there is nothing strange in their also being understood as judges in the likeness of Christ. The great Isaiah, too, cries out to us somewhere, making plain both the godlike kingship of Christ himself and the proclamation of the holy apostles themselves: “Behold, a righteous king shall reign, and rulers shall rule with judgment.” In former times those of the tribe of Judah reigned over Jerusalem, while those who served at the holy tabernacle and had received the lot of the priesthood were appointed to judge: “For the lips of a priest shall guard judgment, and they shall seek the law from his mouth.” But once the shadow in the law had, as it were, been drawn in, and worship in spirit and truth had been brought in through Christ, the world needed more illustrious judges. So the divine disciples were then called to this task and entered into the place of the teachers of the law. That is why God said to the mother of the Jews, I mean Jerusalem, through the voice of the Psalmist: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you,” that is, “those who are called your sons have taken over the rank of the fathers.” And to our Lord Jesus Christ he said: “You will make them rulers over all the earth.” One can see this fulfilled. For we have taken as our rulers, and have as judges for the whole world, the holy disciples. Through their instructions the very mystery of Christ is proclaimed, since they are stewards of the saving word and guides in what must be done. They reject as counterfeit whatever does nothing to benefit those being taught, and they counsel that what is by nature beneficial should be taken up. So “Dan,” he says, meaning those who from time to time are appointed to judge nations and peoples, will rule as powerfully and with as much glory as one of the tribes of Israel. And he means, I think, the royal tribe, Judah, and no other. For how could anyone doubt that those whom the Savior appointed as teachers of all under the sun are held in the highest honor, and have reached the summit of glory, among his worshippers? Yet their rule would not be entirely free of hardship. They were to experience many countless evils. They would be hindered, and would not find the course of their apostleship wholly free of dangers. He hints at this in a figure when he says, “Let Dan be,” that is, the mob of persecutors will be to Dan like a serpent sitting on the road, on the path, biting the horse’s heel, that is, inflicting terrible and inescapable bites. For the bites of vipers are hard to escape, even when they strike only the heel: “He will watch for your head,” it says, “and you will watch for his heel.” Some plotted against the holy apostles to the point of bringing about even their bodily death. And we say they suffered something like what might befall a rider when his horse buckles and, as it were, sinks backward. The rider will be thrown on his back and, having fallen to the ground, I think, will wait for the one who saves. So the divine disciples will wait for the time of their glory and salvation, when they will be called into an unshakable and eternal kingdom, Christ calling out to them: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” For they have finished the race and kept the faith, and so they will receive the unfading crown of glory. But suppose someone prefers the reading that Dan himself will plot against others, rather than that some will lie in wait like serpents on the road against Dan. Then we shall say this: the scribes and Pharisees, who had charge of judging and leading the peoples, attacked Christ like the most venomous vipers. They were caught in the impious act of cutting down with their bites, so to speak, a rider speeding along a bare and smooth path. But though the rider fell, willingly enduring death in the flesh, he will nevertheless come back to life, taking the Father as his helper and support. For the Son, being the power of God the Father, himself brought his own temple back to life. That is why he is said to have been saved by the Father after facing danger as a man, although he is God by nature and himself holds together the whole of creation, visible and invisible, in its well-being. The divine Paul understood it this way when he said of him: “For though he was crucified in weakness, yet he lives by the power of God.”

“Gad: a band of trial shall try him, but he shall try it close on its heels.” Once again he has explained what Gad means: “temptation” or “trial.” It would be fitting, I think, to understand by this the God-hated and arrogant swarm of scribes and Pharisees. They thrust aside the divine preaching of the gospel and placed no value on anything needed for their own good. They gnashed their teeth at Christ. He was teaching things beyond the shadow and the law, he was highly esteemed and admired, and he was astonishing everyone throughout Judea no less by the abundance of his miracles, adding wonders to his teaching on everything that pleases God. So when, in keeping with the prophet’s words, he left Bethany and entered Jerusalem, meek and mounted on a beast of burden, a young colt, the children going ahead acclaimed him, saying: “Hosanna to the son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Some of those running alongside spread their garments on the roads and made his entry a marvel. But the scribes and Pharisees were bursting with rage and, stung by the sharper goads of envy, talked among themselves, all but blaming one another for still delaying when he had to be killed. For they said: “You see that you are getting nowhere. Look, the whole world has gone after him.” Since they feared the crowd of those who already believed, they held back their hands for the time being and refrained from an open attack. But to bring him into conflict with the Roman authorities, they sent some of their own disciples together with those called Herodians, who said: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and defer to no one, for you do not regard people’s status. Is it lawful to pay tax to Caesar, or not?” They were refuted at once when, after the coin had been shown, Christ said to them: “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” They ought to have blushed at this and given up testing him. Instead they launched another test. He had made a kind of whip out of cords and driven out of the temple all those selling sheep and oxen, saying: “Take these things out of here. Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.” They came to him indignant: “By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?” And what did Christ say to this? “I too will ask you a question,” he says, “and you tell me: the baptism of John, where did it come from? From heaven, or from human beings?” And they argued among themselves, it says: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Then why did you not believe him?’ If we say, ‘From human beings,’ we are afraid of the crowd, for they all regard John as a prophet.” And they say, it says: “We do not know.” And what did Christ say to this? “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.” So Gad is a band of trial, that is, the Pharisees who were always putting him to the test. Yet they were tested in return close on their heels, that is, immediately. For it was Christ who, in the prophet’s words, catches the wise in their own wisdom, and who cleverly turned the schemes of the crafty back on them with a counter-question.

“Asher: his bread is rich, and he shall give food to rulers.” Asher, again, means “wealth”; this is the sense of the name. Here too, I think, it may be understood of the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, that is, Christ: the treasure hidden in a field, the pearl of great price, who also says most plainly in the person of Wisdom: “Wealth and glory are mine, and the possession of many things, and righteousness.” He is the one who visited the earth, as David says: “You have greatly enriched it.” The most wise Paul also writes to us about him: “I always give thanks to my God for you because of the grace of God given to you in Christ Jesus, that in every way you have been enriched in him, in all speech and all knowledge.” For although God is rich, he shared our poverty, so that by his poverty we might become rich. To him, then, the rich bread certainly belongs, that is, bread that is very rich and most nourishing. For our Lord Jesus Christ feeds us, not by sending down perceptible manna as he once did for those of Israel, but by making himself dwell in the souls of believers through the Holy Spirit. That is why he said to the Jewish crowds: “Truly, truly, I tell you, it was not Moses who gave you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” And again: “I am the bread of life.” Bread is also understood as life-giving in another sense, one belonging to the more ineffable mysteries. And he gives food to rulers. For I would say that Thrones and Authorities, Principalities and Powers, angels and archangels, and the whole holy and rational creation take Christ as their food, in whatever sense it is fitting to understand this. But he also distributes food to the leaders of the flocks on earth, food that is clearly spiritual: the revelation of the divine mysteries and the knowledge of every virtue, so that they in turn may nourish the peoples under their care with the teachings that lead to life. That is why he says to them: “You received without payment; give without payment.” And elsewhere: “Who then is the faithful and wise servant whom his master will put in charge of his household, to give them their ration of grain at the proper time? Truly I tell you, blessed is that servant whom his master will find doing so when he comes. Truly I tell you, he will put him in charge of all his possessions.” We shall find the teachers of the churches doing this, and before them the holy apostles. The blessed Paul writes to some: “For I long to see you, so that I may share with you some spiritual gift to strengthen you.” And they themselves say that they have been comforted by God, who evidently fills them with the good things from above and enriches them abundantly with the gifts of the Spirit. Asher, then, is Christ, or else those who have become rich in Christ, to whom the rich bread may be understood to belong.

“Naphtali: a stem growing freely, adding beauty to its offspring.” This too, I think, one could apply, and not wide of the mark, to Emmanuel himself, and indeed, if one wishes, to those who have been justified by faith and sanctified in the Spirit. For it was said to the mother of the Jews, I mean Jerusalem, through the voice of Jeremiah: “A beautiful olive tree, well shaded in appearance: so the Lord called your name. At the sound of her circumcision a fire was kindled against her. Great is the affliction upon you. Her branches have become useless, and the Lord of hosts who planted you has pronounced evil against you.” When she ought to have received the care that was due to her (for this, I think, and nothing else is what circumcision signifies), he says that she became useless and was burned, because she refused to recognize the cultivator who was present. He is the one who, by the working of the Spirit as with a very sharp pruning hook, rids us of what is useless, that is, of what is earthy and carnal, so that we may bring forth desire and eagerness for everything admirable. Indeed, we can hear the Savior of us all, Christ, saying clearly: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that bears no fruit he removes, and every branch that bears fruit he prunes, so that it may bear more fruit.” For our Lord Jesus Christ is like the root and the stock of a firmly planted vine for those who have been brought into newness of life. And we, like branches, have grown onto him and hang from him spiritually through union in the Spirit, bound to him by love, luxuriating in the richness that comes from him, and nourished by divine grace to bear the fruit of virtue. The Father himself, together with the Son, watches over our affairs. But it is surely clear that, even if Christ is understood as the vine and the Father as the cultivator, he will cut away in Christ whatever is useless, and will give his care to whatever is capable of thriving and bearing fruit in him. So when the mother of the Jews, the well-shaded and beautiful olive tree, as the prophet calls her, ought to have been seen to have improved, it was then that she perished and fire was kindled in her. That is why the wise John says: “Even now the axe is laid at the root of the trees; every tree, therefore, that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.” And that the famous city was going to fall into calamities that reached the very limit of evil, the prophet Zechariah foretold, saying: “And the mourning of Jerusalem will be like the mourning for a pomegranate grove cut down in the plain.” And again, as though addressing her: “Open your doors, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars. Let the pine wail, for the cedar has fallen, for the mighty have suffered greatly. Wail, oaks of Bashan, for the dense forest has been torn down.” Lebanon is a mountain thickly covered with cedar, a fragrant tree and among the most admired for its beauty. He likens Jerusalem to Lebanon, then, because she had a remarkable multitude of priests, remarkable, I mean, as far as the honors of the law are concerned. For they had been set up as leaders, and like great, tall, straight trees in a forest, they rose above the measure of everyone else and stood far above the peoples under their authority. But Jerusalem, that is, Lebanon, was burned. And those in her who were illustrious and most prominent, who stood at the height of renown, lamented over one another as they fell and perished, having fallen, as it were, into the hands of the mightiest of woodcutters, the Roman generals. But our Lord Jesus Christ, through the very events by which those wicked men perished wretchedly, became a stem growing freely. For he ever delights in unceasing upward growth, and spreads, so to speak, over the whole earth under heaven. God foretold this very thing clearly through the voice of Ezekiel, saying: “And I will take from the choice parts of the cedar; from the top of their heart I will break off a shoot, and I will plant it on a high mountain, and I will hang it on a lofty mountain of Israel. And I will plant it, and it will put forth a shoot and bear fruit and become a great cedar, and every wild animal will rest beneath it, and every bird will rest under its shade. And its branches will be restored, and all the trees of the plain will know that I am the Lord, who brings low the high tree and raises up the low tree, who dries up the green tree and makes the dry tree flourish. I the Lord have spoken, and I will do it.” You see, then, that God the Father took the choice parts of the cedar and planted for us the tree of life, that is, Christ. By “the choice parts of the cedar” he means the tribe of Judah, which always held the rule and was more glorious than the others; from it sprang Jesse and David and the holy Virgin, who gave birth to Jesus. And how could anyone doubt that what was taken from the choice cedar was hung on the tree for our sake, and that it is a fair and most richly flowering plant? We too have sprouted anew by the Father’s counsel, we who were once dry and fruitless trees, while those who were in the moisture and life of the law, that is, those of Israel, have in a way become dry and withered. They were high, and we were low and cast down. But we have been exalted in Christ through faith, while they slipped from their ancient glory and have become low. It is God, then, the Lord of all, who by his own command brings low what is high and lifts up what is low, who dries up the green tree and makes the dry tree flourish. That those of the ancient Synagogue, no different from thorns and thistles, are all but cut away from the holy land, while the multitude of the faithful has sprung up in their place and is likened to the most fragrant of trees, you will learn from God’s words: “And I will make the desert into marshes, and the land into watercourses. I will set in the waterless land the cedar and the box, the myrtle, the cypress and the white poplar.” And further on: “And instead of the thornbush the cypress will come up, and instead of the fleabane the myrtle will come up.” By the cedar you will understand the believers’ hope of incorruption, for the cedar does not rot. By the box, that those in Christ ought not to be thought of as light-minded or frivolous; for they are all wise, since they have the mind of Christ, and boxwood is a solid wood, very dense in itself. By the myrtle, the fragrance of holiness and the evergreen freshness of grace. By the cypress, loftiness and sweet scent; lofty, I mean, in virtue and in the splendor of sound doctrine. By the white poplar, being as it were bright and dazzling white in righteousness; for those in Christ are bright, made radiant by his grace. Naphtali, then, the stem growing freely, is either Christ himself or Christ’s disciples. And when he says, “adding beauty to its offspring,” he would suggest, I believe, something like the following. At first, when Christ was seen in our form, it was not believed that he is God by nature, even though he had become flesh. Indeed, the Jews dared to try to stone him, hurling at him the charge and accusation: “Because you, being a man, make yourself God.” And we shall find even the holy apostles amazed at him as a worker of miracles, yet not yet clearly understanding the mystery concerning him. So when the sea was calmed and the rush of fierce winds was checked at Christ’s command, they, it says, reasoned among themselves, saying: “What sort of man is this, that even the sea and the winds obey him?” Do you see how what he was by nature, that is, God, even though he had become flesh, was not yet known to the people of the world, and his glory was not yet shining brightly? But when knowledge of him had grown among us, it was then believed that he is God by nature, and that every knee shall bow to him, the whole world under heaven worshipping him. So it is as knowledge of him advances toward perfection in us that he is recognized, then indeed, as fairer in beauty than the sons of men. And if “adding beauty to its offspring” should perhaps be understood of us, the meaning is not obscure. For as we continually advance in virtue and attain to better things, that is, as we strain forward to what lies ahead, in the words of the blessed Paul, we rise ever higher toward a more resplendent beauty, spiritual beauty, I mean, so that it may at last be said to us as well: “The King has desired your beauty.”

"Joseph is a son increased; a son increased, envied, my youngest son: turn back to me. Against him they took counsel and reviled him, and the masters of arrows pressed hard upon him; but their bows were broken with might, and the sinews of the arms of their hands were loosed by the hand of the Mighty One of Jacob. From there is he who strengthened Israel, from the God of your father; and my God helped you, and blessed you with the blessing of heaven above, and the blessing of the earth that holds all things, because of the blessing of breasts and womb, the blessing of your father and your mother. You have prevailed over the blessings of the enduring mountains and over the blessings of the everlasting hills; they shall be on the head of Joseph, and on the crown of the brothers whom he led." Once again the word of prophecy carries us on to Emmanuel himself. What it signifies, I think, is nothing other than what I said just now: "giving increase of beauty to the offspring." To say that he has been "increased" certainly signifies, if it is rightly understood, his advance toward what was his from the beginning, and the spreading of the glory that belongs to him by nature. The only-begotten Word of God, being God and from God, emptied himself, as the Scriptures say. He willingly came down into what he was not, clothed himself in this most inglorious flesh, and appeared in the form of a servant, becoming obedient to God the Father unto death. For this reason he is then said to be highly exalted, and, as though he lacked it because of his humanity, to have received almost as a grace the name that is above every name, as the blessed Paul says. But in truth the matter was not a gift of things he did not possess by nature from the beginning; far from it. It should rather be understood as a return and a going back to what was his in the beginning and belonged to him essentially and inalienably. That is why, having taken on the lowliness of humanity for the sake of the divine plan, he said: "Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed." For he was always in glory befitting God, coexisting with his own Begetter before every age and time and before the foundation of the world. So "increase" in Christ must be understood as the advance of his glory, which he has ever more widely and more manifestly, since those in the world recognize that he is God by nature, and as Lord of all he is glorified and worshiped together with God the Father. Yet, though he himself is the maker of the ages, he may fittingly be understood to have become also the youngest. For he appeared in the last times of the age, after the glorious and admirable choir of the holy prophets, and in short after all those before his coming who were reckoned in the rank of sons because of their virtue. That Emmanuel became "envied", that is, an object of zeal, how can anyone doubt? He is an object of zeal to the saints, who strive to follow in his footsteps, are formed after his divine beauty, make him the pattern of what they ought to do, and so carry off the best glory of all. But he may also be understood as envied in another way by those who chose not to love him, I mean the leaders of the Jews, that is, the scribes and Pharisees. They nursed a bitter jealousy within themselves, made his incomparable glory an occasion for envy, and were caught out in many ways. Christ raised the dead who already stank and had decayed, and showed himself stronger than death itself. They ought to have been amazed and moved to see that they must believe, with no more hesitation, but they did not do so; instead they were gnawed by envy and let bitter grief into their minds. He healed the man blind from birth, and they called him a sinner. Hordes of unclean demons were driven out, and they falsely claimed that Beelzebul supplied him with the power. They threw stones, saying most impiously: "It is not for a good work that we stone you, but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God." They were furious and said: "This is the heir; come, let us kill him." So he was envied also by those who chose to hate him, yet he could not be overcome altogether. For though he endured the cross, as God he came back to life and trampled on death, while God the Father all but called out and said: "Turn back to me." For he ascended into the heavens, so that he might also hear him say: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." That they were made to fall beneath him, though they were in labor with every possible rage against him, he taught when he said: "Against him they took counsel and reviled him, and the masters of arrows pressed hard upon him." For the masters of the arrows gathered councils and plotted bitter things. These are the leaders of the peoples, who sharpened against him those who would, as it were, wound him and be driven into him almost like arrowheads, because they dared to do what is unlawful and leapt upon him like wild beasts. But their bows were broken, and the sinews of their arms were loosed by the hand of the Mighty One of Jacob, that is, of God the Father, who is the Lord of hosts, and who also arranged for the Son to be blessed both in heaven and on earth. For the divine Paul writes: "And when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says: Let all the angels of God worship him." And somewhere our great David says: "Let all the earth worship you and sing psalms to you." This, we say, is the blessing from above, and the blessing on the earth below that holds all things, that is, the earth in which, because of Christ, there is now every virtue, and the fruits of piety toward God are very abundant. For somewhere it is said to the Son: "You visited the earth and watered it abundantly; you multiplied it, to enrich it." That both the blessing from above and the blessing from the earth had been given to him, he clearly affirmed: "because of the blessing of breasts and womb, the blessing of father and mother." This clearly and plainly signifies both the begetting of the Only-begotten from God the Father and his birth through the holy Virgin, by which he is understood to be, and appeared as, a man. For being by nature and truly the Son of God the Father, for our sake he endured birth through a woman and a womb, and was nursed at the breast. He did not become man in mere appearance, as some say. He truly appeared as what we ourselves are, and following the laws of nature he also took food, though he himself gives life to the world. That is why the blessed Isaiah made his need of food suited to an infant a kind of sign that the Lord truly became man, saying: "Butter and honey he shall eat." So he was blessed because of breasts and womb. For, as I said before, since he became man and obedient to the Father, he inherited the name that is above every name, and to him every knee shall bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, confessing that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. Yet even though he appeared as one of us, he will still surpass every saint, and in a manner befitting God he will tower above even the renowned fathers of old. For what the Psalmist says, "Who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Or who among the sons of God shall be like him?", the blessed Jacob teaches when he says: "You have prevailed over the blessings of the enduring mountains and of the everlasting hills." By everlasting and most enduring mountains, and by everlasting hills, he means the saints, because they have been lifted up from the earth and give no thought to base things, but seek the things above and soar right up to the heights of the virtues. So even the most illustrious of the fathers, who reached the summit of virtue, come behind the glory of Christ. For they were servants, even if they were afterward ranked among children; but the Lord, as Son, supplied them with the very things through which they became illustrious. That is why they say: "From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace." So the crown of glory will rest by nature on the head of our Savior; but it will no less pass on, as a gift bestowed, to the saints themselves who have come under him. They will wear the unfading crown of glory, and having become partakers of his sufferings they will share in his glory. For it is certain that those who have suffered with him will also reign with him.

"Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will still be eating, and at evening he will distribute food." Rachel first bore the divine Joseph, and after him Benjamin; yet it was Joseph whom his father called the youngest son. Let us grant that this is so. But we say that Benjamin came to be younger than the youngest. Benjamin, then, is the youngest son, and he may fittingly be understood as an image and type of the youngest people. This people was called through the holy disciples after Christ came back to life from the dead and returned to God the Father in heaven. He is likened to a ravenous wolf, I think, because of his fervent appetite for learning, and because he always leaps, and very eagerly, as if on prey, upon whatever nourishes him toward good health, clearly spiritual health. For such people are quick to see what makes for benefit and to seize what profits them, and swift to run from those who are used to doing harm. They are not at all easily frightened, not even if those who are determined to drive them away from good works and words surround them like dogs; rather, they make the attack go numb. For they have learned to say, and very boldly: "Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or persecution, or nakedness, or danger, or sword?" Nor could the false shepherds ever push them off the path they love, though they strike at their kidneys [ditches?] without sparing, as it is written. For such people endure suffering exceedingly well and consider suffering to be life. They have cried out: "For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain." So even if they are likened to ravenous wolves, in the ways we have just shown, they would not, it seems, be wronged as though the comparison were improper. The Savior himself calls himself a lion and a leopard, or panther, saying: "For I am like a panther to Ephraim, and like a lion to the house of Judah. And I will come, and go, and take, and there will be no one to rescue." And he calls those who believe in him beasts of the field, speaking thus through Isaiah: "The beasts of the field will bless me, sirens and daughters of sparrows. For I have given water in the desert and rivers in a waterless land, to give drink to my chosen race, my people whom I acquired to tell of my virtues." You see, then, how he called the chosen race beasts of the field and sirens, that is, the sweetest-voiced of the little birds. They are beasts perhaps because they will not put up with Satan when he tries to tame them and is eager to bring them under his hand; instead they leap upon him, and all but savage those who are determined to drive them toward what is unlawful. They are sirens because they speak most eloquently in telling of Christ's achievements and in singing hymns to his honor. So Benjamin, the wolf, is the new people in faith. He indicates their great readiness to understand what makes for benefit, and also their ability to benefit others, when he says: "In the morning he will still be eating, and at evening he will distribute food." The learner is always somehow like one who is being fed. For lessons are taken into the mind just as food is taken into the stomach. And the teacher falls in no way short of one who feeds. Indeed, the divine Paul likens teaching to food, for he said: "Solid food is for the mature, who by practice have their faculties trained to distinguish good from evil." So Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will still be eating, and at evening he will distribute food. It is as if he said: while still a learner, and before he has reached maturity, he will be able to benefit others, and a very short time will show that those who have only just believed are fit for teaching too. For concerning those from Israel it was said, I think because of their great ignorance and their inner dullness of mind: "Behold, a foolish and senseless people. They have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear." And again: "You who are carried from the womb and instructed until old age." But the wise John writes to those who are in faith and in Christ: "You have no need for anyone to teach you, but as his anointing teaches you about all things." For they have the mind of Christ, who knows all things, and they are quite capable of teaching and exhorting one another. And if it is fitting to say that the prophecy about Benjamin was fulfilled in the blessed Paul himself, this too would hold well and truly. For he who persecuted the Church, and ran at those who love Christ like a wolf, was changed in a very short time into the complete opposite. He preached the faith that he once ravaged, and he gives thanks for having been appointed to the apostleship, although he was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor and a man of violence. For so he says somewhere himself. And he was of the tribe of Benjamin. I also say that the divine David himself clearly recalled his story, saying in the sixty-seventh psalm: "There is Benjamin the younger, in ecstasy. The rulers of Judah, their leaders, the rulers of Zebulun, the rulers of Naphtali." For the blessed disciples, being Jews and of the blood of Israel, became guides of those justified in Christ through faith, and with them was the one from the tribe of Benjamin, who writes and says: "For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you." For he preached to Gentiles and Jews our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

We have only just, and with difficulty, finished the book on Genesis, keeping our words as spare as we could. Now, going from strength to strength, as the Psalm sings, and without pausing even briefly for breath, so to speak, we persuade the pen, well practised in good labours, that it must move on. For, if God wills and gives us wisdom, we now take up the chapters of Exodus. These seem to have been passed over when we composed our moral exhortation, since at that time it seemed best to avoid long discussions, as we wished to show how we should understand the manner of worship in spirit and in truth. We divided up all the chapters contained in the five books of Moses and considered carefully in advance the aim of the contemplation in that work. Whatever was in some way necessary for moral instruction, and especially useful for it, we composed in its proper place, and, I should add, in the order most fitting for each. But the passages through which the mystery of Christ was likely to be foreshadowed, as far as possible, still in the shadows of the law, we reserved for the work that follows it. Now that we have chosen to labour at this, beloved Palladius, I know that you will contend alongside us through prayer. The task is by no means easy to traverse for people like us, but it may become at least partly passable if Christ again widens the path to it. For he is the way, and he is the door, and in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. We will compose this book without going through every chapter in order and leaving nothing out, for very many of them, as I have just said, we have already included selectively, and they will be clearly found in the other treatise. But whatever appears useful for our present aim we will examine as precisely and finely as we can, and so come straight to the truth. And since the aim of the book points to the redemption through Christ, it is altogether necessary first to show that the human race had been in no small danger and had already been brought to the very extremity of misery. For only in this way, and in no other, would the account of the help proceed in fitting order: "For my power," it says, "is made perfect in weakness." And I think that even the most skilled and highly esteemed physicians, if they are ever to be admired for the things in which they are wise, must have a sick person set before them, on whom the display of their skill can be made.

So then, let us now say that once, when a famine pressed hard, fell unbearably upon the sons of Israel and weighed on them, they went down from the land of Canaan into Egypt, some seventy-five souls, as it is written. As time went on, their race grew into a multitude beyond counting. For it is written: "But the sons of Israel increased and multiplied and became abundant and grew exceedingly strong; and the land multiplied them exceedingly." But the one who had come to rule over the land of the Egyptians regarded the growth of the Hebrews in numbers with suspicion. So he plotted against them and set taskmasters over them, to afflict them in their work. The manner of affliction was sweat over digging, long and unpaid brickmaking, and also building strong cities for Pharaoh, that is, cities fortified with towers, or cities so broad and long that they seemed to others quite [impregnable], evidently because of the multitude of their inhabitants. These were Pithom and Rameses and other cities. But the tyrant's scheme turned out contrary to his hopes. For the more those being punished were humbled, it says, the greater the sign [?] of their increase, and the more numerous they became, since God willed to benefit those who were being wickedly abused through what usually does harm. When the tyrant perceived this, he added another plot to their labours. He ordered the midwives of the Jews, when they attended women already in labour and childbirth, to strangle the sex that he regarded with suspicion, that is, the male, but to keep the female alive. For he thought the female sex worthy of no account, as feeble and unwarlike, easily given to cowardice, and made delicate by the law of nature. But the midwives did not do the impious deed, and for this they pleased God. What then did the wretch do? He threw off the disguise from his anger and encouraged shamelessness in the ways of impiety. For Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying: "Every male that is born to the Hebrews, throw into the river, and every female, keep alive."

3. But let the narrative of the history stop here. Let us now set our minds to the innermost contemplations and explain this. Since the mind of man is diligently bent on evil from his youth, through lack of the good things from above practically the whole race on earth was perishing, and a kind of famine of the heavenly teachings was devouring us. We can see this in the prodigal described in the form of a parable, who devoured his father's property in a foreign land and longed to be filled with the carob pods that the pigs ate. In this way we ran after more earthly things, abandoning what is better and the duty of desiring what is more profitable, through which we would likely not have missed the favour from above and would have been seen to be rich in closeness to God. Having slipped away, then, from everything that could hold us up in well-being and in being with God, we no longer made the one who is by nature and truly Lord the steward of our affairs. We departed from the God-loving life, as from a holy land, and all but flowed down into a baser and uglier life, one lying under the devil. So we became like those who went down from Canaan into Egypt and came under the hand of Pharaoh and the Egyptians. The Egyptians were extraordinarily devoted to the worship of demons and left no form of wickedness unpractised, and so they would show in themselves, as in an image, Satan himself and those under him, whom they also considered gods: beings driven out of the best understanding and sick with the mist and darkness of ignorance. And since we had come under a terrible and accursed master, I mean Satan, we were worn down with clay and brickmaking, I mean with earthly pursuits and the most loathsome endeavours in it, which are not accomplished without sweat. For the distraction of this life is not free from toil, even if it may be vain. And Satan appointed the unclean demons, that is, the powers under him, as taskmasters, so to speak, over those he wronged, to oversee the works dearest to him. These load down the mind of every person on earth with the manifold excesses of the passions, fearing, I suppose, that if they were to lift the eye of their understanding to God at leisure, they might free their necks from slavery to him; for human nature is very freedom-loving. That our vain distraction, the toils of the flesh, and the eagerness that looks to earthly things are counted as, and indeed are, glory and wealth for the unclean demons and for Satan himself is shown in a riddle by the Israelites, worn down with clay and brickmaking, building cities for Pharaoh. And that he loathes the male, that is, what inclines toward courage, plainly courage in virtue; that he all but drowns what is warlike by plunging it into the swamps of pleasures; and that he welcomes what is not strong and brings it under his own yoke without a fight as useless: all this is shown quite clearly by the command that the male must be thrown into the waters but the female kept alive. For things that are visible and evident may become types of more hidden things. So, sick with sin from of old and from our fathers, and oppressed by lack of good things, we wretches were yoked, perhaps even unwillingly, to Satan, the leader of wickedness, and were made subject to the taskmasters of wickedness, I mean the unclean demons. Our condition was at the very extremity of all evil, with nothing lacking to make it wretched and miserable, except that God had mercy, and rescued and saved us. And how he did this we shall learn from what follows and is connected with it. For we will bring forward what is written about the divine Moses as an image and outline of the salvation through Christ.

"Now there was a certain man of the tribe of Levi who took one of the daughters of Levi as his wife, and she conceived and bore a male child. Seeing that he was a fine child, they hid him for three months. When they could no longer hide him, his mother took a basket and smeared it with bitumen and pitch, put the child in it, and placed it in the marsh by the river. And his sister watched from a distance to learn what would happen to him. Then Pharaoh's daughter came down to bathe at the river, and her maids were walking along the river. Seeing the basket in the marsh, she sent her maid and took it up. When she opened it, she saw a child crying in the basket, and Pharaoh's daughter spared him and said: 'This is one of the Hebrews' children.'
