And his sister said to Pharaoh's daughter: 'Do you want me to call a nurse for you from among the Hebrews to nurse the child for you?' She said: 'Go.' So the girl went and called the child's mother. Pharaoh's daughter said to her: 'Take care of this child for me and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages.' So the woman took the child and nursed him. When the child had grown up, she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, saying: 'I took him out of the water.'" For since God the Father at last had mercy on the world under heaven, which was enslaved to an impious tyrant and most savage robber, he did not spare his own Son, as it is written, but gave him up for us all. For the Son who is from him and in him by nature, being in his form and equal to him, lowered himself into self-emptying and became like us. As the wise evangelist John says, "he came to his own." For he was sent, as he himself says somewhere, "to the lost sheep of the house of Israel"; "but his own did not receive him." Therefore he also accused them severely through the voice of Isaiah, saying: "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I have begotten sons and raised them up, but they have rejected me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's manger, but Israel has not known me, and my people have not understood me." So since those of the blood of Israel stumbled and did not recognize the one who is by nature and truly Lord, the worshippers of idols were called in through faith, and the impious and most loathsome multitude of the godless recognized the Redeemer. And this, then, was what was foretold to Israel through the voice of the prophets: "I have set watchmen over you. Hear the sound of the trumpet. And they said: We will not hear. Therefore the nations have heard, and those who shepherd their flocks. Hear, O earth: behold, I am bringing evils on this people, the fruit of their turning away, because they did not heed my word, and they rejected my law." Look, then, look clearly at the mystery, as it appears in the story of Moses, as I said just now. The divine Moses was born of the tribe and blood of Levi. And Emmanuel himself also bore this character, holy and innocent, and a high priest wholly sacred, even though he is understood to be of the tribe of Judah, so that he might be believed to be both the one praised and a king. And his priesthood was not according to the flesh, as indeed it was for the leaders of the Jews, but belonged to him as God and King of all, in holiness and glory. So the type lies in fleshly things, so that the truth may be above the flesh, that is, Christ. He is understood as a newborn child because of the innocence of the Godhead, or because he became a new creation. For having stripped off the old state of corruption, we have passed in him into newness of life. And the infant is like a new creation. That the newborn child is a symbol of innocence is easy to see, if one chooses to show it, from the Saviour's own words. For once some women eagerly sought him out and brought infants to him, so that he might lay his hands on them, as it is written. But the disciples, thinking them a nuisance of a crowd, kept them away. But he said to them: "Let the children be, and do not stop them from coming to me; for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these." And once, when a debate arose among them about who was greatest in the kingdom of heaven (for so the wise evangelist tells us), "he took a child," he says, "and stood it in their midst, and said: Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you turn and become like these children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven." And what it means to turn and to love to become like children blessed Paul made clear when he wrote: "Brothers, do not be children in your minds, but be infants in wickedness; and in your minds be mature." It is settled, then, that Christ is signified in an infant because of the innocence of the Godhead. Moses' father, too, is passed over in silence in the sacred Scriptures by design. For it would have been possible to say: "So-and-so took one of the daughters of Levi." But it says, "There was a certain man," indirectly hinting that Christ too is fatherless according to the flesh, except that he had a supposed father; for he was thought to be the son of Joseph. "But the child was fine," it says. For Christ is called, and is, "fairer in beauty than the sons of men." And elsewhere again the divine David cried out to him: "Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one, in your comeliness and your beauty." But it must be understood that no one would doubt that this is the beauty that belongs to the glory and nature of the Godhead, which is above all. For surely no one would attribute the boasts of the flesh to Christ himself and count them to his glory; far from it. For the whole mystery of his economy in the flesh is, for him, self-emptying and humiliation. And the prophet Isaiah writes somewhere about him: "And we saw him, and he had no form or beauty, but his form was without honour, falling short of all the sons of men." We certainly do not say that the prophet's words disparage the glories of the Godhead. Rather, they lead us to understand that the things of the flesh, compared with the glory of the Godhead, will appear worthy of no account. For the Son appeared in a form that was utterly unlovely. Being God by nature, he became like us. The distance between them is immeasurable, and humanity falls short of God by incomparable differences.

Observe how, when Pharaoh had ordered that every male be put to death, the woman who bore him hid the infant. Afterward she laid him down and shut him in the thibē, that is, the closed box, and cast him into the marshes. But the persecutor's daughter found him right there by the waters and at once took him up. She opened the basket, and finding the infant crying, she understood clearly that he was a Hebrew, and she gave him back to his mother to nurse, promising in turn wages for nursing him. What meaning should we apply to such words? Or what mystery must we look into? Before the coming of our Saviour, the male was not safe from plots on earth. By the male we understand what has spiritual courage, whose fruits are the things pleasing to God. So the male was in danger, since Satan all but plunged into worldly pleasures, as into mud or swamps, those who refused to be feeble and effeminate, I mean in character and ways, and drowned them there. Therefore the Spirit-bearers, astonished, I suppose, at everyone's turning toward what is not right, said: "All have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one." For by then the good had become wholly unpractised among all people, since the inventor of sin did not allow them to act with courage. But Emmanuel came to be with us and was numbered among those who were plotted against, the infant who is male by nature and in truth, that is, who does not know how to grow soft, for he did not grow soft toward sin. At first he escaped the notice of the ruler of this age, for the child, that is, Moses, was hidden. But when he came of age, the Synagogue that bore him, whetted for murder by the devil's stratagems (for Christ according to the flesh came from the Jews), shut him up in a tomb. Moses too would be a clear type of this, laid as it were by his own mother's hand in the so-called thibē and, moreover, cast out. For the synagogue of the Jews estranged Emmanuel from itself. But Pharaoh's daughter, that is, the Church from the Gentiles, although she once had Satan as her father, finds him by the waters, which may be understood as a type of holy baptism, through which and in which Christ is found; and she opens the basket. For those who through faith have found the one who went to death for us, so that he might also go to life for us, have truly believed that he did not remain among the dead, but rather came back to life, trampling on death, and came out of the tomb. And she finds the child crying. We too shall meet with Christ recounting the impiety of the Jews and what was done to him, all but weeping. For he says in distress: "They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. And they looked and stared at me; they divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots." And elsewhere too: "They gave me gall for my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink." And the Church from the Gentiles recognized and believed that Christ came from the Jews. For Pharaoh's daughter said, it says: "This is one of the Hebrews' children." Moreover, that in due time the synagogue of the Jews will receive Christ from the Church of the Gentiles, when they are initiated, clearly, into the mystery concerning him, is shown very easily by the mother who bore the child receiving him from Pharaoh's daughter. For the synagogue of the Jews, having as it were cast Jesus out and rejected him through disobedience, will receive him in the last times, initiated by the voices of the Church. And she herself will then be persuaded that the matter is not without profit but full of great hopes. For see how Pharaoh's daughter promised wages to Moses' mother if she would choose to nurse her own child. So the birth of Moses, and what happened to him, would signify very clearly to those of sound mind the mystery of Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the endless ages. Amen.

6. When we examined the birth of Moses closely, we showed that the mystery of Christ is present in it. The subtlety of its meanings portrays him, in keeping with the divine plan, in a newborn infant: this points to the innocence of the Godhead, to its complete freedom from evil and its utter simplicity, that is, to the fact that he appeared as a new creation. But come, let us look again, in another way as well, at Emmanuel being portrayed in Moses. For Christ is the end of the law and the prophets. "Now it came to pass," it says, "in those many days, that Moses, having grown up, went out to his brothers, the sons of Israel. And when he had observed their toil, he saw an Egyptian man beating a Hebrew, one of his brothers. And he struck the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. Going out on the second day, he saw two Hebrew men fighting, and he said to the one in the wrong, 'Why are you striking your neighbor?' But he said, 'Who made you ruler and judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?' Then Moses was afraid and said, 'Has this matter become so well known?' And Pharaoh heard of this matter and sought to kill Moses. But Moses withdrew from Pharaoh's presence and settled in the land of Midian. When he came into the land of Midian, he sat down by the well. Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, who tended the sheep of their father Jethro. They came and drew water until they had filled the troughs, to water the sheep of their father Jethro. But the shepherds came and drove them away. Then Moses rose up and rescued them, and drew water for them, and watered their sheep. They came to Reuel their father, and he said to them, 'Why have you come back so quickly today?' They said, 'An Egyptian man rescued us from the shepherds, and drew water for us, and watered our sheep.' He said to his daughters, 'And where is he? Why have you left the man like this? Call him, then, so that he may eat bread.' So Moses settled with the man, and he gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses as his wife. The woman conceived and bore a son, and Moses named him Gershom, saying, 'I am a sojourner in a foreign land.'" So much, then, for the story of Moses. Our discourse will now once more build for us a contemplation of the innermost meaning. It gives the history, as far as possible, what properly belongs to it, but whatever seems well able to serve the spiritual explanation, it turns toward the divine plan concerning Christ.

7. You have heard that Moses, having grown up, went out to his brothers. And indeed the inspired Paul writes truly: "But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, born under the law." We must therefore consider how we may reasonably understand the manner of the sending revealed here, and what we shall say the "going out" was. Shall we not grant that the Word from God the Father, having come to be in our condition, that is, having become man, all but went out, and say that he came to be outside the glory befitting God? This must be so if it is true that, though he was rich, he became poor and lowered himself to self-emptying. Indeed, when the divine plan had already been fulfilled, when he was about to go back up to the Father to sit with him and ascend the highest thrones, he says: "Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed." The Lord of heaven and earth, who as God holds in his very being the power over all things, would in no way lose what belongs to him by coming to be in the form of a servant. Yet if he in whom we live and move and have our being were seen among us naked and in the tomb, even though he came back to life again as Life itself, would he not seem to have gone a little outside what is most fitting for him? How then could anyone doubt it? So he went out to his brothers, that is, to the sons of Israel. For theirs are the promises, and theirs are the fathers to whom the promises were made. That is why he said: "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." They were enduring a truly terrible and unbearable oppression, for Satan was leaping upon them as if to crush them, and he purposed to free them and to show them released from all toil. Having in a certain manner killed the one who had chosen to do wrong, he hid him in the earth; that is, he put him in the regions beneath the earth, shutting him up in Hades. This, I say, is what it means to hide the dead Egyptian in the sand. That the God-hated and unclean hordes of demons were driven together into Hades by the ineffable power of our Savior, and were condemned to dwell in the abyss, one could learn very easily from the Gospel readings. For the demons, it says, begged him not to order them to depart into the abyss. Since a great multitude had already been sent there ahead of them, those still left came forward and begged to be spared for the time being from being condemned with the others. That they were tormented, paying the penalty for their cruelty toward us, anyone who wishes can see without effort when he hears them cry out: "Ah, what have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come here before the time to torment us?" So, since Christ had seen the Egyptian pressing unbearably upon those on earth, he hid him away in Hades. Joshua too accomplished this, as in shadows and types, he who brought the sons of Israel across the Jordan and led them as general after Moses. For he shut up the five kings of the Amorites in a cave. In this way the type showed us beforehand, indirectly, that Emmanuel, revealed as king over us after the way of life under the law, would seal up the chiefs of the demons in the depths beneath the earth as in a deep cave. Once the one who pressed upon and afflicted them had been destroyed, "on the second day," it says, when two Hebrews were fighting, Moses stood between them as arbiter and as one who would reconcile in peace those who had quarreled without love for one another. He set himself against their enmity, saying to the one who wanted to overpower his brother, "Why are you striking your neighbor?" But the man said to him, "Who made you ruler and judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?" For Emmanuel, having first shut up Satan as it were in Hades, appeared to the people of Israel as an arbiter of righteousness and a teacher of mutual love. He commanded them to make love for their brothers their aim and to consider nothing better than peace and harmony. That is why he said, "My peace I give to you." They ought to have praised the teaching and admired the reconciler, the giver of peace, the president of love, the guide to the best lessons. Instead they behaved with no small impiety, for they would not accept him as their teacher. Though he says clearly through the voice of the Psalmist, "But I have been set up as king by him on Zion, his holy mountain," they went beyond all shamelessness and opposed him harshly and without love for God. At one time they said, "Who gave you this authority?" and at another, "We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from." They turned the very things by which they were being saved into charges against him, and most foolishly disparaged the manner of his help. For the inspired Moses was accused of having killed the Egyptian, even though the Egyptian was oppressing and pressing upon the flocks of the Hebrews and loading them with unbearable exactions. And Christ buried the evil demons as it were in the abyss, and removed them, however unwilling, from their tyranny over us by driving them out of those who had them. Though he ought to have been admired for this, he did not escape the words of those who make a habit of finding fault. For they dared to say, making the miracle into a charge against him: "This man casts out demons only by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons." Note that Moses looked this way and that, and when he saw no one, he hid the dead Egyptian in the sand. Then he went on and counseled peace to his brothers by blood. For the Lord wages war against Amalek, but with a hidden hand, as it is written. So too the more secret parts of the work were carried out by Christ with no one on earth seeing. For who on earth could know how or when the hordes of demons were condemned and ordered to dwell in the abyss? So, having driven Satan into Hades and first freed those on earth from his oppression, he then called them to the knowledge of virtue. Christ himself says this quite plainly somewhere: "Or how can anyone enter the strong man's house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man? Then he will plunder his house." For having first bound the strong man, as it were, that is, Satan, he transfers his goods to himself through faith; that is, those who once acted under Satan and were counted as useless vessels. But he was impiously mocked for the very things for which he ought to have been greatly admired, and so he had to move away, leaving Judea, where he was born according to the flesh. Yet in truth, as the Word, he was not a Jew, but from above, from heaven, and from the Father. In the same way the inspired Moses was born in Egypt and was a Hebrew of the Hebrews, with his father's noble and holy root. But since his kin by blood reproached him and loaded what he had done on their own behalf with the worst slanders, he then moved to Midian and took refuge in the land of a foreign people. Then, sitting down by the well, he came to the aid of Jethro's daughters. They were seven in number, and as they tended their own father's flocks they were bringing the thirsty animals to the troughs. When they had already drawn the water, and with much sweat, some of the herdsmen took advantage of them. But Moses fought for them, and drawing water with his own hands, he watered their sheep, as it is written. We will take Jethro, then, in the role of the world. He was priest of the Midianites, and he offered worship not to the one who is God by nature and in truth, but to created things rather than to their Creator and Maker, or to things made of stone and the handiwork of craftsmen. The world too had gone astray, worshiping demons and not God. The name Jethro is also interpreted as "superfluity" or "superfluous." Such too is the world, which is entirely superfluity, because those who choose to set their minds on its things do nothing necessary. Instead they become drunk, as it were, on vain distractions and are tossed about toward useless pleasures. It is beyond dispute that for those who wish to live rightly the things of the flesh are superfluous, and that setting one's mind on the things of the world misses the pursuit of what is useful and necessary. This must be so if it is true that "the mind of the flesh is enmity toward God," and that whoever sets his mind on the things of the world makes himself an enemy of God. Truly, then, choosing to set one's mind on the things of the world is superfluity, and so is the world itself. For Christ said somewhere: "What will a man gain if he wins the whole world but forfeits his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?"

8. Moses, then, moved from the land of the Egyptians to Midian, and in the same way Christ moved from Judea to Galilee. Notice that only one daughter of Levi bore the holy Moses, while the daughters of Jethro the Midianite were more, seven in number. For the multitude of the Jews is also one, and from it Christ was born according to the flesh, as in the type of Moses. But the daughters of the world, so to speak, are very many, that is, the flocks of the nations that dwell in it. So Christ left the Synagogue from which he sprang according to the flesh and turned toward the many flocks of the nations. Wicked shepherds were oppressing them, that is, the world-rulers of this world, and he himself saved them. But come, let us describe the manner of the oppression and add to it the manner of the help. Divine Scripture is accustomed to compare to a well the knowledge of God that is implanted in us, by which we are guided in everything we must do. For the knowledge of every good wells up in us as from the spring of the mind, and so does the knowledge of God's glory, as in a mirror and a riddle. Thus he rebuked those who neglected love for God and impiously turned to thinking they should give their reverence to demons, saying through the voice of Jeremiah: "Heaven was astonished at this, and the earth shuddered greatly, says the Lord, for my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns that will not be able to hold water." Falsely named worship is like a broken cistern, for from it no one could draw the word that has the power to give life; but the blameless knowledge of God is truly a spring of life. So the well is for us an image of the implanted knowledge. As long as we use a mind that is upright and unforced in seeking the knowledge of God, we shall come straight to the truth. But if someone is overpowered by the deceits of the demons and turns aside to what seems good to himself, he will spend his own efforts for their benefit. This, I think, is what is meant in a riddle when Jethro's daughters draw the water but their oppressors take it by force. We say that those who have gone astray suffer from such sicknesses, for their implanted knowledge has been turned aside toward what is ugly, that is, toward error and toward what serves the demons. But Christ came to help. He drove off the wicked false shepherds and gave them the living water to drink, that is, his divine and heavenly proclamation. That is why he said: "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink." Let us take Jethro, then, as standing for the world, which is full of superfluity and transience. We say that the seven daughters are the flocks of the nations everywhere, with a multitude signified by each of Jethro's daughters. The wicked and most violent shepherds may reasonably be understood as the hordes of demons, and the helper is Christ, who also makes us drunk with divine streams. When the young women had escaped the oppression of the impious shepherds, they returned to Reuel their father, by whom I mean Jethro. When he asked them the reason for their unusual speed, they at once told him of Moses' help. He immediately welcomed the man into his house and gave him Zipporah in marriage, the foremost and most comely of his daughters, and she bore Gershom. For when Christ had helped the communities of the nations in the world, he became known to the world, as those saved through him initiated it into the mystery that he is able to help and can easily deliver from the hand of those who choose to do wrong. And so the world gladly brings him near, as Reuel did the most holy Moses. It comes about that it takes him into kinship, as it were, presenting to him as a bride, a most beautiful one, the Church from the nations, which is signified by Zipporah. For her name is interpreted "visitation" or "beautiful," and also "grace of breath." For the dawn from on high visited the one who is truly distinguished and beautiful, I mean the Church, and as a gift and a guest-present from heaven he granted her the gift of his own breath, I mean participation in the Holy Spirit. And she bore him Gershom, by which I mean a people who are truly sojourners. For those who have been sealed with the divine Spirit, who have been counted worthy of the visitation from above, and who have been shaped into beauty in the likeness of the Son, are truly sojourners in this world. It would especially suit them to cry out and say: "Here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come, whose craftsman and builder is God." For while they walk on earth, their citizenship is in heaven. They have no craving at all for the affairs of this world, but eagerly lay claim to those of the age to come. For they have resolved to follow, through a truly refined and finely shaped life, Christ, who for our sake lived as a sojourner like us in this world. He did not set his mind on the things of this world, far from it; rather, he appeared to us as a pattern of the life that is above the world and most in keeping with the law. Notice how purposefully Holy Scripture named the father of the seven young women Jethro before the help through Moses came to them, but Reuel after it. Jethro is interpreted "superfluity" or "superfluous," as I said before, and Reuel "shepherding of God." (I use this word because it suits my purpose.) We were saying, when we gave him the role of the world, that the distraction of the world is truly superfluous and vain. The company of young women was in this state before they were helped by Christ. But when they had been delivered from oppression and set beyond the reach of the impious shepherds, then, then indeed he is renamed Reuel, that is, "flock of God" or "shepherding," according to the force of the interpretation. For he came under the hand of the chief shepherd of all, I mean Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

The blessed prophets cared deeply about our state. As bearers of the Spirit who examined things closely, they prayed that the Word of God would show himself a helper and defender to those on earth, and they ascribed to him alone, as God, the power to save those who had reached the depths of misery. They were indeed teachers of the best things, wise and keen-minded men who pointed out the way of salvation. What praiseworthy quality did they lack? They were rightly admired. Yet they could not drive Satan from his tyranny over us, nor chase off the profane hordes of demons. These plundered us wretched people in many ways and all but treated us as prisoners of war. They loaded us with the yoke of slavery and wickedly forced us to think and do whatever they pleased. Like harsh and unrelenting tax-collectors, they ordered us to pay them the dues of worship, as if it were a debt we owed: we had to defile ourselves with earthly pursuits and so choose to think only of the things of the flesh. It was therefore a glorious work of the ineffable nature to overthrow the arrogant and profane greed of the devil, to free those on earth from so very harmful and loathsome a slavery, and to make them workers of virtue from then on. The sacred Scriptures will show us just as clearly that this great and long-prayed-for blessing was to come to those on earth in due time, when the Only-begotten lowered himself into self-emptying and humanity. The passage runs as follows: "After those many days the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel groaned because of their labors and cried out, and their voice went up to God from their labors. And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And God looked upon the children of Israel and made himself known to them." The Egyptians were oppressing the Israelites, laying on them the yoke of forced servitude and setting over them harsh and pitiless taskmasters, who made their life bitter, as it is written. Crushed by such excessive greed, the wretched people wept and lamented and begged to be granted gentleness from above. And God visited them: he "looked upon," it says, "the children of Israel, and made himself known to them." So it is with us. When we are ignorant of God, we are subject to those who wrong us and we wallow in the mire of sin, with bitter and cruel overseers set over us, the unclean demons. But the grace of freedom will surely follow when we come to know God. Those events happened as a type, but they were written for our instruction, as it is written. The type concerns a single nation, those of the blood of Israel. Yet it teaches very well and clearly that the aim of the unclean spirits and of the devil is to push and drive those on earth to toil at vain pursuits and carry out the works of the flesh. That way their minds will have no leisure to look up to the things above, and they will not know the God of all. Otherwise they would then be guided toward what pleases him and turn away from the yoke of that slavery. Since a love of freedom is part of human nature, we sometimes do not approve of our passions. Often, when we come to our senses for a moment, we loathe them and the ugliness of fleshly pleasures. We thirst for help from above, from God, and we cry out loudly against the slavery we never wanted. This, I think, is what it means that the children of Israel groaned to God. And since God is good, he sent his Son from heaven as our Savior and Redeemer, who became like us, that is, a man. Sacred Scripture once again foretold this to us in a riddle. It says: "Moses was tending the sheep of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian. He led the sheep into the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God. And an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the bush. He looked, and the bush was burning with fire, yet the bush was not consumed. And Moses said, 'I will go over and see this great sight, why the bush is not burned up.' When the Lord saw that he was coming near to look, the Lord called to him out of the bush, saying, 'Moses, Moses.' And he said, 'What is it?' And he said, 'Do not come near here. Take the sandal off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.' And he said to him, 'I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' And Moses turned his face away, for he was afraid to look at God." God gave the law as a help, as the prophet says (in his providential plan he had appointed Moses beforehand as a tutor). He made the shadow almost as a way of pointing to more perfect things, since in due time the truth was to come to light. The goal of this tutelage was the mystery of Christ, and the vision taught it very well. The bush is a shrubby, fruitless plant, little different from thorns. A great flame poured around it, for a holy angel in the form of fire was at work there. The flame rose up very high, yet it did no harm at all to the bush in which it appeared. What was happening was truly extraordinary [?] and beyond all reason: fire touching thorns and warming them with the gentlest of touches, as though it had neglected its natural power and rested quite idly on things that can be destroyed. No wonder the divine Moses was astonished at the sight. What, then, does it mean? Sacred Scripture likens the divine nature to fire, because it is all-powerful and can easily consume anything, and it likens human beings, who come from the earth, to wood and to the grass of the field. So at one point it says, "Our God is a consuming fire," and at another, "As for man, his days are like grass; like a flower of the field, so he will flourish." But just as thorns cannot bear fire, so humanity cannot bear divinity. Yet in Christ this came about, and divinity became bearable. For in him the whole fullness of the Godhead dwelt bodily, as the wise Paul testified. He who dwells in unapproachable light, that is, God, made his dwelling in the temple born of the virgin. He lowered himself into a wonderful gentleness and, as it were, veiled the full force of his own nature so that he could be contained, just as the fire was contained by the thorns. The fire on the bush, which kept the wood entirely unharmed, shows in a riddle that he made what is by nature corruptible, that is, the flesh, superior to corruption. For who could doubt that the Word from God, who is life by nature, gave life to his own temple and made it incorruptible and superior to death? So the fire spared the thorn, and the flame became bearable to a small and very weak piece of wood. For, as I said, divinity found room in humanity. This is the mystery that took place in Christ. And the Word of God has dwelt in us too, not demanding penalties or exacting punishment, but shining around us with kindly and most gentle rays. As he himself says somewhere, "God did not send the Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him." So the bush was not burned up, though the flame enveloped it. As I said just now, we have not been made to pay the penalty for our sins. Instead, Christ shines around us through the Holy Spirit and is in us through him, and in him we cry, "Abba, Father." Astonished at the sight, the blessed Moses then added, "I will go over and see this great sight, why the bush is not burned up." But at once the blessed angel stops him, speaking as if in the person of God: "Do not come near here. Take the sandal off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground." He calls the waterless, thorn-bearing wilderness in which the bush stood "holy ground." Any place where Christ is present is holy. And it is very fitting that he appears in a wilderness, since the wilderness is a type of the church drawn from the Gentiles. The sacred word says to her: "Rejoice, thirsty wilderness; let the wilderness exult and blossom like a lily." God also promised somewhere to turn the wilderness into marshes and the thirsty land into watercourses. For the Savior's grace has abounded toward us who have been called from the Gentiles, and like a river flooding us with waters from above it fills us to overflowing. This is what the divine David tells us too: "He turned rivers into a wilderness, and fruitful land into a salt waste, because of the wickedness of those who live in it." So the bush is in the wilderness, and the land that holds it is therefore holy and consecrated to God. As Moses approaches, he is stopped and ordered to take the sandal off his foot. This is a sign of deadness and corruption, since every sandal is made from the remains of an animal that has already died and decayed. Christ, then, cannot be approached by those under the law and its tutelary worship. For one must first wash away the defilement and scrub off the filth of sin, and it is impossible for the blood of bulls to take away sin. No one is justified by the law. And as long as sin has not been abolished, corruption must still prevail and death must still rule over those who remain defiled. So those who want to see the mystery of Christ must first lay aside the worship of types and shadows, which overcomes neither corruption nor sin. Then such a person will understand and enter the holy land, that is, the Church. Christ himself makes clear that those who do not leave the worship of the law are held fast by corruption, when he says, "Truly, truly, I tell you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in yourselves." This mystery was not found among those under the law. It was found among those who have received the faith, have been justified in Christ, and are rich in an instruction better than that of the law, I mean the gospel. So those who have not yet, through faith, thrown off the mother of death, I mean sin, remain under corruption and, as it were, under the law, and such people are far from Christ. But if they are willing to take off the sandal, that is, the corruption that cannot justify, and to accept the grace that truly gives life, then they will draw near to him who justifies the ungodly, that is, Christ. Through him and with him be glory to the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

It is in Christ, and in him alone, that we escape the power of death. As the wise disciple has written for us, "There is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved." Anyone who chose to could learn this in many other ways as well, for the divinely inspired Scripture holds countless bright, clear images that flash out the power of the mystery. So let us gather what serves this purpose and show it through what follows.

Moses and Aaron came forward. They went to Pharaoh and said plainly: "Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Let my people go, so that they may hold a feast for me in the wilderness." And Pharaoh said, "Who is he, that I should obey his voice and let the children of Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go." They said to him: "The God of the Hebrews has called us. So we will go a three days' journey to sacrifice to our God, so that death or slaughter does not fall upon us." And the king of Egypt said to them: "Moses and Aaron, why are you turning my people away from their work? Go back, each of you, to your own work."

The deranged Pharaoh was full of diabolical madness, and so he says he does not know who the God of the Hebrews is. Then he was tormented by plague after unbearable plague, and the land of the Egyptians was destroyed little by little. Their waters were turned into blood. Locusts and hail were brought upon the land, gnats and frogs swarmed, and a darkness was poured down for three days. At last, barely and against his will, he promised to let them go. Yet he would not relent. Afterwards he was harsh and hardened again, and it was extremely hard to bring him to choose to free Israel from its long slavery. Then God planned to send the destroyer against the firstborn of the Egyptians. But because of his love for the fathers, the chosen people must not perish along with the unholy nations. So God laid down the law of the Passover and expressly commanded that the mystery of Christ be carried out before the wrath came. This again lets us understand that death cannot be abolished through Moses or the law. It is the precious blood of Christ that drives off the destroyer and frees the sanctified from corruption. For he is Life from Life, and God of all, as God from God.

The sacred Scripture, then, speaks as follows: "The Lord said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt: This month shall be the beginning of months for you; it shall be the first month of the year for you. Speak to the whole congregation of the children of Israel and say: On the tenth day of this month each man shall take a lamb for his father's house, a lamb for each household. If the household is too small for a lamb, he shall take it together with his nearest neighbor."

After laying down that they must take a lamb, he goes on to prescribe what kind of victim it should be, and when and how it must be sacrificed. "Your lamb," he says, "shall be perfect, without blemish, a year old. You shall take it from the sheep or from the goats, and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month. Then the whole assembly of the congregation of the children of Israel shall slaughter it toward evening. They shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel of the houses in which they eat it. They shall eat the flesh that night, roasted over the fire, and they shall eat unleavened bread with bitter herbs. Do not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but roasted over the fire, the head with the feet and the inner parts. You shall leave none of it until morning, and you shall not break any of its bones. Whatever is left of it until morning you shall burn with fire."

To this the lawgiver adds what follows. He teaches how the diners should be dressed, and how, so equipped, they ought to take part in the most holy common [?]. "This is how you shall eat it," he says: "with your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staffs in your hands. You shall eat it in haste. It is the Lord's Passover."

He also reveals, very clearly, how the slaughter of the lamb will benefit them: "I will pass through the land of Egypt and strike down every firstborn, both man and beast, and on all the gods of the Egyptians I will execute judgment. I am the Lord. The blood shall be a sign for you on the houses where you are. When I see the blood, I will shelter you, and no plague shall come upon you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt." Then again, after some other matters, he says: "For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day you shall remove leaven from your houses." After fixing the punishment for anyone who transgresses, he adds: "The first day shall be called holy, and the seventh day shall be a holy convocation for you."

This, then, is the divine oracle. We will go through it again part by part and try to fit to each part its proper sense, referring the force of what is signified in many ways to Christ himself.

The time of the sacrifice, then, is fixed at the beginning of the year, in the first month. For Christ is the beginning of all things, since he is not recent in any way, because of his birth from God the Father before the ages. He sanctifies at every time, all things from beginning to end, yet the festival falls, as it were, in the month of new things. For the old things had passed away, as blessed Paul puts it: "Behold, all things have become new." And human nature too was blossoming again in Christ into what it had been in the beginning. These instructions were given to the children of Israel while they were still slaves and living under a tyrant's hand, for they were still in the land of the Egyptians. Here again the passage hints in a riddle that the human soul could not in any other way run back to freedom from sin, escape the devil's greed, and pass from its sojourn in the world to the city above, except through participation in Christ and through his love for humanity. As he himself said to the foolish Jews: "Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed." And again: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in yourselves." The land of promise, into which they were hastening to move out of Egypt, may rightly be understood as a type of this life.

The lamb is taken from the tenth day of the month and kept until the fourteenth, so that it may be slaughtered toward evening. "And why is that?" someone may ask, for the matter is truly deep. Tell me, what prevented it from being taken on the first day of the month? And what persuaded God to lay down that the victim be kept for five days and then sacrificed, as described, toward evening? For if we begin from the tenth, we will find a count of five days. Now the fact that the lamb is taken not on the first day but on the tenth of the month seems to signify that many times went before, and that long ages came before us, throughout which God always was, and is, and will be. Immediately after them, as their neighbour, comes this age of ours, divided into five periods, as through the five-day course we have just described. The Saviour's parable will explain what we are looking for very well. It runs like this: "The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard. After agreeing with the labourers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. And going out about the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and to them he said, 'You go into my vineyard too, and whatever is right I will give you.' So they went. Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth, he did the same. And going out about the eleventh, he found others standing there, and he said to them, 'Why do you stand here idle all day?' They said to him, 'No one has hired us.' He said to them, 'You go into my vineyard too.'" Do you see, then, how very clearly and plainly this passage divides our age into five whole periods? We shall reckon the first to be the time when our forefather Adam was still living in paradise. The second comes after it and is signified by the third hour: the time of Noah and those with him. The third, as at the sixth hour, is the time when the God over all called Abraham to the knowledge of the truth. The fourth, as again at the ninth hour, is clearly that of Moses and the prophets. About the eleventh hour, that is, in the fifth period, when the day was already drawing in and the present age was, so to speak, already coming to its end, Christ hired the nations, which no one else had in any way called to knowledge in the earlier periods that had passed. That is why the last of all, beyond everyone else, say: "No one has hired us."

The lamb, then, is taken on the first day of the five, that is, the tenth, which serves as a type of the beginning of the age. It is kept until the last period, that is, the fourteenth, and slaughtered toward evening. This is so that you may understand once more that the mystery of Christ is neither new nor recent, but was kept in the foreknowledge of the Father from the very foundation of the world. He died for us in the last periods of the age, when the spiritual and divine light was not yet shining, but the earth was still steeped in the darkness of ignorance, and the world-rulers of this darkness were defiling the hearts of all with their deceptions. This is why the Saviour, when he came among us, said, "I am the light of the world." And the saints are called "lights in the world, holding forth the word of life." Moreover, they rightly hear this too: "You also are the light of the world," because they are able to enlighten those who are in darkness.

You will marvel again when you find yet another mystical design in this. For the lamb is slaughtered on the fourteenth day of the month, when the orb of the moon has its own glory in full and lights up the world with what is, as it were, a counterfeit light. Yet it is already beginning to wane little by little and, as if by necessity, to draw in the honour and grace that dwell in it. From this you may understand, as you are led by the hand from the image and shadow of the thing set before you to a grasp of truer things, that the ruler of the night, that is, the devil, was glorified throughout the whole world. The moon signifies him as a type, for the moon was appointed to rule the night. By planting the wisdom of the world in the hearts of the deceived like a counterfeit light, he won for himself the fullest glory. But Christ died because of us and for us, the true Lamb, who takes away the sin of the world, and he destroyed the devil's glory. For that glory must wane and be consumed little by little, as the multitude of the nations is now hastening to rise up to peace and love toward God by turning away from it and by faith. And this, then, was what was sung of Christ long ago in the Psalms: "In his days righteousness will rise, and abundance of peace, until the moon is destroyed in return." For in Christ's days righteousness rose through faith, and abundance of peace through turning to God. And besides this, the ruler of the night, that is, the devil, has been destroyed in return. Note that it does not say that the moon will simply be destroyed, but rather that it will be destroyed in return. For the devil is destroyed in return as one who had first destroyed others, and it is surely quite plain to all that he had destroyed humanity.

"Let each take a lamb for each household," it says. For Christ dwells whole in each person through participation in the Holy Spirit, and he is not divided, as Paul says. "But if they are too few," it says, "to be enough for a lamb, he shall take with him his neighbour who is near him." Some cannot by themselves alone understand the mystery of Christ perfectly, or are not equal to comprehending him because their own understanding is weak. Such people will still have their share, by receiving their fellow believers as co-workers and helpers. For by admonishing one another we are sometimes able to rise even to contemplations beyond our own capacity. In just this way that wise eunuch, when he was listening to the prophecy about Christ, asked Philip: "I beg you, about whom does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?" You see how, by taking his neighbour with him (for all of us who belong to the one common word of faith are near to one another), he was shown through his inquiry to be already a partaker of the spiritual lamb. For he at once asked to be baptized, and was in fact baptized.

"Let the lamb be perfect," it says. For all the marks befitting God were present in Christ. "But let it also be male," the lawgiver declared. For he it was, and is, who sows the seeds of the knowledge of God in all of us, as in a delightful land, as the prophetic word also puts it, bringing humanity to perfection for God the Father through the proclamation of the gospel. Besides this, let it be a year old. This is either with respect to time, so that it may not be as though imperfect, with its year not yet complete; or else because those who reap the benefits of the passion were going to celebrate the most divine feast of the passion each year. It says that it is to be taken from the lambs and from the kids. Under the law the lamb is understood as a pure and spotless sacrifice, while goats are always brought to the altar for sins. You will find this too in Christ. For the same one was both a spotless victim, offering himself to God the Father as a fragrant aroma, and a kid slaughtered for our sins.

After the slaughter it commands that the doorposts and lintel of the houses be smeared with the blood. As it seems to me, it wishes to signify nothing other than this: that by the august and precious blood of Christ we make secure our own earthly house, that is, the body, driving out through participation in life the deadness that came from the transgression. For participation in Christ is life and sanctification. And when we throw the destroyer himself into confusion, keeping the plotting demon very far away through this anointing, we put to death the passions that arise from the movements of the flesh. By the doors of the house we have just spoken of you will understand our senses. Through them the quality of things is conveyed to everyone's heart, and a countless multitude of desires pours in. The prophet Joel also gives them the name of doors, when he says: "Like thieves they will come in through our windows"; for they had not been anointed with the blood of Christ.

It commands the meat to be eaten on this night, that is, in the present age. For Paul too called it so, saying: "The night is far gone; the day is at hand." Here he plainly calls the age to come "day," for Christ himself gives it light. So they will eat the meat in this age, it says. For as long as we are in this world, we shall partake of Christ through the holy flesh and the precious blood, in a way that is still more bodily. But when we have reached the day of his power, as it is written, and have risen into the splendour of the saints, we shall be sanctified again in some other way, the way known to the dispenser and giver of the good things to come. Besides, partaking of his holy flesh, and likewise drinking the saving blood, contains a confession of the passion and of the death of Christ, which he underwent for our sake in the divine economy. For so he himself says somewhere, when he was laying down for his disciples the laws concerning the mystery: "For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim my death." So in the present age, by partaking of the things just named, we fittingly proclaim his death. But when at last he comes in the glory of the Father, it will no longer be timely to offer him the confession of the passion. Instead we shall know him purely as God, face to face, as Paul says. "For we shall glorify him," it says, "as Master." For having died once, he dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him, as Paul says. That is why he said: "Even though we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we know him so no longer." For then we shall know him more brightly, not from what makes him man but from what makes him true God, since the economy for which he became flesh will have been completed. For the discourses about the incarnation will, presumably, cease. A greater knowledge will come in, and from him a divine understanding of the salvation that is in glory befitting God will shine forth in us.

It commands that the lamb's meat be roasted with fire and eaten, because those who rise to the comprehension of Christ must be fervent in spirit. Paul too bids them be aglow in the spirit. "And they will eat unleavened bread with bitter herbs," it says. Here it hints in a riddle that those who have become partakers of Christ ought to nourish their soul on desires that are unleavened, as it were, and most pure, training it in a way of life without guile and unmixed with wickedness. They should not for that reason refuse the bitterness of trials, according to what someone has said: "My child, if you come to serve God, prepare your soul for temptation; set your heart straight and endure." — "But you shall not eat any of it raw," it says. What, then, does this mean? Whoever eats raw food does not eat in a way that can be digested; such food does not even give way to the teeth at all. Those would rightly be said to do this who do not grind the doctrine about Christ fine through inquiry, putting it to the fire and testing it, in keeping with David's song: "And in my meditation a fire will be kindled." It also forbids eating it boiled in water, hinting that a watery and slack conception of him will not be good food for the minds of believers. A watery conception of him is to think that he is not God by nature, and to bring him down to the rank of created things. Some in their ignorance do not shrink from doing this. They drag what is said of him in the economy, because he became man, to suit their own will, and make it, as it were, food for the impiety within them. "So you shall not eat it boiled in water," it says, "but roasted with fire," both for the reason already given and because the words of the Lord are fire-tried. For all the words about his divinity are hot, with nothing watery or chilled in them, as again the one who speaks in the book of Psalms says: "Your word is thoroughly tried by fire, and your servant has loved it."

Again, it commands them to eat the head with the feet and the entrails, because it wants the whole knowledge of the whole mystery concerning him to dwell in the minds of believers. For before all else we must know that the Word was in the beginning, being God, in the Father and with the Father. That is the head, since it is the beginning of the whole mystery. Second, we must know that, being God, he will come again as judge to bring the economy concerning us to its end. This is what the feet signify to us, since they are the end of the whole body. By the entrails you will understand the doctrine of the incarnation, which is hidden and, as it were, in the middle. So through these things the faith is complete, and through such knowledge Christ is whole and perfect in us. It is for this reason, I would think, that John said: "He who is, who was, and who is coming."

Then again the lawgiver commands, saying: "You shall leave none of it until morning." In this riddle, it seems, he forbids delays, which are not good, in the desire to understand perfectly. Let the perfect and true knowledge of him not be put off, he says. Nor should anyone hold back for some later occasion the full partaking of him, once they have had a share in him and mean to lay hold of him at all. Yet this is what those do who have tasted the doctrines about Christ through catechesis but keep back the illumination of the Spirit and the grace of baptism for a long and untimely postponement, until old age, as they say. Great harm comes of this, and unexpectedly. For in the first place, the hope that such a person will even carry out his intentions is not secure. And even if his aim is finally achieved, he is sanctified, but he has only the forgiveness of his offences. He brings the talent back to his master barren, having had no time to earn anything more with it.

"And you shall not break a bone of it," it says. For bones are always beyond the power of our teeth to eat. Such to the human mind is the hidden doctrine of his divinity, which is, so to speak, white as bone. For we believe that he is Son by nature and that he has been begotten of God the Father, and we understand this very rightly; but we inquire no further, as the saint says. For who knows how to tell the manner of the begetting? And how can the prophet not be right when he cries out: "Who will declare his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth"? So by the bones he means here the firmness of doctrines that surpass the mind. The lawgiver does not allow us to break these. But the heretics, who pervert what is right, break the whole to their own harm. For they pry into the manner of the divine and ineffable begetting, sick with a folly beyond compare, and not taking to heart what is written: "Who has measured the heaven with a span?" This we rightly decline to do: we soberly shrink from breaking the lamb's bones and instead accept by faith the things beyond us. It is necessary, however, to remember that this text was also fulfilled in a more historical sense in our Saviour, when Pilate's soldiers did not break his legs, as it is written.

It says that whatever is left of it until morning must be burned. Here again it calls the illumination in the age to come "morning," when we shall see our King and God face to face, no longer as now in a riddle and a mirror, in shadow and in part, as Paul says. So, because the contemplation of him that is as in a riddle will then be in a sense done away with by a brighter knowledge, it says, again as a type, that whatever is left of it until morning will be burned with fire.

He bids the diners be dressed like this: "Let your loins be girded," it says, "and your sandals on your feet, and your staffs in your hands. And you shall eat it in haste. It is the Lord's Passover." To have one's loins girded would be a symbol of vigour and of a youthful spirit, according to what God said to righteous Job: "Gird up your loins like a man." And again, of someone in the prophets: "And he will have his loins girded with righteousness," that is, vigorous and courageous for righteousness. The sandal signifies a will that is ready to walk without delay toward whatever God wishes. For Paul too writes in this sense: "and having shod your feet with the readiness of the gospel of peace." And besides this, the prophet Jeremiah: "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, but to fear the Lord your God and to walk in all his ways?" The staff in the hand points to the hope that props us up and sustains us in endurance, according to what is found in the prophets: "Hope in the Lord, and lean upon God." Again, it commands that the lamb be eaten in haste. In this it very clearly sketches out that whoever has come to share in Christ must not appear sluggish or slack in good works, but must bring an intense and fervent eagerness to whatever he thinks will profit him. And think again of blessed Paul writing: "Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it."

Since I hold that we should hunt for what is profitable on every side, I shall turn to another interpretation. The law does not wish the one sanctified through Christ to be seen living in luxury and ease, but clothes him in the dress that suits travellers. In this, it seems, it hints at two things: either that what is in type and shadow will one day pass over and run toward the truth; or that whoever has once partaken of Christ should use his eagerness for the good like swift and nimble feet to go on to every virtue, running past the loathsome pleasure of the world. He at once adds the reason why the one we have just described must be seen in this guise, saying: "It is the Lord's Pascha," that is, a passing over. For we pass over from life in the world to a way of life dear to God. Then again he at once makes clear to them what benefit they gain from this, and how great it is. He announces that he will strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt. But for those who have eaten the lamb, he says, the blood will be a sign, so that by it they come under his shelter and are not destroyed when he strikes in the land of Egypt. For God punishes the disobedient and unheeding, who have no share in the holiness that comes from Christ. But he recognizes only those who appear anointed with the blood of the true lamb, and he counts them alone worthy of his good care. He does not let the sanctified perish along with the ungodly, but grants them a special kindness.

For seven whole days he commands those who ate the holy lamb to keep to unleavened bread. In this, as it seems to me, he urges those sanctified through Christ to nourish their soul as well on desires that are most pure and far removed from all wickedness. "Let the first day and the seventh be called holy," it says. For the time at the beginning of our creation was holy, when our forefather Adam had not yet left paradise through his transgression, but was still living in it and still keeping the commandment he had been given. And the time at the end is holy again, through Christ, who justifies by faith those who come to him and brings us back to what we were in the beginning. So the whole mystery of our Saviour was prefigured for us in these things. That is why he himself said, very aptly, to the Jews: "If you believed Moses," he says, "you would believe me; for he wrote about me."

We have been redeemed from the futile way of life handed down to us from our fathers, as it is written, "not with perishable things, with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot, foreknown before the foundation of the world but revealed in the last time." For he who is God by nature, in the form of God the Father and equal to him, was seen on earth and lived among human beings, since the Only-begotten has also been called firstborn. For somewhere in the Psalms he speaks about us to his Father and God in heaven: "I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise." Having taken human things upon himself, and in the divine plan having brought down what is his own into our condition, he is not ashamed to call us brothers, since through him we have been called to sonship. And it is indeed true, and attested by the facts themselves, that the Father gave his own Son as the ransom for the salvation of us all. So, as Paul says, "We were bought with a price, and we are not our own." Rather, one died for all, so that all of us might no longer live for ourselves but for him who died and was raised for us. Now, that each of those who have been saved through Christ, and have richly gained a kind of conformity to him through sanctification in the Spirit, owes his own life to God becomes clear when the all-wise Moses addresses the people of old: "And it shall be, when the Lord your God brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to your fathers, and gives it to you, that you shall set apart for the Lord every male that opens the womb. Every one that opens the womb among your herds or among your livestock, whatever males are born to you, you shall consecrate to the Lord. Every one that opens the womb of a donkey you shall exchange for a sheep; and if you do not exchange it, you shall redeem it. Every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem." And when the assembly was gathered at one time at Horeb, he comes with the same words and lays down the law again, saying: "The firstborn of your sons you shall give to me. So shall you do with your calf, your sheep and your beast of burden. Seven days it shall be with its mother, and on the eighth day you shall give it to me. And you shall be holy men to me."

It is fitting, then, that the God of all asks for all to be dedicated to him, and insists that we must consecrate the males to him. The firstborn of the Egyptians perished, while beloved Israel was saved with all its households and escaped the destroyer, having been anointed with the blood of the lamb as a type of Christ, who for our sake was among the dead in order to abolish death. For this reason those who had been saved would rightly no longer belong to themselves. Rather, it would be fitting that he who had put himself in danger for them should henceforth possess them as his own. Think of those who are able to rescue people who have fallen into barbarian hands, and who free them from an unexpected slavery by enduring battle against their captors: from then on they all but hold the position of master, having won the captives with their own blood. By the same reasoning, I think, our Lord Jesus Christ bound the band of unclean demons and laid down his own blood for us. Having thus driven off death and destroyed corruption, he makes us his own from then on, as people who no longer live their own life but rather his. For had he not died for us, we would not have been saved; and had he not been among the dead, the grim power of death would not have been shaken. So too the divine Paul initiated those saved through Christ into this mystery, saying: "I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me." Just as the Israelites, then, all but lived the life of the slaughtered lamb, so we too no longer live our own life but the life of Christ who died for us, even though he came back to life again. For he was Life by nature, being God. Our life, then, must be holy, for such is the life of Christ. And if we choose to live in holiness, we shall be enriched with his admirable image. Conformed to him who for our sake became like us, who is Only-begotten as God and firstborn because of his humanity, we shall truly be a sacred victim, an offering dedicated and acceptable to God the Father. The firstborn males, then, are sanctified because they are understood as an image of Christ. Mothers brought their babies, and our Lord Jesus Christ received them very gladly and said to the holy disciples: "Let the children come, and do not hinder them from coming to me; for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these." You should understand this passage in the same way: God the Father loves the firstborn as one marked out by the image of Christ. And only the males among the firstborn are chosen. For it was necessary, truly necessary, that the beauty most fitting to Christ be preserved for him, and for those formed after his image, in the form, as it were, of the firstborn. For he is at once firstborn and male, because he knows no weakness toward sin, and the female is a type of weakness. Those who bear the image of Christ must therefore reject an effeminate mind. They must utterly shake off, as truly accursed and hateful to God, what is soft, slack and feeble, and keep up their vigour; and they must choose a manly eagerness for what is needful, I mean for achieving virtue. Every firstling of a donkey is exchanged for a sheep. What is the reason? By the law the donkey is unholy and profane, while the sheep is sacred; so the sheep is offered in place of the donkey. Here again the law hints to us that in Christ even the profane becomes holy, and the unholy too, and that through him even the unacceptable is accepted. For since we were sinners and unclean, he became a holy sacrifice for us, a fragrant aroma. He died for sinners, the righteous for the unrighteous, the pure for the unclean, just as the sheep dies for the donkey. The firstborn of human beings are redeemed with gifts, as is reasonable, that is, with a price fixed beforehand. For what reason? Because whatever had been wholly dedicated and consecrated to God would in every case have had to be sacrificed. But God, who created all things in incorruption, will not have human beings killed. For he did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living, as it is written. Nor, like the unclean demons, does he take pleasure in those who perish. Rather, he commands that a ransom be paid in their place, as though we were declaring outright that we owe him our own life. This is what he brings home by commanding that the so-called didrachm be paid. But the true ransom, given for all, is to be understood as Christ himself, through whom and in whom we have conquered corruption; for he gave himself for us. He said that the lamb must spend seven full days with its mother and be brought on the eighth. For it was not slaughtered as soon as it was born from the womb. God prescribed that it should first gradually gain strength on its mother's milk and grow a little sturdier, and then, only then, be fit to be a fragrant aroma. This too would be a type of a mystical and necessary practice, which is kept to this day among us, who are accustomed to consecrate the rational flock to God, the ruler of all. For we do not bring those who have only just been called, and have just set out on the first steps of faith, to the divine and bloodless sacrifice while they are still uninitiated. Rather, we first instruct them while they still run, as it were, beside their mother, that is, the Church, and we fatten them with a word like milk, tender and suited to infants. The divine Paul writes in this way to those who are not yet mature: "I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able to take it, and even now you are still not able." And again in another letter: "For everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, since he is an infant. But solid food is for the mature, who through practice have their faculties trained to distinguish good from evil." So when they have grown to maturity and been well nourished by the words of catechesis, we bring them on the eighth day. That is, the time in which they were infants has passed, and another time has followed it, in which the mystery of Christ may be set before them at the right moment and in a fitting way. For the eighth day signifies for us the time of the resurrection, when Christ, having endured death for us, came back to life. We are conformed to him spiritually by dying through holy baptism, so that we may also attain the resurrection. Paul will confirm this when he writes: "For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life." We are reborn, then, through faith into the knowledge of the truth, and are already enriched with conformity to our Lord Jesus Christ, who for our sake and among us is the firstborn. Then we drink the spiritual and pure milk and grow up to the measure of the stature of his fullness, as it is written. Then, and only then, shall we all be sacred, an offering dedicated to God, dying to the world but living spiritually and in holiness to God. This, I think, is what is meant by the firstborn of the livestock being slaughtered at his altar. The divine Paul writes to those who have been sanctified in this way: "For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God." The death of the saints, then, is sacred, and it seems to me that the blessed David had something like this in view: "Precious in the sight of the Lord," he says, "is the death of his holy ones." The meaning we have just set out would fit, I think, not only those from the nations who turn to the knowledge of the truth, but above all those called from the worship of the law to justification in Christ and sanctification in the Spirit. The lamb, or the calf, was nourished with its mother for seven days and brought on the eighth. By this, I think, God was indicating in a riddle (for the law is a shadow) that those who were to become sacred and to be offered up to God as a fragrant aroma first had to be schooled through types, through lessons, as it were, that were not very manly but rather suited to infants. And the time most suited to such perfection is the mystery of Christ, which the eighth day signifies. Through the worship of the law, then, God was inaccessible, but he becomes accessible through Christ alone. For through him we have gained access, as after the seventh day: that is, once the sabbath-keeping of the law has passed, or, to speak more generally and take the part for the whole, the worship of the law. For the law made nothing perfect, but Christ brings us to perfection. Those who have believed are complete in virtue and have perfection in knowledge through Christ, for we have his mind. Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

When the Israelites set out from the land of the Egyptians, having barely thrown off the crushing yoke of slavery, they went through the midst of the sea as on dry land, and crossed it without toil. For the waters stood firm like a wall, yielding to the divine command. After this they saw Pharaoh imperilled with his whole army and drowned in the waters, and saw those who had once been unbearable to them, who had driven them hard without pity, miserably destroyed. Then they raised songs to God and honoured him with hymns of thanksgiving, saying: "Let us sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea. He became my helper and protector, for my salvation." For the God of all worked his wonders to good purpose. He had already shown them a great many most marvellous signs in Egypt, and on top of these he generously enabled those under his care to dash through the sea itself. He did this so that from then on their minds might be well founded and firmly set, and that they might believe that he is not like one of the falsely named gods, the inventions of human craft, mere idols made of wood and stone. Rather, being Lord of all, he commands creation as something lying beneath his feet, and easily accomplishes whatever he chooses. And so that they might profit by marvelling still more, he bade them journey on, to be enriched still further, and hasten to the land promised to their fathers, under the command and leadership of the all-wise Moses. What came next the sacred Scripture again makes clear: "Moses," it says, "led the Israelites away from the Red Sea and brought them into the wilderness of Shur. They went three days in the wilderness and found no water to drink. And they came to Marah, and could not drink the water of Marah, for it was bitter. That is why the place was named Bitterness. And the people grumbled against Moses, saying, 'What shall we drink?' And Moses cried out to the Lord, and the Lord showed him a tree, and he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There he gave him statutes and ordinances and judgments, and there he tested him and said: 'If you will listen carefully to the voice of the Lord your God, and do what is pleasing in his sight, and give ear to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will not bring upon you any of the diseases that I brought upon the Egyptians; for I am the Lord who heals you.' And they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees; and they encamped there by the waters." See, then, how by design he does not let those he has redeemed drift into idleness, untested and revelling in the broad ease of good cheer. Otherwise they might gradually forget him who had the power to save, and easily slip back into the error of Egypt. For hardships draw people together toward God. So the prophet says: "Lord, in affliction we remembered you; in a little affliction your discipline was upon us." So, as they crossed a vast and thirsty land, they came to lack the necessities of life. They found no water to drink, and their thirst dragged on into the third day before what they longed for was at last found. But even this was entirely useless. For the water of Marah was bitter, and could not save the thirsty from death. They grew distressed at this and cried out against their mediator, and Moses was at a loss. Then God, who knows all things, showed him a tree; he threw it into the waters, and they were marvellously changed into a sweet and most drinkable stream. Having drunk and been refreshed, they marvelled at the divine sign. After this they encamped at twelve springs of water, where there were also seventy palm trees, and there they lived for a time in plenty. Through shadow and types, then, God was assuring them that the way of salvation could be found in faith and in no other way. For this reason he also commanded them to slaughter the lamb in Egypt, and wanted them to believe that, anointed with its blood, they would ward off the death that had been launched against the firstborn. Would not anyone say, and quite rightly, that what was done was a preliminary exercise of faith? For how, tell me, would death be terrified by the slaughter of a sheep? But the thing was a type of a mystery. For Christ rescues by his own blood those who are sanctified in faith, and shows them to be stronger than death and corruption. Now what, again, is the meaning of the events at Marah? Come, let us explain as far as we can.

The divinely inspired Scripture likens the divine word to water. Just as physical water gives life to bodies, so the divine word, if it reaches the mind, will benefit it greatly. So Christ too, speaking to the crowds of the Jews, cried out: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." And to the woman from Samaria: "Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again." The Israelites, then, had just abandoned the God-hated worship of the Egyptians and had turned their minds to doing whatever God might wish. But they had not yet been trained in the laws from above, and had not yet tasted the spiritual waters, so the mind within them was, as it were, dry and thirsty. Then at last they came upon Marah, but they could not drink the water, for it was bitter. When Moses had thrown in the tree, the water was freed from its natural bitterness. What, then, is Marah?
