I would say it is the letter of the law. For the law is bitter, since it punishes. As the divine Paul said: "Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses." Do you see that it was bitter and hard to bear, perhaps even for those who wished to keep it? So the divine disciples said plainly to those who, after the coming of faith, were tying people once again to the worship of the law: "Now, then, why do you put God to the test by placing on the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?" And the blessed Paul calls the commandment given through the all-wise Moses a ministry of condemnation. He spoke thus: "For if the ministry of condemnation had glory, the ministry of righteousness abounds in glory much more." And elsewhere he said: "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life." By "letter", I think, he clearly means the law, and by "Spirit" the worship in spirit, that is, the worship of the Gospel. For the law is bitter, and Marah means "bitter". There is no need to argue that the instruction of the law, taken by itself and insofar as it consisted of types, cannot give life. For no one is justified before God by the law, as it is written. But the law itself will then become life-giving, and will be freed from the bitterness of the letter, if it becomes receptive to the mystery of Christ. For Christ is the end of the law, for the salvation of everyone who believes, when the law is understood, that is, spiritually. And what happened at Marah would be a clear type of this as well. For the tree signifies the Saviour's cross, or the mystery connected with it. If those under the law accept it, they will find even what is bitter sweet. For to those who believe in Christ the law is no longer fault-finding and punishing but now gives life, since the history is well reshaped for us into spiritual contemplation and guides us to Christ, who is life and the giver of life. Then indeed, then the law will also set statutes and judgments for us. For it will carry us straight to what pleases God, will show the path to every kind of excellence, and will free us from fear and from the expectation of punishment. For "I will not bring upon you," it says, "any plague that I brought upon the Egyptians." So for those under the law who have received this mystery there is good hope of escaping punishment. And this, I think, is what the Saviour himself said to the crowds of the Jews during his stay among them: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life." And again: "Whoever believes in the Son is not judged." Once we have received the statutes of Christ, then indeed we shall come to Elim, which means "ascent". For we are raised from our former infancy to a mature mind, and having attained the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, we shall delight in the springs of spiritual waters. These twelve springs depict for us the company of the holy apostles; and we shall also come upon the seventy palm trees. For it is written that after the holy apostles the Lord appointed seventy others. That the divine disciples are truly springs, pouring out for us the divine and saving word that is necessary for life, the God of all would clearly show to those justified under the law, when he says: "Draw water with joy from the springs of salvation." And of every saint the divine Psalmist says: "The righteous will flourish like a palm tree." Do not be surprised at this, for Christ himself is called by this name in the divinely inspired Scripture. For somewhere the spiritual bride, that is, the Church, speaks again of the bridegroom from above and from heaven, I mean Christ: "I said, I will go up to the palm tree; I will take hold of its heights." For this plant is always flourishing, sweet and deep-rooted, and has a white heart. And spiritually Christ is something like this, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

Once again the God of all works wonders. He goes from strength to strength, as it is written, and finds ways where there seem to be none. Everywhere he provides for his own glory and shows in many ways that he alone can accomplish, without effort, even things beyond reason, things at which we rightly must marvel. So he is seen through all things to be God, not like one of those made gods by human craft or impiously exalted, but God by nature and in truth. From the glorious things he accomplishes, one can quite easily see his pure nature. As its own proper good, that nature has all-conquering power that nothing can resist in whatever it chooses to do. Along with this it also has patient forbearance. One may see what I mean very clearly in the passage now before us. For it is written: “On the fifteenth day of the second month after they had come out of the land of Egypt, the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, and the children of Israel said to them: Would that we had died, struck down by the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the pots of meat and ate bread to the full! For you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole congregation with hunger. And the Lord said to Moses: Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you, and the people shall go out and gather each day's portion day by day, so that I may test them whether they will walk in my law. And on the sixth day they shall prepare what they bring in, and it shall be twice as much as they gather day by day.” For the firstborn of the Egyptians, as we have already said, had perished, and the Israelites were being sent out of the country without even being allowed, so to speak, to take provisions. They carried out their dough before their kneaded lumps were leavened. Equipped simply with whatever came to hand, they went out in haste, and the fear was equal for the Egyptians who drove them out and for those being driven out. The Egyptians expected to be added before long to those already dead unless they obeyed the divine commands and drove Israel out of the country. The Israelites thought that if they were caught lingering and lost their chance of escape [?], they would surely face a struggle to the death and be in danger without mercy. So they departed without any thought for the journey. They barely snatched up what was at hand, and out of necessity they all but stole from their homes the things easiest to carry. When they had eaten even these, they were at a loss where in the desert they might find what they needed to live. Then they slid into longing for the food of Egypt. They forget that they had been rescued from the worst of all evils and from slavery in Egypt, and they practically cry out against the help they had been given. They are angry that they have been redeemed, and they put the fill of an unclean belly ahead of freedom, which all people long for intensely and pray for above everything. The affair troubles the mediator, that is, Moses. But God at once promises to supply them with an abundance of food, and he still treats them gently, although they had offended him greatly. To want to receive from him what is needed for life would deserve no blame at all, but the murmuring grieves him deeply. Indeed the Savior himself taught us to say in prayer: “Give us today our daily bread.” But when we say this, we are in no way accusing the Master. Rather, we are asking him for what we need to live. The Jewish people, however, should have asked for food. Instead they are angry that they were redeemed, and in their great folly they insult so holy and precious a grace, as if it had robbed them of the things they enjoyed most, I mean bread and meat. So they murmur and cry out impiously. But God bears with them and promises them an abundance they did not expect. And by his ineffable power he sends down the quail in the evening, and at dawn the manna. As the divine David said: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels.” He proved by experience and by deeds themselves that God is able to give bread and prepare a table in the wilderness. In the same way our Lord Jesus Christ worked similar wonders: he broke five loaves and fed many in the wilderness, and twelve baskets of fragments were gathered up. The way these miracles are worked lies wholly beyond inquiry. So let things beyond understanding be honored by faith, and let God hear from all who marvel at him: “I know that you can do all things, and nothing is impossible for you.”

Let this be enough for our discussion of what is perceptible to the senses. What, then, is the meaning of the spiritual contemplation? What riddle of the law must we explore, we who are so eager to hunt down the truth? From these things too we shall learn that life under the law is beyond dispute inferior to the life of the gospel. It is not free from the charge of loving the flesh and has not been delivered from earthly desire. The divine life of the gospel, by contrast, is spiritual and blameless, and its beauty cannot be compared. We shall draw the demonstration and proof for each from the divinely inspired Scripture, testing carefully what it says about both. For it says: “Evening came, and quail came up and covered the camp. In the morning, when the dew around the camp had ceased, behold, on the face of the wilderness there was something fine like coriander seed, white like frost on the ground. When the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another: What is this? For they did not know what it was. And Moses said to them: This is the bread which the Lord has given you to eat. This is the word that the Lord has commanded: Gather of it, each of you, for those who belong to you, an omer a head, according to the number of your persons. Each of you, gather with those of your tent. And the children of Israel did so, and they gathered, some more and some less. They measured it by the omer, and the one who gathered much had nothing left over, and the one who gathered less had no lack; each gathered for those who belonged to him. And Moses said to them: Let no one leave any of it until morning. But they did not listen to Moses. Some left part of it until morning, and it bred worms and stank. And Moses was angry with them.” And again, a little later: “Moses said to them: This is the word which the Lord has spoken: Tomorrow is a holy sabbath, a rest to the Lord. Bake what you will bake, and boil what you will boil, and whatever is left over, lay it aside to be kept until morning. And they laid it aside until morning, as Moses had commanded them, and it did not stink, nor was there a worm in it.” So he commanded each person to gather what was sufficient for himself. Yet he did not at all forbid anyone who might choose to gather for those who were absent too, and so to shine by the law of love. But he utterly forbade keeping it until morning, and allowed this only before the sabbath, so that the law of rest would not be dishonored. For none was to be found on the sabbath, because God did not send it down, and by this means he all but compelled them to refrain from work on the sabbath. But some paid little heed to the divine oracles and kept it over on days before the sabbath, and, as the holy text says, “it stank and bred worms, and Moses was angry.” They also ran out to gather on the sabbath, and God was indignant. For it is written thus: “On the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, and they found none. And the Lord said to Moses: How long will you refuse to listen to my commandments and my law? See, the Lord has given you this day as a sabbath. That is why he gave you bread for two days on the sixth day. Stay, each of you, in your homes; let none of you go out of his place on the seventh day.” What explanation, then, would fit these words and suit them best? Why did the quail come in the evening, while the manna was given in the light, at daybreak? For my part, I think we should investigate first of all what the quail is in the shadow, and what the manna is.

3. That the life of the Jews was not delivered from fleshly desires one may reasonably conclude. Their seeking the meat of Egypt for food clearly proves it, and shows that their mind was overcome by their leanings toward it, indeed all but held in tyranny. But our own state is not seen in these things. For we have been sanctified in Christ and are beyond the impurity of the flesh. The divine Paul will bear witness to this when he writes: “Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.” What does “crucified” mean? It stands for “have handed over to death,” a spiritual death, clearly, because they refuse to live according to the flesh and do not choose to set their minds on passing things. Rather, they put to death their members that are on earth, fornication, passion and evil desire. They walk on earth, but long intensely for the citizenship above. For they remember the holy text that cries out: “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not carry out the desire of the flesh.” So the mind of the Jews is feeble and very easily overcome by the assaults of the passions, for it still loves the things of the flesh and is defeated by what is more earthly. These things, as I said, are signified to us by the quail. God grants them to those who seek them. He does not himself draw them into desires, but he does not yet give them the strength to triumph boldly over the passions. For the excellence of life and complete sanctification did not belong to those under the law. They were reserved instead for those in the Spirit. That is why God promised through the prophet a new covenant, not like that first one, since that one was not without fault, but another, a spiritual covenant that is able to perfect believers in conscience. And see how the quail fly to the synagogue of the Jews in the evening, as it were. For it says: “Evening came, and quail came up.” The event hints to us indirectly that the lover of earthly things is not in spiritual light but in night and darkness, as it were. And this is not a false account of the matter, for the mind of the Jews has not been freed from ignorance and hardness, that is, from a spiritual mist. That is why Christ also called out to them, saying: “I am the light of the world.” So those who have not yet believed are in a mist, as if in darkness, for they did not come to the light. And somewhere Christ said about the Pharisees and the people under their authority: “Leave them; they are blind guides of the blind.” The mind of the Jews, then, is without light. Therefore they are sick with the things of the flesh and all but hang on what is more earthly.

We shall therefore take the manna to be a shadow and type of the teachings and gifts given through Christ. These are from above, from heaven, and there is nothing earthly in them anywhere. Rather, they have no share in fleshly foulness, and they are truly the food not only of human beings but also of angels. For the Son has revealed the Father to us in himself. Through him we have come to believe the doctrine of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, and we have been well guided into every path of virtue. And the food of spirits is right and genuine knowledge of these things. The bestowal of the teachings that come through Christ would be as in light and in daytime. That is why the manna was given to the people of old as the day was dawning and the light was spreading. For the day has dawned in us who believe, as it is written. The morning star has risen in the hearts of all, and the sun of righteousness has risen, that is, Christ, the giver of the spiritual manna. He himself will assure us that the perceptible manna was still only an image, while he is the truth, when he says to the Jews: “Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die. I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.” For our Lord Jesus Christ nourishes us for endless life, both by his counsels to godliness and through the mystical blessing. He himself, then, and what comes through him, is truly the divine and life-giving manna. Whoever has eaten this rises above corruption and will escape death. This is not true of those who ate the perceptible manna. For the type did not bring salvation; it only sketched the outline of the truth. When God sent the manna down from above like rain, he commanded each person to gather what was sufficient, but also allowed some, if they chose, to gather for those who lived in the same tent. For he says, “Each of you, gather with those of your tent,” and “You shall not leave any of it until morning.” For we must fill ourselves with the divine teachings of the gospel. Christ distributes his grace to us in equal measure, to small and great alike, and nourishes all equally for life. Yet he wants the stronger to gather for the others, to toil for their brothers, to lend them their own labors and to make them sharers in the gifts from above. And I think this is what was said to the holy apostles themselves: “Freely you have received; freely give.” For gathering, as it were, a great deal of manna for themselves, they were eager to distribute it to those who lived in the same tent, that is, the Church. The divine disciples continually admonished and instructed, led people on to everything praiseworthy, and ungrudgingly set before everyone a share in the grace with which they themselves had been enriched by Christ. So the blessed Paul writes to some: “For I long to see you, so that I may impart some spiritual gift to you, so that you may be strengthened.” But the words “Each of you, gather with those of your tent” might be understood in another way: they should not gather all together indiscriminately or mixed up, but by family or by tents. In that case you will understand it like this. We must fill ourselves with the divine words together with those who share our faith, and seek the spiritual manna. We must not foolishly carry it off together with those who think otherwise and are practically foreigners. This is indeed what we do: we drive the heterodox and perverse away from the churches, and together with those who are our own in faith we are enriched with food from heaven. He said not to leave any until morning. Here again the law hints that using the types after their time has passed, the time when they were still useful and necessary, brings one wholly and entirely under judgment and punishment. For what was kept bred worms, and this too would be a clear sign of punishment and corruption. For all who keep the shadow after the truth has been revealed will be subject to corruption and punishment. We say that something of this kind happened to those to whom the blessed Paul writes: “You have been severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen from grace.” And again: “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Did you suffer so many things in vain, if it really was in vain?” So he forbids keeping it until morning, so that by “morning” you may understand the time after the law, when the coming of Christ appeared and the divine light shone on us. Yet the Israelites did keep it until morning when they were about to keep the sabbath, and this at God's command. What, then, does it mean that what was gathered beforehand for the sabbath was kept and did not spoil, and that Moses was not angry with those who kept it? Through faith we have arrived at the sabbath rest understood in Christ, that is, at rest and cessation from sins. We do not reject as useless the instruction of the law that has been stored up in us and laid by beforehand, as it were, which leads us by the hand to Christ, for the law is a tutor. Rather, if we hold to it together with the teachings of the gospel, we shall not be far from deserving praise, and God is not angry with those who do this. Indeed the Savior himself teaches this when he says to us: “Every scribe who has been made a disciple of the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old.” So the manna stored up in us through the law is blameless, even if it is kept during the spiritual sabbath rest. For we who keep sabbath in Christ turn to the shadows given through Moses so that we may seek the truth within them. But God made gathering on the sabbath accursed and liable to punishment, or rather, he did not send the manna down at all. For when we keep sabbath spiritually in Christ, we shall no longer gather the things found in types. We shall not cling to fleshly circumcision, nor sacrifice oxen or sheep. Rather, we shall set aside the grossness of the types, since we have the truth itself, that is, Christ.

I think the account given of the passages before us is now sufficient and clear. But since we find this chapter in the book called Numbers as well, with some further details added to the narrative, I thought it necessary not to pass over without examination what the book of Exodus leaves unsaid. In this way readers may gain a fuller understanding. It is written, then: “The mixed multitude among them had a strong craving, and the children of Israel also sat down and wept and said, ‘Who will feed us meat? We remember the fish we used to eat in Egypt for nothing, and the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions and the garlic. But now our soul is dried up; our eyes see nothing but this manna.’” Then it continues: “And Moses heard them weeping by their clans, each at the door of his tent. And the Lord’s anger blazed out fiercely, and in Moses’ eyes it was evil.” See, then, how very easily Israel is led astray. Not only is it unable to help others, but it suffers from weakness even in what concerns itself alone. The mixed multitude fell sick with this utterly outlandish and disgusting craving, and those who ought to have rebuked them and persuaded them to choose more fitting thoughts fell sicker still. The inspired Moses was greatly distressed, and he told the God of all plainly that he alone could not bear so heavy and unbearable a burden. To prove it, he pointed out how impossible and hard to obtain the thing was, saying, “Where am I to get meat to give to all this people to eat?” He had sunk so far into despondency that he now wished to depart this life: “If this is how you deal with me,” he says, “kill me outright, so that I may not see my misery.” God supports him and orders him to choose seventy men from the whole congregation to help him and share his care. For the Lord said to Moses, “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you yourself know to be elders of the people and their officers, and bring them to the tent of witness, and let them stand there with you. I will come down and speak with you there. I will take some of the spirit that is upon you and put it on them, and they will bear the burden of the people with you, so that you will not bear it alone.” When this was done (for he at once presented those who were more distinguished than the rest), the God of all filled them with the Holy Spirit. After this, giving in to the cravings of those who wept, he sent the quails down on them. They lay in heaps around the camp, and the people gathered them up with great delight and devoured them like beasts, with no regard for having enough or for restraint. They had gathered and salted a countless multitude of birds, and the eating of meat went on for a month of days, until at last a deadly plague struck them; and as the prophet says, “Hades has widened its throat and opened its mouth without ceasing.” For, it says, “the meat was still between their teeth before it was used up, and the Lord was angry with the people, and the Lord struck the people with a very great plague. And the name of that place was called the Graves of Craving, because there they buried the people who craved.” Though they lacked nothing good, and were free to enjoy without reproach the rich supply of manna, they longed for meat and leeks, and named cucumbers and melons, onions and garlic. So when they had eaten, they perished before long. God gives the quails, not because he approves of the craving, but rather to prove by deeds that nothing is impossible for him. Then, as was fitting, he punishes those who had been caught by shameful pleasures. The wretched Jews suffered something of the same kind at the time of our Savior’s sojourn on earth. For those events were shadows of these, and what happened long ago appeared beforehand as types of what came later. When the truer manna, Christ, came down to us from above, from heaven, able to nourish us and promising endless life, they foolishly chose instead the enjoyment of earthly things, which is truly worldly and utterly insipid; and so they inevitably offended not only the God of all but also the inspired Moses himself. For it is written, “And the Lord’s anger blazed out against his people, and in Moses’ eyes it was evil.” For the mind of the saints always follows the judgments of God. That the Jewish people everywhere preferred temporal and fleshly things to the good things from above, one may learn from the parable in the Gospel. Those sent out with the invitation wanted to gather guests for the wedding, but the guests went off, it says, one to his own field, another to his business. And their excuses were, for one, “I have married a wife,” and for another, “I have bought a field, and I cannot come.” That Moses himself also cried out against the disobedience of the Jews, our Lord Jesus Christ will confirm when he says, “Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. The one who accuses you is Moses, on whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me.” Moses regards it as a very heavy burden to be able to bear with Israel any longer. But God consecrated others, seventy in number, as we have already said. For the law alone, of which Moses may fittingly be understood as a type, is not able to lead us by the hand. That is why many others are appointed, seventy in number, to supply what was lacking in him, and they appear in a perfect number, for the number seventy signifies this. And who, again, are these? Those who after Moses were brought forward through Christ to be leaders, whose firstfruits and fathers are the inspired disciples. God is said to take some of the spirit that was upon Moses and put it in those who had been chosen, for no other reason than that we may believe that it is by the one Holy Spirit that God sanctifies both the saints before us and ourselves. For just as the Father is one, and likewise the Son is one, so too the Holy Spirit is one, the same one in the prophets and in us. Being one, it should not be thought of as divided among many; rather, it remains undivided even in the wide distribution of gifts, and is present perfectly in all. It should be noticed that the God of all commanded the chosen men to be gathered to the number of seventy, but the full number was not assembled. Two were missing, Medad and Eldad. Yet God filled these too with the Spirit, though they came late, for they prophesied in the camp. Some of those around Moses were jealous, and even said that they ought to be stopped. But Moses, foreseeing the mystery of Christ, said, “Would that the Lord’s people were all prophets, when the Lord puts his spirit upon them!” From this too we shall understand that the law cast its net and brought many to God, training them for the mystery of Christ. Yet it could not bring them all; and those who came late Christ himself sanctified. For the Gentiles were called to the knowledge of the truth, not through Moses or the law, but by the power of God the Father, who revealed his own image, that is, the Son, to those who did not know him; and having called them, he made them holy, anointing them with the Spirit. Those under the law are jealous of those in Christ, who have been justified by faith and sanctified in the Spirit. But Moses rejoiced, since he had foreknown the mystery. So the Jewish people, in their unreasonable jealousy of the saints in Christ, do not think as Moses thought. Winding our discourse back, as it were, to the beginning, we say this. In the first section it was clearly shown that the Jewish people are still fleshly, while the people of those who are in faith and in Christ are different, holy and truly better; and that the visible manna served as a shadow and type of the gifts that come through Christ. We were also taught that if we keep the shadows of the law even after the time set for them, we shall offend God and become hateful to the saints themselves, for Moses was embittered against those who had kept the manna. In the second section one can see that the Jews, by dishonoring the spiritual manna, turning away from the things from above that come through Christ, leaning instead toward earthly things and bending without measure toward foul pleasures, perished conspicuously. For they ought by all means to have counted the things of God as better, and to have crowned with faith the Savior and Redeemer of us all, I mean Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, forever. Amen.

No one could behold the divine nature, whatever it may be. It is utterly beyond sight; indeed it surpasses every mind and the power of speech, and it alone is known by itself alone. You will learn this from Christ himself, who cries out: “No one knows who the Son is except the Father, and no one knows who the Father is except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” So the Only-begotten has shown us the surpassing beauty of the God and Father by setting himself forth as a radiant image. That is why he says, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” And we have beheld the Son, both with the eyes of the heart and with the eyes of the flesh, when he lowered himself to self-emptying and came down into our condition. Yet he is God, existing in the form of the God and Father and in equality with him, and begotten from him by nature. Baruch too spoke, pointing, I think, to the Word himself: “This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him. He found out every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel whom he loved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among men.” And the divine David had clearly cried out to us beforehand: “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting. Out of Zion comes the splendor of his beauty. God will come openly, our God, and will not keep silent.” He did indeed come down in the form of fire upon Mount Sinai. But Christ makes it certain that those events were a type and nothing more. The multitudes of the Jews supposed that they had truly beheld the ineffable nature, while Moses acted as mediator, standing among them at Horeb and gathering them into assembly beneath Mount Sinai. And because the piercing blast of trumpets, darting upward, terrified those who heard it, they supposed among themselves that they had also heard the divine voice. But God has plainly shown that this was a childish way of thinking, when he says: “You have not heard his voice, nor have you seen his form, and you do not have his word abiding in you, because you do not believe the one whom he has sent.” So we who have believed have beheld the Father in the Son, and we have received his Word as well. That is how we have been redeemed. For, as it is written, no envoy, no angel, and not the law given through Moses saved us, but the Lord himself. That what I say is true we shall also learn from Scripture. It runs as follows: “And he said: I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. And Moses turned away his face, for he was afraid to look before God.” Observe the weakness of the law. The God of all reveals himself; but though he shows himself openly, Moses turns away his face. This too may be a clear sign to us that the sons of Israel themselves did not behold the glory of the Son, which befits God, even though he showed himself to them and all but led them by the hand to knowledge of him. That is why he said through the voice of Isaiah: “I was found by those who did not seek me; I became manifest to those who did not ask for me. I said, Here I am, to a nation that did not know me. All day long I stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.” So they did not behold the glory of Christ, because they turned away the eyes of their understanding. And this, I think, is what was said about them through the voice of the prophet: “And they turned to me their backs and [?] their faces.” The divine Paul also writes: “To this very day, when the Old Covenant is read, the same veil remains unlifted, because only in Christ is it taken away. Yes, to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart. But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.” But we who have believed are not afraid to look before God; rather, as the divine Paul himself says again, “With unveiled face we behold the glory of the Lord as in a mirror.” So Moses turns away his face. God then tells him that he must go with the elders of the sons of Israel to the senseless Pharaoh and make it clear that God has summoned the people of Israel to sacrifice to him in the wilderness. He adds that they will have to plunder the Egyptians, each woman receiving from her neighbor and from the woman lodging with her articles of silver and gold, and clothing. Then, it says, “Moses answered and said: But if they do not believe me or listen to my voice (for they will say, ‘God has not appeared to you’), what shall I say to them? And the Lord said to him: What is that in your hand? He said: A rod. And he said: Throw it on the ground. And he threw it on the ground, and it became a serpent, and Moses fled from it. And the Lord said to him: Stretch out your hand and take hold of its tail. So he stretched out his hand and took hold of the tail, and it became a rod in his hand. This is so that they may believe you that the Lord, the God of your fathers, has appeared to you, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.” For Moses was afraid that the sons of Israel might think him a lover of lies and a teller of idle tales. He would be claiming that the God of all had appeared to him and had told him to order them to break away resolutely, at last, from the greed of the Egyptians. That is why God commanded him to work wonders and to do things beyond human nature, and changed the rod into a serpent, so that Moses would be recognized not as someone who had truly come on his own initiative, but as the bearer of decrees from above, from God. The true sign, in which all of us have believed, is the Word's descent into our condition, and this is signified by the rod that fell to the ground. How, and in what way, I shall again try to explain as best I can.

The divinely inspired Scripture likens the Word who sprang from God to a rod, because all things are supported by him. “By the word of the Lord,” it says, “the heavens were made firm.” And again: “The Lord upholds the righteous.” We have indeed been brought under the Father through the Son, and the Son himself shows this to be true when he says: “And I will make them pass under my rod.” In another sense, too, the rod is a symbol of kingship, and the God and Father of all reigns through the Son. The rod of Aaron that budded in the holy of holies might signify him. He is the rod from the root of Jesse, and the rod that comforts all of us spiritually and holds believers up so that they stand firm, as is sung in the Psalms to the God and Father of all: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me.” The rod, then, is the Son. But as long as he was, so to speak, in the hand of the Father and in the heights of the Godhead, not yet having become like us, we wretched ones went on living without God in the world. We went astray, worshiping the creation, and we lay subject to the greed of unclean spirits. But then he all but left the heights of his own glory and, as it were, the hand of the Father (I speak rather corporeally here, for the sake of what the contemplation can teach us). He came down from heaven to earth and became like us, conformed to those on earth, who are full of wickedness. The Son himself called them wicked when he said: “If you then, who are wicked, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” So we say that he was, in a manner of speaking, also changed into a serpent, but only because of his likeness to us and his coming to share our form. For man is wicked when compared with the gentleness of God. So the rod changed into a serpent. The Only-begotten became man and was reckoned among the lawless. He was counted with us as wicked, though by nature he is good, or rather is goodness itself. We received the Only-begotten when he had become like us, but the multitudes of the Jews did not love him; they ran away from him, as it were. This will be made clear from the sacred Scriptures, for Moses fled from its face. Because they thought him wicked, they did not dare to believe, but instead killed him and crucified him with wicked men. Yet in due time Christ will be laid hold of, and it will be recognized that he is in no way wicked, but is rather the spiritual support and strength of those who believe. This we shall learn from the event itself. For God turns Moses back as he flees, and when Moses took hold of the serpent, it became a rod in his hand. So to those who do not know him, he seems to be wicked because of his likeness to us; but if anyone takes hold of him through faith, he finds a rod and a support. The divine sign of the rod, then, was worthy enough and able to persuade the people of Israel, or rather everyone on earth, that God had visited them. But those who are gravely ill are hard to persuade, and those who have lost hope of escaping the burdens hanging over them are hard to lead, so more wonders were needed. Such people are brought to docility only with difficulty.

Again God spoke, evidently to the holy Moses: “Put your hand into your bosom. And he put his hand into his bosom, and his hand became leprous, like snow. And he said again: Put your hand into your bosom. And he put his hand into his bosom and brought his hand out of his bosom, and it was restored again to the color of his flesh.” Now the power to rid someone of leprosy is surely, above all, something worthy of God. Diseases that have become so savage that they will not yield even to the skill of physicians would presumably need, in their case, the power from above alone. Nothing can resist that power; for it every path is open and every task easy. And leprosy is an incurable disease. By healing Moses' leprous hand, the God of all let it be understood that what men despair of and what is impossible for us is possible with him, and that nothing at all is too steep for him. From this those who had been called, that is, those of Israel's blood, would know that their misfortune might be hard to escape, yoked as they were to the wickedness of the Egyptians and suffering, as it were, an extreme disease, namely slavery under them. Yet the physician is resourceful. He knows how to remove with ease even diseases that are very hard to get rid of, and he is able to do it, without toil and in no great length of time. For as soon as Moses put his hand into his bosom, it was freed from the disease. But I think the matter also hinted at something else for us. During the long years they spent in Egypt, the people of Israel had broken away from the virtue that had been familiar to them from of old and from their fathers. They had settled instead into the local customs and sunk very deep into decline. As the prophet says, they worshiped the creation rather than the Creator. They slid into every kind of uncleanness and came to have a mind all but dead and grown cold. For leprosy is a sign of uncleanness and deadness. Through the miracle God revealed this mystery: if he received them and, as it were, took them into his bosom again, their uncleanness would not be hard to drive away, and they would very easily shake off the defilement of spiritual deadness. So much, then, for this point. Now I shall try to explain how the mystery of Christ was again foreshadowed, as it were, in Moses' hand made leprous and then cleansed. Our divine evangelist John testifies very well that “all things came into being through the Son, and without him not one thing came into being.” And since the Father is active in everything through him, the divinely inspired Scripture calls the Son the Father's hand, his arm and his right hand. Thus the divine Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” For the wretched Jews have remained hard and unbridled, gravely sick with disobedience. David said that the heavens themselves were made firm by the word of the Lord, while through the voice of the prophets the God and Father declared: “With my hand I made the heaven firm.” He addressed others as well: “For I am your God, who strengthened you and helped you and kept you safe with my righteous right hand.” So it is the custom of the divinely inspired Scripture to call the Son a hand. See, then, how Moses' hand is hidden in his bosom, then brought out and seen to be leprous, then brought back into his bosom again and at once freed from the affliction. If we consider the mystery and the manner of the incarnation, and strive to perceive where it stands and how, we shall find that something like this took place. The Son was, in a certain way, in the bosom of the God and Father, and through him the Father made all things. He is the lofty arm, the all-powerful hand, the wondrous right hand. But when he went out, in a certain way, into his own place, he became man and took on our infirmities, as the prophet says, and so he came to be suspected and considered unclean. For human nature is unclean before God, if what the prophet Isaiah says is true: “All our righteousness is like the rag of a menstruating woman.” So, as far as human nature is concerned, he who is all-pure and dwells in unapproachable light came to be reputed unclean. That is the error the wretched Jews fell into. They called him a drunkard and a Samaritan, and said he was born of fornication, and on top of all this a sinner. For they said to the man born blind who had been healed: “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.” But I do not think they would ever have sunk to such folly as to say such a thing and open an unguarded mouth against him, if they had known that he was God by nature. As man he came to be reputed unclean. But when he had carried out his most skillful plan of salvation on our behalf, he finally ascended to the Father and came to be in his bosom. Then indeed he shook off even the appearance of having shared our deadness and uncleanness. He is glorified as God; he is glorified by all as Lord, as Holy of holies, as the one who illumines the creation and the spirits of men, and who himself supplies to those on earth the power to crush everything that can defile. The Son accepted human conditions for our sake as part of the plan of salvation. He came to be under the law and was reckoned among the lawless, but he returned again to the honor and glory that were innate to him and were his from the beginning. He himself makes this certain when he says to the Father in heaven: “Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.” Do you see that he is eager to be rid of what had come in between? He did not undertake the plan of salvation in the flesh unwillingly, yet he was hastening toward the glory of the Godhead and the dignity that surpasses all things. That is why the blessed Paul too says: “Even though we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we know him so no longer.” For he came back to life from the dead and ascended to the Father with the flesh. But, Paul says, we no longer know him according to the flesh, that is, as still subject to the passions of the flesh. I mean the natural and blameless passions. Before the precious cross he is said to have been hungry, to have grown weary from his journey and to have been deeply grieved, and even to have endured death on the wood for our sake. But now we do not know him as subject to these things. For having died once, he dies no more. Christ is incorruptible, life by nature and the giver of life, since he came forth from the life of the Father.

After the wonder worked so marvelously with the leprous hand, God makes the people more steadfast with a third sign. For he said again: “If they do not believe you because of these two signs, nor listen to your voice, you shall take some of the water of the river and pour it out on the dry ground; and the water that you take from the river will become blood on the dry ground.” Observe again how the disobedience of the Jews was foreknown. They are always hesitant, slow to understand and hard to bring over to the truth. They disbelieved the manner of the incarnation and the wonders worked in the meantime. Only late, and with difficulty, did they believe at the last sign. Perhaps not all of them did, but at least the remnant chosen by grace, as the blessed Paul writes. And what is the last sign? Christ's death on the wood, and his return to life, which was joined to that death and followed close upon it. That the Savior's death, and the great and admirable mystery of the resurrection from the dead, was given as a sign to the sons of Israel will be made clear from the Savior's own words. For once, after he had displayed countless signs, the Pharisees came to him and said mockingly: “Teacher, we want to see a sign from you.” He said to them: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights.” It is easy to see that the death of Emmanuel won many, not only from among the Jews but from among the Gentiles as well. For he said again, at one time, “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself,” and at another, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” Do you see how he showed us the fruit of his death through a vivid illustration? According to the Savior's words, then, this was the last sign for us. On it rests the faith not only of those from Israel but also, as I said, of those from the other multitude, I mean the Gentiles. In what way, then, was this very thing signified? “You shall take,” it says, “some of the water of the river and pour it out on the dry ground; and the water that you take from the river will become blood on the dry ground.” Water is a type, or sign, of life. It is truly necessary for life and most needful for those on earth. So the Son, who is truly life, sprang forth as if from a river: from the Father who gives life to all things. Just as he is light from light, so he is life from life. Moses was taught that the Son did not come into existence outside the God and Father but is from him by nature, and we are taught it no less. For “you shall take,” it says, “some of the water of the river.” Then Moses was commanded to pour it out on the ground. In a riddle, this is the mystery of the incarnation. The Only-begotten, who is life and was begotten as if flowing forth from the life of the God and Father, was in a certain way mingled with the humanity that comes from the earth, just as water mingles with the ground. For all the fullness of the Godhead dwelt in Christ bodily. He was, so to speak, united with human nature in a way that no one could conceive or express. But the water was changed into blood. The one who is life by nature, that is, the Word from God the Father, entered into union with flesh, or rather with complete humanity, our own nature, as part of the plan of salvation. Because of that union he came to be regarded as having endured death itself as well. For we say that he died for us, not suffering this in his own nature (for, being life, he could in no way die), but by making the death of his own flesh his own. Observe that if Moses had not poured the water out on the ground, it would not have been changed into blood, which is a clear sign of death. For the Word from God, considered apart from the flesh, is life and gives life. But once he dwelt in the flesh, then indeed they say that he died, in his humanity. This, then, is the extraordinary and conspicuous sign that drew the remnant of Israel into faith like a net, while the multitude of the Gentiles too was called in along with them. Who would not be won over to obedience, seeing that death, once terrible and dreadful for those on earth to meet, has lost its strength, that corruption has been abolished, and that human nature has been raised to the hope of endless life? Just as we died together with Adam, so we have been raised together with Christ, and the divine Paul will bear witness, writing to us: “For as in Adam we all die, so also in Christ we shall all be made alive.” For he purchased us with his own blood and gave his own life as the ransom for the life of all.

But even after such awe-inspiring wonders had been performed, Moses is distraught; he is overcome by fear and has not yet found the courage to undertake the mission. When God commanded that he must go to Pharaoh and plainly announce that he should let Israel go "to sacrifice to me in the wilderness," he shuddered greatly at the task. He objected openly that he was admittedly a man of few words and had a defective tongue: "For I have not been eloquent, neither yesterday nor the day before, nor since you began to speak to your servant; I am weak of voice and slow of tongue." He plainly insisted that he was not capable of delivering them from the yoke of slavery, and said: "I beg you, Lord, appoint someone else who is able, whom you will send." And when God promised to grant him a tongue and to open wide his mouth, saying that he himself is the giver of wisdom and speech, Moses drew out his refusal still further, saying that someone else who was able ought to be appointed. In this, then, he offends God. "And the Lord," it says, "was angered with wrath against Moses, and said: Is not Aaron your brother the Levite here? I know that he will speak for you." And to this he adds: "He will be your mouth, and you will be for him in the things pertaining to God." Do you see how the slowness of speech of the law was sketched in outline long ago, as in the divine Moses? For the law is not adequate to proclaim the divine oracles, nor is it supremely eloquent or fluent so as to set out exact knowledge of what is beneficial, as Christ is—the true Levite, of whom Aaron was a type. For the law given through Moses barely brings us to the first principles of the oracles of God; it is an elementary introduction for infants, a tutor of the foolish, scarcely conveying to us, through type and shadow, a very dim knowledge of what we ought to do. But the one who is truly most capable, our great high priest, mighty for the mission—that is, Christ—has shown us the truth set free from shadows. For he is not slow or hesitant of tongue, or short of words as Moses was, but exceedingly eloquent, above all because he is the Word of wisdom of God the Father. And consider how the law is not able to deliver from slavery those who toil under the spiritual Pharaoh, that is, Satan; nor could the divine Moses have benefited the earth at all, although he won the most brilliant glory for his virtues, had Christ not been with him and helping him. You may learn that this is so, and that we have spoken truly, from the fact that Aaron was joined to him. Moses converses, but Aaron makes the word clear. For unless the law is understood spiritually, with Christ revealing to us what is in it, its meaning will be dark and obscure to those who hear it. And indeed the Jews, not having the one who interprets the writings of Moses, that is, Christ, have remained ignorant. That is why the divine Paul said: "For to this very day the same veil remains unlifted at the reading of the old covenant, because only in Christ is it done away with. Indeed, to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart. But whenever one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." Rightly, then, did the God of all say to Moses, the revealer of sacred things, concerning Aaron: "He will speak for you, and he will be your mouth, and you will be for him in the things pertaining to God." Of course, we do not say that Moses is closer and nearer to God than Emmanuel is. For the one is Son, and from God the Father by nature, while the other is among us, counted among the household servants, even if he is called a true one. Yet in a certain sense Moses seems to have been for him "the things pertaining to God." For Christ, as a man, was placed under the law and kept the ordinances of Moses. He was circumcised on the eighth day, and he paid the contribution of the two drachmas, although by nature he was a free Son. He also ate the Passover, although again he himself was the true Lamb who takes away the sin of the world. In this way, then, Moses is said to have been for him "the things pertaining to God." And that Israel would refuse to believe even the divine signs worked through Christ, Moses himself would show, since he did not give his faith even to the wonders themselves. Therefore we shall assign the role of Moses to those of Israel, since they were called through him and were trained by the laws given through him. So then, that the law is not sufficient for redemption, but that the precious blood of Christ is enough for us for this (for through it alone death has been conquered), would become clear, and very easily, from what follows as well.

For the divine Moses sets out from the land of the Midianites, taking his wife and children, and at length came to Egypt, faithfully carrying out what God had commanded. And when he was now not far from the land of the Egyptians, the God of all said to him: "As you go and return to Egypt, see that you perform before Pharaoh all the wonders I have put in your hands." And after other words: "And you shall say to Pharaoh: Thus says the Lord: Israel is my firstborn son. I said to you: Send my people away, so that they may serve me. But you were not willing to send them away; see then, I will kill your firstborn son." "And it came to pass," it says, "on the way, at the lodging place, that an angel of the Lord met him and sought to kill him. And Zipporah took a stone and circumcised the foreskin of her son, and fell at his feet and said: The blood of my child's circumcision has stopped. And he went away from her, because she said: The blood of my child's circumcision has stopped." For an angel in a form like ours sprang upon him and attempted to kill him, but was only just appeased when Zipporah circumcised her son—I mean Gershom, who was also the firstborn, and whose name means "sojourner." Whom the destroyer was trying to kill, the sacred Scripture has not clearly indicated; perhaps it was Moses, and by this circumcision of the child the destroyer was driven off against his will. Here again the type makes plain that death has been conquered by the blood of Christ. And the holy multitude of the fathers has been saved—or rather the whole race from the beginning, before him. For he died for all, and the death of all has been undone in him. For it is not by the blood of prophets but by the blood of Christ, who came last of all, that we escape the destroyer together with him. "For to this end," it says, "Christ died and lived, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living." And if it should be said that the destroyer sprang upon Gershom, and not rather upon blessed Moses, you will understand this once again: it is not through circumcision according to the law—that is, the fleshly and perceptible kind—that death has been driven off, but through the circumcision that is in Christ, through the Spirit, which he has worked in the firstborn and new people, a sojourner on earth but enrolled once more as a citizen of the city above, the heavenly one. This is the circumcision which the spiritual Zipporah—that is, the Church, which comes from Midian and from the nations—performed with a stone. And the stone too would be a type of the Spirit, because of its all-powerful and unbreakable nature, and indeed because it comes from rock. For the Spirit is Christ's, and the Rock is Christ, as the wise Paul also writes. One should also know that Joshua, who came after Moses long ago, circumcised the sons of Israel with knives of stone, signifying to us in a figure the circumcision not made with hands through Christ, by which death too is defeated. This is the spiritual circumcision of wickedness, the putting away of vice and pleasures. For concerning circumcision of the flesh, the divine Paul writes to us: "Circumcision is nothing." And a wise and holy word has cried out to us: "Be circumcised in Christ," through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

“Enter through the narrow gate,” Christ called out to his friends. By the narrow gate and the constricted entrance he means, I think, the endurance of suffering and a patience worthy of all praise. Through these, those who have chosen to set their minds on things above may win high esteem in rich measure, and be made radiant by exercises that train them in courage and virtue. Distinguishing oneself in battle bears witness to a soldier's valour. In the same way, the ability to bear well the toils that come from being tested shows that a man is strong and noble, strong, I mean, in his power to achieve the virtue that pleases God, and it makes him illustrious, conspicuous and full of every praise. Indeed the Saviour's disciple has given full assurance that such a man will be admired in every way and on every count, saying: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been approved he will receive the crown of life.” And those who have reached such strength and won such conspicuous glory say: “You have tested us, O God; you have refined us by fire as silver is refined. You laid afflictions on our back; you set men over our heads. We went through fire and water, and you tested us to bring us to refreshment.” For toil ends in delight, and for those who contend nobly afflictions widen the straight road. God, who knows hidden things, knows all things before they come to be (for all things are naked and laid bare before him). Yet he waits for the outcome of events and for the steadfastness of those who are tested from time to time. He wants them to appear worthy of rewards not only to himself, by foreknowledge, but still more to be applauded by angels and men as people who have excelled and whose virtue has been attested by their very deeds. That is why blessed Paul says of himself and the other saints, as of those who had contended very well and won, that they became “a spectacle to the world, both to angels and to men.” So Israel is tested in many ways. Even if it is shown to be still sick with feebleness, God is thereby admired for his exceedingly great gentleness in bearing with those who offend, and the mystery is sketched out for us all the more in each of the events.

Just now we went through the account of the quail and the manna, and showed Israel to be gravely sick with weakness and love of pleasure. But look: here it is again, not long afterwards, seen provoking God. For again it is written: “And the whole congregation of the children of Israel set out from the wilderness of Sin, by their encampments, at the word of the Lord, and they encamped at Rephidim; and there was no water for the people to drink. And the people reviled Moses, saying, ‘Give us water, that we may drink.’ And Moses said to them, ‘Why do you revile me? And why do you test the Lord?’ And the people thirsted there for water, and the people murmured against Moses, saying, ‘Why is it that you brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?’ And Moses cried out to the Lord, saying, ‘What shall I do with this people? A little more and they will stone me.’ And the Lord said to Moses, ‘Go on ahead of this people. Take with you some of the elders of the people, and take in your hand the rod with which you struck the river, and go. Behold, I stand there before you come, on the rock in Horeb. And you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and my people shall drink.’ And Moses did so before the children of Israel. And he called the name of that place Temptation and Reviling, because of the reviling of the children of Israel, and because they tested the Lord, saying, ‘Is the Lord among us or not?’”

This is what the divine oracle told us in Exodus. But in Numbers it sets out a fuller narrative, as it were, in detail, and I think it necessary to bring this forward too. By examining each point correctly and with precision, we may gain a sufficient knowledge of what happened long ago in type, and, besides this, the beauty of spiritual contemplation. It is written, then: “And the children of Israel, the whole congregation, came into the wilderness of Zin in the first month, and the people stayed in Kadesh; and Miriam died there and was buried there. And there was no water for the congregation, and they gathered together against Moses and Aaron. And the people reviled Moses, saying, ‘Would that we had perished when our brothers perished before the Lord! Why have you brought the congregation of the Lord into this wilderness, to kill us and our children? And why is it that you brought us up out of Egypt to come into this evil place? It is a place where there is no sowing, no figs, no vines, no pomegranates, nor is there water to drink.’ And Moses and Aaron went from the presence of the congregation to the door of the tent of witness, and they fell on their faces, and the glory of the Lord appeared to them. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Take the rod, and assemble the congregation, you and Aaron your brother, and speak to the rock before their eyes, and it will give forth its waters; you shall bring water out of the rock for them, and give drink to the congregation and their livestock.’ And Moses took the rod that was before the Lord, as the Lord had commanded, and Moses and Aaron assembled the congregation in front of the rock. And he said to them, ‘Hear me, you disobedient ones: shall we bring water out of this rock for you?’ And Moses lifted up his hand and struck the rock with the rod twice; and much water came out, and the congregation drank, and their livestock. And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron, ‘Because you did not believe so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this congregation into the land that I have given them.’ This is the water of contradiction, because the children of Israel reviled before the Lord, and he was sanctified among them.”

They were journeying through dry country and passing across a great stretch of thirsty land, and they were worn out by the toils of the march. So if even some small thing of the kind that usually causes distress occurred, they raised an intolerable outcry against Moses and Aaron. They had witnessed a great many admirable divine signs, and had learned by experience how surpassing the divine power is. Yet they still feared that it might somehow fail in the task, I mean, of supplying what they needed to live, providing them with food from every quarter and furnishing them with water. They are overcome by faintheartedness, for they have a childish and unmanly mind. If they meet with even some small thing that naturally causes vexation, they at once fall upon their guide and cry out impiously against him because he had ever become their mediator and they had been called to freedom through him. They count as blessed those who perished in the earlier fits of faintheartedness. Those men had been seized by desire for the meat of Egypt; then, having eaten the deadly quail, they were condemned to death. That is why they say: “Would that we had died when our brothers perished before the Lord! And why have you brought us up into this wilderness, to kill us and our livestock?” What cowardice! How unable to bear suffering their temper was, how very ready their mind to sink into despondency! After only a little thirst, the hardships of Egypt now seemed better to them than what came from God. The yoke of slavery, once bitter, was now somehow sweet. Pharaoh was no longer hard to bear, harsh as he was. The clay was not hateful, nor the savagery of the taskmasters; now everything was pleasant. The feebleness of their understanding persuades them to sink to such a depth of folly. Hear also, if you will, their charges against Moses' mediation: “Why is it,” they say, “that you brought us out of Egypt to come into this evil place? It is a place where there is no sowing, no figs, no vines, no pomegranates, nor is there water to drink.” See how Israel is carried away into unmanliness. It leans without restraint toward passing pleasures and lays eager claim to worldly delights. It welcomes a full belly but spurns hope, and has no hold on the land promised to the fathers. It does not realize that, always and in every way, toils come before the choicest gifts, for no one could win the finest rewards without sweat. Israel, then, does not know how to excel, or how to stand up vigorously against the assaults of the passions. That achievement was not kept for those under the law; rather, it was prepared beforehand for those in Christ.

It would have been reasonable for God in his indignation not to grant them even a supply of water. Yet even though they had sunk to such perversity, he wanted them to be helped toward faith by still other miracles, so Moses is commanded to strike the rock with the rod. But God knew that Moses too would grow a little fainthearted at the uprisings of the people and would falter in his faith. That is why he says in Exodus: “Take with you some of the elders of the people, and take in your hand the rod with which you struck the river, and go. Behold, I stand there before you come, on the rock in Horeb; and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and let my people drink.” And in Numbers: “Take the rod, and assemble the congregation, you and Aaron your brother. And speak to the rock before their eyes, and it will give its waters to them. And you shall bring water out of the rock for them, and give drink to the congregation.” Notice how, to confirm him in faith, he brings to mind the wonder worked in Egypt, saying: “Take in your hand the rod with which you struck the river.” It is as if he said: “The rod that changed a great river into blood, by the ineffable power of God who accomplishes such things, will very easily bring water out of the rock as well.” Then he strengthens him in another way, adding: “Behold, I stand there.” “You will not be alone,” he says, “nor will you be the one who performs the miracle. Rather, I will make the rock the mother of many streams. I will prepare the miracle beforehand and wait for your service. Speak to the rock, and I myself will be the power of your words.” Such words ought to have given him courage, yet Moses faltered. For he said: “Hear me, you disobedient ones: shall we bring water out of this rock for you?” Then he strikes the sheer rock twice with the rod, as though none of what was expected would happen, even if the rock were struck. He struck it twice, although in Egypt he had transformed the waters into blood by stretching out [?] the rod only once. Nevertheless God gave the stream, though he was greatly provoked by all this, so that the suspicions of the foolish might not charge him with any appearance of weakness. But Moses is rebuked, it says: “You yourselves shall not bring this congregation into this land which I have given them, because you did not believe so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel.”

Come, then: let us once again reshape the form of the history into the mystery of Christ and say what is fitting. Let us track the divine Scriptures closely, and strive to set forth the force of their meanings in a way that suits the sacred writings well.

So then, when Miriam had died in the first month, the people thirsted. Then, at God's command, the divine Moses strikes the rock with the rod, while the elders of the people stand beside him, and Aaron too. They speak to the rock, and it pours out its stream abundantly and gives drink to the congregation and their livestock, as it is written. What, then, shall we say is hinted at in its turn by Miriam's death? How should she be understood at all? And what necessary meaning is served by saying that she died in the first month? We shall take Moses, then, to stand for the law and Aaron for the priesthood, and we shall assign the role of Miriam to the worship under the law. Indeed God said to rebellious Jerusalem through the voice of a holy prophet: “And I sent before your face Moses and Aaron and Miriam.” Do you see that he placed her with Moses and Aaron to lead Israel? For through the mediation of the all-wise Moses, and under the presidency of Aaron, that is, the dignity of the priesthood exercised through worship in types, Israel according to the flesh at that time gained the worship of God.

That the figure of Miriam is necessarily brought in alongside Moses and Aaron is also easy to see, without any effort, from the following. When Pharaoh perished in the Red Sea together with his bodyguards and was drowned with his whole army, Moses sang the thanksgiving and composed the hymn. And the women went out dancing, and Miriam took her tambourine, as it is written, perhaps sending up a deep and piercing sound to accompany the songs. In these types there was a subtle riddle of the true contemplation. The manner of the song and the sound of the tambourines would suggest that the law itself, that is, Moses, and together with him Miriam, that is, worship in shadows and types, proclaim the extraordinary and admirable power of God who rules all things. So one may assign the role of worship under the law to Miriam, just as one assigns that of the law to Moses and that of the priesthood to Aaron.

So when Miriam died in the first month, that is, at the beginning of the year according to the laws of the Hebrews, when the mystery of the holy Passover itself is celebrated, the people thirsted. In the first month of the year, which is also called the month of new things, the worship in shadows and types all but died. In a certain manner it was drawn in and taken out of the way. How, or in what manner? The only-begotten Word of God shone upon us in our own form, as in the month of new things. That is why he who speaks said himself: “I am here, like the seasons upon the mountains, and as in the month of new things.” In the same way he called the Church from the Gentiles, saying: “Arise, come, my companion, my fair one, my dove, for behold, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. The flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come.” For we have blossomed again in Christ to newness of life, and the time of his coming to dwell among us has been shown to be a spiritual spring for us, making human nature flower and bear fruit. It was then, then, when the worship in shadows had been drawn in and Miriam, as it were, had died, that the people thirsted and found themselves short of spiritual waters. But the stream of Christ burst forth abundantly. By this I mean, once again, the oracles given through him and the mystical instruction in spirit and in truth. The divine Paul understood this and writes: “For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.” He is likened to a rock because he cannot be broken or shaken, for the divine and supreme nature stands firmly founded in its own goods.

We must consider, then, in what way the water was given. The elders of the law were gathered together and Aaron stood by, and words were spoken to the rock; but Moses strikes it, and twice at that. The elders of the people and the priests ran together, and those instructed under the law, that is, Israel in the person of Moses, spoke against Christ. They accused him before Pilate and impiously cried out, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!” Then they also afflicted him with two blows. They killed the Author of life, and then, as if adding a second blow to the first, they wanted to persuade people that he had remained among the dead. For Christ came back to life, trampling down death. But when the soldiers whom they had posted to guard the tomb came and reported this, they ordered them to say, recklessly, that his disciples had stolen him away unnoticed, and so they slandered the august mystery of the resurrection itself. So the blow was struck twice. Yet the rock gave forth its stream abundantly, though Israel had behaved so outrageously toward him. It gave drink to the whole congregation and flooded the inhabited world with sacred and divine streams. For this is how he promised to bestow himself on us, saying through the prophet: “Behold, I turn toward them like a river of peace, and like a torrent overflowing with the glory of the nations.” And David sings somewhere: “The rushing streams of the river gladden the city of God.” And he says also to the Father and God in heaven: “How you have multiplied your mercy, O God! The sons of men shall hope under the shelter of your wings. They shall be drunk with the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight. For with you is the fountain of life.”

Notice that it was after their unbelief had gone before that Moses struck the rock with the rod. For Israel disobeyed and behaved outrageously toward Christ; Moses was rebuked, and Aaron with him. “For you shall not bring the children of Israel,” he says, “into the land that I have given them.” What will bring us into the inheritance of the saints and into the truer land of promise is not the law in types, nor the feebleness in shadows of the priesthood that belongs to it. For we shall not please God through blood, nor shall we be distinguished before God by earthly boasts. Rather, we shall walk toward the city above and come into the inheritance of the fathers, with Christ as our guide, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

Our Lord Jesus Christ spoke to the herds of the Jews, who would not accept the redemption that comes through faith but utterly despised the benefit of his oracles, and who supposed that the law given through Moses would be enough, and enough by itself, to bring them into intimacy with God. He said to them: "No one comes to the Father except through me." And again: "I am the way, and I am the door." In saying this he cannot be speaking falsely, since he is the truth. God the Father can be approached in no other way than through the one who alone is Son by nature; for whoever has come to know him will surely know also the Father from whom he has appeared. That is why he said to those who chose to disobey him while claiming to know the God of all: "If you knew me, you would know my Father also." Moses, of course, became a tutor to the people of older times, a mediator and leader, and the bearer of the laws from God, and indeed the best among the saints. For he heard God say plainly: "I know you above all, and you have found favor with me." Yet the law is not effective, nor is it able to bring about intimacy with God perfectly; but through the mediation of Christ we gain this too. For he is our peace, according to the Scriptures; in him alone is perfection in knowledge, and every good gift, and through himself he has all but brought us to the Father. That is why he said: "I desire that, just as I and you are one, so they too may be one in us." So Moses was indeed a mediator, but only as in type and shadows; the true mediator is Christ, to whom we are joined in relation, if indeed it is true that he came down into our condition and became man, so that we too might become partakers of his divine nature, being bound to God by participation in the Holy Spirit and by grace. We shall come to know these things once more by fixing the eye of our mind on the sacred Writings. For, it says, the Lord said to Moses: "Go down and charge the people, and sanctify them today and tomorrow. Let them wash their garments, and let them be ready for the third day. For on the third day the Lord will come down upon Mount Sinai before all the people. And you shall set bounds for the people round about, saying: Take heed to yourselves that no one goes up the mountain or touches any part of it. Whoever touches the mountain shall surely die. No hand shall touch him; he shall be stoned with stones or shot through with a dart. Whether beast or man, he shall not live. But when the voices and the trumpets and the cloud depart from the mountain, they shall go up on the mountain." For the Israelites, while they were in bondage in Egypt, had slipped into the false worship of the Egyptians. They bowed down to human inventions and offered their worship to things made of stone or of some other material, suffering from a pitiable delusion, and, as the prophet says, saying to the wood, "You are my God," and to the stone, "You gave birth to me." Since the Creator wished to bring them back from that ancient and profane false worship to the knowledge of the truth, it was necessary that they should not seem to be worshiping a God who does not exist, deceived by the words of Moses. That is why he profitably grants them a vision of God in types. For people tend to hold what they see with firmer faith. So he promises to come down openly, and before long. And he wanted them to know that those called to this honor, to become hearers and beholders of God, that is, of his divine and ineffable glory, must surely have the purity he loves best: it was fitting for them to be rid of fleshly uncleanness and, besides this, to be well clothed, so that the form of a festival might be rightly and fittingly represented. For it is truly a festival, and an admirable one, to be granted so glorious a vision.
