Further, he commands them to purify themselves, to keep away from intercourse with women, and to extend their continence to the third day. And he ordered them to wash their very garments. When this had been carried out, "it came to pass," it says, "on the third day, as morning came, that there were voices and lightnings and dark clouds on Mount Sinai. The sound of the trumpet resounded loudly, and all the people in the camp were terrified. And Moses led the people out of the camp to meet God, and they stood at the foot of the mountain. Mount Sinai was all smoking because God had come down upon it in fire; the smoke went up like the smoke of a furnace, and all the people were greatly amazed. And the sounds of the trumpet grew louder and louder. Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice." For the supreme and exalted nature, which is beyond everything created, is barely seen even by the mind. But since the vision of God had of necessity to be brought about for them through more visible things, the manner of the dispensation necessarily proceeded through many terrors. There were voices and lightnings bursting forth together, and a dark cloud gathered as well, so that creation too might be seen serving the God of all and bowing its neck to him as a slave. So Moses brought Israel out, shuddering with dread, and set them by the mountain, having perhaps first initiated them by telling them that they would suffer no harm but would meet a gentle and good Master. As the mountain blazed, smoke at once shot upward, and a shrill blast of the trumpet sounded: faint at first, then a second blast after it, and shortly advancing to a weighty and fuller sound. Then the God of all comes down in the form of fire upon Mount Sinai, "and the Lord called Moses to the top of the mountain. And Moses went up, and the Lord said to Moses: Go down and charge the people, lest they draw near to God to gaze, and a multitude of them fall. And let the priests who draw near to the Lord God be sanctified, lest the Lord destroy some of them. And Moses said to God: The people will not be able to come up to Mount Sinai, for you charged us, saying: Set bounds about the mountain and sanctify it. And the Lord said to him: Go, get down, and come up, you and Aaron with you. But let not the priests and the people try to come up to God, lest the Lord destroy some of them." He commands only the mediator—I mean Moses—to go up the mountain; he admits none of the others, and declares the mountain forbidden ground to them. And he threatened death if anyone chose to disregard this. He did not seek to be thought cruel or harsh or unapproachable—it would be quite foolish to think so—but wanted them to know and understand that being able to come near God, who is utterly exalted and of supreme preeminence, belongs to those of exceptional honor and glory. Besides, it would have been utterly absurd for people reared in the customs of the Egyptians, who knew that the precincts of unclean demons were not open to just anyone who wished, but that only chosen persons, after being purified, presumably according to their laws, were scarcely permitted to enter the innermost places, to think it a matter of no consequence to approach the God of all and to gaze upon such august and holy places, in which his divine and ineffable glory appeared. Here is another explanation, for I say that we ought to be eager to hunt down what leads to benefit by many paths. It was not right for the people and their leader to be honored equally by God—the one who was to act as tutor and those under him, the minister of the law and those for whom the laws were given. Rather, it was surely better and wiser, and most profitable to those who would be under him, that he should receive an exceptional glory. You will see from another passage too that what I say is true. For the Master of all said to Moses, the sacred initiator: "Behold, I come to you in a pillar of cloud, so that you may hear me speaking to you, and they may believe you forever." So everything was done in good order and according to the dispensation.

But, as I said, this was at the beginning a kind of shadow-sketch of the coming of our Saviour. He was to shine upon those on earth as on the third day, that is, in the last time, in which the Word became flesh and appeared to us, according to the Scriptures. It also proclaimed beforehand the cleansing that in due time would be set before believers by him and through him. For "Charge the people," it says, "and let them be ready for the third day. For on the third day the Lord will come down upon Mount Sinai." And Moses makes clear what the manner of the preparation is, saying: "For three days do not go near a woman." And he plainly insisted that they must wash even their garments. Now in saying that they must not lie with women but must keep away from intercourse with them, he signifies very well the mortification of the pleasures of the flesh. And in requiring that even their garments be cleansed, he sketches for us in some way the cleansing by water—and clearly also by the Spirit, which frees from defilements. For as the blessed Paul writes, those who have chosen to mind the things of Christ and walk in the Spirit have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires; they put to death their members that are on earth: fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire. And they make for themselves a bright garment, the grace from above, or even Emmanuel himself. For "put on," it says, "our Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh to gratify its desires." These things, then, Moses commanded the people of that time to do. But we too have heard the law itself proclaiming in riddles what pleases Christ: both cleansing by water and the mortification of fleshly desires. For the law commanded that those who were defiled be sprinkled with water for the purification of the flesh, and that a man with a discharge be sent out of the camp as unclean—disparaging, I think, the whole business of incontinence and showing the pleasure of the flesh to be profane. Accordingly, we who have been justified in Christ and sanctified through the Spirit have been commanded to hate even the garment defiled by the flesh. So the law prepares the way and shows in advance the beauty of the gifts given through Christ, though still in crude types. Let us look closely, if you please, at the very manner of the appearing. "It came to pass," it says, "on the third day, as morning came, that there were voices and lightnings and a dark cloud on Mount Sinai. The sound of a trumpet resounded loudly." For, as I said, the Only-begotten came and descended from heaven, not in the first time, not at the beginning of this age, nor in the second and intermediate time, but as in the third and last, and as at dawn and at the beginning of day—that is, when the spiritual mist that was in us had already been driven away, and the night, as it were, was passing, and the darkness had vanished. For the one who through deceit and greed was supposed to be the god of this age darkened the whole earth spiritually, carrying it away into the error of many gods and into every kind of uncleanness. But the God and Lord of all, that is, Christ, appeared to us and showed us a truly longed-for day, which the inspired David also mentioned when he said: "This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it." And the most wise Paul has written somewhere that "the night is far spent, and the day is at hand," and again: "We are not of the night or of darkness, but sons of light and sons of the day." So the Only-begotten came down at dawn, as on the third day. And there were lightnings on Mount Sinai, and a dark cloud. The lightning is a type of the divine light and the spiritual radiance—that is, the radiance in the Spirit—which through Christ illumines all things and runs through everything under heaven. That is how the prophet cried out to Christ, the God and Saviour of all: "Your lightning appeared to the world." We certainly do not say that he was speaking of the lightning that comes with rain; rather, as I said just now, he meant to signify by the name of lightning the shining forth of the spiritual light. And the darkness might suggest that the mystery of Christ is truly hard to discern. Indeed, the blessed David himself, understanding it in this way, I think, cried out beforehand: "He made darkness his hiding place; round about him was his tent, dark water in the clouds of the air. From the brightness before him the clouds passed." For the mystery of Christ is so hidden that it needs initiation from above and revelation from God. Peter, at any rate, when he rightly understood God the Word who had appeared in the flesh, who is truly Son, heard: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." And Paul too affirmed that the mystery was made known to him by revelation from God. So the darkness indicates the obscurity of this knowledge. And the trumpet sounded loudly, showing how resonant the gospel oracles are. Indeed, God said somewhere through the voice of the prophets to the people of the Jews: "I have set watchmen over you. Listen to the sound of the trumpet. But they said: We will not listen. Therefore the nations have heard, and those who shepherd the flocks among them. Hear, O earth: Behold, I am bringing evils upon this people, the fruit of their turning away, because they did not heed my word and they rejected my law." For the trumpet sounded among them through the watchmen sent by God, that is, the holy apostles, for they were appointed as watchmen over us. But they said, "We will not listen." Therefore the nations heard. And we shall find the holy disciples themselves saying openly to the people of the Jews: "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it away and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. For so the Lord has commanded us." The blessed Isaiah also likens to a trumpet the clear voice of Christ's preaching, when he speaks of the time of his coming: "And it shall be in that day that they will blow the great trumpet." The law too was a trumpet, but it was weak-voiced and slow of tongue. That is why Moses too was so, because the law sounded, and scarcely, in Judea alone, where God was known. But the great trumpet is Christ, or the preaching that comes through him, which resounds through everything under heaven. For he said: "This gospel will be preached in all the world, as a testimony to all the nations." And the outcome of events has borne witness that this saying is true, for no one has been left without hearing of the glory of our Saviour. "And Moses," it says, "led the people out of the camp to meet God, and they stood by Mount Sinai." See the tutelage of Moses: it brings them to God. For it tutors them toward Christ, and sets those who are for a time under its tutelage at the mountain, but it does not bring them up onto it. By "mountain" here you should understand the transcendent and surpassing knowledge of the mystery of Christ. For it is very lofty, and least accessible to those under the law, but more fitting for us who have been sanctified in the Spirit. As the Saviour himself said: "To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given"—meaning the Jews. And in words addressed to the Father and God on our behalf, in the form of a prayer, he says: "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden all these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing in your sight." So Moses sets them by the mountain, but does not bring them up onto it; for, as I said just now, we gain what is perfect and lofty in wisdom and knowledge through Christ rather than through Moses. The one was a servant and a tutor; the other, as Lord of all, has appeared as the giver of perfect knowledge to us. For in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, as it is written. When God came down in the form of fire, then, there was smoke darting up as from a furnace, rolling very high and, I suppose, spreading over all the people. For the Word of God came down from heaven to us for our sake like a refiner's fire, as the prophet says. And he baptized us with the Holy Spirit and with fire—a spiritual fire that consumes the rubbish within us, melts away the filth of sin, and does not let the mind grow cold and drift toward unnatural pleasures. In this way we have been made fervent in spirit, and it is Christ who worked this very thing in us. That is why he said: "I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what more do I wish, if it is already kindled?" So it was in keeping with the dispensation that he appeared to the people of old in the form of fire—though not without smoke. Through this too we shall understand that those who fall into sloth and choose to despise his divine glory will have to weep and lament. For in smoke one cannot help shedding tears. And who could doubt that the God-hated and accursed will depart into the outer darkness? "There," it says, "will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." So the smoke suggested that the people we are speaking of shed bitter tears over their negligence. He added also that the sounds of the trumpet grew much louder as they went on, so that at first only a few could barely hear them, but later many, or rather the whole assembly. For the trumpet, most clear-voiced and sending forth a piercing sound, is the gospel preaching, as we have already said. At first, he means, it was heard in Judea alone; but as time went on, the inspired disciples went about through everything under heaven, preaching everywhere, so that the sacred trumpet sounded from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, or rather to the very ends of the earth, and from east to west. This, I think, is what is meant by the sounds of the trumpet growing louder. After this, God charges the blessed Moses to warn the people: "Lest," it says, "they draw near to God to gaze, and a multitude of them fall; and let the priests who draw near to the Lord God be sanctified, lest the Lord destroy some of them." See, then—see once more from these words—that it is impossible to draw near to God through the tutelage of Moses. For God does not accept those who choose to win approval still in types and shadows, which is what the things of Moses are; rather, he seeks in us the beauty of the truth. And Christ is the truth, through whom we have gained access and have come near to the Father, ascending, as it were, a mountain, to the knowledge of him. For having come to know the Son, we have come to know the Father through him and in him. So it is through him that we have gained access, not through Moses, that is, not through the law. And by commanding that even the priests be sanctified, he clearly showed beforehand that the priesthood under the law was not yet perfectly holy; otherwise he would not have commanded it to be sanctified, since that implies it still needed sanctification. But our high priest, Christ, is blameless and Holy of holies, and the guarantor of a better covenant, as Paul says. Therefore the first covenant has ceased, and there has been a change of the priesthood itself, since it did not possess blamelessness and supreme holiness. For it made no one perfect in conscience, but rather introduced teachings about washings and instructions about sprinklings for the purity of the flesh. The power of the priesthood under the law scarcely reaches even that far. So, since it did not possess perfect holiness, but was to be sanctified in due time in Christ, when the types were refashioned into truth, he commanded it to be sanctified. And by adding, "lest the Lord destroy some of them," he gave us to understand that death is the penalty for those who honor the priesthood under the law once the priesthood through Christ has been revealed in the world. Through Christ both the peoples and the very race that was of old august and holy are sanctified, and whatever has not been sanctified by him is utterly profane and unclean. That is why he said to the people of the Jews: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins." That the Israelites, having become unruly, were going to be sent away for a time, and would return to God in no other way than through Christ, is readily shown by God's words to the most excellent Moses, spoken in keeping with the dispensation: "Go, get down, and come up, you and Aaron with you." Do you see how Moses was sent away, and then does not return alone, but goes up again with Aaron accompanying him and hastening with him—Aaron, who was a type of Christ the great priest? For through him, as I said, the Father can be approached. Those under the law, that is, Israel, have been sent away for a time. But in the last times they will recognize the holy and innocent high priest, that is, Christ, and through him they will come to God the Father, ascending as if to a mountain, to the august and great mystery of the dispensation, by which Christ has saved us all. Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, unto the ages of ages. Amen.

Those of the blood of Israel were called to God through the law, with Moses at that time acting as mediator and minister. But, as the divinely inspired Paul writes, "The law made nothing perfect." The perfection of the law and of the prophets, however, is understood to be Christ, for all redemption comes through him. Since "there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved," in him too is all perfection through sanctification in the Spirit. Through him we have been called to the Father, and with him we shall go up to the city above. Indeed, he said plainly: "In my Father's house there are many dwelling places. If it were not so, I would have told you: I am going to prepare a place for you. And if I go to prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you may be also." For he soared up into heaven as the first portion and, as it were, the firstfruits of humanity. And no one could doubt that he will bring us up as well. He who does not know how to lie confirms this, and has held out the hope to those worthy to attain it. For in due time we shall be citizens of heaven, since Christ, as I said, has gone up before us. The most wise Paul will confirm that this is true, for he has written: "For Christ did not enter a holy place made with hands, a copy of the true one, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf." For he was, and is, and will be God by nature, with his own Father and in the sight of the one who begot him. But he appears on our behalf because he became man. He did this so that we too, who had been cast out of the Father's sight both through the transgression in Adam and through the sin that tyrannized over us, might come into his sight again through Christ, and be restored to what we were at the beginning, while the things that had crept in meanwhile pass away into nothing. So we have been called in Christ to the city above as well, and we are counted worthy of the watchful care of God the Father, and through him and in him we have been taught to worship God, the Maker and Father of all. The law also foretold this to us in a riddle. For the God of all came down in the form of fire on Mount Sinai and laid down for the Israelites the ordinances by which they might properly enter on the first steps of righteousness. For the law is like a preliminary introduction to more perfect things, the elements and the foretelling of the teachings given through Christ. "And to Moses," it says, "he said: Come up to God, you and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, and they shall worship the Lord from afar. Moses alone shall draw near to God, but they shall not draw near, and the people shall not go up with them." When the all-wise Moses had reported these things, all the people answered with a loud voice, saying: "All the words that the Lord has spoken we will do, and we will listen." And what came after this? "Moses," it says, "wrote down all the words of the Lord. And rising early in the morning, Moses built an altar at the foot of the mountain, and twelve stones for the twelve tribes of Israel. He sent the young men of the sons of Israel, and they offered whole burnt offerings and sacrificed calves to the Lord God as a sacrifice of deliverance. Moses took half of the blood and poured it into the bowl, and half of the blood he poured against the altar. And taking the book of the covenant, he read it in the hearing of the people, and they said: All that the Lord has spoken we will do, and we will listen. Then Moses took the blood and sprinkled it on the people, and said: Behold the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you concerning all these words." When the sacrifice had been completed and all the people had been sprinkled with the blood of the covenant, "Moses went up," it says, "with Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of the people of Israel, and they saw the place where the God of Israel stood. Under his feet was something like a work of sapphire brick, like the very form of the firmament of heaven in its clearness. And of the chosen ones of Israel not one was missing. And they were seen in the place of God, and they ate and drank." Come, then, come, let us say what is fitting about each of the passages that have been read. Let us begin straight away with the meaning of what lies before us, and see what Christ has done for us, drawn out as if on a tablet. In the divinely inspired Scripture, both the Church above, the Church in the heavens, that is, heaven itself, and the Church on earth, which is made in the likeness of the one above, are called a hill and a mountain, because of the lofty and elevated virtue of those who dwell in them. For the mind of the saints is not low or downcast. It rises above the more earthly way of thinking and above fleshly desires, and soars instead on high. And what was said through the voice of David is true: "For the mighty gods of the earth have been greatly exalted." And the Psalmist will again confirm that those who have chosen to live in this way, and have climbed at last to virtue, should fittingly lodge in the dwelling places above. He says: "Who shall go up the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? One who has innocent hands and a pure heart, who has not given his soul to vanity and has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor. He has not lent his money at interest and has not taken bribes against the innocent. He shall receive a blessing from the Lord and mercy from God his Savior. This is the generation of those who seek the face of the God of Jacob."

Heaven, then, which is the Church of the firstborn, is a mountain that the saints can climb, but the profane and unholy cannot set foot on it. So the God of all commanded Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel to go up the mountain. And he said: "They shall worship the Lord from afar. Moses alone shall draw near to God, but they shall not draw near, and the people shall not go up with them." Now the sons born of Aaron signify the priestly race to us, and the elders signify those chosen for their merit. Aaron, in turn, represents Christ himself for us, the holy and guileless high priest. Through him we have received the birth that comes through Spirit and water, and we are called "a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation." So in due time we, the chosen and holy, shall go up to the city above, with Christ the great priest present with us and leading us. For our sake he became like us, and he worships along with us, although God is his Father by nature. Moses draws near, but the Son is with us who are far off. For before the mystery of the incarnate economy came about, Moses was closer to God, as the mediator who laid down the law. But since the Son came to be with us, though he is God by nature and Lord of all, he does not disdain our measure, and in accordance with the economy he consents to be regarded as standing even behind Moses. Indeed, he came to be with us under the same law, although as God he is the lawgiver. That he came under the law is easy to see: he was circumcised on the eighth day. He also paid the two-drachma tax, although as the Son he was free by nature. The sacred Scripture itself will suffice, for it says that Emmanuel was born under the law. And you will understand from other passages too that, because of his humanity and because he came under the law like us, he is regarded as placed second to Moses. For the God of all commanded the most excellent Moses to release Israel from unbearable bondage by saying to Pharaoh: "The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, has summoned us." But Moses, standing for the law, confesses that he is powerless to redeem. Then, as Moses shrinks back and hesitates, God joins to him the divinely inspired Aaron, as a type of Christ, who is all-powerful and through whom all redemption comes. For he said to Moses: "See, I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet. You shall tell him all that I command you, and Aaron your brother shall speak to Pharaoh." You see that Aaron again acts as mediator, while Moses plays the part of the lawgiver. This is why blessed Paul also ascribes the law itself to Moses, although it was [?] by God. For he writes: "Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses." We, then, the holy and chosen, go up to the dwelling places above as up a mountain, while the rest of the multitude stays below. For "the people," it says, "shall not go up with them"; for, as the Savior says, "Many are called, but few are chosen." But we do not go up without Christ. At that time Aaron was with those who worshiped and was counted among those still far off. In the same way Christ is far off with us for our sake, so that we too, with him and through him, may be near the Father. For clearly everything was arranged on our account and for our sake. Just as he came to be with us among the dead, so that we might come to life with him and through him (for he came back to life, having trampled down the power of death), so he came to be with us at a distance, though he is near, so that we in turn might draw near to the Father with him and through him. And this has indeed been accomplished. For having become partakers of him through the Spirit, we have been united through him to God the Father, if indeed we are truly partakers of the divine nature, as the Scriptures say. The God of all commanded the holy and chosen to go up on high and climb the mountain together with Moses and Aaron. Those who have come to this glory and are eager to truly go up on high, so as to come near to God, must first be purified by the blood of Christ. He gave his own life in exchange for the life of all, and offered up the flesh he had taken on as a fragrant aroma. For he brought himself to God for us as a spotless victim and a spiritual whole burnt offering. All this the divinely inspired Moses again prefigured for us, guided by the illumination of the Spirit to the knowledge of things to come. For I think it was because he understood this that, before his own journey up and that of those who had been called, "he wrote down all the words of the Lord." What this in turn prefigured we shall say at once. Those who long for the journey up on high must, I think, have the law of God engraved on mind and heart, and then cry out to him as if from a lyre: "I have hidden your words in my heart, so that I may not sin against you." For just as it contributes greatly to life and brings salvation to remember the words of God at all times, so, I think, forgetting them tends to bring destruction. So the blessed Moses writes down all the words of the Lord. He himself proclaimed about them to those he was tutoring, or rather to us ourselves: "And you shall speak of them when you sit in your house and when you walk on the road, when you lie down and when you rise up." And rising early in the morning, he built an altar. Around it he set twelve stones for the twelve tribes of Israel. And he sent the young men of the sons of Israel, who, it says, offered whole burnt offerings and sacrificed calves to God as a sacrifice of deliverance. Now the altar is very clearly a type of the Church of Christ, which lies, so to speak, on the mountain. For we say that the other Church, the mother city of the firstborn, whose architect and builder is God, is on high, as on a mountain. So the altar represents the Church for us. And very fittingly Moses set the twelve stones around it for the twelve tribes of Israel. By this he all but declared in advance to those of the blood of Israel that the place most fitting for them is the Church of Christ, and that perhaps they will need to cry out: "I will go around your altar, O Lord, to hear the voice of praise." That the Father sent the Son as Savior and Redeemer to them above all and before the others, the Son himself will make clear when he says: "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." But since they slipped into outlandish folly and treated him outrageously, Christ of necessity passed over to the Gentiles. So Moses signified in advance that the altar of Christ was the place most fitting for them, as I said just now, by setting around it the twelve stones for the twelve tribes of Israel. From what took place one may also learn that those admired for courage (clearly a spiritual courage, according to God), those with a strong and vigorous mind, would in due time serve as priests of the mystery of Christ. For the young men were sent, and they brought the whole burnt offerings. We find that the holy apostles did this. They traveled, so to speak, over the whole earth, serving him as priests and bringing him whole burnt offerings, that is, those distinguished by blameless faith and thoroughly equipped by their earnest pursuit of virtue. For it is not, it is not, the work of a feeble understanding to be able to initiate others clearly into the mysteries, nor of a mind that is sick and weak and given to sliding down into worldly desires. It belongs to a mind so equipped and so youthfully vigorous that it can say: "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain." Such a person is a young man, and among the very bravest. It is fitting for him to consecrate the whole burnt offerings to God, along with spiritual sacrifices, to take up the spiritual priestly service, and to complete the sacrifice of salvation. This was also very well prefigured by the calves that were offered. For sometimes, because of its great strength, and because the bull is the highest of the clean animals, Christ is likened to a full-grown bull; at other times he is likened to a young calf. And you see again why: the Only-begotten became man and came under the yoke of servitude, if indeed it is true that he appeared in the form of a servant. But although, as far as the mystery of the flesh is concerned, he came to be with us under the yoke of servitude, he had no experience of servitude, because he was of the nature that is from above and free. This is why he is likened to a calf: he is both under the yoke and outside the yoke. For a calf has no experience of the yoke, even though its kind is by nature meant to bear the yoke. Again, even though he came under the law as under a yoke, he was free; for he was above the law, being lawgiver and God. And in the third place, if you like, he wore flesh taken from the earth, which, as Paul says, is sick within itself with the law of sin. As far as the nature of the flesh is concerned, he seems to have been placed under the yoke of sin too, but he had no experience of it. "For he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the just requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit." For this reason, then, Christ is fittingly called a calf, and also because he became a new creation; for he himself is the firstfruits of those called to this. And Moses showed that those who [?] and long to draw near to God had to be sanctified by the blood, when he sprinkled the whole people with blood, and the book itself as well. From this we shall learn again that the law by itself is ineffective for sanctification. For see how it too is sanctified by the sprinkling of blood. The law by no means washes away sins; the grace of the mysteries given through Christ accomplishes this. And it was very fitting that Moses, the initiator into sacred things, rose early in the morning and set up the divine mystery itself, setting twelve stones around it, as I said before, and sacrificing calves. For when it was already dawn and morning, when the Morning Star was all but shining out and the spiritual day was rising for us, when the night had already passed and the demonic darkness had fallen idle, then the beauty of the Church shone out brilliantly, possessing the venerable altar on which the mystery of Christ is performed. And the tribes of the earth stood around it, represented by the stones as by patterns. Indeed, the divinely inspired Paul, recasting the image of the pattern into the truth, writes to those sanctified in Christ: "In him you too, as living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house, into a holy priesthood." Then the young men brought the whole burnt offerings and became spiritual ministers. Then, yes, then we came into the presence of the Father and stood before him, offering as our attendance upon him a vigorous understanding, ready for every good thing. The divine David himself clearly foretold this to us, speaking in the person of believers to the God of all: "In the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you, and you will look upon me; for you are not a God who wills lawlessness, nor will the evildoer dwell beside you." Sanctified, then, and purified by blood, though still in types, "Moses and Aaron went up the mountain, with Nadab and Abihu and seventy of the elders of Israel, and they saw what was under his feet, a work like sapphire brick, like the work of the firmament of heaven in its clearness. And of the chosen ones of Israel not one was missing. And they were seen in the place of God, and they ate and drank." You hear how they beheld what is called the place of God, in the form of the firmament of heaven. For heaven is bright, and its highest, ethereal color is like sapphire. And heaven is the most fitting place for God, the place where he rests, dwelling among angels. For the Holy One dwells among the holy, and in a manner reclines upon those who walk the city above, because of their excellent nature, finely polished for the excellence of life. For we believe that the multitude of spirits above is holy. So what was under his feet appeared to those who had gone up the mountain "in the form of the firmament of heaven in its clearness," it says. For it was necessary, truly necessary, that those who had once been sick with the error of many gods and had worshiped the creation, and who were then called to the knowledge of God, should see, both usefully and necessarily, that he has heaven itself under his feet. They had to see that he who redeems them from the ancient deception is Lord of all, since he brought all things into existence. And those who went up, once they came into the place of God, ate and drank. This will show that those who in due time enter the city above are to share richly in the divine gifts and to delight in the spiritual good things that come from Christ. But in what I said just now, Moses alone was commanded to draw near to God, while the others were to worship from afar, and Aaron was with them. And we said that the Son, who is near to God the Father, our guileless and undefiled high priest, came by his nature to be with us far off, so that through him, and again with him, we too might be found near. That is why he is also called Emmanuel, which means "God with us." Yet even though he came to be with us as man, one can see that the Father was not accessible even to blessed Moses himself apart from the Son's mediation. For he is the way, he is the door, as we have already said. We shall learn this too from what follows. "The Lord," it says, "said to Moses: Come up to me on the mountain and stay there, and I will give you the stone tablets, the law, and the tablets that I have written to give them laws. And Moses rose up with Joshua, who attended him, and they went up the mountain of God." You see that Moses, who received the law while it was still in shadows and letters, is called, but Joshua, though not called with him, goes up with him as a type of Christ. Christ is not called by the Father as the others are, for he is always with him. Rather, as mediator and companion, he makes the way passable for those who are called. For, as I said, it is impossible for us to come into the presence of God the Father in any other way than through his mediation alone. To him, therefore, be glory and might, together with the all-holy Father and the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

Those who have no law to help them are carried off toward anything at all by blind and unconsidered turns of the will. They are very easily carried off even toward hateful things that stand under heavy blame before God and men, though they may seem very much concerned with being blameless. Or rather, if there is something utterly outlandish, such a person sees fit to admire and praise it, and does not know how to tell what is truly acceptable from what is, on the contrary, shameful and suspect. Think of the merchant ships that run across this great, wide sea. If the man at the rudder is skilful and expert, they speed along a straight course. But if he is not very skilled, they are tossed about in every direction, all but yielding to the wave that pushes them, wherever it can drive them. In the same way the human soul, having no law set over it, easily leans toward whatever it pleases, and is drunk with the waves of its own pleasures. We shall find that this is what happened to Israel. Since his mind was not yet firmly set on piety, nor his heart fixed on God, he was caught going backward again, as it were, having come to love the offences of accursed and loathsome idolatry. For this reason the Saviour himself said about them: "When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and does not find it. And it says, 'I will return to my own place.' And when it comes, it finds it unoccupied, swept and put in order. Then it goes and takes seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they enter and dwell there; and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first." Then he added to this: "Truly I tell you, so it will be with this evil generation." At the beginning the evil spirit had been driven out, when they sacrificed the lamb as a type of Christ, were anointed with its blood, and escaped the destroyer. But see, it has broken in again, and far worse than before, if he speaks truly who says about those who have chosen to suffer such things: "It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, having known it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them." What the true proverb says has happened to them: "A dog returns to its own vomit," and "A sow, once washed, returns to wallowing in the mire." From what they dared to do, anyone could see that they touched their own vomit again and set their minds on rolling once more in the mire of the past. For it is written: "When the people saw that Moses was slow to come down from the mountain, the people gathered against Aaron and said to him, 'Rise up and make us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.' And Aaron said to them, 'Take off the gold earrings that are in the ears of your wives and daughters, and bring them to me.' And all the people took off the gold earrings that were in the ears of their wives and brought them to Aaron. He received them from their hands, shaped them with a graving tool, and made them a molten calf. And they said, 'These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.' When Aaron saw this, he built an altar before it, and Aaron made a proclamation, saying, 'Tomorrow is a feast of the Lord.' And rising early the next day, he offered burnt offerings and brought a sacrifice of peace offering; and the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play." The divine Moses was spending his time on Mount Sinai, being thoroughly initiated into the laws. But the people foolishly lost patience at his delay and slid in their derangement so far that perhaps they no longer knew at all that they had come under the God who is almighty. Yet they had seen him in the form of fire on Mount Sinai, had heard his voice with their own ears, and had begged Moses to be their mediator. One might say to them: "You who are filled to the brim with folly! Moses has indeed been delayed. But what has that to do with God, who is always present with those on earth, even if perhaps he is not seen?" Let the divine David cry out, then: "A crooked and embittering generation." And Moses adds to this: "You forgot God who nourishes you." What sort of gods did he need, who had been so wonderfully redeemed? For his sake the hail and the three days' darkness were poured over the land of the Egyptians, and for his sake the firstborn of all perished in a single night. For him the wild and untamed sea gave a way of escape from the cruelty of his pursuers. But if anyone chose to tell every detail, he would spend a long discourse on it all. So while the all-wise Moses delayed, they pressed hard upon Aaron. Seeing that their assault had become all but unbearable (for they had cried out, "Make us gods who will go before us"), he ordered them to bring the earrings of their wives and daughters. And they brought them at once. Aaron showed by the deed itself that they had fallen into the error of Egypt and slipped back into their old follies, when he fashioned for them an image to worship in the form of a calf. For in Egypt the calf was the object of reverence both for the Egyptians themselves and for those who were sick with their delusion. You see, then, how they are carried back to their original state. The unclean spirit has broken in again, and, as the Saviour said, their last state has become worse than the first. I think the divine Aaron asked for the earrings with great purpose, all but signifying by this that they had robbed their own hearing of its proper ornament. They no longer had obedience, but had been carried away into godless and profane disobedience. For when God said, "You shall have no other gods besides me," they applauded the words and honoured them with a splendid vote, saying, "All that God has said we will do and hear"; yet they went looking for carved gods. Do you see how they threw away their readiness to hear? And this, I think, is the ornament of the ears. And see how Aaron mocks what they were attempting. Showing them the image made in the form of a calf, he then declared: "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." But Israel was not redeemed by a calf (how could it have been, or from where?), but with a mighty hand and an uplifted arm, and with signs and wonders. So he speaks ironically, as if to remind them of what God had done, saying, "These are your gods, O Israel." He also offered sacrifices, and they ate and drank as at a feast, "and rose up to play." For apostasy from God is followed by bondage to the things of the flesh: people count uncleanness as luxury, and think fine and sweet delights the very things they ought to lament. That is why the blessed Paul too counted unclean idolatry among the sins of the flesh: "The works of the flesh are evident: fornication, impurity, licentiousness, idolatry." For error is the matchmaker of things still worse, and being carried away from God forces one to suffer the most shameful of all evils. So they were dancing, singing, I suppose, after-dinner songs, and doing and saying the things that drunkards are guilty of. The divine Moses did not know what they had dared to do, but God made it plain to him, saying: "Go, go down quickly from here, for the people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt have acted lawlessly. They have quickly turned aside from the way that you commanded them. They have made themselves a calf, worshipped it, sacrificed to it, and said, 'These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.' And now let me alone, and in the heat of my wrath against them I will destroy them, and I will make you into a great nation. And Moses entreated the Lord his God." Do you hear how fickle and easily led astray Israel is, and how very prone to apostasy? God does not even deign to call them his own people. Although he himself had laid down the law, he assigns the matter to Moses: "They have quickly turned aside," he says, "from the way that you commanded them." That is why Christ too said that the Judge on the divine judgment seat would say to those who think the same way, who put a false face on their impiety and have not truly practised doing good: "Depart from me, you workers of lawlessness; I do not know you." Those, then, would be known to God and truly be his people who hold unbroken to their love for him, keep their faith genuine, stand firm in doing good, and thrust away the sins born of fickleness. Moses, however, pleaded, and asked that the wrath against them all be held back. For the mediator had to imitate Christ, he truly had to. Christ turned away the wrath from above that hung over us because of our many sins, and as the Son gave sinners justification by faith. So this too, once again, is a type of Christ's mediation. By his supplications the divine Moses turns aside the severity of the wrath, and then he goes down from the mountain. But when he learned that they were dancing and the voices of the drunken reached his ears, he smashed the tablets on which the laws were engraved. He no longer thought them worthy of instruction, since they were disobedient and ungrateful, or senseless, with minds all too easily carried away into what was unfitting, and had fallen away so quickly. When he came to the assembly, he crushed the calf. Then he put it into water and, it says, made the sons of Israel drink it. By this he was all but signifying that their impiety would reach their very livers and inmost parts. I think he was perhaps also showing them that their hearts were filled to overflowing with profane and loathsome idolatry. Calling together the chosen men, he ordered them to kill those who were most guilty, sparing neither brother, nor neighbour, nor acquaintance. And twenty-three thousand fell. When he had exacted fitting penalties from those who had committed such shameless impiety, he went back up to God and offered prayers for the rest. Then at last God reluctantly consented. He said that he himself would not go with them, but would rather send an angel with them to watch over them and lead them on the way. At this the people lamented, and God commanded them to take off their robes and all their ornaments and to go on like this in dejection. When this had been done, "Moses," it says, "took his tent and pitched it outside the camp." So much, briefly, for the account of the history. But we shall find that those of Israel dared the same things when the Only-begotten became a man like us. He called them into the kingdom of heaven, as of old he called them through Moses into the land of promise, and he promised to set free those who believed in him. For he had set free from Egypt's greed those of Israel's blood who received in faith the salvation that comes through blood. They sacrificed the lamb, as in types, while Christ was even then fulfilling the mystery. They had the law, which rightly tutored them toward Christ through shadow and types, and they were forever holding up the words of Moses. Yet they paid no regard to Moses himself (for they turned to the teachings and commandments of men), and they shook off the yoke of serving God. For they would by no means accept the one through whom he rules all things, that is, Christ. And what was the reason? They had turned aside to worldly deceit and made the pleasures of this life the object of their most urgent zeal, so naturally they stumbled. When invited to the wedding, they would not come, offering as excuses their wives and the fields they had bought. Since they had slid so far into impiety, the time had already come for Israel to suffer wrath to the uttermost. But the prayers of the saints saved the remnant, though punishment fell on many. For they fell, devoured by the sword and bitter war, and only with difficulty did they recognize that the guilt of their outrage against Christ had turned to evil for them. Having cast off, as it were, the robe of their ancient glory and all spiritual adornment, they suffer greatly from disgrace and remain stripped of all glory. And that Christ himself had departed from them, Moses indicated by moving his own tent far from the camp and leaving the camp behind. For see how Christ, having in a sense fled the Jewish herds, that is, their camps, and their multitude, and having withdrawn very far away, displayed as an unshakable tent the Church from the Gentiles. Declaring it to be his own, he says somewhere through the voice of the Psalmist: "Here I will dwell, for I have chosen it." It was right, then, that from now on those should be seen stripped of adornment and glory who do not have Emmanuel, the Lord of glory, who clothes those who love him with the adornment that comes from faith and virtue. Rejoicing greatly at this, they say: "Let my soul rejoice in the Lord; for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a tunic of gladness. He has set a turban on me as on a bridegroom, and adorned me with ornaments like a bride." Their beauty is indeed outstanding, clearly the spiritual beauty in Christ. Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

"Do you understand what you are reading?" This might rightly be said to the Jewish crowds. They may be thought to have reached such a degree of stupor that the sacred words now call them heartless: "Behold," it says, "a foolish and heartless people. They have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear." Christ himself also showed us that the law given through Moses became completely useless to them because of the greatness of their folly, saying: "You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that testify about me. Yet you refuse to come to me to have life." A hardening has come upon Israel in part. Lacking the illumination of the Spirit, they were sluggish in faith and very hard to move toward choosing and thinking what is useful for salvation. But they would not escape just punishment, because after choosing what was beneficial, they turned instead to incorrigible disobedience. Though they had the light from heaven above, they preferred to walk as if in night and darkness. The prophet hinted at this too when he said of them: "While they waited for light, darkness came upon them; waiting for brightness, they walked in the dead of night." They remained harsh and unbridled, and thought very little of what was profitable for them and of the means by which they could very easily have escaped harm. Christ cried out: "I am the light of the world." And: "While you have the light, walk in the light, so that darkness may not overtake you." But they were like people who have neither mind nor understanding. Therefore they were overtaken by darkness and continue as if in night, with no share at all in the divine radiance and without the divine light; for they do not understand the divinely inspired Scripture at all. And the divine Paul will make clear to us why, saying: "To this very day the same veil remains unlifted at the reading of the Old Covenant, because only in Christ is it taken away. Indeed, to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts. But whenever one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." Look, then, at the mystery shining out in the sacred and more ancient writings. It runs as follows: "And the Lord said to Moses, 'Write these words for yourself, for on the basis of these words I will make a covenant with you and with Israel.' And Moses was there before the Lord forty days and forty nights. He ate no bread and drank no water. And he wrote these words on the tablets of the covenant, the ten words. When Moses came down from the mountain, the two tablets were in Moses' hands. As he came down from the mountain, Moses did not know that the appearance of the skin of his face had been glorified while he spoke with God. And Aaron and all the elders of Israel saw Moses, and the appearance of the skin of his face was glorified, and they were afraid to come near him. And Moses called them, and Aaron and all the rulers of the congregation turned back to him, and Moses spoke to them. After this all the sons of Israel came to him, and he commanded them all that the Lord had spoken to him on Mount Sinai. And when he had finished speaking to them, he put a veil over his face. Whenever Moses went in before the Lord to speak with him, he would take off the veil until he came out. And when he came out, he would tell all the sons of Israel what the Lord had commanded him. And the sons of Israel saw the face of Moses, that it was glorified. And Moses put the veil over his face until he went in to speak with him." The God of the universe writes the law on tablets of stone. But Moses had remained in God's presence for forty days, paying no heed even to human needs, and his face was now made radiant by the touch of the divine light. The chosen men of Israel did not know what to make of the sight, and Aaron least of all. As they were already drawing away and turning to flight, Moses called them back, and so he spoke to the sons of Israel with a veil before his face, using its shade to make the oncoming ray of divine light just bearable for the crowds. "But whenever," it says, "he went in to God, he took off the veil." Understand, then, how even the light of the law itself is somehow too much for the minds of the Jews to contain. But if what is written in it is understood spiritually (for it points to nothing other than the mystery of Christ), it sends divine and most transparent light into the hearts of those who hear it. Yet those of Israel would not listen to such venerable words, nor would they readily grasp the depth of the mystery. Indeed, when Nicodemus heard Christ speaking of rebirth through the Spirit, he answered coldly and feebly, saying: "How can a person be born again when he is old? Can he enter his mother's womb a second time and be born?" And when Christ was persuading him that one must honour by faith things beyond mind and reason, he added: "How can these things be?" And this although the law had foreshadowed the mystery in countless figures. So even the light of the law itself is unacceptable to the Jews, and not only to the feeble and the common crowd, but even to the chosen and holy. For you have heard that Aaron and the elders were afraid of Moses' glory. So Moses put on the veil to very good purpose. For the law has a shading: the thickness of the letter and the dimness of the history. "But when Moses went in before God," it says, "he took off the veil." We shall find this true in our own case too. For when we are brought, as it were, before the face of God the Father, with Christ presenting us, we shall see the glory of Moses without any shading, understanding the law spiritually. For we are transformed from glory to glory, as it is written. How can anyone doubt that the mystery of Christ is in glory, when the blessed Paul clearly cries out about the First and Second Covenants: "For if the ministry of condemnation was glory, how much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory?" The shadow of the law has been abolished, though it was honoured with the glory that came through Moses, that is, the glory on Moses' face. But what has come through Christ remains unshaken and is rich in a glory and grace far better than the old. With the shadings of the law removed, then, we behold the glory of God as in a mirror, as it is written. If we hear of the lamb being slain in a type, let us at once recognize the mystery, knowing the Lamb who for us and on our behalf offered himself to God the Father as a fragrant aroma. And if the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled on those who have been defiled, sanctify them for the purification of the flesh, let us again no less understand the cleansing through Christ. This cleansing, through water and the Spirit, does not free us from fleshly filth, but washes away the stain of defilements in spirit and soul. For we have been sanctified in Christ. We shall usefully add this as well. We decided to carry our account of the chapters of Exodus only this far. This is not because we grew weary of interpreting what follows. It is because, in composing the books On Worship in Spirit and in Truth, we gave due investigation to the construction of the holy tabernacle itself and to each of the things placed in it, that is, the sanctuary and the ark, the table and the lampstand. So it seems that we have left out nothing in our account of what is necessary. For we spent the ninth and tenth books on this. Glory be to our God to the ages of ages. Amen.

The God of all did not make death, nor does he take delight in the destruction of the living. He created all things so that they might exist, and the generations of the world are wholesome. There is no kingdom of Hades upon the earth, as it is written; but through the envy of the devil death entered into the world. This saying may very reasonably be held to be true. For the Creator would not have bestowed such glory and wonder on beings whose nature was to perish easily. Rather, death was brought in out of wrath, because our forefather Adam disregarded the divine commandment and turned aside into disobedience and unruliness. But now it has been abolished, and in Christ, through the obedience of the one man, the charges against us have been taken out of the way. For we have been justified in him, and the divine Paul will bear witness when he writes: "For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous." In the one we were condemned to death, but through Christ we have received mercy and have been renewed to life. For he became obedient to the Father even to death, and laid down his life for us; "and by his bruise we were healed," according to the Scriptures. One might say that, though we fell sick in Adam with the sin that is in the world, we have become in Christ a spiritual and fragrant sacrifice to God the Father, fine and well acceptable, and far better than the shadow in the law. Christ is our firstfruits, and he himself has renewed the way for us. For this is what David says somewhere in the book of Psalms to the Father and God in heaven: "Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you prepared for me. In burnt offerings and offerings for sin you took no pleasure. Then I said, 'Behold, I have come to do your will, O God; I have desired it.'" These things can also be seen again in what is written in Leviticus. It runs thus: "If you offer a sacrifice of firstfruits to the Lord, new grain, parched, coarsely ground groats, to the Lord, then you shall offer the sacrifice of the firstfruits, and pour oil upon it, and put frankincense upon it. It is a sacrifice. And the priest shall offer up its memorial portion from the groats with the oil, and all its frankincense; it is an offering by fire to the Lord."

The sense of the letter, then, is very plain, and I think no great labour is needed in order to understand it precisely. But this much I will say: "groats" means meal made from pulses. In the types, however, the passage takes on the mystery of Christ. He himself is the sacrifice for us, the spiritual firstfruit, that is, the firstfruits of humanity, the firstborn from the dead, the first into incorruption, the firstling, as it were, of those who have fallen asleep. Like a grain of wheat he fell into the earth and died, but like an ear of grain he sprang up many times over. He himself explained this to us, saying: "Unless the grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit." Yet he died not for his own sake but for us. The letter of the law hints at this to us elegantly. For if anyone chooses, it says, to bring a sacrifice of firstfruits as a gift to the Lord, it is to be new, parched, ground groats to God. See, then, how Moses, or rather the letter of the law, urges us to bring fruit from new grain. For Christ, as I said, is the firstfruits of our nature, renewed into newness of life, and in him all things have become new. Yet what is offered in sacrifice comes not only from wheat but also from ground pulses. For just as in the case of wheat he prescribed fine flour, and not the whole grain itself, for the burnt offering, so here too he commanded that the pulses be ground, that is, milled, so that the sacrifice might plainly have, as it were, the character of food. For we are accustomed to make our food not from the whole grain but rather from crushed grain. So Christ is the firstfruit, a fine and most fragrant sacrifice to God, and also most nourishing to us ourselves. For he is the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world, and he has set himself before us, so to speak, as food, like fine flour or groats. The law said that oil must be poured on the sacrifice, and it commanded that the sacrifice also be covered with frankincense. The oil symbolically suggests richness and gladness, while the frankincense elegantly signifies to us what is holy and fragrant. For Christ, as I said, became a sacrifice for us, like the firstfruits of the fields, a firstfruit of spiritual crops. And how or on what ground could anyone doubt that death was for him no occasion of tears or lamentation, but rather brought the end of tears and lamentations and a most joyful hope? For he was not held fast by the gates of Hades, nor did he remain among the dead. Although death prevailed and swallowed up, as the prophet's voice says, God in turn took away every tear from every face; he took away the reproach of the people from all the earth. How, and in what way? Christ came back to life, having trampled on death, so that he might free us too from corruption, and, having thoroughly put an end to the lament over it, might now persuade us to rejoice and cry out: "You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness." So the manner of the sacrifice may fittingly carry gladness, in hope. It might also be understood another way, if one wished. For we have received mercy in Christ, and this, I think, is the meaning of "You anointed my head with oil." And through the frankincense you will understand that Christ's death was not on account of any just causes, that is, offences, but was a most fragrant and wholly blameless sacrifice for us. For it was offered to abolish sin and the death that came from sin and through it. Our forefather Adam received a curse most fitting for his transgressions in the beginning; since he had truly fallen sick with foul-smelling sin, he was for that reason justly condemned. But the Saviour and Lord of all was convicted of nothing improper (for he committed no sin), and he became a fine and fragrant sacrifice for us, like the firstfruits of new crops, and as it were of every kind, I mean of both wheat and pulses. For he died for all, small and great, Gentiles and Jews. Through him and in him we have become a memorial before God the Father. That is why the letter of the law says: "And the priest shall offer up its memorial portion from the groats with the oil, and all its frankincense. For it is an offering by fire to the Lord." For having given offence through many sins, we had all but passed out of the Father's sight. But since Christ became a sacrifice for us, he remembered us and blessed us: "He blessed those who fear him, the small together with the great." Therefore we have also been taught to sing and say: "Blessed are we by the Lord, who made heaven and earth." In yet another way the law makes Christ's sacrifice clear to us, saying: "If his gift to the Lord is a sacrifice of salvation, and he offers it from the cattle, whether male or female, he shall offer it without blemish before the Lord. He shall lay his hands on the head of the gift and slaughter it at the doors of the tent of witness. And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall pour the blood on the altar of burnt offerings round about. And from the sacrifice of salvation they shall bring as an offering by fire to the Lord the fat that covers the belly, and all the fat that is on the belly, and the two kidneys and the fat that is on them, which is by the thighs; and he shall remove the lobe on the liver together with the kidneys. And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall carry them up onto the altar, upon the burnt offerings, upon the wood on the fire, an offering by fire, an odour of fragrance to the Lord." And not only from cattle: if anyone chose to make the burnt offering from sheep, or to make the sacrifice of salvation from goats, it was done in the same ways, and the manner of the sacred rite was one for all. Whether the victim happened to be male or female, the law said that it must be entirely free of every blemish. The meaning of the sacrifice points to Emmanuel himself. For he is the fatted calf, the spotless victim, who takes away the sin of the world, and who was slain for our sake as in the form of a goat; for under the law a goat was slain for sin. But look closely again at the manner of the sacrifice. The letter of the law is not very particular about male and female, and Christ may again be understood as in both. In the male he is understood as leader or guide, for the male is more fitted to rule than the other. In the female he is understood as having come under the law, though he is the leader. For the female is always subject to the male and comes second to him, if indeed she truly stands in a lesser and subordinate measure. Yet what is sacrificed is spotless, and such is Christ. Therefore he said: "The ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me." Indeed, to the Jews he offered his complete blamelessness as proof of his divine nature, saying: "Which of you convicts me of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me?" In this respect, then, the holy victim is spotless. It was slain before the Lord at the doors of the tent, with the hands of the one who brought it laid upon it. Then, once the blood had been poured at the base of the altar, the law said that the inward parts must be burnt whole. For the Son's death was accomplished, as it were, before the eyes of God the Father, as he laid down his own life for the life of the world. For if he speaks truly who says, "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones," how would God the Father not deem the death of the Son himself worthy of his own regard? He certainly honours it and deems it worthy of his watchful care, whereas he turns away from what is loathsome and hateful. That this death was not inglorious would thus be shown at once by the fact that the Father himself was its eyewitness. And it was slain at the very doors of the sanctuary. For Emmanuel died, as it were widening for us the way into the Holy of Holies, and opening the doors of the Church above, in heaven, to those who believe in him. So by Christ's death we gain the power to go on into the very tent of the saints, which the Lord pitched and not man: the heavenly Jerusalem, the beautiful city above, the mother of the saints and nurse of angels. That Christ's death would be holy and sacred is suggested by the command that the blood be poured on the altar itself. It might also signify in another way that he laid down his life for the Church. For the altar is a type of the Church, and the blood a type of the life. The offering up, or consecration, of the inward parts, I mean the fat, the liver and the kidneys, shows again that all that is in Christ is holy, sacred and fragrant. For those learned in such matters say that the desires or appetites for anything at all arise in the liver. The kidney, in turn, is a part of the body whose work is to discriminate, for it separates what is superfluous from what is useful. And in us the mind does something of this kind: if it is wise, it rejects as counterfeit whatever is apt to do harm, and very gladly accepts whatever makes for benefit. And somewhere the blessed David sings, as in the person of Christ: "All my desire is before you." And again: "For you have possessed my kidneys, O Lord." That Emmanuel is full of virtue befitting God would be shown, again as in a type, by the fat. For just as fat forms in the best-fed animals, so in the same way, I think, virtue forms in a mind that is nourished from heaven. Christ, then, is holy and blameless, full of virtue, sacred and fragrant, a spiritual burnt offering, offered as it were in every kind, I mean as calf, ram and goat. For he became a saving sacrifice for us, and gave himself, one for all, he who is worth all. Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

The divine disciples became stewards of the mysteries of our Saviour. They did not seize the honour for themselves, nor did they come to it self-appointed. Rather, they were chosen for apostleship and commissioned to minister, as priests, the saving proclamation, that is, the Gospel of Christ, to all who live under heaven. For he made these initiators illustrious, saying: "Go and make disciples of all nations." So, yielding very eagerly to the Master's decrees, they enlighten the world. They themselves had been given the Father and God in heaven as their teacher, and they made others partakers of the grace. For, naturally enough, they remembered that Christ had moved their minds to this by saying clearly: "Freely you have received; freely give." So the divine Paul writes, and makes clear the deep mystery of the dispensation in the flesh, saying somewhere: "For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the just requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit." For Christ became sin for us, as it is written, and certainly not as one guilty of sin. We are not in the habit of talking such nonsense, since he never knew wrongdoing at all, being God by nature and having come forth from God the Father. But since he became a victim for sin (for Christ our Passover was sacrificed for us), in this sense we say that he also became sin. For he was sacrificed, as I said, so that by his own blood he might win for himself the world under heaven. For we were bought with a price, according to the Scriptures, and we are not our own, but belong to him who became sin for us, so that he might free us from our ancient offences and make us holy through participation in his holy flesh, and of course also in his blood. This the divine law proclaimed to us beforehand, for it is written thus in Leviticus: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying: This is the law of the sin offering. In the place where they slaughter the burnt offerings, they shall also slaughter the sin offering before the Lord. It is most holy. The priest who offers it shall eat it; it shall be eaten in a holy place, in the court of the tent of witness. Everyone who touches its flesh shall be made holy. And if any of its blood is sprinkled on a garment, whatever it is sprinkled on shall be washed in a holy place. And the earthenware vessel in which it is boiled shall be broken; but if it is boiled in a bronze vessel, he shall scour it and wash it with water. Every male among the priests shall eat it. It is most holy to the Lord." Understand, then, how the law commands that the sin be sacrificed, that is, the offering for sin. This was a goat, as a type of Christ, who, as I said, became sin for our sake. For he was reckoned among the lawless and crucified with robbers, and he was even called a curse; for it is written: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree." He lowered himself into these things for our sake as part of the dispensation, yet he was and is holy, not by participation, receiving holiness from another as we do, but rather by nature, as God. For through him, we believe, creation is sanctified. Name the angels, or those who surpass them in glory, or those who are above and higher still, I mean Thrones and Principalities; speak to me even of the Seraphim themselves: these could not be sanctified in any other way than from the Father through the Son in the Spirit. So even though he became sin, he remained what he was, that is, holy by nature as God, and, in the words of John, he does not give the Spirit by measure. And the law clearly indicated that the death of his flesh, which took place for the destruction of the flesh, was holy and unprofaned, and acceptable to God the Father as if ranked with incense, when it said: "In the place where they slaughter the burnt offerings, they shall also slaughter the sin offering before the Lord." Christ is a whole burnt offering, that is, wholly and entirely, not in part, dedicated to God the Father as an odour of fragrance. For this reason he is truly the Holy of holies. For we have been sanctified in him, and he is our entire justification, or rather, as I said just now, the sanctification even of the spirits above. But it says: "The priest who offers it shall eat it." Observe now again that the Church is governed by sacred and divine ordinances in everything that is to be done. The portions of the sacrifice belong to the one who brings it. Anyone brought up in the laws of the Church knows what I mean. And the law shows quite plainly that the place most fitting for the divine rites is the Church of God, and that the mystery of Christ must be celebrated in it, when it adds to what I quoted: "It shall be eaten in a holy place, in the court of the tent of witness." At that time there was one tent in the wilderness, and after it one temple, which Solomon built in Jerusalem. And death was the penalty for those who sacrificed outside the tent. For the sacred letter said thus: "Any man of the sons of Israel who slaughters a calf or a sheep or a goat in the camp, or who slaughters it outside the camp, and does not bring it to the door of the tent of witness to offer it as a gift to the Lord before the tent of the Lord, blood shall be imputed to the man who shed that blood; that soul shall be utterly destroyed from among the people." It is therefore lawlessness and profanation, and liable to the penalty for blood, to like keeping company with the unholy heretics and to cling to communion with them. For they sacrifice the sin offering outside the holy tent; they do not perform the sacred sacrifice in holy places. For the Church is one, just as the temple of old was one, and the tent too was one, foreshadowing still in types the beauty of the Church. We, then, will sacrifice the sin offering as in a holy court, and we will eat of the holy flesh; that is, by sharing in the mystical blessing we will be sanctified. The law will bear witness, saying: "Everyone who touches its flesh shall be made holy." And the sprinkling of the blood of the sacrifice has equal power for mystical blessing. For it said again: "And if any of its blood is sprinkled on a garment, whatever it is sprinkled on shall be washed in a holy place." And what is surprising if it sanctifies the rational living being, I mean man, when even the vessels taken up for the sacred service were sanctified in a manner surely fitting for them? That is why they are not taken for common use, and why some of the vessels are washed out and others broken. For how could things that have served the divine be called back to human uses? And the law indicated that partaking of the flesh of the sacrifice is a holy matter, and would not befit any others than those who are accustomed to wrestle down sin and to show manly courage in virtue, when it said: "Every male among the priests shall eat it. It is most holy to the Lord." Tell me, then: does the law command that the female sex be driven away from the blessing? We do not say that, for she is sanctified along with us. But those things were in types and shadows. By the male and priestly race the law aptly signified those who in Christ are spiritually manly and priestly. We have been called, then, to share in the most fragrant sacrifice, as a holy and acceptable race, as a holy nation, as a royal priesthood, young men and maidens, old men with the young. For in Christ Jesus there is no male and female, but we are all of one, since we partake of the one bread, as it is written. Come, then, and finally, with mouths never closed and voices never ceasing, let us honour with praises the King and Redeemer of all, I mean Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

Sin has reigned over us and has gained the mastery over those on earth, because the mind of man is intently set on evil from his youth, and has chosen without restraint to give way to the downward pull toward what is worse, counting the glory of goodness as nothing. But God, who is rich in mercy and compassion, as it is written, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ, raised us up with him, and seated us with him in the heavenly places. For in Christ we have been enriched with the gentleness that comes from above, and we have washed away sin, that inglorious and utterly wretched thing, having been called through faith to sanctification. And besides this, since we have become partakers of eternal life as well, we shall be acceptable and shall be offered to God the Father as a fragrant aroma. For the blessed Paul writes truly that we are the aroma of Christ to God. Even if sin has at times tyrannized over us, we have nevertheless thrown off the stain, scoured away the filth, and been delivered in Christ from our old infirmities, as a sacred passage will convince us. For it is written thus in Leviticus: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: This is the law of the leper on the day he is cleansed.
