He shall be brought to the priest, and the priest shall go out of the camp, and the priest shall look, and behold, the infection of leprosy has been healed from the leper. And the priest shall give orders, and they shall take for the one who has been cleansed two small birds, living and clean, and cedar wood, and spun scarlet, and hyssop. And the priest shall give orders, and they shall slaughter one of the birds into an earthen vessel over living water. And he shall take the living bird, and the cedar wood, and the spun scarlet, and the hyssop, and he shall dip them, together with the living bird, into the blood of the bird that was slaughtered over living water, and he shall sprinkle seven times the one who has been cleansed of the leprosy, and he shall be clean. And he shall send the living bird away into the open field, and the one cleansed shall wash his garments, and shall shave off all his hair, and bathe in water, and he shall be clean. And after this he shall enter the camp, and shall stay outside his house seven days. And on the seventh day he shall shave off all his hair: his head, his beard and his eyebrows; all his hair shall he shave off. And he shall wash his garments and bathe his body in water, and he shall be clean." Now the historical sense would be plain enough even if no one chose to explain it, but it contains nothing that leads to any benefit unless it is understood spiritually. Come then, let us speak, skilfully reshaping the ineffectual letter into the mystery of Christ. But first it will be useful for us to say a few things that are needed for clarity. Leprosy is an unwelcome disease that befalls the bodies of some people. It is above all a devouring thing, and it is always found to take hold, more and more, of the inner parts of those in whom it occurs. The disease is extremely hard to escape. It does not yield to the science of physicians, that is, to the help of anyone skilled in such matters, but departs only with difficulty, as though nature rose up against it and repelled the harm with God's help. The law, however, said that the leper must be sent out of the camp as unclean. For it was said somewhere to Moses, the revealer of sacred things, by God, who commanded the sons of Israel: "Let them send out of the camp every leper, everyone with a discharge, and everyone who is unclean in soul." Of course we do not say that the law is censuring bodily diseases. It would be utterly foolish for penalties to be laid on those who have fallen ill against their will, when they ought rather to be pitied. Rather, what was given through the all-wise Moses was in types, in labour with the truth. For leprosy deadens the flesh, and sin in turn, when it befalls souls and makes its way into the human mind through dead works, at once renders the mind useless and cold. By the dead works of the flesh we plainly mean the foul and profane passions, and choosing to set one's mind on the things of earth. That is why at the beginning we said that while we were dead in our trespasses, God the Father made us alive together with Christ. So by means of a visible thing the passage carves us toward subtle ideas. For it sends the lepers out of the camp, hinting in a riddle that those who have been deadened by sin, whose minds are all but tattooed with various passions, and who are gravely sick with the ugliness within themselves, must withdraw from the company of the saints and be removed somewhere outside the sacred rolls. For the wicked will by no means be herded together with the righteous, nor the filthy with the profane [?], nor will one who bears the hard-to-wash stain of sin be together with the sanctified. "For what fellowship," it says, "has light with darkness, or what portion has a believer with an unbeliever?" And that those who wish to live rightly must, for their own good, make haste to get away from the wicked, the divinely inspired Scripture itself will again convince us. For God said somewhere to those who were his own: "Depart, depart from their midst, and be separated, you who carry the vessels of the Lord." The vessels of the Lord may be understood as the manifold virtues. That is why the divine Paul also says: "Put on the whole armour of God." So, as in the type of the lepers, God drives away from the company of the saints the one who is sick with sin and defiled. But it was surely quite likely that some of the sick would throw off the disease. For sometimes we leave our sins behind, turning our minds to choose to do and to think what is better and more fitting. What then of the law? Does it not show the way to those who wish to repent? Does it not open the gate of salvation? Do not imagine that it does not. For the Master is good and loves humankind. Hear him saying clearly: "Turn back, you who are turning, and I will heal your wounds." And again, through the voice of Ezekiel: "Turn back and turn away from all your iniquities, O house of Israel, and they shall not become for you a punishment for unrighteousness." What, then, is the way of salvation? Who frees sinners from having to be punished? Who redeems and saves with ease? Our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself as a ransom for all and sanctifies us with his own blood.

Now look with me again at the mystery, still in shadows, in what is written in the law. The leper was brought to the one who served as priest under the law, after the priest had gone outside the gate. When the disease had, as it were, taken a turn for the better and showed that it would cease and come to an end, the rites of cleansing were carried out as the lawgiver saw fit. A pair of clean birds was taken, along with cedar wood and spun scarlet in the form of a cord, and also hyssop, which is a kind of herb. Then one of the birds was slaughtered over water, while the other, together with the things we have just mentioned, was dipped in the water and in the blood of the dead bird, and then, having suffered no harm, it was released. Then the priest sprinkled the one who had been sick with leprosy seven times with the water, and so set him free from the charges laid by the law. He also shaved off his hair, and then, after staying outside for seven days, he entered the camp without blame, and his own house. For we who long carried about the deadness of sin, who were stained by the manifold savagery of the passions, and who were sick, as it were, with a spiritual leprosy (for we had gone astray and worshipped the creation), have been brought to God, the great priest, holy and innocent, in the words of the blessed Paul. And we have been brought by God the Father. For Christ said somewhere, speaking to the Jews: "Do not grumble among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him." For God the Father brings the sick to the Son, as it were by his own power. For the Son came to heal the brokenhearted and to open the eyes of the blind. If, then, we renounce weakness and sluggishness in doing what pleases God, if we have a most industrious heart, cling tightly to works of goodness, and practise a glorious and admirable way of life, acknowledging the one who is Master by nature and in truth, let us say, in the words of the Psalmist: "Bless the Lord, O my soul, who is merciful to all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from corruption, who crowns you with mercy and compassion." Notice how the one who has suffered from leprosy is brought to the priest after the priest has gone outside the gate, far from the camp. For when we had been cast out, as it were, and were living somewhere outside the holy and sacred city (I mean the Church of God), Christ came to us, bearing a likeness to us. And having visited us, he declared us clean through holy baptism and through his body. For he was sacrificed for us, and the fact that he himself endured death on the wood for our sake proved to be a saving medicine for us. This was sketched out for us in shadow in the sacred Scriptures. For two clean birds are taken. And this too was a type of Christ, who is from above and from heaven. For a bird flies through the air, and Emmanuel came down to us from above and from heaven. For he says somewhere: "No one has ascended into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of God." And the wise John also writes: "He who comes from above is above all." And the birds are clean. For the Lord is truly clean and undefiled, knowing no sin. Yet we certainly do not say that we conceive of two Christs, even though two birds are mentioned. Rather, the passage brings before us a wise and necessary contemplation. For the Only-begotten, being God by nature, bore the flesh of the holy Virgin, and is composed, as it were, of two, I mean the supreme nature and humanity, ineffably and beyond understanding. Yet there is one Lord Jesus Christ. The passage, then, contemplates the coming together of two into one. So the law, which signifies the mystery of Christ in many ways, after indicating it by the two birds, said that cedar wood must also be taken. This too would be a type of his holy flesh, which could not suffer corruption, for the wood does not rot. The hyssop, for its part, would be a type of the Holy Spirit, fervent in operation, by which we are made fervent in spirit, the impurity in our inward parts being, as it were, melted away. For hyssop is an herb hot by nature, able to scour out the cold, phlegmy impurity that collects in the inward parts. And Christ, as I said, frees us by the operation of the Spirit from the passions hidden deep within the mind. And it is very fitting that the herb is taken over living water, for we have been baptized in the Holy Spirit and fire, as it is written. The herb, as I said, is hot and receptive of the Spirit's operation. The spun scarlet, again, by itself suggests the manner in which the Only-begotten became man. For the Word, though he was God, was interwoven, as it were, with flesh and blood. And the scarlet will represent blood and flesh, since it appears, and will be, of that colour. The bird, then, is slaughtered over living water, and in this water the remaining bird is dipped together with the other things, and then released having suffered no harm, as I said before. For Christ was sacrificed for us, yet he was the same one both in death and above death. For he was put to death in the flesh, as it is written, but made alive in the spirit, in which he also went and preached to the spirits in prison who had once been disobedient. Insofar as he is understood to be, and became, man, he underwent death; but insofar as he is truly Life and from Life, he was shown to be stronger than death. So the living bird was dipped into the death of the bird that had died, the law signifying in a riddle that although the Word is by nature Life and from Life, he makes the death of his own flesh his own. For the flesh he assumed was not foreign to him but his own. And the leper, sprinkled seven times with water, was thereafter freed from the charges arising from his leprosy. And Christ, as I said, declares us clean too, sanctifying us through holy baptism. This, I think, is what "seven times" indicates. Understanding it in this way, the blessed Paul said: "Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more." So the abundance of grace, and the fact that it is, so to speak, perfectly sufficient for cleansing, is signified by "seven times." After he had been sprinkled, the leper shaved off his hair. For once we have been cleansed through holy baptism, we put away, as it were, the growths of the flesh, that is, the inborn pleasures within us, understood as a kind of hair, together with our other faults; and it is Christ who works this in us. For he is the Word, living and active and sharpest of all, shearing away sins and freeing the mind from the impurity of the passions. Once shaved, then, the leper enters the camp, but not yet his own house. For once we have been cleansed, as I said, we are joined to the saints and from then on live together with the holy and sacred race; and so we enter the house of God as well, but not yet the dwellings above. For that gift is reserved for the saints in the age to come. That is why the one who has been cleansed goes into the camp, and only after spending seven days does he enter his own house. For after the present age, having the cleansing that comes through Christ, we shall also take up our lodging in the dwellings above; and each of the sanctified will lodge in the inheritance to be allotted to him as in his own house. For the rewards do not come to believers at once. Rather, our calling rests on good hopes and on the pledge of the Spirit. But in due time grace will shine forth, and the fulfilment of our hope in Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

Long ago God made plain, through the voice of Ezekiel, how utterly hardened the synagogue of the Jews was, and how disobedient and intractable its ways, when he said: "All the house of Israel are contentious and hard-hearted." So the Saviour himself, since it refused to be saved, also rebuked the perversity within it, saying: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing. See, your house is left to you." For the God of all wished to save it in countless ways. But most of them veered far into unbridled licence and disregarded the mercy from above, and so were swept by terrible and heedless turns into destruction and ruin. He gave laws through Moses by which they could be well trained in the knowledge of virtue and gain a sound knowledge of the truth. He also raised up the holy prophets at various times for their benefit, so that they might have other guides to what is finest, who knew how to shape them into a glorious way of life, a life wholly in keeping with the law, and toward everything worthy of admiration. They ought to have offered thanks to the God of all, gladly received their tutors, thought them worthy of every honour, been remoulded, and very eagerly, toward better things, and chosen to obey the more fitting voice. Instead they were found hard and unyielding, and sick with still worse things. That is why they have perished, and why the prophet Jeremiah says of them: "The house of Israel has fallen; there is no one to raise it up." Look with me at the matter once more, as it is spoken in riddles through the writings of Moses too. For in Leviticus it runs like this: "And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: When you enter the land of the Canaanites, which I am giving you as a possession, and I put an infection of leprosy in the houses of the land you possess, then the owner of the house shall come and report to the priest, saying: 'Something like an infection has appeared to me in the house.' And the priest shall order them to clear out the house before the priest goes in to see the infection, so that nothing in the house may become unclean. After this the priest shall go in to examine the house, and the priest shall see the infection. And look, the infection is in the walls of the house, greenish or reddish hollows, and it appears lower than the surface of the walls. Then the priest shall go out of the house to the door of the house, and the priest shall shut up the house for seven days. And the priest shall come again on the seventh day and look at the house; and look, the infection has spread in the walls of the house. Then the priest shall give orders, and they shall take out the stones in which the infection is and throw them outside the city into an unclean place. And they shall scrape the inside of the house all around, and pour out the mortar they have scraped off outside the city into an unclean place. And they shall take other stones, dressed ones, and put them in place of the stones, and they shall take other mortar and plaster the house. But if the infection comes again and breaks out in the house after the stones have been taken out, and after the house has been scraped, and after the house has been plastered, then the priest shall go in and see whether the infection has spread in the house. It is a persistent leprosy in the house; it is unclean. And they shall pull down the house, and its timbers and its stones and all the mortar of the house they shall carry outside the city into an unclean place." Then, having first declared unclean anyone who sleeps or eats in it, or enters it at all, he brings the priest in again to inspect it. For he says: "But if the priest comes and goes in and looks, and look, the infection has not spread at all in the house after the house was plastered, then the priest shall declare the house clean, because the infection has been healed. And to purify the house he shall take two small birds, clean and living, and cedar wood, and spun scarlet, and hyssop. And he shall slaughter one bird into an earthenware vessel over running water. And he shall take the cedar wood, and the spun scarlet, and the hyssop, and the living bird, and dip them in the blood of the bird slaughtered over running water, and with them he shall sprinkle the house seven times. And he shall purify the house with the blood of the slaughtered bird, and with the running water, and with the living bird, and with the cedar wood, and with the hyssop, and with the spun scarlet. And he shall send the living bird out of the city into the open field, and make atonement for the house, and it shall be clean." In these words the whole mystery of the synagogue of the Jews is clearly revealed to us: both what has already happened to it from beginning to end, and what is yet to happen to it at the hands of Christ. Come, then, let us go through each point again as precisely as we can, and, unfolding the coarseness of the letter, let us strive to lay bare the beauty of the spiritual sense buried within it.

Leprosy, when it occurs in the human body, is a disease that the arts of physicians cannot drive off. Like certain others, it yields only to the great and all-powerful right hand, and is overcome by the all-working power of God. In those who have once been afflicted, the flesh takes on a different appearance from what it had at first. A change of colour comes over it and belies nature, since the flesh is altered into a state contrary to nature. As this happens to the appearance of the body, so we should understand something of the same kind to happen when our will changes and we pass from a better state to a worse. For many people often move from a good disposition to a baser one and depart from what befits their nature, and so they mottle their own soul with wickedness of many kinds, as if keeping in themselves the look of both conditions at once. They neither fall into a complete loss of the good, nor run off into utter wickedness and pathlessness. Since such a condition sometimes arises in us, divine Scripture often makes the leper an image of it, and of whatever else tends to happen to human character and choice. Sometimes it portrays the character of each individual, as though on a painted tablet, taking the person of a single man and setting him before us. But when it wishes to suggest such a condition in a nation, a city or a country, it introduces the figure of a house, because a house contains those who live in it, and so it makes the meaning plural. So when you hear of a leprous house, you are to understand the entire synagogue of the Jews, plainly corrupted by its own passions. It cared little for the oracles God had given it, and inclined instead toward freedom to do whatever gave them pleasure, rather than what would prove good. As for someone reporting to the priest, saying, "Something like an infection of leprosy appears in the house," we by no means say that the lawgiver means a man goes to the priest to accuse his own house. Rather, he goes as one would to a physician, to ask for a remedy for what has befallen him. Since we have granted that the synagogue of the Jews is leprous, come, let us consider as well as we can who it is that reports the disease, and who, in turn, is the priest. Let the role of the one making the report be given to the choir of the holy prophets. Even before the incarnation they reported to Christ, the High Priest of all and Guardian of our souls, the diseases of the Jews' folly and the unholiness and corruption of their ways. They did not do this out of any hatred or hostility toward them. They were overcome by reverence for their Benefactor, and confessed the Jews' offences, though not without tears, while still pleading that the synagogue be shown mercy. Take in this sense, too, the blessed prophet Jeremiah, who laments the leprosy of the Jews and is deeply stung by it, where he prays: "Our sins have stood against us, O Lord. Act for us for your name's sake, for our sins before you are many. Against you we have sinned. Hope of Israel, O Lord, you will save in the time of troubles. Why have you become like a stranger in the land, like a native who turns aside to lodge for the night? Will you be like a man asleep, or like a man who cannot save? Yet you are among us, O Lord, and your name has been called upon us; do not forget us." And again: "Woe is me, my soul! For the godly man has perished from the earth, and there is no one among men who does right. They all go to law for blood; each oppresses his neighbour with oppression. They make their hands ready for evil." In such laments of the prophets we shall recognize the report that Israel had become leprous. The priest, then, orders that the house be cleared out. For God's visitation upon our offences is a most fearful thing, and those who are guilty must be punished. Therefore, because he loves humankind, he commands those already in such evils to love cleansing and to clear away the disease that has struck them, and in this way to forestall the penalty that comes with the visitation. So it is in the words: "Wash your heart clean of wickedness, O Jerusalem, that you may be saved. How long will thoughts of your troubles remain within you?" And what could the "thoughts of troubles" reasonably be taken to mean, if not those very thoughts through which we have fallen into troubles and into the penalties for our offences? See, then, how in these words the priest commands that the causes be cleared away beforehand, the causes for which, one may reasonably suppose, a person would fall under punishment.

Then he says: "And the priest shall go in to examine the house, and he shall see the infection; and look, the infection is in the walls." And again: "The priest shall go out of the house to the door of the house, and the priest shall shut up the house for seven days." For after the warning given out of goodness, and the requirement that the house be cleansed beforehand [?], wickedness appeared again in the form of leprosy. Naturally this roused the priest, who here represents God, to justified indignation. So, having again inspected the infection, that is, the signs and marks of the disease, he shut up the house for a full seven days. For God, though he loves humankind, was grieved, and with very good reason, at the outrages of the people of Israel against the law. He sent them all into captivity, handing them over to the Babylonians for a full seventy years, counting each day as ten. He says the days for which the house is shut up are seven, reckoning a day as ten years, in keeping with what was said to the prophet Ezekiel: "I have assigned you a day for each year." The angel who prays for the synagogue in Zechariah also sets his seal on this account, saying: "Lord Almighty, how long will you withhold mercy from Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, which you have disregarded? This is the seventieth year." Then he says again: "The priest shall return on the seventh day." By the priest's return you are to understand here nothing other than the turning of God's love for humankind back toward the nation, as in the words: "Therefore thus says the Lord: I will return to Jerusalem with compassion, and my house will be rebuilt in it, says the Lord Almighty, and a measuring line will be stretched out over Jerusalem." Or again, as in this passage: "How shall I deal with you, Ephraim? Shall I shield you, Israel? Shall I make you like Admah and Zeboiim? My heart is turned within me; my remorse is stirred. I will not act toward you according to my fierce anger; I will not abandon Ephraim to be blotted out. For I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst." So he says that the priest returns on the seventh day to see the house, "and look, the infection has spread in the walls of the house; and the priest shall give orders, and they shall take out the stones in which the infection is and throw them outside the city." And a little later: "And they shall take other dressed stones and put them in place of those stones." For after the nation had been released from the charge for its past offences, God, who searches out everything within us, surveyed the synagogue of the Jews once more. He found it, as might be expected, no longer leprous throughout, yet not entirely rid of its old wickedness. So he did not direct his anger against all, but only against those who had caused its sickness and had become the occasion of the disease. These he calls stones, indicating certain parts of the whole house, that is, of the nation. Some of them were the kings of various periods who led the people astray into other forms of worship. Others were the false prophets, who spoke out of their own hearts, as it is written, and undermined the piety of those who listened to them. These he orders to be removed from the house, signifying their being set apart, that is, their being cast out to destruction. Such is what God said about Jeconiah: "Earth, hear the words of the Lord: Record this man as a man cast out." And about the false diviners: "Therefore I have cut down your prophets; I have slain them by the word of my mouth." And again: "Therefore the leaders of the people shall be cast out of their houses of luxury; because of their evil practices they have been driven out." And again: "Because of uncleanness you were destroyed with destruction." The bringing in of other stones, clean and dressed, in place of those removed signifies that at various times, by God's counsel, certain people were raised up to prop up the house of Israel again and hold it together in an uncorrupted state, whether kings, or prophets, or saints. So it is in what God said to the blessed Isaiah: "Thus says the Lord of hosts: Go into the chamber, to Shebna the steward, and say to him: What are you doing here, and what business have you here, that you have hewn yourself a tomb here, and made yourself a tomb on high, and carved yourself a dwelling in the rock? Look, the Lord of hosts will cast out and crush a man, and will take away your robe and your glorious crown, and will hurl you into a great and boundless land, and there you will die. And he will turn your fine chariot to dishonour, and the house of your ruler to be trampled underfoot. And you will be removed from your stewardship and from your post. And on that day I will call my servant Eliakim son of Hilkiah, and I will clothe him with your robe, and give him your crown, and put your power and your stewardship into his hands, and he will be like a father to those who live in Jerusalem." "But they shall also take other mortar," he says, "and plaster the house," using "plaster" in the sense of "coat over." This too signifies the exhortation given to Israel through the holy prophets. They coated sinners over with fine and good words and persuaded them to go eagerly toward what pleases God, to scrub off the defilement of the passions, and instead to strive and press on toward whatever the lawgiver knew to be beneficial for those who worship him. Such is the word spoken to them through one of the saints: "Seek good and not evil, that you may live; and so the Lord God Almighty will be with you." After this he says: "But if the infection of leprosy comes again and breaks out in the house after the stones have been taken out, and after the house has been scraped, and after it has been plastered, then the priest shall go in and see whether the infection has spread in the house. It is a persistent leprosy in the house; it is unclean. And they shall pull down the house, and its timbers and its stones and all the mortar of the house they shall carry outside the city into an unclean place." For every method of treatment had been devised for the people of Israel. The removal of the scabby stones had done no good, and the plastering through the prophets, that is, their exhortation, had in the end proved useless. Then the priest enters once more to inspect the leprous house. For the Only-begotten entered this world with a body. When he became man, he came to inspect carefully how great a change, and of what kind, the synagogue would show, from its old wickedness to a thoroughly good way of life. But since he found it still in the grip of its old passions and sick with a persistent uncleanness, he at last orders it to be pulled down and sent away into an unclean place. For the whole order of the Jews under the law has been dissolved, and the nation has been scattered into every unclean place, as was said in the prophets: "And I will scatter them to every wind," or, "I will winnow them among all the nations." In this connection you will also do well to take what the Saviour said about their temple: "Do you see all these things? Truly I tell you, not one stone will be left here on another that will not be thrown down." To this he adds: "Everyone who enters the house during all the days it is shut up shall be unclean until evening. And whoever sleeps in the house shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening." And whoever eats in the house likewise. This clearly indicates that everyone who in any way at all attaches himself to the Jews by sharing their mind will certainly share in their uncleanness as well. Then he brings in the priest yet again to look over the leprous house: "For if the priest comes," he says, "and goes in and looks, and look, the infection has not spread at all in the house after the house was plastered, because the infection is healed." For the synagogue of the Jews was pulled down as unclean because of its outrage against Christ, and it fell away from God's friendship. Yet after it has remained in this state for a long time, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in, as Paul puts it, it will be shown mercy by Christ. As God, he will visit it again in a hidden way and in the last times bring it back to righteousness, that is, to the righteousness that comes through faith in him and love for him. The High Priest of all, then, will come to inspect it once more, and finding it improved, he will at once cleanse it and receive it, as was said through the holy prophets: "On that day, says the Lord, I will gather her who was driven away, and receive her who was crushed, and those whom I drove away; and I will make her who was crushed a remnant." And again in another place: "For the sons of Israel will remain many days without king and without ruler, without sacrifice and without altar, without priesthood and without manifestations. And afterward the sons of Israel will return and seek the Lord their God and David their king; and they will be amazed at the Lord and at his good things in the last days." So when the priest inspects the leprous house, he says, and declares it clean, they shall take, to purify the house, two small birds, living and clean, and cedar wood, and spun scarlet, and hyssop. And again: "He shall dip the living bird in the blood of the bird slaughtered over running water, and with the living bird, and with the cedar wood, and with the hyssop, and with the spun scarlet; and he shall send the living bird out of the city into a clean field, and make atonement for the house, and it shall be clean."

Here again, look closely and you will see clearly the whole mystery of our Savior, and the cleansing that comes through holy baptism. The law commands two birds to be taken, living and clean, so that through these winged creatures you may understand the heavenly one, man and God at once. He is divided into two natures only so far as the account proper to each requires. For he was the Word who shone forth from God the Father, in flesh taken from a woman, yet he was not divided. Christ is one, from both. This is why the birds are taken as two, and yet both are understood as one, but as living and clean. For the Word himself, in himself, is the giver of life and of all purity, and so is the temple from the Virgin, which has the living Word within it. The body was his own, not a garment belonging to someone else. That is why there is one Lord Jesus Christ. Besides the birds, the law also commands cedar wood to be taken, so that by it you may understand that the body of Christ is incorruptible. For it knows no corruption, and cedar resists decay. And when we understand that the holy body of Christ did not decay, the teaching about his resurrection becomes entirely credible. The spun scarlet signifies the confession of our Savior's death. Indeed, the Song of Songs says somewhere of the Church: "Your lips are like a scarlet thread, my sister, my bride." The lips of the Church always proclaim the salvation that comes through the blood of Christ, and she bids whoever comes to her to make the confession of faith in that blood. So the Song rightly compares her lips to a scarlet thread. And sharing in the mystical blessing itself also proclaims the death and resurrection of Christ himself. We first persuade believers to confess these things, and then we bring them to holy baptism and perfect them in the blood of the eternal covenant, as it is written. So by the scarlet the law signifies the confession of faith in the blood of Christ, and by the hyssop the fervor of the Holy Spirit. For the herb is hot and scours away ailments that come from cold. Such too is the working and power of the Holy Spirit in us. So the law says that the one who purifies the leprous house shall take the living bird, the cedar wood, the scarlet and the hyssop, and dip them in the blood of the slaughtered bird over living water, and sprinkle the house with them seven times. "And he shall purify the house with the blood of the bird, and with the living water, and with the cedar wood, and with the hyssop, and with the spun scarlet." Here again the law shows us that the synagogue of the Jews cannot wash away the defilement of its disobedience, or put off the stain of its many different offenses, in any other way than through the blessing that comes from Christ alone, and through confession of him and faith in him, which are of course perfected and sanctified through holy baptism. Notice how the whole Christ is painted for us in these things, and how faith in him and confession of him are signified. By the living bird you may understand the ever-living, life-giving and heavenly Word, and by the slaughtered bird, the precious blood of the temple that suffered. For we say that he suffered in the flesh, but as in his own body. By the wood that does not rot, understand the incorruptible flesh; by the hyssop, the Spirit; by the scarlet, the confession of the blood of the covenant; by the living water, the life-giving grace of baptism. The holy side of our Savior aptly signified this grace in the passion itself, when it sent out water together with the blood. The law says that the house must be sprinkled with this, so that it may be purified, as was said to Ezekiel the prophet: "I will take you from the nations and gather you from the lands, and I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be cleansed." And the law commands that it be sprinkled not just once but seven times. For where sin increased, grace overflowed all the more. Then the lawgiver adds that he shall send the living bird out of the city into the open field, and make atonement for the house, and it shall be clean. We have taken the house just mentioned as a type of the synagogue of the Jews, that is, of the whole nation. Let us grant that a city is something that contains many houses. You may understand our inhabited world to be such a city. It holds many races of people and is girded all around by the firmament as if by a wall, and beyond that we understand the broad and pure field of the worlds above. So when the lawgiver has the bird released into the field outside the city, he is teaching Christ's departure from the world and his ascent into heaven. For when he has come to his God and Father, he will make atonement for all of us and for the synagogue of the Jews, and we shall be cleansed. As John, the wisest of disciples, says: "We have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the whole world." So he was right to say to the Jews: "If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me." Through him and with him [?] with the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

The Only-begotten, who is God by nature and from God the Father, lowered himself into our condition. As it is written, he was seen on earth and lived among men, and he did this for no other reason than that, as the divine Paul says, he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in the things of God, to make atonement for the sins of the people. The law, ordained through Moses for the people of old with angels as mediators, appoints men as priests. They suffer from the common weakness of nature, and because of it they must offer sacrifice for their own sins of ignorance as well as for those of the people. But the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints a Son made perfect forever. That is why he is able to save completely those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them. Christ makes atonement, but not at all for himself, and the saying is true: "For he committed no sin." He makes atonement for us instead. The divine Paul makes this very clear to us when he writes of him: "whom God put forward as a propitiation through faith in his blood." For this reason he also says that Christ entered the Holy of Holies once for all, having obtained eternal redemption, and that by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified. We have been saved, but it is he who takes away our sins and suffers for us. He laid down his own life willingly for us, yet he came back to life. For he was God by nature, and he is in heaven at the right hand of the Father, always living to intercede for the saints, as I said just now. Again, I have said these things as though drawing on the shadow of the law, and I will explain clearly how that stands. It is written in Leviticus: "And the Lord said to Moses: Speak to Aaron your brother, and tell him not to enter the holy place inside the veil at every hour, before the mercy seat that is upon the ark of the testimony, and he will not die. For I will appear in a cloud upon the mercy seat." It was necessary, truly necessary, that Aaron, who was appointed to fulfill the image and type of Christ's priesthood, should not enter the Holy of Holies at every hour, that is, at just any time, for in this he points, as it were, to the beauty of the mystery. Christ entered once, having obtained eternal redemption, as I said. So if Aaron entered the Holy of Holies not once a year but at every hour, as though at any time he liked, it would be an offense against the truth itself through the things that are its types. For this reason God commanded that the rule be kept, so that Aaron might not die. But if death was the penalty for anyone who broke the shadow and insulted the type of the truth, what punishment will there be for those who offend against the truth itself, that is, Christ? This is exactly what the Jews did. They did not accept faith in him and dishonored him in countless ways, even though he said plainly: "I am the truth," that is, the fulfillment of the types in the law. For Christ is the end of the law and the prophets, as the most holy Paul, learned in the law, writes to us. Aaron is therefore forbidden to enter the Holy of Holies continually, so that the beauty of the mystery might shine on us unimpaired and pure even in the shadows themselves. So the entry took place once a year, at one appointed time. And God laid down by law how it should be done so as not to fall short of what was fitting, saying: "This is how Aaron shall enter the holy place: with a calf from the herd for a sin offering and a ram for a whole burnt offering. He shall put on a consecrated linen tunic, linen drawers shall be on his body, he shall gird himself with a linen sash, and he shall put on a linen turban. These are holy garments; he shall wash his whole body with water and then put them on. From the congregation of the sons of Israel he shall take two male goats for a sin offering and one ram for a whole burnt offering. Aaron shall bring the calf for his own sin and make atonement for himself and for his house. He shall take the two goats and set them before the Lord at the door of the tent of testimony, and Aaron shall cast lots over the two goats, one lot for the Lord and one lot for the Sent-Away. Aaron shall bring the goat on which the lot for the Lord fell and offer it for sin. The goat on which the lot for the Sent-Away fell he shall set alive before the Lord, to make atonement over it, so as to send it away, and he shall release it into the wilderness." In these words he explains to us how the sacrifice was done. Next, Aaron brought the calf for his own sin and for that of his house. Once the calf had been sacrificed and the ram had been made a whole burnt offering, according to the law that applied to it, "he shall take," it says, "the censer full of burning coals from the altar before the Lord. He shall fill his hands with finely blended incense and bring it inside the veil, and he shall put the incense on the fire before the Lord, and the smoke of the incense shall cover the mercy seat that is over the testimonies, and he will not die. He shall take some of the calf's blood and sprinkle the altar with his finger; he shall sprinkle some of the blood seven times with his finger." And he adds: "He shall slaughter the goat for sin, the one from the people, before the Lord, and bring some of its blood inside the veil, and he shall do with its blood as he did with the blood of the calf." He commanded all these things to be done to make atonement, I mean, for the uncleannesses of the sons of Israel and for all their sins. The blood of both the calf and the goat was smeared not only on the mercy seat and the inner tent, that is, the Holy of Holies, but also on the altar of burnt offerings itself, in the first tent. For again he said: "He shall go out to the altar that is before the Lord and make atonement on it. He shall take some of the calf's blood and some of the goat's blood and put it on the horns of the altar all around. He shall sprinkle some of the blood on it with his finger seven times, and cleanse it and sanctify it from the uncleannesses of the sons of Israel." And again he adds: "He shall bring the live goat, and Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat. He shall confess over it all the lawless deeds of the sons of Israel, all their wrongs and all their sins. He shall put them on the head of the live goat and send it away into the wilderness in the hand of a man who stands ready. The goat shall carry their lawless deeds on itself into the trackless land, and he shall send the goat away into the wilderness."

This, then, is what was ordained in types for its time, and this is how it was carried out. But now the shadow has passed and the time of reformation has come. So come, let us use fine and discerning thought to carry the aim of the law over into the mystery of Christ. Our Lord Jesus Christ entered the Holy of Holies once for all, having obtained eternal redemption. Yet he entered with the blood of an eternal covenant: not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood, wiping away the sin of the world. He was sacrificed not for any sin of his own but for our salvation. Let us, then, follow the shadows of the law very closely. It was entirely fitting, or rather necessary, for the divine Aaron to offer sacrifice for his own sins of ignorance. Since he was a man, he could not be thought to stand above sinning. But that will not fit Christ at all, far from it. As God, he is rich in sinlessness by his own nature. Yet in him and through him comes the cleansing even of those who have been sanctified, I mean both the priests and the peoples. See how Aaron, in the victims offered for himself, foreshadows the sacrifice we understand in Christ and its spiritual fragrance. There was a calf, and a ram for a whole burnt offering. Again, Christ is understood as in the calf. The offerings brought to God on behalf of the saints are very plentiful, and their forms are very rich. The calf is a sacred animal and ranks above all the others fit for sacrifice. So the calf would hint to us at the perfection of the sacrifice. Then there is the ram for a whole burnt offering, for our Lord Jesus Christ became a sweet-smelling fragrance to God the Father, dispelling in himself what we might call the loathsome stench of the world's sin. Notice that when Aaron is commanded to enter the Holy of Holies at the appointed times and duly to complete the sacrifices for his own sins of ignorance, he is not seen in the vestments of the high priesthood on that occasion. Instead, it says, "he shall put on a consecrated linen tunic, linen drawers shall be on his body, he shall gird himself with a linen sash, and he shall put on a linen turban. These are holy garments, and he shall wash his whole body in water." But this attire was customary for all who performed sacred service, and prescribed by the law. What plausible account of this can we give, as I think, or rather what true one? It was not fitting that Aaron, while sacrificing for his own offenses, should appear in the likeness of Christ, who knew no sin. For the vesture most proper to him, the very attire of the high priesthood, portrayed the beauty of our Savior's kingship and priesthood together. And the law showed clearly that no one can enter the Holy of Holies, the true tabernacle that the Lord pitched and not man, unless he has first been purified by the water of regeneration, since it commanded Aaron to wash in water if he was about to enter the Holy of Holies. He commanded that coals be taken from the altar itself and carried within, that is, inside the veil. And he directs them to fill their hands with fine incense. When this has been done, "the smoke of the incense," it says, "shall cover the mercy seat that is over the testimonies." This was a type of Christ. He is sacrificed as a calf and wholly burnt as a ram, and he fills the whole holy tabernacle, that is, the Church, with spiritual fragrance, so that we will say: "Your name is perfume poured out. That is why the maidens loved you and drew you. We will run after you toward the fragrance of your perfume." But come, let us take the discussion back to the beginning, for that way our explanation of the meanings will keep straight to the proper path. A calf and a ram, then, were the animals brought for sacrifice on Aaron's behalf, while two goats came from the people, along with a ram as a burnt offering. For it is written that there were lots for the goats, one for the Lord and the other for the Sent-Away. We must say what mystery lies in them. Some think that one of the goats is given and released in the wilderness to an unclean demon, an "averter" called the Sent-Away. We say that this opinion is full of outlandish superstition and cannot escape the charges that attach to pagan error. Indeed, to say something greater still without holding back: on such lopsided reasoning, we would find that the law introduces sin against God, even though it draws people away from polytheistic error in many ways, points to the one who is by nature Lord of all, and habitually guides people to the knowledge of the truth. For anyone used to thinking rightly would immediately ask: Why did God command that it be released and handed over like a sacrifice offered to an evil and hostile power, I mean the goat? And what useful purpose would we find Aaron to have served when he laid his hands on the goat and confessed the sins of the sons of Israel? Would the whole affair not then be seen as full of the utmost folly and pagan impiety, and not free of crude thinking? Who could still dispute, or how, that a view so plainly unsound deserves to be rejected?

What, then, was being enacted? Two goats were brought. They were fine animals, equal to each other in size, of the same age and the same color, and without blemish of any kind. Then two lots were written, clearly marking the names of the goats, as the lawgiver intended. One goat was named Lord, and the other Sent-Away. Since the goats were named in this way, one Lord and the other Sent-Away (it had this name because it was sent away), we will understand that "Sent-Away" refers not to a demon but to the animal itself. The goat called Lord (this, as I said, was the name of one of the goats) was slaughtered with fitting honor. With its blood it sanctified the innermost tent, and also the outer altar of burnt offerings, on which the sacrifices prescribed by the law were performed. The other goat, that is, the Sent-Away, was sent out into the trackless land after Aaron had confessed the sins of the sons of Israel over it. Both of them signify Christ. He died as a man and was sacrificed for us, as though in the form of a goat. For the goat was slaughtered for the forgiveness of sins, and it sanctified the Church, which we understand to be typified by the innermost tent, and also those under the law. For, as I said, even the altar of the law was sanctified with the goat's blood. And beyond all dispute, the lesser is blessed by the greater. So perfection does not lie in the law, and worship according to the law cannot sanctify anyone. It necessarily needs Christ, who is able to make perfect, and who sanctifies with his own blood those who practice the worship of the law. That is why the divine Paul, speaking of himself and of those called from the circumcision, says somewhere: "Knowing that a man is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Jesus Christ," that is, so that we might have the justification that comes from him. So he was sacrificed for our sins, according to the Scriptures; but he came back to life and departed to the region that is inaccessible to men, that is, to heaven, carrying away our sins, as it were. For he himself, as it says somewhere, takes away our sins and suffers for us. This, I think, is the Sent-Away. He was sent away, as it were, from our world to the city above, "now to appear in the presence of God on your behalf." The blessed John confirms us in this when he writes: "Little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for those of the whole world." So it is agreed that we have been washed clean in Christ, and by his wound we were healed. He is our advocate, and he has gone up to the region inaccessible to men, of which the wilderness would be a type. For he entered into the world as a forerunner on our behalf, and he himself opened for us the way, new and living, that leads within the veil. Christ, then, is the Sent-Away, bearing our sins as though in the form of a goat. For, as I said, a goat was slaughtered for sins. And the fact that the goats were equal and alike in every respect showed in a riddle that he is one and the same. Since the slaughtered goat could not come back to life (that would have looked like mere wonder-working and nothing else, and the Divine never makes a show of itself, even though it can do all things in marvelous ways), two goats were deliberately taken that matched each other exactly and without flaw. In the same way, in the cleansing of the leper, the lawgiver ordained that two small birds must be brought, one of which was slaughtered while the other was released in the wilderness. For the law has taught us the mystery of Christ through countless very vivid examples. Through him and with him be glory and power to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

The wretched Jews, by letting loose a harsh and boorish tongue against Christ, could be convicted on many counts. And that the matter did not go unpunished for them anyone can see from what actually happened. For Israel the firstborn, who enjoyed the splendid glory that came with this, the beloved and chosen one, has been put behind the Gentiles and has come to be among the last, or rather in every kind of evil. The Lord foretold this to them, saying through Hosea: “Woe to them, for they have strayed from me. They are wretched, for they have acted lawlessly against me. I redeemed them, but they spoke lies against me.” For there is nothing jarring to speak of that they have not dared to say. They have uttered blasphemy, not considering what is written: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who master it will eat its fruits.” And since they behaved outrageously toward him, letting loose their tongue unbridled for slander, as I said just now, for this very reason they have also slipped away from the hope that is in him, and would not listen to him when he says: “This is your lot and your portion, because you disobeyed me, says the Lord.” So then, that they became liable to the charge of a loose tongue and were bound to pay bitter penalties for their outrage against Christ, we shall establish very well from what is written in Numbers as well. It reads as follows: “And Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses on account of the Ethiopian woman whom Moses had taken, for he had taken an Ethiopian wife. And they said, ‘Has the Lord spoken to Moses alone? Has he not spoken to us also?’ And the Lord heard. Now the man Moses was very meek, more than all the people who were on the earth. And at once the Lord said to Moses and Aaron and Miriam, ‘Come out, you three, to the tent of witness.’ And the three came out to the tent of witness. And the Lord came down in a pillar of cloud and stood at the doors of the tent of witness; and Aaron and Miriam were called, and both of them came out. And the Lord said to them, ‘Hear my word. If there is a prophet of the Lord among you, I will make myself known to him in a vision, and I will speak to him in a dream. Not so with my servant Moses: he is faithful in all my house. Mouth to mouth I will speak to him, in plain sight and not in riddles, and he has seen my glory. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?’ And the anger of the Lord’s wrath was upon them, and they went away; and the cloud withdrew from the tent; and behold, Miriam was leprous, white as snow. And Aaron looked at Miriam, and behold, she was leprous. And Aaron said to Moses, ‘I beg you, lord, do not lay sin upon us, for we did not know against whom we sinned. Let her not become like one dead, like a stillborn child coming out of its mother’s womb, and it eats away half her flesh.’ And Moses cried out to the Lord, saying, ‘O God, I beg you, heal her.’ And the Lord said to Moses, ‘If her father had spat in her face, would she not be put to shame? She shall be shut out of the camp for seven days, and after that she shall come back in.’ And Miriam was shut out of the camp for seven days, and the people did not set out until Miriam was cleansed.” These things, then, are akin to what has already been said. They are not far removed from the interpretation given there, but carry a meaning that is its sister and, as it were, grown from the same root. For these too speak of the mystery, and they present the dishonor that befell the synagogue of the Jews for its outrages against him. Yet the nature of the offenses differs somewhat in one small respect. In that earlier passage the Synagogue was leprous and unclean, ruining herself by many and various falls. Here, however, the account depicts for us the charges relating only to the outrage against Christ: it portrays the puffed-up arrogance of the Jews and displays the meekness of him who says, “Learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart.” Besides this, it also presents the loving-kindness of the righteous Judge, who does not bring his wrath upon offenders forever or without end, but after striking binds up the wound, saving and healing. To put it summarily, then, in a few words, the aim of the passage before us tends wholly in this direction. So let us take each of the things said, part by part, and unfold the meaning hidden in them, with God opening a door for our discourse, he who says to those who hope in him: “And I will give you treasures that are dark and hidden; I will open to you things unseen.”

So Aaron and Miriam spoke against the all-wise Moses on account of the Ethiopian woman whom he had taken, and they said: “Has the Lord spoken to Moses alone? Has he not spoken to us also?” These are the two charges in their idle talk against Moses: first, that he took a wife, the Ethiopian, I mean; and second, in addition to this, the saying, “Has the Lord spoken to Moses alone? Has he not spoken to us also?” In the first he faces an indictment for breaking the law; in the second it is claimed that he was not ranked so very high among the great, nor had received any grace beyond the others, if indeed God is seen to have spoken to others too. We shall speak in order, assigning our first discussion to the first accusation, and from there we shall then carry over what is in the types to Christ himself. Now Moses had married a wife long before and made the Midianite woman his partner, Jethro’s daughter, I mean; but after no little time had gone by, he took the Ethiopian woman as a further wife, a foreigner and black. And this although the lawgiver clearly declared that the children of Israel must not intermarry with foreigners at all. For thus it is written: “You shall not give your daughter to his son, and you shall not take his daughter for your son.” On these grounds the great Moses is judged guilty of breaking the law by Aaron and Miriam, who, it seems, had not perceived the mystery that was well arranged through him, once again as in a type. This we shall now make as clear as we can, fitting the nature of the matter very well to Christ himself, on whom we shall now place the role of Moses. For Christ is lawgiver and mediator between God and humanity, just as that man certainly was too. Indeed Moses himself pointed to this when he said: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me.” Aaron will be taken as the figure of the Jewish priesthood, and Miriam will play the part of the Synagogue. So the elders of the Jews accused our Savior Christ, and the Synagogue herself along with them, charging him with transgressing the divine commandments by saying: “If this man were from God, he would not break the Sabbath.” And they were furious with him in another way too, because he betrothed the black woman, that is, the church from the Gentiles, and in a sense married her in addition to the first, that is, the Israelite woman, who again was the Synagogue. That they were furious when the customs drawn from pointless observance, or from what Moses had spoken in types, were being abolished for them is not hard to see for anyone who has once become acquainted with the Gospel writings. And again, that he betrothed the church from the Gentiles while she was still blackened by darkness in knowledge and in conduct (for the true light, which knows how to brighten and whiten, was not yet in her), one could quite easily prove from the prophets. But it seems more fitting to me to show it from the Savior’s own dispensation. He preached, then, to the Samaritans, who were foreigners, and in them laid down beforehand a kind of beginning and foundation of the church from the Gentiles. That they were foreigners and lodged outside the flock of Israel one can see without effort from the following. When he sent out his disciples to proclaim the message of the kingdom of heaven, he said: “Do not go off on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter any city of the Samaritans. Go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” Do you see how he placed them outside the sheep of the house of Israel? So, while he had not yet departed from his marriage to the Israelite woman, that is, the Synagogue, but still seemed in some way to live with her, he in a sense betrothed and married in addition the black foreign woman, that is, the church from the Gentiles. That is why, when talking with the Jews, he said: “And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and there will be one flock, one shepherd.” And he refuted them somewhat more sharply as disobedient when they asked him outright, “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.” Jesus answered them: “I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name bear witness about me. But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep.” For he already called those from the Gentiles his own sheep. At this the Pharisees were greatly enraged and angry with him, as one who loved foreigners and set the things of God at nothing, and appealing to the law they said: “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” For if you did not side with the Samaritans, they say, if you were not a lover of Greeks and a lover of foreigners, you would never have mixed with people from the Gentiles. And if the demon that is among the Greeks were not in you (for they called idolaters demon-possessed because of the devil who was in them), you would not, they say, have treated transgression of the law’s commandments as of no account. And yet what comes through Christ is above all a fulfillment of the law rather than a transgression, according to what he said: “I did not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it.” For it was simply the transformation of the letter into truth. Such, then, is the nature of the accusation about the black woman, and the picture of the perversity shown toward Christ will be taken from what concerns Moses. Next we shall bring in the slander that is neighbor and sister to this one, once again transposing the sense of what is said from type to truth. “For the Lord has not spoken to Moses alone,” they say, “but he has spoken to us also.” The word comes from arrogance, the utterance from empty conceit. Surely those who think rightly ought not to hasten to climb to an equal measure with the one who rightly heard, “I know you above all, and you have found favor with me.” They should rather offer thanks for the honors they have received, not overstepping the rank appointed from above, nor seizing for themselves the honor so given; for that could justly be regarded as having its share in the utmost arrogance. But consider again our Lord Jesus Christ, making plain to the Jews the purpose of God the Father, which is known by nature to him alone, and saying: “I do not speak on my own; but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment about what to say and what to speak.” And again: “The words that I speak are not mine, but his who sent me.” Then consider in turn the lawless scribes and Pharisees, intent on growing insolent against this, and arrogant beyond measure because God had spoken to their fathers, and for this reason choosing to disobey. For they say: “We know that God has spoken to Moses; but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from.” Do you see, then, how by saying they know well that God spoke to Moses, they all but repeat that ancient saying in harsher words: “Has God the Father spoken to Christ alone, and not to our fathers?”—at Sinai, that is, they mean. “And the Lord heard. And the man Moses was very meek, more than all the people who were on the earth.” Miriam and Aaron, it seems, made Moses’ meekness an occasion for arrogance. But at this God is angry, even though Moses held his peace, and comes unsummoned to show just indignation against those who dared to insult him, taking to himself the contempt shown to his true minister. You will understand it the same way in the case of Christ. Because of the meekness and loving-kindness that were in him, the Pharisees were all the more prone to contempt. But it was plain to see, it seems, beyond all dispute, that they would not escape the wrath stirred from above. For God the Father, being insulted in the Son, was bound to take offense. For he knew without being taught, by a knowledge befitting God, the words spat out by the Pharisees in their arrogance.

Then, next after this: “And at once the Lord said,” it says, “to Moses and Aaron and Miriam, ‘Come out, you three, to the tent of witness.’ And the Lord came down in a pillar of cloud and stood at the doors of the tent of witness.” Here again the passage hints that God will be the judge of those who speak against our Savior Jesus Christ, and that he will surely come down in justice to wrath against those who have dared to revile him and to contend for equal honor with him. But the judgment is certainly carried out through the Son, with the one who begot him plainly present with him inseparably, according to the saying, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” And since Miriam and Aaron were seen standing before the righteous Judge, he says: “Hear my words. If there is a prophet of the Lord among you, I will make myself known to him in a vision, and I will speak to him in sleep. Not so with my servant Moses, who is faithful in all my house: mouth to mouth I will speak to him, in plain sight and not in riddles. And he has seen the glory of the Lord.” By this Moses’ preeminence over the others in beholding God is upheld, and his ability to hear the divine words in an extraordinary way is well attested. But you may see this more truly in Christ. For God the Father did not speak in the Son in the way he spoke in the prophets. The prophets were supplied by the Spirit with the knowledge of what they needed to learn; but the Son knows the counsels that are in the Spirit without being taught, since he is the Wisdom and Counsel of the one who begot him. And the blessed prophets received a vision of his glory through riddles, for no one has ever seen God; he is beheld only by the one who is Son by nature. That is how it should be understood in a way befitting God. And the Savior himself will be our witness to this, when he says: “Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.” So it was unreasonable, or rather downright impious, for the Jews to hold up the fact that God had spoken to their fathers and set at naught Christ when he said that he speaks the very things he heard from the Father. For what took place on Mount Sinai consists of shadows and types and riddles, bearing within them a knowledge of what was commanded that was hidden and far from clear. But Christ heard the Father’s words with his own ears, if, because the thought absolutely requires it, one may speak in rather bodily terms. Moreover, the passage also brings out how greatly Christ differs from all the others: “For he is faithful in all my house.” Does it not show by this that the dispensation through the law and the prophets was partial and limited, while that through Christ is general and universal? For the law saved one house, that of Israel; but not so Christ, who purchases the whole world for God the Father through faith in him and through his own blood, as it is written. Why then, it says, “were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?” For this is the same as what was spoken long ago through the prophet to the unholy Pharisees because of their idle and unrestrained talk about Christ: “But you, draw near here, you lawless sons, offspring of adulterers and a harlot. In whom have you taken delight? Against whom have you opened your mouth? Against whom have you let loose your tongue?” For the Pharisees, as though slackening entirely the reins of their God-fighting tongue, made their slander of Christ run very glibly, and, puffed up to overweening arrogance, they belch out the words of their madness. Deeply pained at them, the Psalmist says: “I said to the lawless, ‘Do not act lawlessly,’ and to the sinners, ‘Do not lift up your horn; do not lift up your horn on high, and do not speak injustice against God.’” For they truly acted lawlessly, impiously condemning the very one they ought least to have condemned; and they would be convicted of lifting up their horn on high, since they would not concede to Christ alone the knowledge of the Father’s will, but rather insisted that they themselves knew it, by saying, as was mentioned before, “We know that God has spoken to Moses,” and for this reason were eager to disobey. Then the cloud withdrew from the tent of witness, and at once Miriam appeared leprous, and not merely so, but white as snow. For the divine and pure nature, vexed at the outrages against Christ and the unholy audacities of the Jews and bitterly affected by them, in a sense flew up and departed from the Synagogue, according to what was said by Christ: “I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my inheritance.” For the Lord, who had come down in a pillar of cloud, departs again as a cloud, according to the type in the letter. And since he rightly withdrew from the synagogue of the Jews, she was at once shown to be unclean; and unclean not merely so, but having reached the very extreme of the disease. For to say that the leper was turned exceedingly white conveys how severe the disease was; and what could be whiter than snow? It was indeed to be expected, or rather necessary and beyond doubt, that the synagogue of the Jews, having fallen away from the care of the one who saves, would come to be in every kind of evil. So the untamed and mocking swarm of the rabble is punished with uncleanness and dishonor, according to what the saints rightly said to God: “Fill their faces with dishonor, and they will know that your name is Lord.” But Aaron, who joined Miriam in the accusation, is to good purpose not made leprous with her, even though he owed the Judge the same penalty. For since the priesthood is something precious and great before God, he escaped appearing leprous for this reason, and was punished instead with grief for her who suffered it, according to what was said by God: “Gird yourselves and lament, you priests; wail, you who minister at the altar; go in, in sackcloth, you who minister to God, for sacrifice and drink offering have ceased from the house of our God.” And he comes to the all-wise Moses, saying: “I beg you, lord, do not lay sin upon us, for we did not know against whom we sinned.” For those who were of Israel by race, and no strangers to the synagogue of the Jews by their kinship in the flesh, but had been appointed stewards of the mysteries of our Savior, were to offer up prayers on behalf of those who had sinned through ignorance, even though they themselves had stumbled along with them at the beginning. And they entreat Christ not to join in the Father’s wrath, as Paul did when he said: “Brothers, my heart’s desire and my prayer to God for them is for their salvation.” And the one who said this was both a steward of God’s mysteries and a priestly minister of the divine proclamation, which is what Aaron also was then. But when Moses cries out for the leprous woman and begs that she be healed, God postpones his pardon, saying: “Let her be shut out of the camp for seven days, and after that she will come back in.”

The passage shows us, as in an image, that the divine nature is swift to show mercy and in a sense most ready to be entreated, but is often made harsh by the number or the magnitude of our sins, and draws back from its loving-kindness toward the guilty. In our understanding, at least, it also signifies this: that much intercession of the saints has gone up to God on behalf of Israel; but since it was not fitting that Israel should go unpunished, having been condemned for no ordinary offenses, he put mercy second to justice. That God is often provoked by our sins, so that at times he even hesitates to bestow that gentleness which is most dear to him, is not at all hard to see from the following as well. The slaughter that was to come in its time upon the land of the Jews, when the Babylonians overran it by the law of war, was revealed through the Holy Spirit to Jeremiah the prophet; and as though many had already fallen and the dead were in view, he says to the holy prophet: “Woe is me, for my soul faints over the slain. Run through the streets of Jerusalem, and look, and take note, and search in her squares, to see if you can find a man, if there is anyone who does justice and seeks faithfulness, and I will be merciful to them, says the Lord.” Do you see in these words how he is in anguish over the slain and is readily willing to have mercy on Jerusalem, yet is all but held back by himself, reining in his divine gentleness because of the enormity of the sin, while nonetheless seeking occasions for compassion and wishing to end the effects of his wrath for the sake of a single man? For he proposed that whoever wished should show him one faithful man in the city. So Miriam is sent out, in the grip of leprosy. “But the people,” it says, “did not set out until Miriam was cleansed.” For we too who believe in Christ shall wait for the cleansing of the Jews, clearly the cleansing that comes through faith. And so, after that, leaving behind the tents of this life, we shall set out for the city above and hasten up to the land of promise. The Savior, then, speaks the truth when he says to the Jews: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me.” Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

Exceptional indeed is the lot of those who have chosen to love God, the King of all, for the possession of good things beyond understanding has been prepared for them. The blessed prophet Isaiah will confirm this when he says, "There is an inheritance for those who serve the Lord." And again: "And you will trust in the Lord, and he will lift you up onto the good things of the earth, and he will feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things." The promise, then, must be true, and firmly grounded in every way and altogether. The mouth of God could never miss the truth or ever lie, and it will certainly bring what it has promised to fulfillment. Knowing this, the inspired Psalmist says somewhere: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance; you are the one who restores my inheritance to me." Who, then, are those who serve the Lord, and to whom will so splendid and desirable a lot come? They are those who are eager to accomplish what pleases God, who know how to rush without hesitation toward anything at all that is admirable, and who have resolved to crush every enemy without the least shrinking. They do not rely on their own strength or skill, but hold out the grace from above like a weapon, and have the God of all as their champion and the one who shields them. Being so disposed, they say: "I will not hope in my bow, and my sword will not save me. For you saved us from those who afflict us, and you put to shame those who hate us." The good and the most courageous, and those readier to believe as they ought, he makes most illustrious, distributing good things with a generous hand. But those who have chosen to suffer from disobedience, the most shameful sickness of all, he will surely drive away from the flock of the chosen, and chase away from everything that can give joy. And he will declare to each of them, with perfect justice: "This is your portion, the portion for your disobedience to me." We shall find the peoples of the Jews to have fallen under such charges. They have therefore slipped away from their hope and remained disinherited, although the inheritance was theirs, if indeed it is true that the promises belong to them, as the blessed Paul says. But since they disobeyed the one who called them to these promises, they have remained without a share in them, and, in the Savior's words, "The last have become first, and the first last." This too was proclaimed to us beforehand in the more ancient Scriptures themselves. The passage runs as follows: "And after these things the people set out from Hazeroth and encamped in the wilderness of Paran. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying, 'Send men for yourself, and let them spy out the land of the Canaanites, which I am giving to the sons of Israel as a possession. You shall send them one man for each tribe, according to their ancestral clans, every one a leader among them.' And Moses sent them from the wilderness of Paran at the command of the Lord, all of them men who were leaders of the sons of Israel." These men, then, chosen from the tribes, twelve in number, were set apart from the rest of the multitude. They went up to examine very carefully whether the land was rich or thin-soiled: whether it was good for pasture, fertile and most productive, or dry and barren; whether it nourished cultivated trees and was granted the bearing of seasonable fruits, and whether its grain could grow thick even untended. Beyond this, they were to find out who its inhabitants were: whether they were formidable in strength, hard to defeat in war and not to be faced by just anyone, or easily overcome by those trained in valor. They were also to learn how many cities there were and of what kind, whether bare and unwalled or strongly fortified with towers. Moses added that they must also pluck some of the fruits and bring them back as proof, as it were. Having gone up, then, they hastened to carry out what they had been ordered. Since it was the right season, they surveyed the land and even carried off a cluster of grapes, a strange and unusual thing, a true marvel. They came back unharmed and returned to Moses. Yet they were still divided in their opinions. All of them saw fit to praise the land and reported that it was good and rich, and they brought the fruit taken from it as a witness to this. But some called the nation living on it bold, strong and most warlike, and yielding little to anyone in arrogance. "For we have seen sons of giants there," they said, so tall and huge that those of Israel's blood, I suppose, would look like locusts if compared with their stature. Caleb and Joshua, however, said plainly that the land was good and rich. "And if the Lord chooses us, he will bring us into it." And they affirmed once more that, with God as their champion, they would prevail in what had to be done. But when those of Israel, the great and herd-like multitude, heard such words, they at once fell into forgetfulness of God and lost all memory of the signs in Egypt.
