They were seized with great fear, they shrank from battle, they refused to resist, and they no longer longed for what had been promised. They gave no thought to the all-powerful and invincible hand of their helper, but wailed like children, and expected at any moment to be destroyed by the enemies' swords, together with their wives and dearest ones. They even dared to say that servitude in Egypt had been better for them and the burden of slavery easier to bear. Weeping, they said they must go back to the Egyptians; and when Joshua and Caleb urged them to courage and sprinkled dust on themselves, they tried to stone them. When matters had now come to such a pitch of misery, "the glory of the Lord appeared," it says, "in a cloud over the tent of witness among all the sons of Israel," and he was thinking of destroying them all without delay. But when Moses fell down before him and earnestly entreated him, he consented, though barely. "For the Lord said to Moses," it says, "'I am merciful to them according to your word. But as I live, and my name lives, the glory of the Lord shall fill all the earth. For all the men who have seen my glory and the signs that I did in Egypt and in this wilderness, and have tested me now this tenth time, and have not listened to my voice, shall surely not see the land that I swore to their fathers. Only their children who are here with me, all who do not know good or evil, every inexperienced youth, to these I will give the land. But all who provoked me shall not see it. My servant Caleb, however, because another spirit was in him and he followed me, I will bring into the land which he entered, and his seed shall inherit it.'" See, then, how grievous in God's eyes are the charges of disobedience, and how those who fall under them must endure a penalty hard to bear. This is exactly what we shall find Israel to have suffered when we compare the new things with the older Scriptures and show that the truth agrees with the shadows. Moses urges those chosen from all the tribes to go and examine carefully the land of promise. But when they had gone and come back, some of them, ten in number, spoke against it, and brought upon the whole congregation both fear and an unbelief hateful to God. The remaining two, Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua, urged them to go up and plunder it, and saw fit to praise the land itself, crying out plainly that it was rich and fruitful and excellent for raising crops. But the former fell away from the promise, while the latter, by heaven's vote, were made heirs of what is above and were honored by God.

It is now necessary to say what the true and spiritual interpretation is. Through the books of Moses, that is, through the good things for the saints that are prefigured in them in types, namely the holy land promised to the fathers, the mind of the Jews was in a certain way being sent out ahead. For it is possible, truly possible, to see the mystery of Christ foreshadowed by the types in the writings of the law, together with the sanctification in the Spirit that comes through him and the hope promised to the saints. The lamb in Egypt was sacrificed by those of Israel; they were anointed with its blood, and the destroyer was held back. The shadow announced in advance that death would lose its strength through the death of Christ, and that corruption would from then on pass by those anointed in the Holy Spirit. The law would show us no less that we shall also lay hold of the well-being granted in the beginning, and that man will be brought back again into the paradise of delight. For it commanded them to keep a feast in the seventh month, on the fifteenth of the month, taking in their hands shoots of palm trees, the fruit of a beautiful tree, thick branches of trees, willow and chaste-tree. And it commanded them to receive these not just at any time, but on the first day and on the seventh; and it calls the first day a holy convocation, and the seventh as well. In this it indicated the matter indirectly: paradise was given at the first time, at the beginning of the human race (I mean to Adam), and it will be given also at the last time, that is, at the consummation of the present age, of which the last of the seven days, the seventh, would be a very clear type. The first is holy, and the seventh. For holy was our time when our first father Adam was still keeping the commandment given to him; and holy again is the time at the end. For we have been sanctified in Christ, freed from the charges that arise from sin and made partakers of the Holy Spirit. So through type and shadow Moses, that is, the force of the writings of the law, all but sends ahead those who are quicker to learn and have, as it were, a chosen mind, to make an exact survey of what God has promised. But for those who wish to obtain such august and most glorious goods, the struggle is not against blood and flesh, but rather against principalities and powers and the world-rulers of this age, as it is written. Therefore those who mind the things of the flesh, who have preferred what is temporary and perishing to the delight that lasts forever, shrink from the battle. For see how those of Israel too, brought down by the words of the chosen men to such a depth of cowardice and misery, went on and on about their wives and children. Consider also those who, at the time when Christ the Savior of us all came among us, lost their faith through the words of the Jews. Our Lord Jesus Christ was granting the kingdom of heaven to those who believe. Yet he called them to boldness, clearly a spiritual boldness. And he commanded that those who trusted in him should thoroughly crush the greed of the devil, saying: "Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy." But they would not believe, putting bodily things before love for God. For when they were invited to the wedding, "they all," it says, "began with one accord to make excuses." One said, "I have bought a field"; another, "I have married a wife, and I cannot come." Do you see the kinship of these passions? Do you see the family likeness of these diseases? So the scribes and Pharisees in a certain way spoke against God's promise, by being unwilling to go into it themselves and by not letting others go in either. Therefore they also heard: "Woe to you lawyers, for you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering." For the peoples under their authority perished through the words of their leaders. Thus God says somewhere through the voice of the prophet: "The shepherds have acted foolishly and have not sought the Lord; therefore the whole flock did not understand, and they were scattered." Accordingly the great multitude of the Jews slipped away from the promise and came to have no share in the grace that comes through Christ. Yet the remnant has been saved through Christ. Of this too Caleb the son of Jephunneh would be a clear type, and Joshua as well. They said countless things to those of Israel, spurring them on to courage, calling the land good and desirable, and crying out that they would conquer the nations; yet they very nearly perished. "For all the congregation," it says, "spoke of stoning them." Yet they were in fact made heirs by God. Who, then, is Caleb? His name will make it clear. For it is translated "all heart," and Jephunneh in turn means "the turning." So those who have a heart that is perfect with God are sons of the turning, together with those of Joshua. These, again, would be those who have believed, understood as being represented first, as the firstfruits, by the holy apostles, who called Israel; and in them the remnant would be understood. In calling Israel they were put in danger, yet they were made heirs of the holy land. That the sons of the turning, that is, those who turned from the commandments of the law to the worship and grace that come through faith, have a whole, that is, a perfect heart with God, one may learn from Paul, who writes plainly that he regards the things of the law as refuse and counts them loss because of the surpassing worth of the knowledge of God, so that he may gain him and have the righteousness that comes from him. Israel, then, will slip away from the promise, yet will not perish entirely, but will be saved in a small portion; for this, I think, is the remnant. You will understand this well, as I have already said, when you see Caleb brought in by God's promise, with the Savior somehow yoked to him and running beside him; for that is what the name Jesus means. Indeed, the divine angel Gabriel himself, when he announced to the holy Virgin the manner of the Only-begotten's becoming man, said: "Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great, and will be called Son of the Most High." Did only the remnant of the synagogue of the Jews, then, inherit the promises and enter the sacred land? Far from it. The new people, the people of faith, came in together with it, as it were. For the God of all promised to bring in every young child together with Caleb. The divine David also indicated this to us when he said concerning the inheritance of the saints: "Let this be written for another generation, and the people that is being created shall praise the Lord." For the inheritance has been kept not for those who were being tutored under the law, but for another generation. And what is this other generation? The new people, as I said, the people of faith. For we have been created in Christ for newness of life, having put off the old man with its passions and desires. For Christ is said to have created the two peoples into one new man, making peace, and reconciling both to the Father in one Spirit. So the infants brought in together with Caleb would be a type of the new people. To these the divine disciple also wrote: "Like newborn infants, long for the spiritual and pure milk, so that by it you may grow up to salvation, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good." And you will clearly learn that the divine Paul too understood the things in the law in this way, and refashioned the type found in the letter into the truth, since he wrote to the Hebrews: "Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion, on the day of testing in the wilderness, where your fathers tested me, put me to the proof, and saw my works. For forty years I was provoked with that generation, and I said, 'They always go astray in their heart.' They did not know my ways, and I swore that they shall not enter my rest." And so that we too, thrusting away accursed unbelief and casting it as far as possible from our own souls, may be found heirs of the promise, he addressed them again: "Take care, brothers, that there is not in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, leading you to fall away from the living God. Rather, exhort one another every day, as long as it is called 'today,' so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. For we have become partakers of Christ, if indeed we hold the beginning of our confidence firm to the end, while it is said: 'Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion.' For some who heard rebelled, but not all who came out of Egypt through Moses. And with whom was he provoked for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, if not to those who disobeyed? And we see that they could not enter because of their disobedience." Their unruliness, their refusal to yield to the divine commands, brought about the loss of their hope for those who chose to practice it, while the opposite would be of no small benefit; and he will persuade us of this no less when he says: "Let us therefore fear lest, while the promise of entering his rest still remains, any of you should seem to have fallen short of it. For indeed we have had the good news preached to us, just as they did. But the word they heard did not benefit them, because it was not united by faith with those who heard it." For we who have believed in the Savior and Redeemer of us all enter into his rest. I mean Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, forever. Amen.

The inspired prophet Jeremiah rebuked the Jews for their love of learning, and very rightly, when he said: “How can you say, ‘We are very wise, and the law of the Lord is with us’? The false reed of the scribes was made in vain. The wise were put to shame; they were dismayed and caught, because they rejected the word of the Lord. What wisdom is in them?” The scribes and Pharisees were greatly puffed up over their knowledge of the laws. They raised their brows high and looked down on the common crowd. Yet they suffered badly from simple-mindedness, and the facts themselves exposed them as unwise and lacking in understanding. For they rejected the wisdom from above and from heaven, the Word from God the Father, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption. That is why they became reprobate and senseless, foolish and blind, as the Savior himself said. They thrust away the divine word and fled as far as they could from life-giving grace. They grieved God sorely by their constant disobedience and were caught out in countless ways, and so they perished by famine. This is what God had said through the voice of the prophets: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will bring a famine on the land: not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. And the waters will be shaken as far as the sea, and from the north to the east they will run about seeking the word of the Lord, and they will not find it.” They could have possessed that word in great abundance, but they most foolishly thrust it away. So they are now punished by divine sentence and deprived of the best things of all, the very things through which they might almost have grown rich in the good things from above. They chose to disobey and impiously outraged the divine and wonderful grace, and so the famine of divine teachings has been brought upon them, and very rightly. But for us who believe in him, Emmanuel has become the bread of life, the Bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world. In him and through him we outrun the God-hated power of corruption. We put on the grace from above and from heaven, that is, incorruption, and so we have been presented to God the Father, radiant and holy. Indeed, which good things of this kind do we not go on being rich in while in the world? The letter of the law leads us to such reflections. It reads as follows: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: When you enter the land into which I am bringing you, and you eat of the bread of the land, you shall set apart an offering, a portion reserved for the Lord, the firstfruits of your dough. You shall set apart a loaf as an offering; just like an offering from the threshing floor, so shall you set it apart: the firstfruits of your dough. And you shall give it as an offering to the Lord throughout your generations. But suppose you go astray and do not do all these commandments which the Lord spoke to Moses, all that the Lord God commanded you by the hand of Moses, from the day on which the Lord gave you commandment and onward throughout your generations. If it was done unintentionally, without the congregation’s knowledge, then the whole congregation shall offer one young bull from the herd, without blemish, as a whole burnt offering, for a fragrant aroma to the Lord, with its grain offering and its drink offering according to its ordinance, and one male goat for sin. And the priest shall make atonement for the whole congregation of the sons of Israel, and it shall be forgiven them, because it was unintentional; and they have brought their gift, an offering to the Lord, for their sin before the Lord, for their unintentional sins. And it shall be forgiven the whole congregation of the sons of Israel, and the proselyte who comes to join you, because for all the people it was unintentional. But if a single soul sins unintentionally, he shall bring one year-old she-goat for sin. And the priest shall make atonement before the Lord for the soul that acted unintentionally and sinned unintentionally, to make atonement for him. And it shall be forgiven him, whether he is a native among the sons of Israel or a proselyte who has joined them. There shall be one law among them for whoever acts unintentionally.” That is what we find in Numbers. In Leviticus the lawgiver shapes the mystery differently, but the insights it offers are not very different. Come, then, let us recall that passage as well, since it is very necessary for understanding, and weave a single account covering both. Again it is written as follows: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: When you enter the land which I am giving you and reap its harvest, you shall bring a sheaf, the firstfruits of your harvest, to the priest. And he shall lift up the sheaf before the Lord, to be accepted on your behalf; on the day after the first day the priest shall lift it up. And on the day on which you bring the sheaf you shall offer an unblemished year-old sheep as a whole burnt offering to the Lord. Its grain offering shall be two tenths of fine flour mixed with oil, an offering to the Lord for a fragrant aroma to the Lord, and its drink offering shall be a fourth of wine, and of bread. And you shall not eat parched new groats until this very day, until you have offered the gifts to your God. It is a perpetual statute throughout your generations, in all your dwellings.”

A sheaf, then, is the firstfruits of the crops and a symbol of a new and plentiful harvest. Bread, on the other hand, comes from grain that has already been gathered, heaped up on the threshing floor, and perhaps even brought into the storehouses. God commanded those already settled in the land of promise to make these an offering to him, so that Christ might be understood through both. He is the bread from heaven that gives life, and the firstfruits of the dough of those who are being created anew in him into newness of life. For Adam became the firstfruits of the older dough. But he disregarded the commandment he had been given and slipped into transgression, so he was at once accursed, and in him the human race was condemned to death and corruption. Christ, however, is the firstfruits of the second dough. He escaped the curse, clearly because he himself became a curse for us. And he drives out the power of corruption, again because he alone was free among the dead. For he came back to life, having trampled death underfoot. Then, renewed into incorruption, he ascended to the Father almost as a splendid offering and gift, as a kind of firstfruits of humanity. So the bread’s being carried into the holy tabernacle and laid up before God in the Holy of Holies would hint, and very fittingly, at Emmanuel’s ascent into heaven. For he went up not into anything made with hands, nor into copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, “now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf,” as it is written. The bread from heaven and from above gives life, and besides this it releases those on earth from their sins and frees them from their sins of ignorance, as he offers himself on their behalf to God the Father for a fragrant aroma. You will understand this very well if, with the eyes of the mind, you watch the bull being slaughtered as a whole burnt offering and the goat being slaughtered for the people’s sins of ignorance. For, as it is written, “Who can discern his transgressions?” Notice how clearly the lawgiver declared the cleansing through Christ to be incomparably superior to the worship under the law. For he says in effect: “If you transgress the precepts of Moses, and some of you are caught having disregarded a commandment of the legal worship, then, yes then, you will find forgiveness confirmed for you through blood, when a bull is sacrificed and a goat is offered.” And this was a type of Christ. So the law lays down the punishment for transgressors, but the precious blood of Christ releases us from the penalty and frees us from the charges incurred through ignorance. For he laid down his life for us, in order to abolish the sin of the world. So Christ may be understood in the bread as life and life-giver. Again, in the bull he is understood as wholly burnt and offering himself as a fragrant aroma to God the Father. And in the form of the goat he is understood as having become sin for our sake and as slaughtered for sins. The sheaf, in turn, should be understood in another way. What it signifies will be explained as far as possible. One might liken the human race to the ears of grain in a field. It springs up, as it were, from the earth, waits for the ripening proper to it, and in time is cut down by death the reaper. So Christ himself said to the holy disciples: “Do you not say, ‘There are still four months, and then comes the harvest’? Behold, I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are already white for harvest. And the one who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit for eternal life.” So, as I said just now, those on earth may very well be likened to the crops in a field. Christ became like us, springing up like an ear of grain from the holy Virgin. Indeed, he also called himself a grain of wheat, saying: “Truly, truly I tell you, unless the grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” He became an offering to the Father, as it were, on our behalf, in the role of a sheaf, as the firstfruits of the earth, which is shown to be fruitful by what it has brought forth. Though he is understood to be a single ear of grain, as we ourselves are, he is offered not as a single ear but as a sheaf, that is, as one bundle made from many ears. This is a matter necessary for our benefit, and it fulfils the type of a mystery. For Jesus Christ is one, but in the form of a sheaf he is understood to be many, and he is many, because he holds in himself all who believe, clearly by a spiritual union. How else could blessed Paul write: “We have been raised with him and seated with him in the heavenly places”? Since he has become like us, we have become one body with him, and through his body we have gained the riches of unity with him. That is why we say that we are all in him. Indeed, he himself says somewhere to his Father and God in heaven: “I desire that, just as you and I are one, so they too may be one in us.” For “whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit.” He is a sheaf, then, because he holds all in himself and is offered up on behalf of all, and because he is the firstfruits of a humanity made perfect in faith, which must henceforth be brought into the treasuries above in heaven. The law says that the sheaf must be brought on the day after the first day, that is, on the third day. For Christ came back to life from the dead on the third day, and from there he ascended into heaven, into the true tabernacle, into the Holy of Holies. Understood as bread, he was also signified by the bull offered as a whole burnt offering and a fragrant aroma, and indeed by the goat presented for sins of ignorance. In the same way, even if he is understood as a sheaf, he is also himself the year-old sheep, that is, the perfect one. For Christ is all-perfect by his own nature and lacks nothing. Besides this, he is wholly without blemish, for he knew no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. He is also the bright fine flour mixed with oil, that is, a life of richness and gladness. For we live rejoicing in him because of the hope laid up for us, and, watered by the grace of the Holy Spirit, we say in the words of the Psalms: “You anointed my head with oil.” For we have received mercy through faith in Christ, and in a certain way we are burned together with him on the altar, holding the second rank, just as the so-called groats stand in relation to his fine flour. By groats we mean meal made from pulses. For even though Christ became like us in the divine plan, no one would doubt that he is rightly understood to be above us. So his life is incomparably more precious, for it is wholly holy and without blemish. Our condition is lesser and comes after his, ranking as groats do, I mean, compared with fine flour made from wheat. And fine flour is a type of life. Yet the groats are carried up to the altar together with the fine flour. For, as I said, we are burned together with Christ, and with him we all give off a sweet fragrance, and with him we are acceptable to God the Father. Those who do not have Christ would not be fit for sacrifice at all, for he says, “Apart from me you can do nothing.” And the law says: “You shall not eat new grain until this very day, until you bring the sheaf.” For neither the age of the law nor the choir of the holy prophets had the new food, that is, the teachings given through Christ. Nor did they have the renewal of human nature itself, except perhaps in name alone. But when our Lord Jesus Christ came back to life and, in the role of the sheaf, presented himself to God the Father as the firstfruits of humanity, then, yes then, we too are transformed, as it were, into a new life. For we live according to the gospel, “not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit.” Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

But the inspired David says somewhere: "What shall I give back to the Lord for all that he has given to me?" Words like these would suit us above all. What could we offer that is equal in worth to God the Father? He gave his own Son for us, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. In doing so he almost held back even the tender affection that befits him. For the Son gave himself for our sins, according to the Scriptures, and we have been saved. He was bruised for our sins and suffers pain for our sake, and he endured even the death of the flesh. He did this not to be seen remaining with us among the dead, but so that we, running up to life with him and through him and hastening back to incorruption, might joyfully say: "Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O Hades, is your sting?" What path, then, leads to this? The grace that comes through baptism. Through it we scrub off every stain and are shown to share in the divine nature, since Christ dwells in us through the Spirit. For then, then indeed, our conscience is sprinkled clean from dead works, as blessed Paul writes. We come to share in the mystical blessing and fill our own minds with the grace from above, and we are seen to be enviable and admired. Indeed, which of such things are we not? You would see that what I have said is true if you understand what was decreed about the heifer. "And the Lord spoke," it says, "to Moses and Aaron, saying: This is the ordinance of the law that the Lord has commanded, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, and let them bring you a red heifer without blemish, which has no blemish in it and on which no yoke has been laid. And you shall give it to Eleazar the priest, and they shall bring it outside the camp to a clean place and slaughter it before him. And Eleazar shall take some of its blood and sprinkle some of its blood seven times toward the front of the tent of witness. And they shall burn it up before him: its skin, its flesh and its blood shall be burned up together with its dung. And the priest shall take cedar wood and hyssop and scarlet, and they shall throw them into the midst of the fire where the heifer is burning. And the priest shall wash his garments and bathe his body in water, and after this the priest shall come into the camp, and the priest shall be unclean until evening. And the one who burns it shall wash his garments and bathe his body in water, and he shall be unclean until evening. And a clean man shall gather up the ashes of the heifer." And in what follows: "And it shall be a perpetual statute for the children of Israel and for the proselytes who have joined you and live among you." To this the lawgiver adds that touching a dead body defiles people and makes them profane. Whoever this happens to shall be unclean for seven whole days. He shall be purified with the ashes of the heifer mixed with water, being sprinkled [?] on the third day and also on the seventh. "But if he does not do this," it says, "his uncleanness will remain unwashed." He will also pay the penalty, because he has defiled the tent of the Lord. "His soul," it says, "shall be cut off from Israel, because the water of sprinkling was not sprinkled on him." "And if someone happens to die in a house," it says, then the charge of uncleanness is to be laid against the dwelling itself and everything in it, by which I mean its vessels. And if any of the containers are standing without lids, these too are to count as defiled. "And no less profane," it says, "is anyone who in the open country touches someone who has been slain, or a dead man's bone, or a tomb." By what means, then, did he command such things to be wiped away? We shall explain this, unfolding as skilfully as we can the obscurity of the letter with fitting reasoning.

The heifer, then, wholly blameless, utterly free of every stain and not knowing how to sin, is our Lord Jesus Christ. For he dared to say: "The ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me." And to the Jews he said: "Which of you convicts me of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me?" But notice this. In the sacred writings he is sometimes called a bull-calf and sometimes a heifer. Through the male he is signified as leader, and through the female as being in a lower state and in subjection. For he is God, the leader of all things, and sovereignty over all belongs to him together with God the Father. Yet he willingly came under the law and kept the ordinances of Moses as if Moses were his superior, although Moses was a servant. And this is no wonder, since he was also called a prophet and appeared in the form of a servant, though he is Lord and God of the prophets. The heifer is red, for the mystery of the incarnation was accomplished in blood. It is true that he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross, and came to save the world under heaven by his own blood, and redness would be a very clear sign of blood. He became obedient to the Father and was with us under the law as a man, according to the divine plan, and he was even called a servant, not dishonouring the [?] of the flesh he had assumed. Yet even so he was and is free, because he is God by nature. He is in no way bound by the yoke of slavery and has no experience of it at all. For he comes from above and is above all, having sprung from the very essence of God the Father, which is free. That is why he said that the heifer to be brought must be red and without blemish and have no experience of the toil of the yoke. If the Only-begotten emptied himself and willingly lowered himself into the form of a servant, how could anyone possibly doubt that the lowering was from the heights and the emptying from fullness? And again, the descent was from a freedom that was innate and prior, I mean the descent into the form of a servant. So he is a heifer because he was in subjection and under the law, though he is the leader. He is red because the manner of the divine plan was carried out in blood, on our account and for our sake. He is without blemish because he is sinless, for he knew no sin. He has no experience of work or yoke because of his freedom in the Godhead and his unfamiliarity with slavery, even though he became like us and took the form of a servant. "But they shall give the heifer," it says, "to Eleazar the priest, and they shall bring it outside the camp to a clean place and slaughter it before him." The priest would be a type of those who are holy and sanctified and anointed with the Holy Spirit. For it has been said somewhere to us who have believed, through the voice of a saint: "But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation." To us, then, the holy ones, the chosen race and the holy nation, Christ has been given by God the Father as sanctification and redemption, wisdom and righteousness, Saviour and Redeemer. And as the inspired Paul writes, he suffered outside the gate. Paul said that we too must go there, bearing his reproach, that is, our own cross. The Saviour himself also said this: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me." It is most fitting and beneficial for those who are holy and sanctified to have the dead Christ, as it were, before their eyes. This would be suggested by the law's decree that the heifer must be slaughtered in the priest's sight. And when we remember Christ who died on our account and for our sake, then indeed we marvel all the more at the inspired Paul as he speaks to us of him: "For one died for all, so that the living might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and was raised for us." And again: "For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for us." So let him who endured slaughter for us be set, in a sense, before the eyes of our mind. For in this way we shall no longer live for ourselves but rather for God, as people bought with the blood of Christ, who gave himself for us according to the Scriptures. He commanded, moreover, that the holy tent be sprinkled with blood by the priest's hand, and this seven times. He also commanded that the heifer be burned with nothing at all belonging to it thrown away: the skin and the rest of the body were to be burned along with the flesh and the dung. For Christ sanctifies with his own blood the truer tent, that is, the Church, and he sanctifies it perfectly, that is, abundantly. This, I think, is what the sevenfold sprinkling of the tent with blood means, for a number that reaches up to seven is a sign of perfection. The burning of the heifer with fire after it was slaughtered seems to suggest the testing, even unto death, that Christ underwent for us. For silver is tested in fire, as the Psalms sing: "You have tested us, O God; you have refined us as silver is refined." That Christ was in a certain sense tested through obedience unto death is shown, I think, quite clearly by the following passage. He said somewhere through the voice of Zechariah the prophet, perhaps to those justified by faith, that is, those for whom he died: "And I will say to them: If it seems good to you, weigh out my wages and give them to me; or else refuse." Then the prophet says: "And they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: Put them into the furnace, and see whether it is genuine, in the way that I was tested for their sake." So, as I said, the burning of the heifer with fire after its slaughter would suggest that Christ was tested even unto death. Nothing of it, however, is thrown away. For Christ is holy in his entirety, both the flesh and the skin, that is, both what is hidden under cover and what is visible and at hand. For he was God by nature, though he became like us, yet without knowing sin. Cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet thread are thrown into the ashes. The cedar neatly suggests to us incorruption, for cedar resists rot. The hyssop suggests cleansing, for the herb is a cleanser and by its nature dissolves impurities in the bowels. The scarlet thread very aptly signifies the union of the Word with flesh. For the Word was, as it were, woven together with flesh and blood, and for our sake he was tested by fire and even unto death, as I said just now. His suffering and the manner of his incarnation brought us incorruption and cleansing. For we have been justified in him and have turned away the defilement in our souls and our inmost parts. Saving baptism, and that of power [?], is truly not the removal of dirt from the flesh but the appeal of a good conscience to God. Through it forgiveness of offences comes about, and grace will surely follow the confession of faith. That Christ's death for us has become the way to incorruption and life is beyond all doubt. But the one who burns the heifer and mixes the cedar wood, the hyssop and the scarlet into the ashes, and also the one who gathers the ashes, are unclean until evening, it says, even though they wash their garments and are clean. Perhaps the law is pointing out the weakness of human nature. If our affairs were examined minutely and precisely, none of those appointed to ministry, clearly meaning the divine and holy ministry, would be entirely beyond reproach. Even someone who has chosen to live the best life and is as pure as possible will not have a blameless ministry. For no one is worthy to touch the mysteries of our Saviour. And this is no wonder, for the sacred word will persuade us when it says: "The stars are not pure before him." So if our condition were compared with the purity of Christ, it would be unclean and defiled and liable to divine judgement. One might also, with very good reason, admire the divine Psalmist when he says: "If you, Lord, should mark iniquities, who shall stand? For with you there is atonement." So even the one who seems to be pure is found at fault. For, as I said, complete sinlessness is far beyond human nature, and so is coming near to Christ in our degree of purity. He said that the water of purification must be poured out outside the camp, and not within the camp itself. For the cleansing in Christ lies, as it were, outside the synagogue of the Jews. He departed from it completely, saying: "Behold, your house is left to you desolate." From then on the purifying grace flowed over, as it were, to the Gentiles, and as Paul says: "Those who were far off have come near." For they were called through faith and became rich in the righteousness that is in Christ, while those from Israel chose to disobey. He made clear that the water of purification would very easily scour away every kind of uncleanness when he said that anyone who touches a dead body will be defiled, and will be freed from what has befallen him in no other way than by being sprinkled with the water of purification on the third and seventh day. Death is the corruption of bodies and a symbol of uncleanness. The sprinkling of the water, mixed with the ashes of the heifer and the other things, would be a type of holy baptism. By works of death we mean the unholy and profane passions of the flesh: fornication, impurity, passion, evil desire. So anyone held fast by dead works and by defilements that lead to corruption cannot become clean in any other way. He must be purified and wash away the defilement through holy baptism, on the third and on the seventh day. The third day signifies the time of the resurrection, the last time, as at the end, in which the Only-begotten became man. "And if a house is defiled," it says, "because someone has died in it, those who enter it are unclean. Every utensil and every container without a lid is also abominable. But these too are thoroughly cleansed with the water of purification in the same way, on the third and the seventh day." By the defiled house, the utensils in it and the container without a lid, the lawgiver seems here to be hinting to us at the Lord-killing synagogue of the Jews. Taken all together, they are understood as a house; taken one by one, they are represented by the utensils, for a human being on earth is a vessel. Their mind is not secure but all too ready for defilement and for letting in absolutely anything that is accustomed to do harm. He hints at this through the containers without lids, into which anything that wants to can easily slip, whether lizards or some other creature that lives in houses. But the mind of those justified by faith is not like this. It is secure and covered, and those that are accustomed to do harm cannot get into it. "But even if someone touches," it says, "someone wounded, or a dead man's bone, or a tomb, he too shall be defiled." By the wounded we mean the one who is not sound in heart but wounded, as it were, by worldly desires or worldly or fleshly wishes. A dead man's bone we would take as a remnant of uncleanness. A tomb, again, we would take as a kind of reminder of an uncleanness that has already died. For Satan sometimes strikes the heart. And we ourselves, when we are partly overcome by the passions of the flesh, fall sick. It is not that we are wholly given over to every kind of sin, but we go on living in the world still standing among its remnants. I mean something like this: someone strives to master anger or love of money but does not entirely escape excess. This, I think, is what it means to remain among the remnants of some uncleanness, and the dead man's bone would be a sign of it. And again, when we let our mind sink back into the memory of a passion already conquered, and come close to a pleasure already buried, we sometimes sin no small sin. But we are freed from such charges because Christ scours us clean and purifies us through his own suffering. For he died for us, and by his bruise we were healed. He himself takes away our sins and is our advocate with the Father concerning sins, not only ours but also those of the whole world, as the inspired John wrote to certain people. In him, then, is all cleansing, all justification, sanctification and redemption. With him and through him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living, as it is written. For he created all things so that they might exist, and the generative forces of the world are wholesome. But the firstfruits of the race, that is, Adam, fell sick with disobedience. Disregarding the divine commandment, he offended God the Creator, and for this reason he slipped down into corruption. Human nature became accursed, and the race fell under judgment. And we wretched ones, though we came into being in incorruption, are now like shadows and the grass of the field: after a short and scanty span we fall unexpectedly back, as it were, upon our mother the earth. Hence the saints have cried out in various ways, lamenting our condition. One can hear blessed David crying out openly, "Man has become like vanity," and Isaiah in turn, "All flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass." For, as I said, we have sunk to such a depth of misery and wretchedness that no one could say what our condition might fittingly be compared to, even though the Spirit-bearers are exceedingly wise. But when we were in this state, the Maker did not overlook us. Rather, he judged us worthy of mercy and of regard, and in Christ he declared us free of death and corruption. How, or in what way? It is plain to everyone, even if perhaps no one says it. Yet one can also see the power of the mystery in the older Scriptures themselves. It reads as follows in Numbers: "And they set out from Mount Hor by the way to the Red Sea, and went around the land of Edom; and the people grew disheartened on the way. And the people spoke against God and against Moses, saying, 'Why have you brought us out of Egypt to kill us in the wilderness? For there is no bread and no water, and our soul loathes this worthless bread.' And the Lord sent the deadly serpents among the people, and they bit the people, and many of the people of the sons of Israel died. And the people came to Moses and said, 'We have sinned, for we have spoken against the Lord and against you. Pray, then, to the Lord, and let him take the serpent away from us.' And Moses prayed for the people. And the Lord said to Moses, 'Make yourself a serpent and set it on a pole. And if a serpent bites anyone, everyone who has been bitten and looks at it shall live.' And Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a pole. And whenever a serpent bit someone and he looked at the bronze serpent, he lived." They had been in bondage in Egypt, and weighed down by unbearable slavery they were redeemed by God, and many marvellous signs took place there. Water was changed into blood. Frogs and gnats, and dog-flies too, and onslaughts of hail all but made war on the land of the Egyptians. They were also punished with darkness, and the death of the firstborn struck unbearably at those who had chosen to oppress, while God wondrously kept the Israelites safe. Then, passing through the middle of the sea as if on dry land, they watched the Egyptians perish miserably. They received bread from heaven, for God sent the manna down to them. Christ followed them, understood as being in the rock, and had mercy on them in their thirst with unexpected streams. For the Divine is all-powerful and gives ungrudgingly what sustains life to those devoted to him. Yet those who enjoyed such exceptional blessings are put to the test by slight hardships and found wanting. For they forgot what God had done, were not at all steadfast in believing him, but were rash, easily shaken and quick to lose heart, and against all reason they took no account of the honours they had received. They call the bread from heaven worthless and complain of the lack of water, though they had learned that nothing is impossible for the divine and ineffable nature, which had even made the sheer rock a mother of river streams for them. Because they spoke against God with no excuse at all, they were punished with the bites of the serpents. Then, coming to remember their own offence, they shed floods of tears, confess their wrongdoing and beg the mediator, Moses I mean, to make God compassionate and gentle toward them. Moses fell down and entreated God, and, yielding to the commands from above, he made a bronze serpent and set it on high, and he ordered those who had been struck to fix their gaze on it. And by doing this they were saved.

But what is the meaning, what is the great and wise mystery? That is what we should next inquire into. The letter will not satisfy the more thoughtful, for the mysteries are buried, as it were, in the types. Come, then, let us speak, recasting the narrative from the type into what is universal and more general, that is, into what is true. Displeased with the good things that come from God and from above, we thoughtlessly pursued what is pleasant rather than what is beneficial. We thrust aside the exercises of virtue and devoted ourselves to the most shameful things. So we grieved our Benefactor and offended the Creator in more ways than one. For this reason we have fallen under the bites of serpents. I mean spiritual serpents, which strike us through every sin and drag us down into the bonds of death. At the head, as it were, of the multitude of venomous beasts is the apostate dragon, that is, Satan. By his bites, at the very beginning, man, that is, Adam, utterly perished. And the evil creeps from him, as from a root, into us as well, who came from him. But we have been saved in a certain way, for we have looked upon the serpent, that is, Christ. How, then, is God a serpent, when he is good by nature, or rather goodness itself? Because he became like us, who are evil by our own choice. "He came in the likeness of sinful flesh," and, "He was counted among the lawless." We are evil, though not made so by God; we slid into this baseness because of the sin that tyrannized over us. Christ himself makes this plain when he says, "If you, then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?" So Christ is a serpent, since he is in the likeness of evil, in that he became man. But anyone who looks upon him spiritually will be stronger than corruption, will leap clear of death, will think nothing of bites and will pay no heed to the multitude of venomous creatures. We shall see Christ by rightly understanding the mystery that concerns him and by firmly believing that, being God by nature, he became man, and that, though he was in the likeness of evil, he nonetheless remained good. He became like us not so that he might be seen as evil along with us, but so that he might make us good, transforming us by the Holy Spirit into every form of virtue. The serpent, moreover, is on a pole. For Christ was lifted up on the precious cross, and he himself declared this to the Jews, saying, "When you lift up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he." That the type points to his mystery you may learn from his own clear words: "For just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up." The serpent was bronze because the divine proclamation of the gospel is resonant and rings out most clearly. No one has failed to hear the oracles given through Christ. The mystery concerning him is proclaimed throughout the whole world under heaven, and to him every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. Amen.

"In many parts and in many ways God spoke of old to the fathers by the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages." Some rightly understand that, though he is God by nature, he came down to self-emptying, since he became flesh and dwelt among us, according to the Scriptures. These have been richly endowed with grace that is divine and worth receiving. For "as many as received him, to them he gave power to become children of God," it says. Others thrust away the word that is truly divine and saving. They have slipped from hope, and, wicked as they are, they have perished wickedly, impiously heaping insults on the Saviour and Redeemer of all. Such are these wretched Jews, over whom the prophet Jeremiah himself laments, saying, "Who will give water to my head, and to my eyes a fountain of tears, that I may weep for the people day and night?" They could have been illustrious and enviable, yet they have been deprived of the prosperity that was theirs. How, then, would they not deserve to be counted from now on as no better than the dead? One might fittingly mourn over them and shed a tear out of love and fellow-feeling. They have become bereft of every good, and wayward Israel has been shaken, as it were, from its very foundations. For Christ has passed over to the Gentiles, and the Jew, slow to learn, is now saved only barely and in a very small portion. This, I think, is what is prophetically sung through the voice of Isaiah: "Had not the Lord of Sabaoth left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah." Come, then, if you please, let us contemplate the power of the mystery from the words of Moses themselves. For it is written thus in Deuteronomy: "If someone slain is found in the land that the Lord your God is giving you to inherit, lying fallen in the field, and it is not known who struck him, your elders and your judges shall go out and measure the distance to the cities around the slain man. And the city nearest to the slain man shall be determined, and the elders of that city shall take from the herd a heifer that has not been worked and has not drawn a yoke. And the elders of that city shall bring the heifer down into a rugged ravine that is neither worked nor sown, and they shall hamstring the heifer in the ravine. And the priests and the Levites shall come forward, for the Lord your God has chosen them to stand before him and to bless in his name, and by their word every dispute and every assault shall be settled. And all the elders of that city who are nearest to the slain man shall wash their hands over the head of the heifer that was hamstrung in the ravine, and they shall answer and say: 'Our hands did not shed this blood, and our eyes have not seen it. Be merciful, Lord, to your people Israel, whom you redeemed out of the land of Egypt, so that innocent blood may not be laid upon your people Israel.' And the blood shall be atoned for them. So you shall remove innocent blood from among yourselves, if you do what is good and pleasing before the Lord your God."

Emmanuel, then, was wounded for our sake, for he was bruised because of our sins, according to the Scriptures. He was found to have suffered this in the land of the Jews, outside the gate of Jerusalem. Yet they did not know who struck him, how or in what way. What, then, does the law mean? After all, we say that the outrages committed against Christ were the work of the Jews' impiety. They themselves brought him to Pilate; they themselves would stand convicted of crying out, "Away, away with him, crucify him!" and again, "If you do not put this man to death, you are no friend of Caesar." The inspired disciples, too, clearly denounced their perversity to God the Father in heaven, speaking thus: "For truly there were gathered together in this city against your holy servant Jesus Christ, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel." Most clearly and openly of all, blessed Peter rebukes the Jewish crowds, saying at one point, "You killed the Author of life," and at another, "But you denied the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer to be granted to you." Why, then, does the law say that they do not know who struck him? The saying is mystical and not open to everyone without distinction; it is perhaps known only to those who rightly understand the mystery of Christ. The leaders of the Jews, and those who shared in their impious schemes, thought that they had prevailed, and that it was against Christ's will. Attributing the deed to their own perversity, they rejoiced as though they had won, and they did not know that he suffered willingly and, following the will of the Father, gave himself up for us. So he says clearly to Pilate, "You would have no power over me at all, unless it had been given you from above." Therefore the Father gave up the Son, and, so to speak, he himself is said to have struck Emmanuel. Indeed, in the book of Psalms the person of Christ is introduced speaking to the Father and God in heaven about the impiety of the Jews: "Him whom you struck they persecuted, and they added to the pain of my wounds." So let the Lord-killer no longer be proud. They did not simply prevail, as though Christ were weak; let them learn the truth from Moses, for they do not know who struck him. See, then, Emmanuel wounded in the land of the Jews. But the mystery concerning him is in no way fulfilled among them; rather, it is enacted in figure in the region and land of the Gentiles. For if the slain man is found, it says, they shall take a heifer that has never known yoke or labour, bring it down into a rugged and unploughed ravine, and have it hamstrung by those appointed for sacred service. Then, washing their hands over it, they are to say, "Our hands did not shed this blood." The heifer, then, is a type of Christ, as we have already said. It is a heifer because it has never known the yoke and yet is under the yoke: as man he is under the yoke, and yet he is free of the yoke because he is God by nature. For the Divine is free and subject to nothing that exists; rather, it rules over all things and holds the whole creation in its hands. But although the Son is free by nature, as God, he became one with us as man, and so came under the yoke. Accordingly, together with us he called the Father his God, while we are subject to the authority of the Godhead. So the heifer is under the yoke as far as its nature is concerned, but free of the yoke because of the glory of the Godhead and its complete freedom. Now see the heifer led away into a rugged and unploughed ravine. For after the precious cross, when Christ was found slain, he departed from the land of the Jews and passed over to the region of the Gentiles, which was neither worked nor sown. Before Christ shone upon the Gentiles as well, they lived in the world like dry and unploughed ground, bare of the fruitfulness that pleases God. Indeed, the prophet Isaiah says of it, "Be glad, O wilderness, and its villages; let the wilderness rejoice and blossom like a lily." So the region, or rather the multitude, of the Gentiles may very well be compared to rugged, unworked and utterly fruitless ground. It is there, I said, that the heifer must be hamstrung by the divine ministers. For, as I said, the mystery of Christ is celebrated by us who come from the Gentiles, and, confessing his passion and his return to life from the dead, we approach the mystical blessings. This, I think, is the hamstringing of the heifer. For, as I said, we celebrate the venerable mystery by proclaiming his death and also his resurrection. All who depart from the impiety of the Jews, leaving far behind the city in which he was wounded and found to have suffered, and who come to the rugged and unploughed ravine, will there wash their hands over Christ himself. For they will be washed clean by being baptized into his death. This, I think, is the meaning of "They shall wash their hands over him." And confessing that they had become partners in the impiety of the Jews, they will receive forgiveness. For the Jews, having behaved outrageously toward Christ, wrote the impiety upon their own heads, saying, "His blood be on us and on our children." But those who long for his grace and seek the cleansing that comes through the Holy Spirit all but cry aloud, by the honour they have learned to give him, "Our hands did not shed this blood." Cleansing, then, is in Christ, even if one of the Jews should choose to think rightly. This is what the inspired disciples did before all others, together with those who believed through them. One might fittingly assign to them the role of the elders, for they were honoured and chosen, and they renounced the impiety of Israel through faith in Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

The God of all rescued those of Israel's blood from the house of slavery, as if from an iron furnace. He all but waged war on the Egyptians "with a mighty hand and an uplifted arm," as it is written, and set his wonders against the madness of the oppressors. He worked signs and wonders, and he commanded them to go through the middle of the sea as though on dry land. As the divine David said: "He nourished them in the wilderness, and gave them bread from heaven. Man ate the bread of angels." He made springs of water gush out. Indeed, which of the most marvelous things was not wondrously accomplished? So, as the divine Moses writes: "As an eagle shelters its nest, he received them and took them up on his back." But they sank to such a pitch of ill counsel, perverse reasoning and savage enterprises that they went on disobeying even the Redeemer when he was present in the flesh. And why do I say only this, and pass over what is still worse? They killed him, led on by hot and savage audacity to the very height of impiety. For this reason Jerusalem, the slayer of the Lord, is justly sent away. Shown to be bereft from then on of her close bond with God, she has passed into every kind of evil, bearing on her own head, as it were, a punishment she brought on herself. Emmanuel himself declared this, saying: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing. Behold, your house is left to you desolate." The law itself would show us in a riddle that the synagogue of the Jews, abhorred by Christ, was going to suffer so terrible and unbearable a punishment. For it runs as follows: "If you go out to war against your enemies, and the Lord your God delivers them into your hands, and you take their spoil, and among the spoil you see a woman beautiful in appearance, and you desire her and take her as your wife, then you shall bring her inside into your house. You shall shave her head and pare her nails, and remove from her the garments of her captivity. She shall sit in your house and weep for her father and mother for a month of days. After this you shall go in to her and live with her, and she shall be your wife. And if you do not want her, you shall send her away free, and she shall not be sold for silver. You shall not treat her with contempt, because you humbled her." Now I think it pointless to busy oneself with the narrative sense of the story, and to want to make an art of probing what lies in shadows. Nothing in it is hard to reach: the meaning of what is laid down is quite bare, and is grasped with sweat [?]. So we must proceed to search out the spiritual meaning.

What war, then, is to be understood here, and against whom? Who is the woman beautiful in appearance and most comely? And what, again, is meant by her head being stripped of its hair, and by her being rid of her nails and of the clothes of her captivity? Well, as I have already said, the synagogue of the Jews served the Egyptians like a captive. In the beginning the fathers went down into Egypt, driven there by famine. But a long time passed and made them robust, very bold and beyond counting, so the Egyptians grew terrified that, emboldened by their numbers, they might make war on them and bring their former masters under their own hand. So Israel was harshly afflicted with the sweat of brick-making. But God had pity. As I said, he made war on the Egyptian bonds that were oppressing them beyond endurance. He rescued them and won the victory. Among the spoil he saw Jerusalem, taken by the spear, that is, the multitude of the Jews shining with the beauty of their ancestral nobility; for she was beautiful and admirable because of the fathers. He looked on her and desired her, that is, he held her worthy of love, and all but wished to live with her and make her the mother of good endeavors, so he brought her into his own house. And what does this mean? He pitched the holy tabernacle in the wilderness, so that she might be schooled by the sacrifices of the law and by worship in types, and so learn little by little the mystery of Christ. For the law is a tutor to lead us to Christ, as blessed Paul said. Having brought her into his house, he shaved her and rid her of her nails and of the garments of captivity. Holy Scripture is generally accustomed to use the head to signify the mind, and it likens the hair on the head to the thoughts in the mind. So the shaving of the hair very fittingly points to the putting away of notions. Ancient Israel, once redeemed, was commanded to do exactly this, for God said plainly through the all-wise Moses: "You shall have no other gods besides me." And again: "You shall not do so to the Lord your God. For the abominations which the Lord hated they did to their gods." While they were living in Egypt they held different notions: they thought there were countless gods, they gave worship to the creation rather than the Creator, and they ascribed glory to wood and stones. But once they were called through Moses to the knowledge of the God who alone is true by nature, how can anyone doubt that the time had come to bring them, wholly and entirely, new and different notions? The inspired Paul commanded us too to hasten to achieve this, saying: "Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, so that you may discern what the will of God is, what is good and acceptable and perfect." This, surely, is what the shaving of the head would suggest. The removal of long nails, for its part, hints at the casting off of filth and uncleanness. For people who for some reason like to have their nails longer than they need are very dirty. No one would doubt that Israel, once deemed worthy of a close bond with God, had to leave such things behind, since the law clearly cries out: "You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not bear false witness against your neighbor," and all that goes with these. As for the garments of captivity, I would say that they depict the form of slavery and the pattern of a life lived in baseness. For she was subject to the will of the devil and bowed her neck to his greed, and so she put on love of the flesh like a torn and filthy garment. But when she had been redeemed by the law and was being trained to think and do better things, she stripped off the guilt of her old baseness and from then on wore the instruction of the law like a bright tunic. And this, I think, is what the inspired Paul urges us ourselves to do, when he says: "Having stripped off the old self with its deeds, and having put on the new, which is being renewed according to the image of the one who created it." We too are stripped in holy baptism, all but flinging the garments of captivity down before Satan. Then, having put on Emmanuel himself, we offer thanks to God the Father, saying: "Let my soul exult in the Lord, for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a tunic of gladness." And again Paul, speaking as a lawgiver, said: "Put on our Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires." You see how, when we strip off the things of the flesh as garments of captivity, we take Christ as a bright and divine covering. For he is the tunic of gladness and the garment of salvation. So, it says, once her hair has been shorn and she has removed her long, dirty nails and the clothes of captivity, then, and only then, will she dwell in your chamber and be brought into your house with the standing of a wedded wife. Yet she will weep for her father and mother for a month of days; that is, she will remember those at home. "And after this you shall go in to her, and she shall be your wife." For I think that those who have been called into a close bond with God must rid the mind of absurd notions and idle thoughts (I mean those that lead to sin) and of all filth, and, as the inspired Paul writes, of "the old self, which is corrupted according to the desires of deceit." They must then attend without distraction on the God who has kept them and received them into his fatherly household. For I think that "she shall sit in your house" would signify attending without distraction. Thus blessed David, who knew this to be truly excellent and profitable, says: "One thing I have asked of the Lord, and this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to visit his holy temple." And it would be a very clear sign that the mind is firmly established and filled with love for God if one thinks it necessary to linger always in the divine courts. Yet the Creator was not ignorant of the limits of the human mind. How could he be, or from where? For he speaks truly who says, "He knew our frame." When we depart from life in the world and withdraw the mind from the passions of love of the flesh, we do not usually manage this altogether blamelessly. We are somewhat weak at the beginning, and the mind is carried along by pleasures that lead to evil. It would easily slip into remembering worldly distractions, and would all but embrace very warmly its old ties to them, even if the law should perhaps hold it tight and God should, as it were, drag us back up and transfer us to a higher and incomparably better life. For virtue is uphill, while the path that carries us down to evil is, as it were, very smooth; so we shun the toil and easily take the other road. What, then, does the law say? "She shall weep for her father and mother for a month of days"; that is, she will not immediately welcome living at your hearth, but will remember those at home for a little while. This is what happens to people who fall into captivity. Even if they happen to be held in honor by their captors, and even if abundant luxury is set before them, they still long for home and parents and their own city. They remember their own no less, and sometimes shed tears, their minds filled with pain and grief because they have been deprived of the land that bore them. This is what happened to the flocks of the Jews. They had been redeemed from Egypt and rescued from bitter slavery, and called by God to the freedom that was theirs from of old and from their fathers; yet even so they remembered what they had had in Egypt, and wept, saying: "Would that we had died, struck down by the Lord in the land of Egypt!" They also attacked Moses, saying: "Why have you brought us out into this wilderness?" Those who leave behind accursed love of the flesh and life in the world must at first find it hard to tear themselves away, and must sometimes seek the things of the world. The lawgiver suggests this to us obliquely when he says: "She shall weep for her father and mother for a month of days." We certainly do not say that he commanded them to weep; rather, he permits it and bears with the weak. And he said that those who experience this must be pardoned their failings, because they have not yet acquired endurance. And in fact he pardoned this weakness of the synagogue of the Jews in the wilderness, and did not utterly destroy those who had sinned, even though his anger served a useful end. But he did not always allow us to be sick and to admit memories of our old ties, I mean our ties to the world. He showed this clearly by assigning no long time for weeping: "a month of days," that is, a short and limited span of time. The divine Psalmist too has brought before us some such meaning, when he says to the Church of the Gentiles: "Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father's house, for the king will desire your beauty." So once she has wept for her father and mother for a month of days, it says, she shall then be your wife. For when we depart, as I said, from life in the world, then and only then are we joined to God, in a spiritual union, of course. For whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him. But, it says, "If you do not want her, you shall send her away free, and she shall not be sold for silver." For when the synagogue of the Jews acted impiously and laid hands on Christ himself, because she behaved outrageously toward her own Master, she was then hated and became unwanted, and was all but sent out of the divine and holy hearth. Yet she was not handed over into slavery, nor, as though sold to Satan, made wholly subject to his will. For although Israel slipped away from its close bond with Christ, it did not worship idols. It went on confessing and worshiping the one God who is God by nature, and kept its love for Moses and the law. For the God of all did not reject it, since it had once been deemed worthy of a close bond with him. This is what he teaches us when he says: "You shall not treat her with contempt, because you humbled her." By "humbling" he here means the taking of her virginity, that is, the manner of spiritual union, clearly the union in Christ. Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

"Take up weapons and shield," the prophet Isaiah called out to certain people. And Paul, the wisest of men, says: "Put on the whole armor of God." For those who are known to God, who love virtue and live in company with every noble kind of goodness, wage war above all against every profane and fleshly pleasure in general. Against the devil's perversities they lead out, as it were, their own forces: a faith firmly grounded, an endurance that cannot be shaken, a patience that bears hardship, and an eagerness for diligent work, in all, that is, that is worthy of admiration. But no one, I think, could ever reach such a measure of spiritual strength as to win glory so conspicuous and beyond all wonder unless he had Christ as his defender. And Christ will certainly fight alongside them and gladly be with those who have chosen to set their minds on his things, who have been enriched by the cleansing that comes through him, and who have made it their practice to boast in his reproach. So the divine Psalmist says: "He who dwells in the help of the Most High will lodge in the shelter of the God of heaven. He will say to the Lord, 'You are my protector and my refuge, my God, my helper, and I will hope in him.' For he will rescue me from the snare of the hunters and from a troubling word." And that we shall prevail over our enemies, with God keeping us safe, he himself will prove trustworthy when he says: "Because he came to me, I will rescue him. He has cried to me, and I will hear him; I am with him in affliction; I will deliver him and glorify him." But look at the matter as it is written by the all-wise Moses himself. For he said: "If you go out to encamp for war against your enemies, you shall also guard yourself from every evil word. If there is among you a man who is not clean because of his emission by night, he shall go outside the camp and shall not come into the camp. And toward evening he shall wash his body with water, and when the sun has set he shall come into the camp. And you shall have a place outside the camp, and you shall go out there; and you shall have a peg on your belt. And when you squat down outside, you shall dig with it, and bringing back the earth you shall cover your unseemliness with it. For the Lord your God walks about in your camp to deliver you and to hand your enemy over into your hands. And your camp shall be holy, and no unseemly thing shall be seen among you, lest he turn away from you." Do you hear that those who wish to overpower their enemies and win renown must rid themselves of every defilement? "For our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world-rulers of darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places." These watch human life closely and pry busily into the way each person lives. We must therefore make our way of life blameless and beyond reproach, so that it may not be exposed to their accusations. For the father of sin is both an enemy and an avenger. Those in this world who rise against their enemies by the law of war and battle either receive wounds in the body, as it may happen, or inflict them on others. But it is not so with us: "For our weapons are not fleshly," as it is written. So neither are we struck in the flesh; rather, we are struck in mind and heart when we admit desires and fall into the passions of love for the flesh. We must therefore be fitted with spiritual armor from head to foot, be fenced about with grace from above, and, as far as possible, keep the mind out of range of every spiritual arrow. In this way we shall overcome our adversaries and, rising beyond every passion, we shall keep the beauty of the soul unblemished for God. This is why the law says: "If you go out to encamp for war against your enemies, you shall guard yourself from every evil word." That is: put yourself as far as possible from every accusation; let no word spoken against you about any shameful or disreputable deed be true; avoid reproach of every kind, and let every evil word against you be idle. That we must also unburden ourselves of the charges that arise from fleshly impurity he showed in a riddle, when he commanded that the man defiled by his emission should go outside the camp and must wash with water toward evening, and so afterward return home and, if he wished, into the camp itself. Next I will try to explain what this means and what the sense of such things might be. If some human defilement occurs, the mind having yielded a little to natural necessity and having given entry to desires for what is base, the Master has judged that, as far as that goes, one must be set apart from the multitude of the saints, and he does not allow the clean to dwell with the unclean. For he by no means leaves unrebuked in us the sin that corrupts. But we shall find cleansing in Christ, being purified with water, in accordance, I mean, with the saying "Wash yourselves, become clean." We do this toward evening, that is, in the last times of the age; and one may see this fulfilled in the flocks of the saints. For those who were defiled by outlandish fleshly lusts, who once stayed outside the multitude and camp of the saints, who were somewhere far from the holy flock, have been enriched with the cleansing that comes through holy baptism; those who were far off have come near, shown to be partakers with the saints, and henceforth fellow citizens and sharers in the hope. This happened, of course, at the time of the Lord's coming, which took place, as it were, in the evening, at the very sunset of the present age. He said, then, that those who gain the cleansing that is in Christ must be eager to drive off the charges that arise from love of the flesh. "But you shall have," he says, "a place outside the camp, and you shall go out there; and there shall be a peg on your belt. And when you squat down outside, you shall dig with it, and bringing back the earth you shall cover your unseemliness with it. For the Lord your God walks about in your camp to deliver you and to hand your enemy over into your hands. And your camp shall be holy, and no unseemly thing shall be seen among you." For, as I said, it is fitting above all for those who desire to prevail manfully over spiritual enemies to reject every kind of impurity. But "we all stumble in many ways," and human nature suffers from being prone to slip into wrongdoing, and "no one understands his transgressions," in the words of the Psalmist. So, he says, if it should happen that we are all but shattered by one of the impurities innate in us, and are caught, having fallen sick with something outside the law and outside a life fit for the saints (for "the law of sin dwells in the members" of the flesh), then first, let the faults that come from weakness not be set out plainly and unconcealed, nor in the sight of many, but outside, so to speak, and in secret, as far from the camp as possible; and then let them be covered over by their correction. For "the wise will hide their own shame," as it is written. And when we cease from our offenses and in a sense remake the mind by its inclinations toward the better, so that it chooses what is beneficial, we remove from our midst the ugliness of the faults already committed; and having overcome the foul smell of sin with the fragrance of what follows, we shall enter again into the camp of the saints, that is, into the church of the firstborn. This too is accomplished in Christ. In what way? If we take up our own cross, as he himself said, with a nimble and well-girded mind. For our having a peg on the belt, that is, the wood, perhaps hints at this indirectly. The law, then, is spiritual, and bodily things are wont to sketch the outline of spiritual ones. For we are not in impurity in the eyes of God, who made things this way, when we go to the privy and rid ourselves of the waste of the belly.
