But, as I said just now, things perceived by the senses would be types and images of spiritual things. So we must bury our impurities, "for the Lord God walks about in the camp." For Christ dwells in us and walks about in us; and if he sees some unseemly and ugly thing in us, he rises up at once and leaves, for "a holy spirit of wisdom will flee deceit," as it is written, "and will withdraw from senseless thoughts." But if he finds us clean and scoured, superior to passions and defilements, he will gladly dwell in us and deliver us from the hand of our enemies. Therefore he says: "You shall be holy, for I am holy." And again: "Come out from there, and touch nothing unclean, and I will welcome you, says the Lord." For when we have been cleansed in this way, our Lord Jesus Christ will receive us with joy; through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

The divine Paul was very wise when he said that the people of old were tutored by the writings of Moses toward the mystery of Christ. For this is how things stand, and the saying is true. If we turn what was decreed through Moses toward the truth, we shall find in it a most beautiful spiritual meaning. But if we cling tightly, as it were, to the letter and do not let go of what lies in types, we shall hear the prophet saying: "You have sunk very deep into your seat." For we shall find nothing lofty and truly profitable in the shadows, though we shall declare the commandment entirely blameless. This is why the divine Moses put a veil over his face, signifying, I suppose, to the more discerning that the law is twofold: the truth lies innermost, while the shadow is laid over it like a face, and what is outwardly visible is a superfluous covering over what is hidden. So Moses teaches us in Deuteronomy that the initiators into the new covenant in Christ would in due time speak the word given through him, but would lead people toward the truth and give an account clearer than the letter, interpreting it more spiritually. It is written thus: "And Moses and the council of elders of Israel gave command, saying: Keep all these commandments that I command you today. And on the day you cross the Jordan into the land that the Lord your God is giving you, you shall set up great stones for yourself and plaster them with plaster, and you shall write on the stones all the words of this law, when you cross the Jordan, when you enter the land that the Lord, the God of your fathers, is giving you, a land flowing with milk and honey, as the Lord, the God of your fathers, told you. And when you cross the Jordan, you shall set up these stones, which I command you today, on Mount Ebal, and you shall plaster them with plaster. And you shall build there an altar to the Lord your God, an altar of stones; you shall not lift iron upon them. Of whole stones you shall build the altar to the Lord your God. And you shall offer burnt offerings on it to the Lord your God, and you shall sacrifice a peace offering, and you shall eat and be filled and rejoice before the Lord your God. And you shall write on these stones all this law." Notice again, I ask you, that he commanded that the words that were to come from him should be treated as no secondary matter, but be thought worthy of the greatest possible care. These were the words of the holy apostles. I will try, as far as I can, to explain each part thoroughly.

"If it should come about," he says, "that we cross the Jordan and march into the land of promise we have so longed for, then, at that very time, set up great stones on a height, plaster them, and write on them all this law very clearly." The great stones set up on high signify for us the choir of the holy apostles, who are truly great and lofty and conspicuous. For as far as virtue and the glories of the life in Christ are concerned, nothing compares with them. We find them standing far above those of our own time, and very greatly surpassing them. For tell me, who in his right mind would compete on equal terms with those holy and renowned men, whom Christ even called his own friends? "No longer," he says, "do I call you servants; you are my friends." He called them the light of the world and the salt of the earth, and commanded that they be seen adorned with dignities proper to himself; he made them benefactors and appointed them physicians for the whole world, saying: "Heal the sick, cast out demons, cleanse lepers, raise the dead; freely you have received, freely give." So the stones are great, and lie as if on a mountain. For the brilliance of their glory and the eminence of their renown make them appear set very high, as if on a mountain. But who are those who set up the stones? Those who cross the Jordan: those who have believed in the holy Christ and are enriched with the grace that comes through holy baptism. They, surely, set up over themselves as teachers and initiators into the mysteries the disciples of our Savior, the truly holy and chosen stones, of whom a prophetic oracle has told us: "For holy stones roll upon the earth." For the divine disciples were all but rolled out over all who live under heaven, traveling about the inhabited world, showing to people everywhere the beauty of the godliness that was in them, and proclaiming the true pearl, the one precious stone, that is, Christ. And the plastered stones bear the law written on them very clearly. For in the holy apostles we shall find the spiritual meanings of the law plainly and openly, no longer overshadowed by the letter, nor having the shadow as a dim covering, but bright and pure. For the teaching of the saints is spiritual. So they speak the law brightly; and this, I think, is what it means to write it very clearly on the plastered stones, as it is written. And once the stones bearing the law had been set up, he said that an altar must be built of other whole stones, that is, uncut and unharmed by blows of iron. And what might be the meaning of this? Christ is the precious cornerstone, and he has been laid in the foundations of Zion. For we are supported on him, having received him as a kind of secure and unshakable base. And we, like living stones, are built upon him as a spiritual house, into a holy temple, into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit. But no less are we also a kind of altar, gathered together in spiritual unity, giving off the fragrance of faith in Christ, and offering through him to God the Father, like the sweetest-smelling incense, the glories that come from the virtues. So the divine Paul writes to us: "Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship." So we ourselves are stones too, but whole and unstruck. For those who, as I said, give off the fragrance of Christ himself make a complete dedication of their minds: they are not divided toward the things of the world, nor do they still bear the wounds of profane and loathsome sin. Rather, just as Christ is undivided, so they too are single-minded and true, devoted to God alone and refusing even to seem divided toward the things of the flesh and the world. Having dedicated himself in this way, the holy Paul writes: "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain." It is necessary to remember that he gave us the same law elsewhere, saying: "If you make me an altar of stones, you shall not build it of hewn stones, for you have lifted your tool upon it, and it is defiled." So the stones are whole and unstruck, in the senses we have just described. "But you shall eat," he says, "and be filled there, and rejoice before the Lord your God." For to those who have reached such a height of glory that they can give off the fragrance of Christ, it would be very fitting indeed to be filled with the holy and divine food, and also to rejoice spiritually in the eyes of God. This too is accomplished when those who have believed in our Lord Jesus Christ partake of the mystical blessings in the churches; through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

The wise John understood very rightly both the mystery of Christ and the measure of Moses' ministry, and so he declared: "The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ." The law was quick to anger. It laid bitter penalties on transgressors at once and without delay. In short, it accused wickedness and pronounced condemnation on sin. For "sin," it says, "is not counted where there is no law." And again: "I would not have known sin except through the law." Christ, however, releases us from our offenses. He justifies by grace, he sanctifies those who have believed, and he brings to fulfilment what was promised long ago to the fathers. Paul will again make clear that both these things are true, when he writes: "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life." By "letter" he means the shadow in the law. By "Spirit" he means worship in spirit and truth, that is, the worship of the gospel, which Christ has established anew for people throughout the whole world. Since the first was not blameless, a place had to be sought for the second. And God made the first one old by promising a new one. When Moses had, so to speak, withdrawn and been removed from the scene, Christ in a sense rose up in his place and was shown to be our leader. Through him and in him we shall be brought into the kingdom of heaven and receive a blessedness that lasts through the endless ages, living a pure and holy life free from all blame. The very things ordained through Moses for the people of old have also trained us to be disposed and to think this way. For it is written: "And Moses called Joshua and said to him before all Israel: Be courageous and strong. For you shall go in before this people into the land which the Lord swore to our fathers to give them, and you shall give it to them as their inheritance. And the Lord who goes with you will be with you. He will not let you go, nor will he forsake you. Do not fear, and do not be afraid." The all-excellent Moses was about to depart from affairs here and be transferred to the dwellings above, and so the divine Joshua in a sense rises in his place and succeeds to the leadership. In the same way, when the old and ancient letter and the worship in the law were coming to an end and, as I said before, had all but withdrawn, the Only-begotten came down to us from heaven and took our form. He rules over all things as God and has held this splendid dignity from the most ancient times. Yet because he became like us, he fittingly allows it to seem that he is called to the beginning of a reign. That is why he said: "But I have been established as king by him" (clearly by God the Father) "on Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the decree of the Lord." Moses has yielded to the glory of Christ, so let no one bring him back into the middle again. Let the types no longer hold sway, and let no one try to prise the shadow back up. "The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new." If anyone chooses to do this, let him know that he dishonors the divine economy, forcibly overturns what God has decided, and undoes the great and venerable mystery. Whoever still clings to the types after Jesus has been revealed will lie very far from the sacred rolls. He will be shown to be disinherited and to have no share at all in the gifts that come through Christ. The divine Paul clearly rebukes some in Galatia who had fallen into this, when he writes: "O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified? This only I want to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith? Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now being made perfect in the flesh?" Then he adds: "You who are justified by the law have been cut off from Christ; you have fallen from grace. For through faith we eagerly await the hope of righteousness." The great Moses was truly faithful and among the most distinguished of all. But he was a servant, and this was his measure: he was the mediator and minister of the law that condemns. Now his Master has come among us and brought us the grace that justifies. So let the law be silent, the accuser of sin, the ministry of condemnation, through which God has shut up all things under sin so that he might have mercy on all, as it is written.

But what did the great Moses say to Joshua? "Be courageous and strong. For you shall go in before this people into the land which the Lord swore to our fathers to give them, and you shall give it to them as their inheritance." See, then, how the law foretells. Moses was not unaware of the Savior's glory. He knew of his incomparable preeminence over every saint, and indeed over all rational creation. He knew of that invincible hand, that all-powerful and unconquerable authority. He was all but struck with amazement as he beheld enemies falling, death made powerless, Satan fleeing, the beast once invincible and hard to overcome now terrified and defeated, the mouth of sin stopped, lepers cleansed, demons trembling, and the raging sea calmed by a single word. Moses was not unaware that the law given through him had justified no one, for it was impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sin. But our Lord Jesus Christ will free the world from its ancient charges. Since he himself is the truth and is holy by nature, he sanctifies believers by his own blood and makes them superior to death and corruption. He will bring them into the very kingdom of heaven, the truly lovely and holy land of the dwelling above, the beautiful city in heaven, the Church of the firstborn, whose designer and builder is God. Moses makes it plain that God the Father will struggle alongside the Son who became one of us and will work with him in everything, for he adds: "And the Lord who goes with you will not let you go, nor will he forsake you." The Son is all-powerful and has invincible authority, since he is God by nature. Yet he is said to be helped by the Father because of his humanity. Such language, and indeed the thing itself, befits the form of a servant and the very manner of the economy in the flesh. So that he may be believed to have become one of us, the Son even takes on the weakness proper to a human being, saying to his Father and God in heaven: "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you let your holy one see corruption."

The instruction given through the law was perhaps not known to anyone before the Lord's coming, in the sense of being understood spiritually. After Christ shone forth, however, it came to be admired, and when the Holy Spirit came down upon us, it was placed, as it were, before the eyes of small and great alike. Through the Spirit we understand even the depths of God. This too is clear from the following passage, which reads: "And Moses wrote all the words of this law in a book and gave it to the priests, the sons of Levi, who carry the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and to the elders of the sons of Israel. And Moses commanded them on that day, saying: After seven years, at the time of the year of release, at the feast of Tabernacles, when all Israel comes together to appear before the Lord your God in the place which the Lord will choose, you shall read this law before all Israel in their hearing. Assemble the people, men and women and children, and the stranger who is in your cities, so that they may hear, and learn to fear the Lord their God, and give heed to do all the words of this law." You hear that he wrote the law. He also charged those who had been chosen, I mean the priests and the elders as well, to assemble everyone when the seventh year had come, at the time of release, at the feast of Tabernacles: young and old, women and children. Then, when they had gathered, they were to read the law to them. Many and countless ages were to pass by before Christ would shine forth and the time of his incarnation would be revealed. One can learn this from the requirement that the reading take place every seven years. In divine Scripture the number seven signifies a multitude, as I think it does in the words "The barren woman has borne seven." And again: "Do not trust your enemy for ever, for there are seven wickednesses in his heart." And the author of Proverbs said somewhere: "The righteous man will fall seven times, and rise again." Observe that during the seven years before the release, that is, in the times before the Lord's coming, the law was not read. For not reading it at all is the same as being unable to understand any of it, even if someone happens to read it. But, as I said, it became known to small and great only when the time of release arrived. The law commanded the people of old: "Every seven years you shall make a release, and you shall make it in this way: remit every private debt that your neighbor owes you." And again: "If you acquire a Hebrew servant, he shall serve you six years, and in the seventh year you shall let him go free from you." At the end of the ages, as it were at the end of seven years, our Lord Jesus Christ remitted our debts and released those who had sinned. As in the gospel parable, he forgave them when they were debtors. They were slaves of sin and yoked to Satan, but by the spirit of freedom he made them radiant and splendid. The time of release appeared at the time of Tabernacles, which points to the mystery of the resurrection, when the tent of each of those who lie in the earth, that is, the body, is pitched again. Christ came back to life from the dead, trampled on death, despoiled Hades, and said to those in bonds, "Come out," and to those in darkness, "Be uncovered." Then he renewed the beauty of human nature by the Holy Spirit, as in the firstfruits of our race and of those being created anew for sanctification, and breathed on the holy apostles, saying: "Receive the Holy Spirit." Then the eyes of our understanding were opened. Then we were enlightened and came to understand the law that had long been hidden and was perhaps known to none of the ancients. Then we were gathered even from the ends of the earth into the place he had chosen, that is, the Church. There the chosen and holy initiators and teachers interpret for us the law that was given in shadows and types. Thus the divine Paul transforms the types very well into spiritual contemplation when he writes: "For if the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who have been defiled, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ?" When the Israelites were slaughtering the lamb and devoting themselves to shadows, he referred the type of the mystery to Christ and said: "Christ our Passover has been sacrificed." And he writes to others: "Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not hear the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. The son of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, but the son of the free woman through the promise. These things are an allegory. For these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar. Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children. But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother." So when we are initiated into the law spiritually, we receive the fear of God within ourselves. Moses also showed, in a veiled way, that the force of worship in types and shadow would in due time be drawn back. For it is written that when Moses had finished writing all the words of this law in a book, to the very end, he commanded the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, saying: "Take this book and place it beside the ark of the covenant of the Lord our God." Notice, then, that he ordered the law to be laid at one side of the ark, and not in the very middle. This was because the new decrees given through Christ were all but present, and the older commandment had to give way to them. It had, as it were, to make room or step out of the middle so that something else might be brought in. It is not thrown out of the holy ark, for the law given through Moses is received in the churches. Yet it has not been placed in the first position. It has been drawn back, as it were, and remains at the side, giving way, as I said, to things incomparably higher, that is, to the divine decrees of the gospel. Through these Christ has trained us in the knowledge of God and in every kind of virtue. Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
